Generalizing Causal Decision-Making:
Markov Equivalence, Transportability and Counterfactuals

Min Woo Park alsdn0110@snu.ac.kr Affiliation: Sanghack Lee sanghack@snu.ac.kr Affiliation: Seoul National University Affiliation: Seoul, Republic of Korea
Abstract

Structural causal bandits use causal knowledge to guide exploration when reward mechanisms are unknown. This paper extends the approach to partially known causal structure, information from other environments, and realizable counterfactual actions. First, we develop graphical criteria for minimal intervention sets under Markov equivalence and characterize possibly-optimal minimal intervention sets for maximal ancestral graphs. A search algorithm finds sets that are possibly optimal in at least one graph represented by a partial ancestral graph. Second, we derive target reward bounds from source distributions through partial transportability, accounting for non-manipulable variables. Dominance relations provide further bounds for action pruning and restricted exploration, with a regret guarantee under valid prior bounds. Third, we formulate counterfactual structural causal bandits over actions supported by specified experimental capabilities. Graphical characterizations of minimality and possible optimality yield algorithms that remove equivalent or dominated choices while preserving an optimal action. Experiments with specified structural causal models examine how these reductions and transferred bounds affect learning. Together, these results clarify how causal knowledge and experimental capabilities determine which actions merit exploration and guide learning within the retained action space.

††shortheadings: Generalizing Causal Decision-Making / Park and Lee††firstpage: 1
keywords
Causal Inference, Causal Decision-Making, Markov Equivalence, Transportability, Counterfactual Inference, Multi-Armed Bandits

1 Introduction

Sequential decision-making requires an agent to choose actions while learning their consequences. In a multi-armed bandit (MAB), the agent repeatedly selects an action and observes its reward, balancing the value of gathering information against the value of choosing a promising action (Thompson, 1933; Robbins, 1952; Lai and Robbins, 1985; Auer et al., 2002; Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020). An unstructured bandit treats the reward distributions of different actions as unrelated. In many applications, however, actions intervene on variables in a common causal system, and their effects are therefore connected.

For example, a physician choosing treatments must consider how they affect the same underlying biological mechanisms. An education policy may change several factors that influence later employment, such as access to training and acquired skills. In both cases, treating every combination of interventions as an unrelated action can require unnecessary exploration. Causal knowledge helps determine which interventions can affect the outcome and which choices can be excluded without losing an optimal decision (Bareinboim et al., 2024).

Structural causal models (SCMs) describe such systems through mechanisms that generate each variable from its causes and unobserved inputs (Pearl, 2000). An intervention replaces selected mechanisms while leaving the others intact. This representation connects the effects of different actions and supports questions that a list of unrelated reward distributions does not answer. Causal decision-making uses these relationships to inform learning and action selection (Zhang and Bareinboim, 2019; Zhang and Bareinboim, 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Kumor et al., 2021; Zhang and Bareinboim, 2022; Ruan et al., 2024; Zhang and Bareinboim, 2025; Richens and Everitt, 2024; Richens et al., 2025; Mueller and Pearl, 2023; Bareinboim et al., 2024).

Early work on causal bandits demonstrated how causal information can improve exploration (Bareinboim et al., 2015; Lattimore et al., 2016; Forney et al., 2017). Subsequent studies considered additional information or restrictions, including access to observational and interventional distributions and assumptions on causal mechanisms (Zhang and Bareinboim, 2017; Lu et al., 2020; Bilodeau et al., 2022; De Kroon et al., 2022; Feng and Chen, 2023; Varici et al., 2023). Structural causal bandits (SCBs) (Lee and Bareinboim, 2018; Lee and Bareinboim, 2019) provide the starting point of this paper. In an SCB, an action specifies both the variables to intervene on and the values assigned to them.

Fig. 1 separates the SCB framework into two stages. Offline action space optimization uses graphical equivalence and dominance relations in the known causal structure to remove unnecessary interventions while retaining at least one optimal action in every compatible SCM. This optimization requires neither the mechanisms nor the reward means to be known. During online learning, the agent selects an intervention from the reduced action space, observes the reward generated by the environment’s SCM, and uses the accumulated observations to guide subsequent choices.

Contributions.

The central question of this paper is which actions remain worth exploring given the agent’s causal knowledge and experimental capabilities. We extend SCBs in three complementary directions, each addressing a different limitation of the starting formulation.

  • ⊳\triangleright

    Markov equivalence. Observational data generally do not determine a unique causal diagram. Sec. 4 develops action space optimizations when the agent knows only a Markov equivalence class, represented by a partial ancestral graph. We characterize minimal intervention sets for ancestral graphs, distinguish whether their minimality can be witnessed by one compatible model, and establish a graphical characterization of possibly-optimal minimal intervention sets for maximal ancestral graphs. A search algorithm identifies sets that are possibly optimal in at least one represented maximal ancestral graph (Park et al., 2025).

  • ⊳\triangleright

    Transportability. Data collected elsewhere can inform a target decision problem, but differences between environments and restrictions on manipulation limit what can be transferred. Sec. 5 first reviews the existing formulation of structural causal bandits with non-manipulable variables. It then develops partial transportability and dominance bounds for target rewards, combines information from available source experiments, and uses the resulting bounds to prune actions and restrict exploration. A regret guarantee describes the behavior of the proposed policy under valid prior bounds (Park and Lee, 2026b).

  • ⊳\triangleright

    Counterfactuals. Some systems allow different mechanisms to receive different versions of an input on the same unit. Sec. 6 uses realizability to specify the counterfactual actions supported by these capabilities. We extend minimality and possible optimality to this action space, derive graphical characterizations, and construct a reduced collection that preserves an optimal action (Park and Lee, 2026a). The required capabilities are stated explicitly, because a mathematically defined counterfactual need not be experimentally available.

Relation to earlier publications.

This paper brings together and revises our studies of structural causal bandits under Markov equivalence (Park et al., 2025), transportability (Park and Lee, 2026b), and counterfactual interventions (Park and Lee, 2026a). The revisions include corrected graphical statements, algorithms, and proofs, together with new or recomputed experiments. The opening paragraphs of Secs. 4, 5 and 6 identify the changes relative to each publication; the statements and experimental results presented here are the revised versions.

Organization.

Sec. 2 introduces the causal and graphical foundations. Sec. 3 develops the bandit objective and action space optimization. Secs. 4, 5 and 6 present the three extensions, and Sec. 7 brings the results together. The appendices provide supporting proofs and experimental model specifications.

2 Causal and Graphical Preliminaries

This section introduces the notation used throughout the paper, the semantic framework represented by structural causal models (SCMs), and the necessary background results on which our work builds. A large part of this section follows Jaber (2022); Bareinboim et al. (2022); Zhang (2023) and Bareinboim et al. (2024).

The SCM and intervention notation supports every subsequent section. Readers can proceed to Sec. 3 after the material on SCMs and causal diagrams. The material on maximal ancestral graphs (MAGs), partial ancestral graphs (PAGs), and Fast Causal Inference (FCI) prepares the partial-structure setting in Sec. 4.

2.1 Basic Notation

Following standard conventions, we use a capital letter, such as XX, to represent a variable, with its corresponding lowercase letter, xx, denoting a realization of the variable. Boldface letters are used to represent sets of variables or values, denoted by 𝐗\mathbf{X} or 𝐱\mathbf{x}. The domain ΩX\Omega_{X} is the set of possible values of XX, and Ω𝐗=×X∈𝐗ΩX\Omega_{\mathbf{X}}=\bigtimes_{X\in\mathbf{X}}\Omega_{X}. For a discrete distribution PP, its support consists of the assignments in the domain that have positive probability; it may vary across environments and interventions. We consistently use P⁡(𝐱)P(\mathbf{x}) as an abbreviation for P⁡(𝐗=𝐱)P(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}). We denote by 𝟙{𝐗=𝐱}\mathds{1}\{\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}\} the indicator function. Two values 𝐱\mathbf{x} and 𝐳\mathbf{z} are consistent if they share common values for 𝐗∩𝐙\mathbf{X}\cap\mathbf{Z}. We denote by 𝐱∖𝐙\mathbf{x}\setminus\mathbf{Z} the value of 𝐗∖𝐙\mathbf{X}\setminus\mathbf{Z} consistent with 𝐱\mathbf{x} and by 𝐱∩𝐙\mathbf{x}\cap\mathbf{Z} the restriction of 𝐱\mathbf{x} to the variables in 𝐙\mathbf{Z}.

A graph 𝒢=⟨𝐕,𝐄⟩\mathcal{G}=\langle\mathbf{V},\mathbf{E}\rangle is defined over a set of nodes (vertices) 𝐕\mathbf{V} and a set of edges 𝐄\mathbf{E}. A graph is directed if all its edges are directed (→\to). We use mixed graphs whose edges may be directed or bidirected (↔\leftrightarrow); either type may be absent.

2.2 Structural Causal Models

A structural causal model (SCM) is a versatile and expressive framework that provides a principled way to represent and reason about causal relationships. Its generality makes it applicable across a wide range of domains. We use an SCM as the semantic framework to represent the environment in which the agent operates.

Throughout this paper, we consider recursive SCMs, so that each exogenous realization determines a unique value of every endogenous variable. Unless stated otherwise, all variables and mechanisms considered below satisfy this convention.

Definition 0 (Structural Causal Model (Pearl, 2000)).

An SCM ℳ\mathcal{M} is a quadruple ⟨𝐔,𝐕,ℱ,P⁡(𝐔)⟩\langle\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V},\mathcal{F},P(\mathbf{U})\rangle, where:

  • •

    𝐔\mathbf{U} is a set of exogenous variables that are determined by factors outside the model and follow a joint distribution P⁡(𝐔)P(\mathbf{U});

  • •

    𝐕\mathbf{V} is a set of endogenous variables representing observed variables inside the model;

  • •

    ℱ={fV}V∈𝐕\mathcal{F}=\{f_{V}\}_{V\in\mathbf{V}} is a set of functions (mechanisms) such that v=fV​(𝐩𝐚V,𝐮V)v=f_{V}(\mathbf{pa}_{V},\mathbf{u}_{V}) where 𝐏𝐚V⊆𝐕∖{V}\mathbf{Pa}_{V}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{V\} and 𝐔V⊆𝐔\mathbf{U}_{V}\subseteq\mathbf{U};

  • •

    P⁡(𝐔)P(\mathbf{U}) is a probability distribution over the exogenous variables.

2.3 Pearl’s Causal Hierarchy

An SCM induces all quantities within Pearl’s Causal Hierarchy (PCH) (Pearl and Mackenzie, 2018; Bareinboim et al., 2022). The three layers of the PCH correspond to distinct regimes of reasoning about an environment: seeing, doing, and imagining (Table 1).

The first layer ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1} represents observational distributions, such as P⁡(Y∣x)P(Y\mid x); the second layer ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} represents interventional distributions, e.g., P⁡(Y∣d​o​(x))P(Y\mid do(x)), using the d​odo-operator (Pearl, 1995). The highest layer ℒ3\mathcal{L}_{3} represents counterfactual distributions, such as P⁡(Yx∣X=x′)P(Y_{x}\mid X=x^{\prime}) (Heckman and Robb Jr, 1985; Heckman and Robb, 1986): the distribution of YY under intervention d​o​(X=x)do(X=x) among units whose observed treatment is x′x^{\prime}. Such distributions underlie quantities such as the effect of treatment on the treated (Heckman and Robb Jr, 1985; Heckman and Robb, 1986).

2.3.1 Observational Distributions

An agent perceives the deployed environment through its sensors by “seeing”, which can be formalized through the first layer of the PCH (ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1}).

Definition 0 (Observational distributions (Bareinboim et al., 2022)).

An SCM ℳ=⟨𝐔,𝐕,ℱ,P⁡(𝐔)⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V},\mathcal{F},P(\mathbf{U})\rangle defines a joint probability distribution P⁡(𝐕)P(\mathbf{V}) such that for each 𝐘⊆𝐕\mathbf{Y}\subseteq\mathbf{V}:

P(𝐲)=∑𝐮𝟙{𝐘(𝐮)=𝐲}P(𝐮),\displaystyle P(\mathbf{y})=\sum_{\mathbf{u}}\mathds{1}\{\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{y}\}P(\mathbf{u}), (1)

where 𝐘⁡(𝐮)\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{u}) is the solution for 𝐘\mathbf{Y} after evaluating ℱ\mathcal{F} with 𝐔=𝐮\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{u}11 1 We write sums for expectations over exogenous variables when these variables are discrete; for general exogenous distributions, the corresponding expressions are understood as integrals with respect to P⁡(𝐔)P(\mathbf{U}). The same sum-to-integral convention applies to expectations over endogenous variables. For non-discrete endogenous variables, distributions are defined analogously on measurable events rather than only on point events. .

Therefore, observational distributions are computed using the following procedure:

  • 1.

    For each exogenous realization 𝐔=𝐮\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{u}22 2 One can view the realization as a situation or a unit (Pearl et al., 2016)., the environment evaluates functions in ℱ\mathcal{F} according to a topological order (i.e., any variable on the left-hand side is evaluated after those on the right-hand side); and

  • 2.

    The probability P⁡(𝐮)P(\mathbf{u}) is accumulated for each realization 𝐔=𝐮\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{u} consistent with 𝐘=𝐲\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{y}.

Example 0 (Clinical system (Zhang, 2023; Bareinboim et al., 2024)).

In a clinic treating patients with a chronic disease, physicians must choose a treatment. There are two possible treatments, X=0X=0 and X=1X=1. The agent’s goal is to identify the treatment that maximizes the probability of patient recovery (YY). Consider an SCM ℳ\mathcal{M} that models this system:

ℳ={𝐔={U}𝐕={X,Y}ℱ={fX(u)=𝟙{u<0.8}fY(x,u)=𝟙{u<0.4−η⋅x}P(𝐔)={U∼𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚏(0,1)},\displaystyle\mathcal{M}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{U}=\{U\}\\ \mathbf{V}=\{X,Y\}\\ \mathcal{F}=\begin{cases}f_{X}(u)=\mathds{1}\{u<0.8\}\\ f_{Y}(x,u)=\mathds{1}\{u<0.4-\eta\cdot x\}\end{cases}\\ P(\mathbf{U})=\{U\thicksim\mathtt{Unif}(0,1)\},\end{cases} (2)

where the coefficient η\eta is a real number bounded in (0,0.4)(0,0.4).

In words, the physician prescribes treatment X=0X=0 for senior patients (U≥0.8U\geq 0.8); otherwise, the alternative treatment X=1X=1 is prescribed. The recovery YY depends on the treatment XX and the patient’s age UU.

By passively observing patient outcomes and collecting data, the agent can estimate the mean recovery rate as follows:

P⁡(Y=1)\displaystyle P(Y=1) =P⁡(X=0,Y=1)+P⁡(X=1,Y=1)\displaystyle=P(X=0,Y=1)+P(X=1,Y=1) (3)
=P⁡(X=0,Y=1)+P⁡(Y=1∣X=1)​P​(X=1)\displaystyle=P(X=0,Y=1)+P(Y=1\mid X=1)P(X=1) (4)
=P⁡(U≥0.8,U<0.4−η⋅X)⏟=0+P⁡(Y=1∣X=1)​P​(U<0.8)\displaystyle=\underbrace{P(U\geq 0.8,U<0.4-\eta\cdot X)}_{=0}+P(Y=1\mid X=1)P(U<0.8) (5)
=0.8⋅P⁡(Y=1∣X=1).\displaystyle=0.8\cdot P(Y=1\mid X=1). (6)

The agent may also estimate the recovery rate among patients who received each treatment. Among patients who received treatment X=0X=0, the recovery rate is:

P⁡(Y=1∣X=0)\displaystyle P(Y=1\mid X=0) =P⁡(U<0.4−η⋅X∣U≥0.8)\displaystyle=P(U<0.4-\eta\cdot X\mid U\geq 0.8) (7)
≤P⁡(U<0.4∣U≥0.8)\displaystyle\leq P(U<0.4\mid U\geq 0.8) (8)
=0.\displaystyle=0. (9)

Similarly, the recovery rate for X=1X=1 is:

P⁡(Y=1∣X=1)\displaystyle P(Y=1\mid X=1) =P⁡(U<0.4−η⋅X∣U<0.8)\displaystyle=P(U<0.4-\eta\cdot X\mid U<0.8) (10)
=0.5−1.25​η.\displaystyle=0.5-1.25\eta. (11)

Therefore, the mean recovery rate is given by:

P⁡(Y=1)\displaystyle P(Y=1) =0.8⋅P⁡(Y=1∣X=1)\displaystyle=0.8\cdot P(Y=1\mid X=1) (12)
=0.4−η.\displaystyle=0.4-\eta. (13)

Since the coefficient η\eta lies in (0,0.4)(0,0.4), we can conclude:

P⁡(Y=1∣X=0)<P⁡(Y=1∣X=1).\displaystyle P(Y=1\mid X=0)<P(Y=1\mid X=1). (14)

This result from an observational study suggests that treatment X=1X=1 is better than treatment X=0X=0.

2.3.2 Interventional Distributions

The agent interacts with the environment through the notion of “doing”; that is, by intervening (acting) on the SCM (environment), thereby modifying the original system. We formally define the environment that arises under such interventions using submodels.

Definition 0 (Submodel (Bareinboim et al., 2024)).

Let ℳ=⟨𝐔,𝐕,ℱ,P⁡(𝐔)⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V},\mathcal{F},P(\mathbf{U})\rangle be an SCM, and let 𝐱\mathbf{x} be a particular realization of a set of variables 𝐗⊆𝐕\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}. A submodel ℳ𝐱\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{x}} of ℳ\mathcal{M} is an SCM ⟨𝐔,𝐕,ℱ𝐱,P⁡(𝐔)⟩\langle\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V},\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{x}},P(\mathbf{U})\rangle where:

ℱ𝐱={fV:V∈𝐕∖𝐗}∪{fX=x:X∈𝐗,x is the value of X in 𝐱}.\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{x}}=\{f_{V}:V\in\mathbf{V}\setminus\mathbf{X}\}\cup\{f_{X}=x:X\in\mathbf{X},x\text{~is the value of~}X\text{~in~}\mathbf{x}\}. (15)

In words, an intervention is modeled by replacing the original mechanisms associated with variables 𝐗\mathbf{X} with constant values 𝐱\mathbf{x}, as represented by the do-operator, i.e., d​o​(𝐗=𝐱)do(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}) (for short, d​o​(𝐱)do(\mathbf{x})). The outcome under the intervention is called the potential response (Pearl, 2000).

Definition 0 (Potential response (Bareinboim et al., 2022)).

Given an SCM ℳ=⟨𝐔,𝐕,ℱ,P⁡(𝐔)⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V},\mathcal{F},P(\mathbf{U})\rangle, let 𝐗\mathbf{X} and 𝐘\mathbf{Y} be two sets of variables in 𝐕\mathbf{V}, and let 𝐮\mathbf{u} be a realization of 𝐔\mathbf{U}. The potential response 𝐘𝐱​(𝐮)\mathbf{Y}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{u}) is defined as the solution for 𝐘\mathbf{Y} obtained from the system ℱ𝐱\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{x}} with 𝐔=𝐮\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{u} in ℳ\mathcal{M}.

For a fixed intervention 𝐱\mathbf{x}, the potential response becomes a random variable by evaluating it at the random exogenous variables: 𝐘𝐱=𝐘𝐱​(𝐔)\mathbf{Y}_{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{Y}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{U}), with 𝐔∼P⁡(𝐔)\mathbf{U}\sim P(\mathbf{U})33 3 The notation 𝐘𝐱​(𝐮)\mathbf{Y}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{u}) is borrowed from the potential-outcome framework (Neyman, 1990; Rubin, 1974).. Its distribution is induced by P⁡(𝐔)P(\mathbf{U}); averaging a scalar potential response gives its expectation. We next define the resulting interventional distribution.

Definition 0 (Interventional distribution (Bareinboim et al., 2022)).

An SCM ℳ=⟨𝐔,𝐕,ℱ,P⁡(𝐔)⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V},\mathcal{F},P(\mathbf{U})\rangle induces a collection of joint probability distributions over 𝐕\mathbf{V}, one for each intervention 𝐱\mathbf{x}. For each 𝐘⊆𝐕\mathbf{Y}\subseteq\mathbf{V}:

P(𝐲𝐱)=∑𝐮𝟙{𝐘𝐱(𝐮)=𝐲}P(𝐮).\displaystyle P(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{x}})=\sum_{\mathbf{u}}\mathds{1}\{\mathbf{Y}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{y}\}P(\mathbf{u}). (16)

Hence, the interventional distribution can be evaluated as follows:

  • 1.

    Replace the mechanism of each X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X} with its value in 𝐱\mathbf{x}; the resulting ℱ𝐱\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{x}} defines the submodel ℳ𝐱\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{x}}.

  • 2.

    For each realization 𝐔=𝐮\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{u}, the environment evaluates functions in ℱ𝐱\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{x}} according to a topological order.

  • 3.

    The probability P⁡(𝐮)P(\mathbf{u}) is accumulated for each realization 𝐔=𝐮\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{u} consistent with 𝐘=𝐲\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{y} in the submodel ℳ𝐱\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{x}}.

In words, the interventional distributions induced by d​o​(𝐱)do(\mathbf{x}) in an SCM ℳ\mathcal{M} are distributions over the endogenous variables in the submodel ℳ𝐱\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{x}}. We denote the interventional distribution over 𝐘\mathbf{Y} induced by d​o​(𝐱)do(\mathbf{x}) interchangeably as P𝐱​(𝐲)P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}), P⁡(𝐲𝐱)P(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{x}}), or P⁡(𝐲∣d​o​(𝐱))P(\mathbf{y}\mid do(\mathbf{x}))44 4 We mainly use do-operator notation for ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} quantities..

Example 0 (Continued).

Suppose that the patient’s age UU is unavailable to the agent, so the agent observes only the treatment XX and the outcome YY. Consider an intervention d​o​(X=x)do(X=x) that sets treatment XX to a constant x∈{0,1}x\in\{0,1\}. The submodel ℳx\mathcal{M}_{x} induced by d​o​(X=x)do(X=x) is given by:

ℳx={𝐔={U}𝐕={X,Y}ℱx={fX=xfY(x,u)=𝟙{u<0.4−η⋅x}P(𝐔)={U∼𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚏(0,1)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{x}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{U}=\{U\}\\ \mathbf{V}=\{X,Y\}\\ \mathcal{F}_{x}=\begin{cases}f_{X}=x\\ f_{Y}(x,u)=\mathds{1}\{u<0.4-\eta\cdot x\}\end{cases}\\ P(\mathbf{U})=\{U\thicksim\mathtt{Unif}(0,1)\}.\end{cases} (17)

Evaluating the patient’s recovery YY in the submodel ℳx\mathcal{M}_{x} gives:

PX=0​(Y=1)\displaystyle P_{X=0}(Y=1) =P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(X=0))\displaystyle=P(Y=1\mid do(X=0)) (18)
=P⁡(U<0.4−η⋅X∣d​o​(X=0))\displaystyle=P(U<0.4-\eta\cdot X\mid do(X=0)) (19)
=P⁡(U<0.4)\displaystyle=P(U<0.4) (20)
=0.4.\displaystyle=0.4. (21)

Similarly, the patient’s recovery rate under treatment d​o​(X=1)do(X=1) is:

PX=1​(Y=1)\displaystyle P_{X=1}(Y=1) =P⁡(Y=1∣d​o​(X=1))\displaystyle=P(Y=1\mid do(X=1)) (22)
=P⁡(U<0.4−η⋅X∣d​o​(X=1))\displaystyle=P(U<0.4-\eta\cdot X\mid do(X=1)) (23)

Given that η>0\eta>0, we can conclude:

PX=0​(Y=1)>PX=1​(Y=1).\displaystyle P_{X=0}(Y=1)>P_{X=1}(Y=1). (26)

Thus, treatment X=0X=0 yields a higher recovery rate under intervention. This reverses the observational ranking in Eq. 14: patients receiving the two treatments differ in UU, whereas an intervention fixes the treatment while preserving the population distribution of UU. The example therefore distinguishes observational association from the effect of intervening on treatment.

2.4 Causal Diagrams

While SCMs provide precise semantics for the distributions underlying the PCH, they are typically not directly observable by the learning agent in practice. As a result, reasoning about the system requires explicit assumptions about the underlying causal model. These assumptions are commonly represented using a causal diagram.

Definition 0 (Causal diagram (Pearl, 1995; Bareinboim et al., 2022)).

Consider an SCM ℳ=⟨𝐔,𝐕,ℱ,P⁡(𝐔)⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V},\mathcal{F},P(\mathbf{U})\rangle. Then 𝒢\mathcal{G} is said to be a causal diagram of ℳ\mathcal{M} if it is constructed as follows:

  • 1.

    Add a vertex for every endogenous variable in 𝐕\mathbf{V}.

  • 2.

    Add a directed edge (V→WV\to W) if VV appears as an argument of fW∈ℱf_{W}\in\mathcal{F}.

  • 3.

    Add a bidirected edge (V↔WV\leftrightarrow W) if the corresponding 𝐔V,𝐔W⊆𝐔\mathbf{U}_{V},\mathbf{U}_{W}\subseteq\mathbf{U} are dependent55 5 That is, there is no partition 𝐔¯V,𝐔¯W\overline{\mathbf{U}}_{V},\overline{\mathbf{U}}_{W} over 𝐔\mathbf{U} such that (1) 𝐔V⊆𝐔¯V\mathbf{U}_{V}\subseteq\overline{\mathbf{U}}_{V} and 𝐔W⊆𝐔¯W\mathbf{U}_{W}\subseteq\overline{\mathbf{U}}_{W}; and (2) independence 𝐔¯V⟂⁣⟂𝐔¯W\overline{\mathbf{U}}_{V}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}\overline{\mathbf{U}}_{W} holds in P⁡(𝐔)P(\mathbf{U}). Furthermore, we say that VV and WW are confounded, and the underlying cause is referred to as an unobserved confounder. or the corresponding functions fVf_{V}, fWf_{W} share some UV​W∈𝐔U_{VW}\in\mathbf{U} as an argument.

We focus on recursive SCMs, i.e., acyclic causal diagrams. Intuitively, there is a directed edge from an endogenous variable VV to WW (V→WV\to W) whenever WW “listens to” VV in determining its value. Similarly, a bidirected edge between VV and WW (V↔WV\leftrightarrow W) indicates the presence of shared unobserved factors that influence both variables.

While an SCM ℳ=⟨𝐔,𝐕,ℱ,P⁡(𝐔)⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V},\mathcal{F},P(\mathbf{U})\rangle contains explicit quantitative information about the structural mechanisms ℱ\mathcal{F} and the exogenous distribution P⁡(𝐔)P(\mathbf{U}), a causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G} encodes only qualitative information about which variables may66 6 A directed edge V→WV\to W encodes the possibility of a causal mechanism by which WW listens to VV, but not its necessity. A similar interpretation holds for bidirected edges. More formally, the graphical constraints (assumptions) are not represented by the edges present in the diagram, but rather by the missing edges. In particular, a missing edge indicates that one variable cannot be an argument of the other, or that the corresponding exogenous inputs are independent. In summary, edges represent possible dependencies, while missing edges encode independence assumptions. serve as inputs to the functions fV∈ℱf_{V}\in\mathcal{F} and how the exogenous variations are related. Hence, the diagram abstracts away the specific forms of the mechanisms ℱ\mathcal{F} and the distribution P⁡(𝐔)P(\mathbf{U}), retaining only qualitative information about their arguments and independence structure.

Example 0 (Continued).

Let us consider the running example ℳ\mathcal{M}. Fig. 2(a) illustrates an abstraction of ℳ\mathcal{M}. The causal mechanisms ℱ\mathcal{F} are structural functions of the form:

ℱ={x=fX​(u)y=fY​(u,x).\displaystyle\mathcal{F}=\begin{cases}x=f_{X}(u)\\ y=f_{Y}(u,x).\end{cases} (27)

To apply the graphical construction, we start the process by examining each of the endogenous variables 𝐕={X,Y}\mathbf{V}=\{X,Y\} and adding them as nodes in the causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The corresponding diagram is illustrated in Fig. 2(c)77 7 In causal diagrams, bidirected edges are drawn as dashed lines for clarity. .

For concreteness, we consider an additional instance of the following form:

ℳ′={𝐔={UX,UY,U1,U2}𝐕={X,Y}ℱ={x=fX​(uX,u1,u2)y=fY​(x,uY,u1,u2)P⁡(𝐔)={U∼𝚄𝚗𝚒𝚏⁡(0,1):∀U∈𝐔}.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{\prime}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{U}=\{U_{X},U_{Y},U_{1},U_{2}\}\\ \mathbf{V}=\{X,Y\}\\ \mathcal{F}=\begin{cases}x=f_{X}(u_{X},u_{1},u_{2})\\ y=f_{Y}(x,u_{Y},u_{1},u_{2})\end{cases}\\ P(\mathbf{U})=\{U\thicksim\mathtt{Unif}(0,1):\forall U\in\mathbf{U}\}.\end{cases} (28)

Take the exogenous variables to be mutually independent, so the displayed uniform marginals specify their joint distribution. In this setting, ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} induces the same causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G}, where 𝐔X={UX,U1,U2}\mathbf{U}_{X}=\{U_{X},U_{1},U_{2}\} and 𝐔Y={UY,U1,U2}\mathbf{U}_{Y}=\{U_{Y},U_{1},U_{2}\}. The diagram gives a compact summary of the possible directed and confounding relationships between XX and YY, while omitting the identities and number of exogenous variables and the quantitative forms of the mechanisms.

2.4.1 Graphical Notation

If there is an edge between two vertices XX and YY in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we say that the two vertices are adjacent in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, denoted by Y∈𝙰𝚍𝚓​(X)𝒢Y\in\mathtt{Adj}(X)_{\mathcal{G}} or X∈𝙰𝚍𝚓​(Y)𝒢X\in\mathtt{Adj}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}}. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices, with a specified edge connecting each consecutive pair. When two vertices are joined by both a directed and a bidirected edge, the path specifies which edge is traversed. If a path consists of directed edges with the same orientation, we say the path is directed. A non-endpoint vertex is a collider on a path when both adjacent path edges have arrowheads at that vertex, as in A→B←CA\to B\leftarrow C. Otherwise, it is a non-collider on that path. A path is a collider path if all its non-endpoint vertices are colliders.

We use kinship notation for graphical relationships: parents (𝙿𝚊\mathtt{Pa}), children (𝙲𝚑\mathtt{Ch}), ancestors (𝙰𝚗\mathtt{An}), and descendants (𝙳𝚎\mathtt{De}).

  • •

    𝙿𝚊​(X)𝒢\mathtt{Pa}(X)_{\mathcal{G}} (parents of XX in 𝒢\mathcal{G}): the set {Zi}\{Z_{i}\} such that there exists a directed edge Zi→XZ_{i}\to X in 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

  • •

    𝙲𝚑​(X)𝒢\mathtt{Ch}(X)_{\mathcal{G}} (children of XX in 𝒢\mathcal{G}): the set {Zi}\{Z_{i}\} such that there exists a directed edge X→ZiX\to Z_{i} in 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

  • •

    𝙰𝚗​(X)𝒢\mathtt{An}(X)_{\mathcal{G}} (ancestors of XX in 𝒢\mathcal{G}): the set {Zi}\{Z_{i}\} such that there exists a directed path Zi→⋯→XZ_{i}\to\cdots\to X in 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

  • •

    𝙳𝚎​(X)𝒢\mathtt{De}(X)_{\mathcal{G}} (descendants of XX in 𝒢\mathcal{G}): the set {Zi}\{Z_{i}\} such that there exists a directed path X→⋯→ZiX\to\cdots\to Z_{i} in 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Ancestors and descendants include the variable itself. For a set of variables, we define 𝙰𝚗​(𝐗)𝒢=⋃X∈𝐗𝙰𝚗​(X)𝒢\mathtt{An}(\mathbf{X})_{\mathcal{G}}=\bigcup_{X\in\mathbf{X}}\mathtt{An}(X)_{\mathcal{G}}, and similarly for other relationships.

The 𝐗\mathbf{X}-lower-manipulation of 𝒢\mathcal{G} removes all directed edges out of variables in 𝐗\mathbf{X}, denoted as 𝒢𝐗¯\mathcal{G}_{\underline{\mathbf{X}}}, while the 𝐗\mathbf{X}-upper-manipulation of 𝒢\mathcal{G} removes all edges with an arrowhead at a variable in 𝐗\mathbf{X}, including bidirected edges, denoted as 𝒢𝐗¯\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}. We denote the set of variables in 𝒢\mathcal{G} by 𝐕⁡(𝒢)\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{G}). A subgraph 𝒢⁡[𝐕′]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{V}^{\prime}], where 𝐕′⊆𝐕⁡(𝒢)\mathbf{V}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{G}), is defined as a vertex-induced subgraph in which all edges among the vertices in 𝐕′\mathbf{V}^{\prime} are preserved. We define 𝒢\𝐗\mathcal{G}\backslash\mathbf{X} as 𝒢⁡[𝐕⁡(𝒢)∖𝐗]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{G})\setminus\mathbf{X}] for 𝐗⊆𝐕⁡(𝒢)\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{G}).

Definition 0 (Latent projection (Verma and Pearl, 1990)).

The latent projection of a causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G} over 𝐕\mathbf{V} onto 𝐗⊆𝐕\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V} is a mixed graph over 𝐗\mathbf{X}. It retains the edges in 𝒢⁡[𝐗]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{X}] and, for every pair of distinct vertices Vi,Vj∈𝐗V_{i},V_{j}\in\mathbf{X}, includes the following additional edges:

  • 1.

    Add a directed edge Vi→VjV_{i}\to V_{j} if there exists a directed path from ViV_{i} to VjV_{j} in 𝒢\mathcal{G} such that every non-endpoint vertex on the path is not in 𝐗\mathbf{X}.

  • 2.

    Add a bidirected edge Vi↔VjV_{i}\leftrightarrow V_{j} if there exists a path between ViV_{i} and VjV_{j} in 𝒢\mathcal{G} with arrowheads at both endpoints, such that every non-endpoint vertex is a non-collider and lies outside 𝐗\mathbf{X}.

We denote by 𝒢​⟨𝐗⟩\mathcal{G}\langle\mathbf{X}\rangle the latent projection of 𝒢\mathcal{G} onto 𝐗\mathbf{X}.

2.4.2 Graphical Constraints

The structure of a causal diagram imposes constraints on the data generated by any causal model that is consistent with the diagram. One such constraint is conditional independence (CI), which can be inferred from the causal diagram via the d-separation criterion.

Definition 0 (d-separation (Pearl, 2000)).

In a causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G}, let XX and YY be distinct vertices and let 𝐙⊆𝐕∖{X,Y}\mathbf{Z}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{X,Y\}. A path pp between vertices XX and YY is a d-connecting (active) path relative to a set 𝐙\mathbf{Z} if:

  • 1.

    every non-collider on pp is not a member of 𝐙\mathbf{Z}; and

  • 2.

    every collider on pp is an ancestor of some member of 𝐙\mathbf{Z}.

Two variables XX and YY are said to be d-separated by 𝐙\mathbf{Z} if there is no d-connecting path between XX and YY relative to 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. Furthermore, two disjoint sets 𝐗\mathbf{X} and 𝐘\mathbf{Y} are said to be d-separated by 𝐙\mathbf{Z} if every variable in 𝐗\mathbf{X} is d-separated from every variable in 𝐘\mathbf{Y} by 𝐙\mathbf{Z}; this is denoted as (𝐗⟂⁣⟂𝐘∣𝐙)𝒢(\mathbf{X}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}\mathbf{Y}\mid\mathbf{Z})_{\mathcal{G}}88 8 Probabilistic independence statements are denoted as (𝐗⟂⁣⟂𝐘∣𝐙)P(\mathbf{X}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}\mathbf{Y}\mid\mathbf{Z})_{P}..

We now present a key result that relates d-separation statements derived from a causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G} to constraints on the distribution P⁡(𝐕)P(\mathbf{V}).

Theorem 12 (Probabilistic implications of d-separation (Pearl, 2000)).

If 𝐗\mathbf{X} and 𝐘\mathbf{Y} are d-separated by 𝐙\mathbf{Z} in a causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G}, then 𝐗\mathbf{X} is independent of 𝐘\mathbf{Y} given 𝐙\mathbf{Z} in every distribution PP compatible with 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Conversely, if 𝐗\mathbf{X} and 𝐘\mathbf{Y} are not d-separated by 𝐙\mathbf{Z} in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, then 𝐗\mathbf{X} and 𝐘\mathbf{Y} are dependent given 𝐙\mathbf{Z} in at least one distribution PP compatible with 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

For concreteness, we consider the causal diagram in Fig. 3. The path p=⟨X,W,T,Y⟩p=\langle X,W,T,Y\rangle is active relative to 𝐙={W}\mathbf{Z}=\{W\} since T∉𝐙T\notin\mathbf{Z} is a non-collider and W∈𝐙W\in\mathbf{Z} is a collider. Alternatively, the path is blocked relative to 𝐙′={W,T}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\{W,T\} since T∈𝐙′T\in\mathbf{Z}^{\prime} is a non-collider along pp. Moreover, p′=⟨X,W,Y⟩p^{\prime}=\langle X,W,Y\rangle is blocked relative to 𝐙′\mathbf{Z}^{\prime} since W∈𝐙′W\in\mathbf{Z}^{\prime} is a non-collider along p′p^{\prime}. Hence, XX and YY are d-separated relative to 𝐙′={W,T}\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}=\{W,T\}. Therefore, Thm. 12 states that:

(X⟂⁣⟂Y∣W,T)𝒢⟹(X⟂⁣⟂Y∣W,T)P.\displaystyle(X\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}Y\mid W,T)_{\mathcal{G}}\implies(X\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}Y\mid W,T)_{P}. 2.5 Ancestral Graphs and Causal Discovery

Recovering causal structures.

Causal discovery addresses the reverse direction: inferring from P⁡(𝐕)P(\mathbf{V}) which causal diagrams could have generated it (Pearl, 2000; Spirtes et al., 2000).

In practice, assumptions regarding model simplicity (à la Occam’s razor) are used to avoid situations in which a saturated model would otherwise be preferred. A growing literature focuses on constructing equivalence classes of causal diagrams, acknowledging the difficulty of identifying a single true causal diagram from data (Zhang, 2008b; Hauser and Bühlmann, 2012; Kocaoglu et al., 2017; Greenewald et al., 2019; Squires et al., 2020; Choo and Shiragur, 2023; Zhou et al., 2025).

The simplest and most abundant form of data is observational, and conditional independence is a key property that is imprinted in the data by the underlying causal diagram via d-separation, as discussed earlier. Consequently, causal diagrams that encode the same set of d-separations imply the same CIs in the generated data. Hence, the goal is to leverage the CIs in the data to learn the equivalence class of the true, but unknown, causal diagram.

Markov equivalence class.

The following definition formally introduces this equivalence class, known as the Markov equivalence class (MEC) (Richardson and Spirtes, 2002; Zhang, 2006; Zhang, 2008b).

Definition 0 (Markov equivalence).

Two graphs are in the same Markov equivalence class (MEC) if they imply the same set of conditional independence statements.

We use ℰ\mathcal{E} to denote a Markov equivalence class. To denote a particular equivalence class to which a model 𝒢\mathcal{G} belongs, we write ℰ⁡(𝒢)\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{G}).

Ancestral graphs.

Ancestral graphs are designed to capture graph structures without explicitly modeling latent variables. While directed edges between vertices in a causal diagram represent a possible direct causal link between them, in ancestral graphs, directed edges instead represent ancestral relationships. Similar to the absence of directed cycles in causal diagrams, ancestral graphs do not permit an almost directed cycle, which occurs when X↔YX\leftrightarrow Y is present while XX is an ancestor of YY.

Maximal ancestral graphs.

We consider the case without selection variables, so undirected edges are excluded. A mixed graph is called a maximal ancestral graph (MAG) if:

  • 1

    (Ancestral). It does not contain any directed or almost directed cycles; and

  • 2

    (Maximal). There is no inducing path relative to the empty set99 9 An inducing path relative to 𝐔\mathbf{U} is defined as a path where (1) every non-endpoint vertex not in 𝐔\mathbf{U} is a collider, and (2) every collider is an ancestor of at least one endpoint. between any two non-adjacent vertices.

A MAG entails a conditional independence model via m-separation, defined below. Its path-blocking conditions are the same as those used for causal diagrams above; the different name indicates that we now apply them to ancestral graphs1010 10 We use the notation ℳ\mathcal{M} to denote a MAG when focusing on ancestral graphs, rather than an SCM..

Definition 0 (m-separation).

Let XX and YY be distinct vertices and let 𝐙⊆𝐕∖{X,Y}\mathbf{Z}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{X,Y\}. A path pp between vertices XX and YY is an m-connecting (active) path relative to a set 𝐙\mathbf{Z} if:

  • 1.

    Every non-collider on pp is not a member of 𝐙\mathbf{Z}; and

  • 2.

    Every collider on pp is an ancestor of some member of 𝐙\mathbf{Z}.

Two variables XX and YY are m-separated by 𝐙\mathbf{Z} if there is no m-connecting path between XX and YY relative to 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. Two disjoint sets 𝐗\mathbf{X} and 𝐘\mathbf{Y} are said to be m-separated by 𝐙\mathbf{Z} if every variable in 𝐗\mathbf{X} is m-separated from every variable in 𝐘\mathbf{Y} by 𝐙\mathbf{Z}.

In general, a MAG represents a set of causal diagrams that entail the same conditional independence and ancestral relations among the observed variables. For each causal diagram, there is a unique corresponding MAG over the observed variables that preserves their ancestral relations and the conditional independence relations implied by the graph after marginalizing the latent variables. Distinct MAGs can imply the same conditional independence relations among the observed variables. To illustrate, consider the causal diagrams 𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{1} and 𝒢2\mathcal{G}_{2} in Fig. 4. While they yield the same conditional independence relations:

(A⟂⁣⟂B)P​ and ​(A⟂⁣⟂Y∣B,C)P\displaystyle(A\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}B)_{P}\text{~and~}(A\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}Y\mid B,C)_{P} (30)

they correspond to distinct MAGs, ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}, respectively. The following graphical constructs are key to deriving a graphical characterization for when two MAGs are Markov equivalent.

The skeleton is obtained by ignoring all endpoint marks. A triple ⟨A,B,C⟩\langle A,B,C\rangle is unshielded if AA and BB are adjacent, BB and CC are adjacent, and AA and CC are not adjacent. A path is uncovered if every consecutive triple on the path is unshielded. This condition concerns vertices two steps apart; it does not, by itself, prohibit every edge between nonconsecutive vertices.

Definition 0 (Discriminating path).

A path p=⟨X,⋯,W,Z,Y⟩p=\langle X,\cdots,W,Z,Y\rangle is a discriminating path for ZZ if:

  • •

    pp includes at least three edges;

  • •

    ZZ is a non-endpoint vertex on pp, and is adjacent to YY on pp; and

  • •

    XX is not adjacent to YY, and every vertex between XX and ZZ is a collider on pp and is a parent of YY.

For example, consider the MAG in Fig. 4(c). The path p=⟨A,C,B,Y⟩p=\langle A,C,B,Y\rangle is a discriminating path for BB between AA and YY. The path includes at least three edges, AA is not adjacent to YY, and CC is a collider along pp and a parent of YY. Using this structure, we have the following graphical characterization for when two MAGs are Markov equivalent.

Lemma 0 (Graphical characterization of MEC (Spirtes and Richardson, 1997; Zhang, 2007)).

Two MAGs over the same set of vertices are Markov equivalent if and only if:

  • 1.

    they have the same adjacencies;

  • 2.

    they have the same unshielded colliders; and

  • 3.

    for every path that is discriminating for the same vertex in both graphs, that vertex has the same collider status on the path in the two graphs.

In words, two MAGs are Markov equivalent if they have the same skeleton and the same unshielded colliders (also known as v-structures), and if every discriminating path common to both graphs identifies a collider in one graph if and only if it identifies a collider in the other.1111 11 Determining whether two MAGs are Markov equivalent is tractable, with a worst-case runtime of 𝒪⁡(|𝐕|3)\mathcal{O}(\lvert\mathbf{V}\rvert^{3}) (Zhao et al., 2005; Wienöbst et al., 2022).

For example, ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2} in Figs. 4(c) and 4(d) are Markov equivalent because:

  • 1.

    they have the same adjacencies A∗⁣→C,B∗⁣→C,B∗⁣→YA\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}C,B\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}C,B\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}Y and C∗⁣→YC\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}Y.

  • 2.

    they have the same unshielded collider A∗⁣→C←⁣∗BA\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}C\mathrel{\leftarrow\!\!\ast\!}B.

  • 3.

    the path p=⟨A,C,B,Y⟩p=\langle A,C,B,Y\rangle is a discriminating path for BB in both graphs, and BB is a non-collider on pp in both graphs.

This characterization of equivalent MAGs motivates the formulation of a partial ancestral graph (PAG), which is a partial mixed graph (PMG) representing an equivalence class of MAGs. A PAG shares the same adjacencies as every MAG in ℰ⁡(ℳ)\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{M}) and displays all and only the invariant edge marks. To make this precise, we first introduce PMGs and then PAGs.

Partial mixed graphs.

A partial mixed graph (PMG) has endpoint marks drawn from tails (−-), arrowheads (>\mathord{>}), and circles (∘\circ). A circle mark implies an undetermined mark that can be either an arrowhead or a tail. We use the ?\bm{?} mark to denote a wildcard that represents either a tail (−-) or a circle (∘\circ), but not an arrowhead (>\mathord{>}). In addition, we use an asterisk (∗*) as a wildcard to denote any possible mark.

In a PMG, if every edge mark on a path consists of circles, the path is called a circle path, and each edge is called a circle edge (∘−∘\,\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}\,). An edge is a partially directed edge (∘⁣→\,\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}) if it has both a circle and an arrowhead. A circle component is a maximal set of vertices connected by circle paths. A vertex incident to no circle edge forms a singleton circle component. Furthermore, [𝒬][\mathcal{Q}] denotes the set of MAGs represented by the PMG 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and similarly [ℳ][\mathcal{M}] denotes the set of causal diagrams conforming to the MAG ℳ\mathcal{M}.

A path ⟨V0(=X),V1,⋯,Vk(=Y)⟩\langle V_{0}(=X),V_{1},\cdots,V_{k}(=Y)\rangle is possibly directed from XX to YY if, for every i<ki<k, the edge between ViV_{i} and Vi+1V_{i+1} has no arrowhead at ViV_{i} and no tail at Vi+1V_{i+1}. We use kinship notation for graphical relationships in PMGs, with the prefix 𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜\mathtt{Poss}: possible ancestors (𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}) and possible descendants (𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙳𝚎\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{De}).

  • •

    𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(X)𝒬\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(X)_{\mathcal{Q}} (possible ancestors of XX in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}): the set {Zi}\{Z_{i}\} such that there exists a possibly directed path from ZiZ_{i} to XX in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

  • •

    𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙳𝚎​(X)𝒬\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{De}(X)_{\mathcal{Q}} (possible descendants of XX in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}): the set {Zi}\{Z_{i}\} such that there exists a possibly directed path from XX to ZiZ_{i} in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

Both possible ancestors and possible descendants include the variable itself. For a set of variables 𝐗\mathbf{X}, define:

𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(𝐗)𝒬=⋃X∈𝐗𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(X)𝒬,\displaystyle\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(\mathbf{X})_{\mathcal{Q}}=\bigcup_{X\in\mathbf{X}}\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(X)_{\mathcal{Q}}, (31)

and define 𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙳𝚎​(𝐗)𝒬\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{De}(\mathbf{X})_{\mathcal{Q}} analogously.

Partial ancestral graphs.

A partial ancestral graph (PAG) (Richardson and Spirtes, 2002; Zhang, 2006; Zhang, 2008b; Zhang, 2008a; Ali et al., 2005), denoted by 𝒫\mathcal{P}, is a PMG that represents a Markov equivalence class of MAGs. Every MAG ℳ\mathcal{M} represented by a PAG has the same skeleton as 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and the non-circle marks in 𝒫\mathcal{P} are identical to those in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Every circle in 𝒫\mathcal{P} corresponds to a non-invariant mark among the represented MAGs. The PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P} in Fig. 4(e), for instance, encodes every MAG obtained by orienting circle marks incident to AA and BB as either >\mathord{>} or −-, including both ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}. Therefore, {ℳ1,ℳ2}⊆[𝒫]=ℰ⁡(ℳ1)=ℰ⁡(ℳ2)\{\mathcal{M}_{1},\mathcal{M}_{2}\}\subseteq[\mathcal{P}]=\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{M}_{1})=\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{M}_{2}).

Fast Causal Inference (FCI).

Assume the causal Markov condition and faithfulness with respect to the true MAG ℳ∗\mathcal{M}^{\ast}, with no selection bias. The causal Markov condition states that graphical separation implies conditional independence in the observational distribution; faithfulness requires the converse. For pairwise disjoint sets 𝐗,𝐘,𝐙⊆𝐕\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}\subseteq\mathbf{V}, faithfulness states that:

(𝐗⟂⁣⟂𝐘∣𝐙)P⟹(𝐗⟂⁣⟂𝐘∣𝐙)ℳ∗.\displaystyle(\mathbf{X}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}\mathbf{Y}\mid\mathbf{Z})_{P}\implies(\mathbf{X}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}\mathbf{Y}\mid\mathbf{Z})_{\mathcal{M}^{\ast}}. (32)

Given an oracle for these conditional independence relations, FCI (Spirtes et al., 2000; Zhang, 2008b) recovers the PAG representing the Markov equivalence class of ℳ∗\mathcal{M}^{\ast}. With finite data, conditional independence tests estimate this oracle information.

Alg. 1 gives an oracle-level schematic of FCI, using an exhaustive search for separating sets to simplify the presentation. Its three phases describe the logical steps of recovering adjacencies, identifying unshielded colliders, and completing invariant orientations.

In Phase 1, we initialize a complete graph over the nodes in 𝐕\mathbf{V} consisting of circle edges (∘−∘\,\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}\,). For every pair of nodes XX, YY, we remove the edge between XX and YY if there exists a separating set 𝐙\mathbf{Z} such that (X⟂⁣⟂Y∣𝐙)P(X\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}Y\mid\mathbf{Z})_{P}. By the end of Phase 1, we obtain the skeleton of the resulting PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

In Phase 2, we identify all v-structures by testing ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0}:

  • ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0}.

    For each unshielded triple ⟨X,Z,Y⟩\langle X,Z,Y\rangle in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, orient it as a collider X∗⁣→Z←⁣∗YX\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}Z\mathrel{\leftarrow\!\!\ast\!}Y if and only if ZZ is not in 𝖲𝖾𝗉𝗌𝖾𝗍⁡(X,Y)\mathsf{Sepset}(X,Y).

Fig. 5 illustrates ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} and the arrowhead orientation rules ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}–ℛ4\mathcal{R}_{4}.

Finally, in Phase 3, we apply the orientation rules of Zhang (2008b) other than ℛ5\mathcal{R}_{5}–ℛ7\mathcal{R}_{7} until none applies. These three rules are omitted because selection bias is excluded. Fig. 6 illustrates the tail orientation rules ℛ8\mathcal{R}_{8}–ℛ10\mathcal{R}_{10}.

  • ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}.

    If X∗⁣→Z∘−∗YX\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}Z\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}Y, and XX and YY are not adjacent, then orient Z∘−∗YZ\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}Y as Z→YZ\to Y.

  • ℛ2\mathcal{R}_{2}.

    If X→Z∗⁣→YX\to Z\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}Y or X∗⁣→Z→YX\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}Z\to Y, and X∗−∘YX\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y, then orient X∗−∘YX\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y as X∗⁣→YX\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}Y.

  • ℛ3\mathcal{R}_{3}.

    If X∗⁣→Z←⁣∗YX\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}Z\mathrel{\leftarrow\!\!\ast\!}Y, X∗−∘W∘−∗YX\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}W\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}Y, XX and YY are not adjacent, and W∗−∘ZW\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Z, then orient W∗−∘ZW\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Z as W∗⁣→ZW\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}Z.

  • ℛ4\mathcal{R}_{4}.

    If ⟨X,⋯,W,Z,Y⟩\langle X,\cdots,W,Z,Y\rangle is a discriminating path between XX and YY for ZZ, and Z∘−∗YZ\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}Y, then orient Z∘−∗YZ\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}Y as Z→YZ\to Y if Z∈𝖲𝖾𝗉𝗌𝖾𝗍⁡(X,Y)Z\in\mathsf{Sepset}(X,Y); otherwise orient the triple ⟨W,Z,Y⟩\langle W,Z,Y\rangle as W↔Z↔YW\leftrightarrow Z\leftrightarrow Y.

  • ℛ8\mathcal{R}_{8}.

    If X→Z→YX\to Z\to Y, and X∘⁣→YX\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y, orient X∘⁣→YX\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y as X→YX\to Y.

  • ℛ9\mathcal{R}_{9}.

    If X∘⁣→YX\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y, and p=⟨X,Z,W,⋯,Y⟩p=\langle X,Z,W,\cdots,Y\rangle is an uncovered possibly directed path from XX to YY such that ZZ and YY are not adjacent, then orient X∘⁣→YX\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y as X→YX\to Y.

  • ℛ10\mathcal{R}_{10}.

    Suppose X∘⁣→YX\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y, Z→Y←WZ\to Y\leftarrow W, p1p_{1} is an uncovered possibly directed path from XX to ZZ, and p2p_{2} is an uncovered possibly directed path from XX to WW. Let UU be the vertex adjacent to XX on p1p_{1} (UU could be ZZ), and VV be the vertex adjacent to XX on p2p_{2} (VV could be WW). If UU and VV are distinct, and not adjacent, then orient X∘⁣→YX\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y as X→YX\to Y.

Fig. 7 illustrates how FCI works. We can learn the PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P} in Fig. 7(e) from observational data generated by the causal diagram in Fig. 4(a). Nodes AA and BB are not adjacent in 𝒫\mathcal{P} because (A⟂⁣⟂B)P(A\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}B)_{P}, and AA and YY are not adjacent since (A⟂⁣⟂Y∣B,C)P(A\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}Y\mid B,C)_{P}. Hence, Phase 1 results in the skeleton in Fig. 7(b).

In Phase 2, the v-structure A∘⁣→C←⁣∘BA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C\mathrel{\leftarrow\!\!\circ\!}B is identified since C∉𝖲𝖾𝗉𝗌𝖾𝗍⁡(A,B)C\notin\mathsf{Sepset}(A,B), leading to Fig. 7(c). In Phase 3, C∘−∘YC\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y is oriented as C→YC\to Y by ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} since the triple A∘⁣→C∘−∘YA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y is unshielded, which gives Fig. 7(d). Moreover, B∘−∘YB\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y is oriented as B→YB\to Y by ℛ4\mathcal{R}_{4} since ⟨A,C,B,Y⟩\langle A,C,B,Y\rangle is a discriminating path between AA and YY for BB, and B∈𝖲𝖾𝗉𝗌𝖾𝗍⁡(A,Y)B\in\mathsf{Sepset}(A,Y). This yields the PAG in Fig. 7(e).

Under the oracle, Markov, and faithfulness assumptions stated above, FCI returns the PAG of the true MAG. Moreover, its orientation rules are sound and complete in the sense that they identify all and only the edge marks that are invariant within the represented Markov equivalence class. To state these properties precisely, we first define orientation soundness and completeness for a general PMG.

Soundness and completeness of orientations.

Fix a nonempty target class 𝒥\mathcal{J} of MAGs with a common skeleton, determined by the input PAG and any additional orientations. Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be a PMG on this skeleton.

  • •

    Soundness. Every tail or arrowhead in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} agrees with the corresponding mark in every MAG in 𝒥\mathcal{J}.

  • •

    Completeness. Every endpoint mark that is invariant across 𝒥\mathcal{J} is displayed as a tail or arrowhead in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

Thus, when orientations are sound and complete, each circle in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} has both a tail witness and an arrowhead witness in 𝒥\mathcal{J}. For the PMGs used below, the represented class [𝒬][\mathcal{Q}] is understood relative to the input PAG and the incorporated additional orientations.

For example, consider the PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P} in Fig. 4(e), with target class 𝒥=[𝒫]\mathcal{J}=[\mathcal{P}]. The arrowheads at CC on A∘⁣→CA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C and B∘⁣→CB\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C are invariant, as are both endpoint marks of B→YB\to Y and C→YC\to Y. Soundness means that these displayed arrowheads and tails agree with every MAG in 𝒥\mathcal{J}. Completeness means that all such invariant marks have been displayed.

The MAGs ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2} in Figs. 4(c) and 4(d) are two members of the class that witness the variation represented by the remaining circles. In ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1}, the edges A↔CA\leftrightarrow C and B↔CB\leftrightarrow C have arrowheads at AA and BB, whereas in ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}, the corresponding edges A→CA\to C and B→CB\to C have tails at those endpoints. Thus, neither endpoint mark is invariant, and the PAG correctly retains circles at AA and BB. Its orientations are nevertheless complete: every remaining circle reflects variation within the target class rather than a missing invariant orientation.

Visibility.

In the context of ancestral graphs, it is crucial to be able to identify edges that are not confounded. A directed edge X→YX\to Y is visible if no DAG whose corresponding MAG is the given MAG (or belongs to the class represented by the given PAG) contains an inducing path between XX and YY, relative to its latent vertices, that is into XX. We refer to any edge that is not visible as invisible. For induced subgraphs, we retain the model class specified by the full PMG 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a DAG over observed vertices 𝐕\mathbf{V} and latent vertices 𝐔\mathbf{U} whose corresponding MAG belongs to [𝒬][\mathcal{Q}]. A directed edge X→YX\to Y in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}] is visible relative to this class if no such DAG contains an inducing path into XX between XX and YY in 𝒢⁡[𝐀∪𝐔]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}\cup\mathbf{U}], relative to 𝐔\mathbf{U}. The latent vertices are retained when the observed vertex set is restricted to 𝐀\mathbf{A}.

Lemma 0 (Graphical characterization of visibility (Zhang, 2006; Maathuis and Colombo, 2015)).

A directed edge X→YX\to Y in a MAG or PAG is visible if and only if there exists a vertex ZZ not adjacent to YY for which at least one of the following conditions holds:

  • 1.

    ZZ and XX are joined by an edge with an arrowhead at XX.

  • 2.

    A collider path from ZZ to XX has an arrowhead at XX, and all its non-endpoint vertices are parents of YY.

The criterion is evaluated in the full MAG or PAG, relative to its represented causal model class. For a PAG, a graphical visibility witness is preserved in every represented MAG. Conversely, if the criterion fails in the PAG, there is a represented MAG in which the directed edge is invisible (see Lemma 104). For an induced subgraph retaining the full graph’s model class, a visibility witness may lie outside the retained observed vertices; the criterion should therefore not be recomputed using only the induced subgraph.

Fig. 8 illustrates the conditions. Throughout this paper, purple directed edges indicate visibility. For concreteness, C→YC\to Y in the PAG in Fig. 7(e) is visible, indicating that the two nodes are not confounded in any causal diagram in the MEC represented by the PAG. Note that A∘⁣→C→YA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C\to Y satisfies the first condition of Lemma 17. Moreover, consider the edge B→YB\to Y in the MAG of Fig. 4(c), which is visible by the second condition of Lemma 17. The path ⟨A,C,B⟩\langle A,C,B\rangle forms a collider path into BB, and CC on this path is a parent of YY.

3 Structural Causal Bandits

Many canonical decision-making settings, such as multi-armed bandits (MABs), Markov decision processes (MDPs), and dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs), can be represented within the semantic framework of structural causal models (SCMs) (Zhang, 2023; Bareinboim et al., 2024). In this section, we introduce the MAB framework, examine it through a causal lens, and generalize it within the SCM framework, resulting in what is known as structural causal bandits (SCBs) (Lee and Bareinboim, 2018; Lee and Bareinboim, 2019).

3.1 Multi-Armed Bandits

The multi-armed bandit (MAB; simply, bandit) problem is a sequential decision-making problem. One can view this problem as a sequential game between an agent and an environment (i.e., a bandit instance). The game is played over TT rounds. In each round t∈{1,2,⋯,T}t\in\{1,2,\cdots,T\}, the agent first chooses an action AtA_{t} from a given set 𝒜={ai}i=1|𝒜|\mathcal{A}=\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\lvert\mathcal{A}\rvert}, and the environment then reveals a reward YtY_{t}. The agent cannot access future information when choosing actions; its action distribution may depend on the observed history:

Ht−1=⟨A1,Y1,⋯,At−1,Yt−1⟩.\displaystyle H_{t-1}=\langle A_{1},Y_{1},\cdots,A_{t-1},Y_{t-1}\rangle. (33)

A policy π={πt}t=1T\pi=\{\pi_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} assigns an action distribution πt(⋅∣Ht−1)\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid H_{t-1}) to each history. At round tt, the agent samples AtA_{t} from this distribution using internal randomness independent of the environment’s randomness. Deterministic policies are included as a special case. The agent interacts with the environment by following a policy. The objective of the agent is to maximize the total reward, which is a random quantity depending on both the agent’s actions and the rewards generated by the environment. Conditional on the selected action At=aA_{t}=a and the past history, YtY_{t} has distribution νa\nu_{a}, which does not change with tt. All reward means are assumed finite. In the SCM formulation, each round uses a fresh independent draw of the exogenous variables from the same distribution P⁡(𝐔)P(\mathbf{U}).

Unstructured vs. structured bandits.

The fundamental challenge in bandit problems is that the environment is unknown to the agent. The agent only knows that the true environment lies in some set 𝒞\mathcal{C}, called the environment class.

An environment class 𝒞\mathcal{C} is called unstructured if 𝒜\mathcal{A} is finite and playing an action provides no information about the reward distributions of other actions (Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020). Environment classes that are not unstructured are called structured. An important feature of structured bandits is that the agent can often gain information about some actions without explicitly playing them.

Cumulative regret.

Let ν={νa:a∈𝒜}\nu=\{\nu_{a}:a\in\mathcal{A}\} be a stochastic bandit instance, and let μa\mu_{a} denote the mean reward of action a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. Let a⋆a^{\star} be an optimal action, i.e., μa⋆=maxa∈𝒜⁡μa\mu_{a^{\star}}=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\mu_{a}. The cumulative (pseudo-)regret of a policy π\pi on instance ν\nu is defined as:

RT𝒜​(π,ν)=T​μa⋆−∑t=1TμAt,\displaystyle R_{T}^{\mathcal{A}}(\pi,\nu)=T\mu_{a^{\star}}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu_{A_{t}}, (34)

which compares the cumulative mean reward of always playing an optimal action with the sum of the mean rewards of the selected actions over TT rounds.

Define the suboptimality gap as Δa≜μa⋆−μa\Delta_{a}\triangleq\mu_{a^{\star}}-\mu_{a} for a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. By the standard regret decomposition (Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020), we have:

RT𝒜​(π,ν)=∑a∈𝒜Δa​NT​(a),\displaystyle R_{T}^{\mathcal{A}}(\pi,\nu)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Delta_{a}N_{T}(a), (35)

where NT​(a)N_{T}(a) denotes the number of times action aa is selected up to time TT. This decomposition shows that minimizing expected cumulative regret amounts to controlling the expected number of pulls of suboptimal actions, weighted by their gaps:

𝔼​RT𝒜​(π,ν)=∑a∈𝒜Δa​𝔼​NT​(a).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}R_{T}^{\mathcal{A}}(\pi,\nu)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\Delta_{a}\mathbb{E}N_{T}(a). (36)

The expectation is taken with respect to the probability measure induced by the interaction between π\pi and ν\nu. When clear from context, we omit the dependence on π\pi and ν\nu.

3.2 Structural Causal Bandits: Where to Intervene?

We begin by noting that a standard bandit can be viewed as the simple causal model shown in Fig. 9(a). Interventions on XX correspond to actions with ΩX={x1,x2,⋯,xk}\Omega_{X}=\{x_{1},x_{2},\cdots,x_{k}\}, and the action space 𝒜={ai}i=1k\mathcal{A}=\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k} is defined as:

𝒜={ai=d​o​(xi):xi∈ΩX}.\displaystyle\mathcal{A}=\{a_{i}=do(x_{i}):x_{i}\in\Omega_{X}\}. (37)

The variable YY denotes the reward, and UU represents an unobserved confounder. Then νai\nu_{a_{i}} can be written as follows:

νai=P⁡(Y∣d​o​(xi))=Pxi​(Y).\displaystyle\nu_{a_{i}}=P(Y\mid do(x_{i}))=P_{x_{i}}(Y). (38)

Eq. 38 states that a standard bandit can be modeled as an SCM associated with the two-node causal diagram in Fig. 2(c), highlighting that the classical formulation is a special case of a causal model.

Example 0 (Clinical system; continued).

Revisit the clinical-system example. This can be seen as an example of a bandit problem. The environment corresponds to SCM ℳ\mathcal{M} in Eq. 2 and the action space is defined as:

𝒜={d​o​(X=0),d​o​(X=1)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{A}=\{do(X=0),do(X=1)\}. (39)

Furthermore, the bandit instance can be written as follows:

ν={PX=0​(Y)=𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.4),PX=1​(Y)=𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.4−η)},\displaystyle\nu=\{P_{X=0}(Y)=\mathtt{Bern}(0.4),P_{X=1}(Y)=\mathtt{Bern}(0.4-\eta)\}, (40)

as shown in Eqs. 21 and 25.

A careful reader may naturally ask:

“Why should we restrict ourselves to this simple setting?”

In particular, there is no need to limit the analysis to a two-node structure with a single manipulable variable XX. In what follows, we generalize the bandit formulation to arbitrary SCMs, which we refer to as structural causal bandits.

Structural causal bandits.

We now formalize the structural causal bandit (SCB) (Lee and Bareinboim, 2018; Lee and Bareinboim, 2019) problem in which an agent interacts with an environment modeled by an SCM ℳ=⟨𝐔,𝐕,ℱ,P⁡(𝐔)⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V},\mathcal{F},P(\mathbf{U})\rangle that includes a reward variable Y∈𝐕Y\in\mathbf{V}. In this setting, each action corresponds to an intervention on some set of variables 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\}, with an assigned value 𝐱∈Ω𝐗\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_{\mathbf{X}}. That is:

𝒜={do(𝐱):𝐱∈Ω𝐗,𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}}.\displaystyle\mathcal{A}=\{do(\mathbf{x}):\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_{\mathbf{X}},\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\}\}. (41)

We refer to each 𝐗\mathbf{X} as an intervention set (IS). We use the terms arm, action, and intervention interchangeably, depending on the context. The mean reward of an action is denoted by μ𝐱=𝔼⁡[Y∣d​o​(𝐱)]\mu_{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid do(\mathbf{x})]. Whenever a maximizing action is used, we assume that the maximum is attained and select one maximizer using a fixed tie-breaking rule. This is automatic for finite action spaces. For a fixed intervention set 𝐗\mathbf{X}, we denote a best action by:

𝐱∗∈arg⁡max𝐱∈Ω𝐗⁡μ𝐱.\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{\ast}\in\arg\max_{\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_{\mathbf{X}}}\mu_{\mathbf{x}}. (42)

Similarly, we denote the optimal action in 𝒜\mathcal{A} by:

𝐱⋆∈arg​max𝐱∈Ω𝐗𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}⁡μ𝐱.\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{\star}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_{\mathbf{X}}\\ \mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\}\end{subarray}}\mu_{\mathbf{x}}. (43)

For convenience, we identify d​o​(𝐱)do(\mathbf{x}) with the variable-indexed assignment 𝐱\mathbf{x} whenever the intervention target is clear. Assignments to different variable sets remain distinct actions, even when their numerical values coincide. The empty assignment denotes d​o​(∅)do(\emptyset).

Let At∈𝒜A_{t}\in\mathcal{A} denote the random intervention selected at round tt, using the assignment notation above. We define the suboptimality gap by Δ𝐱=μ𝐱⋆−μ𝐱\Delta_{\mathbf{x}}=\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}-\mu_{\mathbf{x}} and the cumulative regret as follows:

RT𝒜=T​μ𝐱⋆−∑t=1TμAt=∑𝐱∈𝒜Δ𝐱​NT​(𝐱),\displaystyle R_{T}^{\mathcal{A}}=T\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu_{A_{t}}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{A}}\Delta_{\mathbf{x}}N_{T}(\mathbf{x}), (44)

where NT​(𝐱)N_{T}(\mathbf{x}) denotes the number of times d​o​(𝐱)do(\mathbf{x}) is selected up to time TT.

In this setting, the agent knows the causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G} and the reward variable YY. The diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G} specifies the environment class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, consisting of SCMs conforming to 𝒢\mathcal{G}, while the structural functions ℱ\mathcal{F} and the exogenous distribution P⁡(𝐔)P(\mathbf{U}) remain unknown. Thus, the agent has access to qualitative structural information but not to the quantitative parameterization that determines the reward distributions. Graphical characterizations range over compatible SCMs, with domains chosen as part of the model; a particular bandit instance fixes these domains.

Example 0 (Two manipulable variables).

Consider an MAB environment induced by the following SCM ℳ\mathcal{M}:

ℳ={𝐔={U1,U2}𝐕={X1,X2,Y}ℱ={fX1​(u1)=u1fX2​(x1,u2)=x1⊕u2fY​(x2,u2)=x2⊕u2P⁡(𝐔)={U∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.5):∀U∈𝐔}\displaystyle\mathcal{M}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{U}=\{U_{1},U_{2}\}\\ \mathbf{V}=\{X_{1},X_{2},Y\}\\ \mathcal{F}=\begin{cases}f_{X_{1}}(u_{1})=u_{1}\\ f_{X_{2}}(x_{1},u_{2})=x_{1}\oplus u_{2}\\ f_{Y}(x_{2},u_{2})=x_{2}\oplus u_{2}\\ \end{cases}\\ P(\mathbf{U})=\{U\thicksim\mathtt{Bern}(0.5):\forall U\in\mathbf{U}\}\end{cases} (45)

where ⊕\oplus denotes the exclusive-or operator. Assume that U1U_{1} and U2U_{2} are mutually independent. The causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G} associated with ℳ\mathcal{M} is shown in Fig. 9(c). Consider an agent deployed in ℳ\mathcal{M} whose goal is to minimize expected cumulative regret:

𝔼​RT𝒜=∑𝐱∈𝒜Δ𝐱​𝔼​NT​(𝐱)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}R_{T}^{\mathcal{A}}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{A}}\Delta_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbb{E}N_{T}(\mathbf{x}) (46)

by intervening on the manipulable variables 𝐕∖{Y}={X1,X2}\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\}=\{X_{1},X_{2}\}. The collection of intervention sets is given by:

{∅,{X1},{X2},{X1,X2}}.\displaystyle\{\emptyset,\{X_{1}\},\{X_{2}\},\{X_{1},X_{2}\}\}. (47)

This collection is precisely the power set of the manipulable variables, and therefore contains 2|{X1,X2}|=42^{|\{X_{1},X_{2}\}|}=4 possible intervention sets. This setting can be translated into a traditional MAB instance in which each action corresponds to assigning specific values to a subset of {X1,X2}\{X_{1},X_{2}\} under intervention. In this example, this yields 991212 12 That is, 1+2+2+41+2+2+4, corresponding to the numbers of actions induced by each of the four intervention sets. actions:

𝒜={𝐱∈{0,1}|𝐗|,𝐗∈{∅,{X1},{X2},{X1,X2}}}.\displaystyle\mathcal{A}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{\lvert\mathbf{X}\rvert},\mathbf{X}\in\{\emptyset,\{X_{1}\},\{X_{2}\},\{X_{1},X_{2}\}\}\}. (48)

We provide two structural properties that arise in the SCB setting: equivalence and partial orders. These properties capture dependencies among different actions and can be understood through do-calculus (Pearl, 1995) and related tools.

  • Rule 2.

    P⁡(𝐲∣d​o​(𝐰,𝐱),𝐳)=P⁡(𝐲∣d​o​(𝐰),𝐱,𝐳)P(\mathbf{y}\mid do(\mathbf{w},\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{z})=P(\mathbf{y}\mid do(\mathbf{w}),\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}) if (𝐗⟂⁣⟂𝐘∣𝐖∪𝐙)𝒢𝐖¯​𝐗¯(\mathbf{X}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}\mathbf{Y}\mid\mathbf{W}\cup\mathbf{Z})_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{W}}\underline{\mathbf{X}}}}.

To provide intuition, let us consider the following example, where the action space can be reduced using graphical information derived from these properties. The first reduction corresponds to removing intervention sets that are equivalent to some proper subset, while the second corresponds to removing intervention sets that are never strictly better than some other intervention set.

Example 0 (Continued).

The main question is whether one can do better by exploiting the causal invariance implied by ℳ\mathcal{M} and represented by 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Property 1. First, using Rule 3 of do-calculus, we have:

P⁡(y∣d​o​(x1,x2))=P⁡(y∣d​o​(x2)),\displaystyle P(y\mid do(x_{1},x_{2}))=P(y\mid do(x_{2})), (49)

since (X1⟂⁣⟂Y)𝒢X2¯(X_{1}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}Y)_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{X_{2}}}}. In words, intervening on X1X_{1} has no additional effect on YY once X2X_{2} is intervened upon. Therefore, the corresponding expected rewards are equal:

μx1,x2=μx2,\displaystyle\mu_{x_{1},x_{2}}=\mu_{x_{2}}, (50)

for any x1∈ΩX1x_{1}\in\Omega_{X_{1}} and x2∈ΩX2x_{2}\in\Omega_{X_{2}}. Consequently, actions of the form d​o​(x1,x2)do(x_{1},x_{2}) are redundant, and it suffices to consider only the 55 actions induced by the remaining three intervention sets:

𝒜={𝐱∈{0,1}|𝐗|,𝐗∈{∅,{X1},{X2}}}.\displaystyle\mathcal{A}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{\lvert\mathbf{X}\rvert},\mathbf{X}\in\{\emptyset,\{X_{1}\},\{X_{2}\}\}\}. (51)
