P⁡(y)\displaystyle P(y) =∑x1P⁡(y∣x1)​P​(x1)\displaystyle=\sum_{x_{1}}P(y\mid x_{1})P(x_{1}) (52)
=∑x1Px1​(y)​P​(x1),\displaystyle=\sum_{x_{1}}P_{x_{1}}(y)P(x_{1}), (53)

by Rule 2 of do-calculus with (X1⟂⁣⟂Y)𝒢X1¯(X_{1}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}Y)_{\mathcal{G}_{\underline{X_{1}}}}. Equivalently, μ∅=∑x1μx1​P​(x1)\mu_{\emptyset}=\sum_{x_{1}}\mu_{x_{1}}P(x_{1}). Thus, we can derive:

μ∅\displaystyle\mu_{\emptyset} =∑x1μx1​P​(x1)\displaystyle=\sum_{x_{1}}\mu_{x_{1}}P(x_{1}) (54)
≤∑x1μx1∗​P​(x1)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x_{1}}\mu_{x_{1}^{\ast}}P(x_{1}) (55)
=μx1∗.\displaystyle=\mu_{x_{1}^{\ast}}. (56)

Hence, d​o​(∅)do(\emptyset) is never better than d​o​(x1∗)do(x_{1}^{\ast}) and can therefore be excluded from consideration. Thus, it suffices to consider only the 44 actions induced by the remaining two intervention sets:

𝒜={𝐱∈{0,1}|𝐗|,𝐗∈{{X1},{X2}}}.\displaystyle\mathcal{A}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{\lvert\mathbf{X}\rvert},\mathbf{X}\in\{\{X_{1}\},\{X_{2}\}\}\}. (57)

This conclusion holds for any SCM consistent with 𝒢\mathcal{G}, showing how causal structure can reduce the action space while retaining at least one optimal action. Eliminated actions may tie with retained actions, but cannot achieve a higher reward than the best retained action.

We now formalize these two reductions, beginning with equivalence among actions.

3.2.1 Property 1: Equivalence among Actions

We begin by recalling Rule 3 of do-calculus, which gives conditions under which an intervention has no effect on the outcome variable. Since actions correspond to interventions (including the null intervention), we consider whether:

P⁡(y∣d​o​(𝐱,𝐰))=P⁡(y∣d​o​(𝐱))\displaystyle P(y\mid do(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}))=P(y\mid do(\mathbf{x})) (58)

holds. By Rule 3 of do-calculus, this equality is valid if (Y⟂⁣⟂𝐖∣𝐗)𝒢𝐗∪𝐖¯(Y\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}\mathbf{W}\mid\mathbf{X})_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}\cup\mathbf{W}}}}, which implies that μ𝐱∪𝐰=μ𝐱\mu_{\mathbf{x}\cup\mathbf{w}}=\mu_{\mathbf{x}}. When this condition holds, the actions d​o​(𝐱,𝐰)do(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}) and d​o​(𝐱)do(\mathbf{x}) are equivalent in terms of their induced reward distributions. Consequently, it suffices to play one action from each equivalence class.

Minimal intervention sets.

Ideally, one would like to restrict attention to a smaller subset of actions, provided that it still contains an optimal action. Motivated by this observation, we introduce the notion of a minimal intervention set (MIS).

Definition 0 (Minimal intervention set (Lee and Bareinboim, 2018)).

A set 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} is an MIS relative to ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle if there is no proper subset 𝐙⊊𝐗\mathbf{Z}\subsetneq\mathbf{X} such that, for every SCM conforming to 𝒢\mathcal{G} and every assignment 𝐱∈Ω𝐗\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_{\mathbf{X}}, μ𝐱=μ𝐱∩𝐙\mu_{\mathbf{x}}=\mu_{\mathbf{x}\cap\mathbf{Z}}1313 13 We refer to 𝐗\mathbf{X} and 𝐙\mathbf{Z} as equivalent if the equality holds..

We denote by 𝕄𝒢,Y\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y} the collection of MISs with respect to ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle. In words, an MIS is a set for which no proper subset is equivalent in terms of the induced reward. Whether a set is an MIS can be determined through a simple procedure based on ancestral relationships.

Proposition 0 (Proposition 1 in Lee and Bareinboim (2018)).

𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} is an MIS with respect to ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle if and only if 𝐗⊆𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢𝐗¯\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}}.

Intuitively, this characterization states that, for 𝐗\mathbf{X} to be an MIS, each variable X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X} must have a directed path to YY that does not pass through any other variables in 𝐗∖{X}\mathbf{X}\setminus\{X\}. Such a path is called proper with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X}: only its starting vertex belongs to 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Note that ∅\emptyset and every singleton {X}\{X\} with X∈𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢∖{Y}X\in\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}}\setminus\{Y\} are MISs.

Example 0 (Continued).

Let us consider the causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G} shown in Fig. 9(c). Since ∅\emptyset, {X1}\{X_{1}\}, and {X2}\{X_{2}\} are MISs in this graph, it remains only to test {X1,X2}\{X_{1},X_{2}\}:

{X1,X2}⊈𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢X1,X2¯={X2,Y}.\displaystyle\{X_{1},X_{2}\}\nsubseteq\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{X_{1},X_{2}}}}=\{X_{2},Y\}. (59)

Therefore, it follows that:

𝕄𝒢,Y={∅,{X1},{X2}},\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y}=\{\emptyset,\{X_{1}\},\{X_{2}\}\}, (60)

and the corresponding action set 𝒜\mathcal{A} is given in Eq. 51.

3.2.2 Property 2: Partial Orders among MISs
Possibly-optimal minimal intervention sets.

We now explore partial orders among MISs. Given a causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G}, it is possible that interventions on certain variables always perform at least as well as interventions on others, regardless of the parameterization of the underlying model. Formally, there may exist two sets of variables 𝐖\mathbf{W} and 𝐗\mathbf{X} such that:

μ𝐰∗≤μ𝐱∗\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{w}^{\ast}}\leq\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}} (61)

for every SCM consistent with 𝒢\mathcal{G}. In this case, it is unnecessary to consider actions over Ω𝐖\Omega_{\mathbf{W}}. Motivated by this observation, we define the notion of possibly-optimal MIS, which captures this partial order among MISs.

Definition 0 (POMIS (Lee and Bareinboim, 2018)).

Let 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} be an MIS with respect to ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle. If there exists an SCM conforming to 𝒢\mathcal{G} such that μ𝐱∗>μ𝐰∗\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}}>\mu_{\mathbf{w}^{\ast}} for all 𝐖∈𝕄𝒢,Y∖{𝐗}\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y}\setminus\{\mathbf{X}\} where 𝕄𝒢,Y\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y} is the collection of MISs with respect to ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle, then 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a possibly-optimal minimal intervention set (POMIS) with respect to ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle.

We denote by ℙ𝒢,Y\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G},Y} the collection of POMISs with respect to ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle. Possible optimality means that the graph alone cannot rule out the intervention set; the best action in the actual SCM must still be learned.

Consider an MIS 𝐖∈𝕄𝒢,Y\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y} and a disjoint set of variables 𝐗\mathbf{X}. It follows that:

μ𝐰=∑𝐱𝔼𝐰​[Y∣𝐱]​P𝐰​(𝐱).\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{w}}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}}[Y\mid\mathbf{x}]P_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{x}). (62)

Suppose that, by Rule 2 of do-calculus, conditioning on 𝐱\mathbf{x} can be exchanged with intervention. Then, we can derive the following for every fixed 𝐰\mathbf{w}:

μ𝐰\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{w}} =∑𝐱𝔼𝐰​[Y∣𝐱]​P𝐰​(𝐱)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}}[Y\mid\mathbf{x}]P_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{x}) (63)
=∑𝐱μ𝐱𝐰​P𝐰​(𝐱)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\mu_{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{w}}P_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{x}) Rule 2 (64)
≤∑𝐱μ{𝐱𝐰}∗​P𝐰​(𝐱)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\mu_{\{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{w}\}^{\ast}}P_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{x}) (65)
=μ{𝐱𝐰}∗.\displaystyle=\mu_{\{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{w}\}^{\ast}}. (66)

Let 𝐙⊆𝐗∪𝐖\mathbf{Z}\subseteq\mathbf{X}\cup\mathbf{W} be an MIS equivalent to 𝐗∪𝐖\mathbf{X}\cup\mathbf{W}. Then, we have:

μ𝐰∗≤μ𝐳∗.\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{w}^{\ast}}\leq\mu_{\mathbf{z}^{\ast}}. (67)

Building on this observation, we introduce two graphical concepts for characterizing POMISs. Let 𝖼𝖼​(X)𝒢\mathsf{cc}(X)_{\mathcal{G}} be the c-component (Tian and Pearl, 2003) containing XX in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, namely, the maximal set of vertices connected to XX by bidirected paths, and 𝖼𝖼​(𝐗)𝒢=⋃X∈𝐗𝖼𝖼​(X)𝒢\mathsf{cc}(\mathbf{X})_{\mathcal{G}}=\bigcup_{X\in\mathbf{X}}\mathsf{cc}(X)_{\mathcal{G}}.

Definition 0 (Unobserved confounders’ territory (Lee and Bareinboim, 2018)).

Given information ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle, let ℋ=𝒢⁡[𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢]\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{G}[\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}}]. A set of variables 𝐓⊆𝐕⁡(ℋ)\mathbf{T}\subseteq\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{H}) containing YY is called a UC-territory on 𝒢\mathcal{G} with respect to YY if 𝙳𝚎​(𝐓)ℋ=𝐓\mathtt{De}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathbf{T} and 𝖼𝖼​(𝐓)ℋ=𝐓\mathsf{cc}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathbf{T}. A UC-territory 𝐓\mathbf{T} is said to be minimal if no 𝐓′⊊𝐓\mathbf{T}^{\prime}\subsetneq\mathbf{T} is a UC-territory.

Let 𝐓\mathbf{T} be a minimal UC-territory on the causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G} with respect to YY. Then 𝐖=𝙿𝚊​(𝐓)𝒢∖𝐓\mathbf{W}=\mathtt{Pa}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{G}}\setminus\mathbf{T} is called an interventional border (IB) for 𝒢\mathcal{G} with respect to YY.

The minimal unobserved confounders’ territory (MUCT) is the smallest set containing YY that is closed under descendants and c-components within 𝒢⁡[𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢]\mathcal{G}[\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}}].

To compute it, start from {Y}\{Y\} in ℋ=𝒢⁡[𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢]\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{G}[\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}}] and repeatedly add the c-components and descendants of the current set in ℋ\mathcal{H} until the set stops changing. Every UC-territory contains each stage of this construction, so its limit is the unique MUCT. Its closure properties support the use of Rule 2 to exchange conditioning on its border with intervention.

We denote by 𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(𝒢,Y)\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{G},Y) and 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒢,Y)\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{G},Y) the MUCT and IB with respect to ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle, respectively. The following theorem provides a complete characterization of POMISs.

Equipped with Thm. 28, one can systematically reduce the action space using the information ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle. Restricting attention to POMISs preserves the optimal achievable reward while reducing the candidate action space. The schematic comparison in Fig. 11 illustrates the potential reduction in expected cumulative regret from restricting the action space to MISs or POMISs.

4 Structural Causal Bandits under Markov Equivalence

The SCB formulation in the preceding section assumes that the agent knows the causal diagram. Under the causal Markov and faithfulness assumptions, observational conditional independences generally identify only a Markov equivalence class. Causal sufficiency, the absence of unobserved common causes of the observed variables, restricts the graph class but does not, by itself, resolve all orientations (Verma and Pearl, 1990; Spirtes et al., 2000; Chickering, 2002; Tsamardinos et al., 2006). Additional assumptions on functional forms, noise distributions, or variation across environments may provide further identification (Perry et al., 2022; Peters et al., 2016; Ghassami et al., 2017; Heinze-Deml et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2020; Ghassami et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021). In the presence of latent variables and without selection bias, we represent the observational Markov equivalence class by a PAG.

Under these assumptions, observational conditional-independence information identifies a PAG, which may encode a super-exponential number of maximal ancestral graphs (MAGs). Each such MAG, in turn, represents an infinite number of causal diagrams over supersets of the observed variables. Therefore, considering all causal diagrams consistent with a PAG is computationally prohibitive. Directly identifying conditions for MIS and POMIS at the level of ancestral graphs would circumvent this difficulty. Our key contributions in this section are as follows:

  • •

    We generalize MIS and develop graphical criteria for ancestral graphs, enabling an agent to identify and exclude variables that have no effect on the reward.

  • •

    We extend POMIS to ancestral graphs and establish a necessary and sufficient graphical condition for MAGs.

  • •

    We present a search algorithm that is sound and complete for POMIS membership in at least one represented MAG.

Relation to the published version.

This section revises Park et al. (2025). The counterexample in Sec. 4.1.2 disproves the sufficiency of Theorem 2 of Park et al. (2025). For Proposition 6 of Park et al. (2025), only the implication from PAG-level POMIS membership to membership in some represented MAG is retained (Prop. 42). The search associated with Theorem 4 of Park et al. (2025) instead characterizes the union of the POMIS collections of the represented MAGs (Sec. 4.2.2). Definition 6 of Park et al. (2025) is corrected by removing 𝐗\mathbf{X} before computing possible ancestors, excluding paths that pass through intervened variables (Def. 44). Our revision of Algorithm 1 of Park et al. (2025) uses an MIS precheck, omits the preliminary orientation step, and tests proper paths and the corrected IB (Algs. 3 and 58). Accordingly, Sec. 4.3 reports corrected action spaces and new experiments with horizon 50,00050{,}000 and 100100 repetitions; these replace the published arm counts and regret results.

4.1 Generalizing Minimal Intervention Sets

In this section, we generalize the notion of a minimal intervention set (MIS) to ancestral graphs, so that it applies not only to causal diagrams but also to MAGs and PAGs. We first provide complete graphical conditions for MIS in MAGs and PAGs. We then show that MIS membership in a PAG need not have a common witnessing MAG. To address this issue, we introduce definitely minimal intervention sets (DMISs), which require a single compatible SCM to witness the absence of equivalence to every proper subset. Here, definitely refers to this common witness, not to minimality in every MAG represented by the PAG.

4.1.1 Minimal Intervention Sets for Ancestral Graphs

We use 𝒟\mathcal{D} to denote either a causal diagram or an ancestral graph (MAG or PAG) over 𝐕\mathbf{V}. The existence arguments below quantify over the graphical model class, without fixing an observational distribution or a parametric family.

Definition 0 (MIS).

Given ⟨𝒟,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{D},Y\rangle, a set 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} is an MIS if, for every 𝐙⊊𝐗\mathbf{Z}\subsetneq\mathbf{X}, there exist an SCM 𝒮\mathcal{S} conforming to 𝒟\mathcal{D} and an assignment 𝐱∈Ω𝐗\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_{\mathbf{X}} such that μ𝐱𝒮≠μ𝐱∩𝐙𝒮\mu^{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathbf{x}}\neq\mu^{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathbf{x}\cap\mathbf{Z}}1414 14 The superscript identifies the SCM used to evaluate the reward mean..

For any causal diagram, we can explicitly construct a compatible binary SCM 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} to provide the witnesses used below (Lemma 116). Each variable equals one when its private uniform noise falls below a threshold that increases with its parents’ values, while shared latent variables represent the bidirected edges. Setting a previously unintervened variable to one strictly increases its mean, and positive parental effects propagate this increase along directed paths. Along a proper directed path to YY, no other intervention interrupts this propagation, so the reward mean strictly increases.

We say that ZZ is a definite collider if both edges have arrowheads at ZZ. If (1) one of the edges is out of ZZ; or (2) both edges have a circle mark at ZZ (i.e., X∗−∘Z∘−∗YX\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Z\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}Y) and there is no edge between XX and YY, then we say that ZZ is a definite non-collider. A path is said to have a definite status if every non-endpoint node along it is either a definite collider or a definite non-collider. In a PAG, m-separation is tested over definite-status paths: a path is m-connecting given 𝐙\mathbf{Z} if every non-collider is outside 𝐙\mathbf{Z} and every collider is an ancestor of 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. If no such path connects the queried sets, they are m-separated.. For this purpose, we extend the definition of a proper path in Sec. 3 to possibly directed paths from X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X} to YY. Each such path is not disturbed by other intervening variables, and thus aligns with the characterizations of MIS for causal diagrams and MAGs. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be a PAG over the set of variables 𝐕\mathbf{V}.

Proposition 0 (Graphical characterization of MIS for PAGs).

𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} is an MIS relative to ⟨𝒫,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{P},Y\rangle if and only if for every variable X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X}, there exists a proper possibly directed path from XX to YY with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X} in 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 34] (If) Fix an arbitrary 𝐙⊊𝐗\mathbf{Z}\subsetneq\mathbf{X} and choose W∈𝐗∖𝐙W\in\mathbf{X}\setminus\mathbf{Z}. By hypothesis and Lemma 95, there is an uncovered proper possibly directed path pp from WW to YY relative to 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Taking a subsequence preserves properness.

Replace every ∘⁣→\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to} edge in 𝒫\mathcal{P} by a directed edge and orient its circle components into DAGs without unshielded colliders, orienting every circle edge incident to WW out of WW. Such a choice is possible by the construction in the proof of Lemma 103; Lemma 94 ensures that the resulting MAG ℳ\mathcal{M} belongs to [𝒫][\mathcal{P}]. The first edge of pp now points out of WW. Each consecutive triple of pp is unshielded and cannot become a collider, so the subsequent edges must also point towards YY. Thus, pp is a proper directed path in ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Use the causal diagram with the same directed and bidirected edges as ℳ\mathcal{M}. By Lemma 116, it admits an SCM 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} with μ𝐗=𝟏𝒮∗>μ𝐙=𝟏𝒮∗\mu_{\mathbf{X}=\bm{1}}^{\mathcal{S}^{\ast}}>\mu_{\mathbf{Z}=\bm{1}}^{\mathcal{S}^{\ast}}. This SCM conforms to 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Since 𝐙\mathbf{Z} was arbitrary, 𝐗\mathbf{X} is an MIS. The witnessing MAG and SCM may depend on 𝐙\mathbf{Z}, as permitted by Def. 30. The case 𝐗=∅\mathbf{X}=\emptyset is vacuous.

(Only if) Suppose that some Z∈𝐗Z\in\mathbf{X} has no proper possibly directed path to YY. Any proper directed path in a represented MAG would appear as a proper possibly directed path in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Hence no ℳ∈[𝒫]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}] contains such a directed path from ZZ. The separation argument in the only-if part of Thm. 31, applied to this vertex, gives P⁡(y∣d​o​(𝐱))=P⁡(y∣d​o​(𝐱∩(𝐗∖{Z})))P(y\mid do(\mathbf{x}))=P(y\mid do(\mathbf{x}\cap(\mathbf{X}\setminus\{Z\}))) for every assignment and every SCM conforming to any such MAG. The equality therefore holds throughout the model class of 𝒫\mathcal{P}, so 𝐗\mathbf{X} is not an MIS.

Enumerating minimal intervention sets.

The characterizations in Theorems 31 and 34 lead to MISs (Alg. 2), which returns the complete collection 𝕄𝒟,Y\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{D},Y} for a MAG or PAG 𝒟\mathcal{D}. The algorithm begins with the empty intervention set and adds one variable at a time. It stops extending a set as soon as one of its variables loses every proper possibly directed path to YY.

First, let 𝐀=𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒟\mathbf{A}=\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{D}} and retain the induced graph ℋ=𝒟⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{D}[\mathbf{A}]. No MIS can contain a variable outside 𝐀\mathbf{A}. Moreover, every vertex on a possibly directed path to YY belongs to 𝐀\mathbf{A}, so this restriction preserves all paths needed by the MIS condition. The graph ℋ\mathcal{H} is then kept fixed throughout the recursion.

The variables in 𝐀∖{Y}\mathbf{A}\setminus\{Y\} are arranged in a fixed list ℓ\ell:

  • •

    For a MAG, we use a reverse topological order of its directed edges. That is, whenever U→VU\to V, the vertex VV precedes UU.

  • •

    For a PAG, we order its circle components by reversing the partial topological order returned by Alg. 12.

For the PAG case, this is the order in which Alg. 12 extracts the components. Within each component, variables are ordered by increasing shortest-path distance to YY in the underlying undirected graph of 𝒟\mathcal{D}; ties can be resolved arbitrarily.

For a PAG, processing circle components in this reverse partial topological order supports early pruning before recursion. To see this, suppose that every possibly directed path from an upstream candidate WW to YY passes through already selected downstream variables. Deleting those selected variables excludes WW from the remaining possible ancestors of YY, so the algorithm discards this extension before making a recursive call. Processing downstream components first therefore allows such upstream candidates to be eliminated as soon as they are considered.

The same order also preserves paths across different circle components. Each step between distinct components on a possibly directed path leads to a component appearing earlier in the order. A variable selected later from a different component therefore cannot lie on a proper possibly directed path from an earlier selected variable to YY. Adding that later variable cannot block the earlier variable’s path. Thus, reverse partial topological order prevents this source of failed recursive calls between components. Within a single component, however, a later choice can still block an earlier variable’s path. Thus, the algorithm retains the test for all selected variables.

For a current intervention set 𝐗\mathbf{X}, subMISs recomputes 𝐀=𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℋ∖𝐗\mathbf{A}=\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{H}\setminus\mathbf{X}}. These are the vertices that can still reach YY without passing through any variable in 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Write 𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙲𝚑​(X)ℋ\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{Ch}(X)_{\mathcal{H}} for the set of vertices adjacent to XX whose incident edge has no arrowhead at XX. Each selected XX must have a first step into 𝐀\mathbf{A}, giving the test:

𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙲𝚑​(X)ℋ∩𝐀≠∅​ for every ​X∈𝐗.\displaystyle\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{Ch}(X)_{\mathcal{H}}\cap\mathbf{A}\neq\emptyset\text{\quad for~every~}X\in\mathbf{X}. (82)

Possible ancestors include YY itself, so a single possibly directed edge from XX to YY can satisfy this test. For a MAG, the first step and the remaining path must be directed. The test is applied to all selected variables after every addition. Although a new variable may have a path to YY, selecting it can interrupt a path used by an earlier variable. Keeping ℋ\mathcal{H} fixed allows the algorithm to inspect the first step from every selected variable; only the graph used to compute 𝐀\mathbf{A} has those variables removed.

If the test fails, the call returns an empty collection. Otherwise, it records 𝐗\mathbf{X} and tries each remaining variable Wi∈𝐀W_{i}\in\mathbf{A}. The recursive call receives 𝐗∪{Wi}\mathbf{X}\cup\{W_{i}\} and only the variables after WiW_{i} in the list. In particular, the initial call records ∅\emptyset, because its test has no selected variable to check.

Proposition 0.

MISs​(𝒟,Y)\textsf{MISs}(\mathcal{D},Y) returns exactly 𝕄𝒟,Y\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{D},Y}. Every MIS is generated once, and the recursion terminates.

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 35] We first justify the test 𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙲𝚑​(X)ℋ∩𝐀≠∅\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{Ch}(X)_{\mathcal{H}}\cap\mathbf{A}\neq\emptyset for every X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X} in Eq. 82. If X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X} has a proper possibly directed path to YY, its first adjacent vertex VV is outside 𝐗\mathbf{X}. The remaining path avoids all of 𝐗\mathbf{X}, so V∈𝐀V\in\mathbf{A}. Conversely, if V∈𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙲𝚑​(X)ℋ∩𝐀V\in\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{Ch}(X)_{\mathcal{H}}\cap\mathbf{A}, there is a possibly directed path from VV to YY in ℋ∖𝐗\mathcal{H}\setminus\mathbf{X}. Prepending XX gives a proper path: XX cannot already occur on the remaining path, and no other selected variable occurs there. This also covers V=YV=Y, when the remaining path has zero length. Thus, the test is equivalent to requiring a proper path for every selected variable. By Theorems 31 and 34, every recorded set is an MIS.

Next, suppose an intervention set 𝐗\mathbf{X} fails the test at a variable X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X}. Adding more intervention variables only removes additional vertices from the graph in which the remainder of its path must lie. It cannot create a path for XX that avoids the enlarged intervention set. Therefore, no superset of 𝐗\mathbf{X} is an MIS, and stopping this branch cannot omit a valid output. Likewise, if an unselected variable WW is outside 𝐀=𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℋ∖𝐗\mathbf{A}=\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{H}\setminus\mathbf{X}}, it has no path to YY avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X} and cannot be added in any valid extension.

To establish completeness, fix an MIS 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. All its variables belong to 𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒟∖{Y}\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{D}}\setminus\{Y\}. List them in the order inherited from ℓ\ell. Every prefix 𝐗\mathbf{X} of this list is an MIS: the proper paths for the variables of 𝐙\mathbf{Z} avoid 𝐙\mathbf{Z} except at their starting vertices, and hence also avoid the smaller set 𝐗\mathbf{X} except at their starting vertices. For the next variable W∈𝐙∖𝐗W\in\mathbf{Z}\setminus\mathbf{X}, its proper path for 𝐙\mathbf{Z} avoids 𝐗\mathbf{X} entirely. Thus W∈𝐀=𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℋ∖𝐗W\in\mathbf{A}=\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{H}\setminus\mathbf{X}}, and the algorithm visits the branch that adds it. Inductively, it reaches and records 𝐙\mathbf{Z}.

Finally, each recursive call passes only the suffix after its newly selected variable. Selected indices therefore increase strictly. A given set has only one increasing sequence of indices, so it is generated on only one branch. The list becomes shorter at every recursive step, establishing termination.

Enumeration cost.

Let κ=|𝕄𝒟,Y|\kappa=\lvert\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{D},Y}\rvert be the total number of MISs returned, let n=|𝐕|n=\lvert\mathbf{V}\rvert and mm be the number of edges, and let r=|𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒟∖{Y}|r=\lvert\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{D}}\setminus\{Y\}\rvert be the number of initial candidates. We first express the cost in terms of κ\kappa. Each call that passes Eq. 82 records exactly one distinct MIS. Thus, there are exactly κ\kappa such calls. Each starts at most rr recursive calls, while a call that fails the test stops immediately. Thus, the total number of calls is at most 1+r​κ1+r\kappa. For a MAG with the reverse topological order above, no call fails the test, and the number of calls is exactly κ\kappa.

With adjacency-list graph operations, computing the remaining possible ancestors and checking all selected variables takes 𝒪⁡(n+m)\mathcal{O}(n+m) time per call. Copying a suffix or a selected set takes at most 𝒪⁡(r)\mathcal{O}(r) time. We also account for the collection unions in the algorithm. Each output belongs to the returned collections of at most r+1r+1 calls along its branch, and each such collection can be copied at most rr times while processing the remaining candidates. Repeated copying therefore contributes at most 𝒪⁡((r+1)2​κ)\mathcal{O}((r+1)^{2}\kappa) time. This is absorbed by the bound below because r+1≤nr+1\leq n. A straightforward implementation of the preliminary ordering takes 𝒪⁡(n3)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}) time, giving the conservative total bound:

𝒯MISs=𝒪⁡(n3+(r+1)​κ​(n+m)).\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\texttt{MISs}}=\mathcal{O}(n^{3}+(r+1)\kappa(n+m)). (83)

For a fixed number κ\kappa of output MISs, this bound is polynomial in the graph size. It counts both the unsuccessful calls and the cost of collecting the outputs, rather than only the cost of checking a single candidate.

However, κ\kappa itself can be exponential. For example, a MAG consisting of rr candidate vertices X1,⋯,XrX_{1},\cdots,X_{r}, the reward YY, and the edges Xi→YX_{i}\to Y has κ=2r\kappa=2^{r}. Every subset of the candidate vertices is an MIS because each selected variable has a directed path to YY. Thus, polynomial dependence on a fixed output count does not imply polynomial time for all input graphs. The recursion reduces unnecessary exploration by rejecting an invalid set together with all of its extensions.

Possible vacuousness.

One might expect that if 𝐗\mathbf{X} is an MIS relative to ⟨𝒫,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{P},Y\rangle, then it is also an MIS relative to ⟨ℳ,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{M},Y\rangle for some MAG ℳ\mathcal{M} conforming to the PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P}. However, this is not always the case, i.e., 𝐗\mathbf{X} need not be an MIS for any MAG represented by 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

For concreteness, consider the PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P} in Fig. 12 where 𝐗={A,B}\mathbf{X}=\{A,B\} is an MIS with respect to ⟨𝒫,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{P},Y\rangle since both AA and BB have proper possibly directed paths to YY (i.e., A∘−∘YA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y and B∘−∘YB\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y, respectively). However, we will demonstrate that at least one of AA and BB is irrelevant to the reward YY in every conforming MAG. To see this, consider binary SCMs with mutually independent exogenous variables UA,UB,UY∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(ϵ)U_{A},U_{B},U_{Y}\sim\mathtt{Bern}(\epsilon), where 0<ϵ<120<\epsilon<\frac{1}{2}. First, for the proper subset 𝐙1=∅\mathbf{Z}_{1}=\emptyset, we can construct an SCM 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} as follows:

𝒮1={𝐔={UA,UB,UY}𝐕={A,B,Y}ℱ={fA​(y,uA)=y⊕uAfB​(uB)=uBfY​(b,uY)=b⊕uYP⁡(𝐔)={UV∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(ϵ):∀UV∈𝐔}.\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{1}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{U}=\{U_{A},U_{B},U_{Y}\}\\ \mathbf{V}=\{A,B,Y\}\\ \mathcal{F}=\begin{cases}f_{A}(y,u_{A})=y\oplus u_{A}\\ f_{B}(u_{B})=u_{B}\\ f_{Y}(b,u_{Y})=b\oplus u_{Y}\end{cases}\\ P(\mathbf{U})=\{U_{V}\thicksim\mathtt{Bern}(\epsilon):\forall U_{V}\in\mathbf{U}\}.\end{cases} (84)

Its corresponding MAG is shown in Fig. 12(b). Here, μ∅=2​ϵ​(1−ϵ)\mu_{\emptyset}=2\epsilon(1-\epsilon) while μ{a,b}∗=μb∗=1−ϵ\mu_{\{a,b\}^{\ast}}=\mu_{b^{\ast}}=1-\epsilon with b∗=1b^{\ast}=1. Thus, μa,1≠μ∅\mu_{a,1}\neq\mu_{\emptyset} for every a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\} in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}. That is, there exists an SCM 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} such that:

μ𝐱∗≠μ𝐳1∗\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}}\neq\mu_{\mathbf{z}_{1}^{\ast}} (85)

Next, for the proper subset 𝐙2={A}\mathbf{Z}_{2}=\{A\}, since μa=μ∅=2​ϵ​(1−ϵ)\mu_{a}=\mu_{\emptyset}=2\epsilon(1-\epsilon), we again have μa,1≠μa\mu_{a,1}\neq\mu_{a} for every a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\} in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}. That is, there also exists an SCM 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} such that:

μ𝐱∗≠μ𝐳2∗\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}}\neq\mu_{\mathbf{z}_{2}^{\ast}} (86)

An analogous construction applies to 𝐙3={B}\mathbf{Z}_{3}=\{B\} using 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} (Fig. 12(c)), defined as follows:

𝒮2={𝐔={UA,UB,UY}𝐕={A,B,Y}ℱ={fA​(uA)=uAfB​(y,uB)=y⊕uBfY​(a,uY)=a⊕uYP⁡(𝐔)={UV∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(ϵ):∀UV∈𝐔}.\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{2}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{U}=\{U_{A},U_{B},U_{Y}\}\\ \mathbf{V}=\{A,B,Y\}\\ \mathcal{F}=\begin{cases}f_{A}(u_{A})=u_{A}\\ f_{B}(y,u_{B})=y\oplus u_{B}\\ f_{Y}(a,u_{Y})=a\oplus u_{Y}\end{cases}\\ P(\mathbf{U})=\{U_{V}\thicksim\mathtt{Bern}(\epsilon):\forall U_{V}\in\mathbf{U}\}.\end{cases} (87)

Hence, there also exists an SCM 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} such that:

μ𝐱∗≠μ𝐳3∗\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}}\neq\mu_{\mathbf{z}_{3}^{\ast}} (88)

These witnesses establish that {A,B}\{A,B\} is an MIS for 𝒫\mathcal{P}. However, a common witnessing SCM would have a corresponding MAG in which neither intervention variable is redundant. By Thm. 31, both AA and BB would then have proper directed paths to YY. On this three-vertex skeleton, this requires A→Y←BA\to Y\leftarrow B, creating an unshielded collider absent from 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Hence no such MAG, and therefore no common witnessing SCM, exists.

4.1.2 Definitely Minimal Intervention Sets

To address this vacuousness, we propose the concept of definitely MIS, which ensures that an MIS in a PAG remains an MIS in some consistent MAG.

For an MIS, the witnessing SCM may depend on the proper subset being compared. A DMIS requires a single SCM to work for all proper subsets; the distinguishing assignment may still depend on the subset.

Definition 0 (Definitely minimal intervention set).

Given ⟨𝒟,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{D},Y\rangle, 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} is a DMIS if there exists an SCM 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} conforming to 𝒟\mathcal{D} such that, for every 𝐙⊊𝐗\mathbf{Z}\subsetneq\mathbf{X}, there exists an assignment 𝐱∈Ω𝐗\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_{\mathbf{X}} satisfying μ𝐱𝒮∗≠μ𝐱∩𝐙𝒮∗\mu^{\mathcal{S}^{\ast}}_{\mathbf{x}}\neq\mu^{\mathcal{S}^{\ast}}_{\mathbf{x}\cap\mathbf{Z}}.

The collection of DMISs is denoted by 𝔻𝒟,Y\mathbb{D}_{\mathcal{D},Y}. Since DMIS is stricter than MIS, their inclusion relation is as follows.

Proposition 0.

If 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a DMIS with respect to ⟨𝒟,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{D},Y\rangle, then it is also an MIS.

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 37] Let 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} be the common SCM in Def. 36. For each 𝐙⊊𝐗\mathbf{Z}\subsetneq\mathbf{X}, that definition supplies an assignment 𝐱\mathbf{x} with μ𝐱𝒮∗≠μ𝐱∩𝐙𝒮∗\mu^{\mathcal{S}^{\ast}}_{\mathbf{x}}\neq\mu^{\mathcal{S}^{\ast}}_{\mathbf{x}\cap\mathbf{Z}}. Choosing the same 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} for each subset satisfies exactly the quantifiers in Def. 30. For causal diagrams and MAGs, which have no circle marks, MIS and DMIS coincide.

Proposition 0.

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be either a causal diagram or a MAG. If 𝐗\mathbf{X} is an MIS with respect to ⟨𝒟,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{D},Y\rangle, then it is also a DMIS.

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 38] If 𝒟\mathcal{D} is a causal diagram, let 𝒢=𝒟\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{D}. If 𝒟\mathcal{D} is a MAG, let 𝒢\mathcal{G} have exactly its directed and bidirected edges, so its corresponding MAG is 𝒟\mathcal{D}. In either case, Prop. 23 and Thm. 31 imply that every X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X} has a proper directed path to YY in 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Fix the SCM 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} supplied by Lemma 116. For any 𝐙⊊𝐗\mathbf{Z}\subsetneq\mathbf{X}, choose W∈𝐗∖𝐙W\in\mathbf{X}\setminus\mathbf{Z} and apply that lemma to its proper path. Then μ𝐗=𝟏𝒮∗≠μ𝐙=𝟏𝒮∗\mu_{\mathbf{X}=\bm{1}}^{\mathcal{S}^{\ast}}\neq\mu_{\mathbf{Z}=\bm{1}}^{\mathcal{S}^{\ast}}. The same SCM works for every proper subset and conforms to 𝒟\mathcal{D}. This establishes DMIS membership. If 𝐗=∅\mathbf{X}=\emptyset, any conforming SCM witnesses the vacuous requirement. This equivalence between MIS and DMIS for causal diagrams and MAGs stems from the fact that the relevant ancestral relations are determined, namely, 𝐗⊆𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒟𝐗¯\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{D}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}}. We now turn to DMIS for PAGs, where ancestral relations are not fully determined, thereby creating a notable gap between MIS and DMIS. Recall the PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P} in Fig. 12(a), where {A,B}\{A,B\} is an MIS but not a DMIS.

Proposition 0.

𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} is a DMIS relative to ⟨𝒫,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{P},Y\rangle if and only if there exists a MAG ℳ\mathcal{M} conforming to 𝒫\mathcal{P} such that 𝐗\mathbf{X} is an MIS relative to ⟨ℳ,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{M},Y\rangle.

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 39] (If) Suppose that 𝐗\mathbf{X} is an MIS for some ℳ∈[𝒫]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}]. By Prop. 38, there is one SCM 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} conforming to ℳ\mathcal{M} such that every proper subset of 𝐗\mathbf{X} is distinguished by an assignment. Since this SCM also conforms to 𝒫\mathcal{P}, it witnesses DMIS membership for the PAG.

(Only if) Let 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} witness that 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a DMIS for 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Since 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} conforms to 𝒫\mathcal{P}, choose a MAG ℳ∈[𝒫]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}] to which it conforms. The same SCM and assignments witness that 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a DMIS for ℳ\mathcal{M}. By Prop. 37, it is an MIS for ℳ\mathcal{M}. Thus, a DMIS has a common witnessing SCM, whereas an MIS for a PAG may rely on different SCMs for different proper subsets. The following examples illustrate the difficulty of expressing this common-witness requirement as a direct graphical criterion.

The difficulty for PAGs is that the proper paths required for different intervention variables must occur in the same represented MAG. In Fig. 12(a), the vertices AA and BB cannot both be ancestors of YY in one represented MAG, because A→Y←BA\to Y\leftarrow B would create an unshielded collider on the uncovered path A∘−∘Y∘−∘BA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}B.

Consider the uncovered circle path A∘−∘C∘−∘Y∘−∘DA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}C\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}D in the PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P} shown in Fig. 13(a). Every consecutive triple on this path must remain a non-collider in every represented MAG. This restricts the orientations that could make both AA and DD ancestors of YY, as follows. Consider any MAG represented by 𝒫\mathcal{P} (Figs. 13(b), 13(c) and 13(d)) where A∘−∘CA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}C appears as a directed edge out of AA (e.g., ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}). This results in C→Y→DC\to Y\to D, as the path is of definite status. In contrast, if any MAG contains D→YD\to Y, this leads to Y→C→AY\to C\to A, as in ℳ3\mathcal{M}_{3}. The important observation is that A→CA\to C ensures that D∉𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℳD\notin\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{M}}, whereas D→YD\to Y ensures that A∉𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℳA\notin\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{M}} for any MAG ℳ∈[𝒫]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}]. This shows that AA and DD cannot simultaneously be ancestors of YY in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Hence, {A,D}\{A,D\} is not a DMIS relative to ⟨𝒫,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{P},Y\rangle.

We consider a more involved example in Fig. 14. In 𝒫\mathcal{P}, 𝐗={X,Z}\mathbf{X}=\{X,Z\} is an MIS because XX and ZZ each have a proper possibly directed path to YY with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X}, namely X∘−∘A∘−∘YX\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}A\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y and Z∘−∘B∘−∘YZ\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}B\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y, respectively. These paths are realized as directed paths in ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}, separately.

However, realizing both paths in a single MAG requires X→AX\to A and Z→BZ\to B, which forces A→ZA\to Z and B→XB\to X to avoid new v-structures. These orientations produce the directed cycle X→A→Z→B→XX\to A\to Z\to B\to X. The alternative choice of distinct first neighbors, X→BX\to B and Z→AZ\to A, is symmetric. A shared first neighbor instead creates a v-structure, either X→A←ZX\to A\leftarrow Z or X→B←ZX\to B\leftarrow Z. Since these cases exhaust the possible first neighbors, no MAG represented by 𝒫\mathcal{P} admits proper directed paths from both XX and ZZ to YY with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Hence 𝐗\mathbf{X} is not a DMIS.

Remark 0 (On the graphical characterization of DMISs).

The example in Fig. 14 provides a counterexample to the graphical characterization of DMISs for PAGs in Park et al. (2025). The paths X∘−∘A∘−∘YX\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}A\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y and Z∘−∘B∘−∘YZ\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}B\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}Y meet the condition in Theorem 2 of Park et al. (2025): no uncovered path can have both starting edges as its end edges, because any connecting path contains a shielded triple involving the adjacent vertices AA and BB. Hence, {X,Z}\{X,Z\} satisfies the stated graphical condition but is not a DMIS, disproving its sufficiency.

We leave the development of a direct graphical criterion for DMIS membership for PAGs, together with a polynomial-time decision algorithm, to future work.

4.2 Generalizing Possibly-Optimal Minimal Intervention Sets

We now refine the notion of a possibly-optimal minimal intervention set (POMIS) by defining it over DMISs rather than MISs. This refined notion is consistent with the existing literature and serves as a natural extension, as supported by Props. 38 and 37, which imply that MIS and DMIS coincide for causal diagrams and MAGs.

Definition 0 (Possibly-optimal minimal intervention set (POMIS)).

Let 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} be a DMIS relative to ⟨𝒟,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{D},Y\rangle. If there exists an SCM conforming to 𝒟\mathcal{D} such that μ𝐱∗>μ𝐰∗\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}}>\mu_{\mathbf{w}^{\ast}} for all 𝐖∈𝔻𝒟,Y∖{𝐗}\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{D}_{\mathcal{D},Y}\setminus\{\mathbf{X}\}, we say that 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a possibly-optimal minimal intervention set (POMIS) relative to ⟨𝒟,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{D},Y\rangle.

For a PAG, this definition compares 𝐗\mathbf{X} against the DMISs of the entire represented model class within one SCM. All reward means and maximizing assignments in this comparison are evaluated in that same SCM. The following proposition relates this comparison to POMIS membership in a represented MAG.

Proposition 0.

If 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} is a POMIS relative to ⟨𝒫,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{P},Y\rangle, then there exists a MAG ℳ\mathcal{M} conforming to 𝒫\mathcal{P} such that 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a POMIS relative to ⟨ℳ,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{M},Y\rangle.

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 42] Let 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} witness that 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a POMIS relative to ⟨𝒫,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{P},Y\rangle. Since 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} conforms to 𝒫\mathcal{P}, choose a MAG ℳ∈[𝒫]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}] to which it conforms.

First, we will show that 𝐗\mathbf{X} is an MIS relative to ⟨ℳ,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{M},Y\rangle. For the sake of contradiction, suppose 𝐗\mathbf{X} is not an MIS relative to ⟨ℳ,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{M},Y\rangle. Then, repeatedly removing a graphically redundant subset yields an MIS 𝐙⊊𝐗\mathbf{Z}\subsetneq\mathbf{X} such that μ𝐱=μ𝐱∩𝐙\mu_{\mathbf{x}}=\mu_{\mathbf{x}\cap\mathbf{Z}} for every assignment 𝐱\mathbf{x} and every SCM conforming to ℳ\mathcal{M}. In particular, under 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast}, maximizing over assignments gives μ𝐱∗=μ𝐳∗\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}}=\mu_{\mathbf{z}^{\ast}}. By Prop. 38, 𝐙\mathbf{Z} is a DMIS for ℳ\mathcal{M} and hence for 𝒫\mathcal{P}. This contradicts the strict optimality of 𝐗\mathbf{X} against every other DMIS in 𝔻𝒫,Y\mathbb{D}_{\mathcal{P},Y} under 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast}.

Thus, 𝐗\mathbf{X} is an MIS, and therefore a DMIS, for ℳ\mathcal{M}. Moreover, 𝔻ℳ,Y⊆𝔻𝒫,Y\mathbb{D}_{\mathcal{M},Y}\subseteq\mathbb{D}_{\mathcal{P},Y}, since an SCM witnessing DMIS membership for ℳ\mathcal{M} also conforms to 𝒫\mathcal{P}. The strict inequalities witnessed by 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} therefore hold against every member of 𝔻ℳ,Y∖{𝐗}\mathbb{D}_{\mathcal{M},Y}\setminus\{\mathbf{X}\}. Consequently, 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a POMIS relative to ⟨ℳ,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{M},Y\rangle.

Failure of the converse.

The converse of Prop. 42 does not hold. To see this, consider the PAG shown in Fig. 12(a). The empty set is a POMIS for both MAGs shown in Figs. 12(b) and 12(c). In each MAG, the edge entering YY is invisible, so its endpoints may be confounded in a represented causal diagram. POMIS membership here asserts the existence of a compatible SCM in which the empty intervention is strictly optimal among MISs; it need not be optimal in the SCM displayed earlier. However, in every compatible SCM, at least one of AA and BB is not an ancestor of YY, so intervening on that variable leaves the distribution of YY unchanged; that is, either P⁡(y∣d​o​(a))=P⁡(y)P(y\mid do(a))=P(y) or P⁡(y∣d​o​(b))=P⁡(y)P(y\mid do(b))=P(y). Since both singleton intervention sets are DMISs for the PAG, the empty set cannot be strictly better than every other DMIS.

MUCT and IB for ancestral graphs.

We now investigate the graphical characterization of POMISs for MAGs and PAGs. To this end, we extend the notions of MUCT and IB to these graph classes. The main challenge is that ancestral graphs do not display the underlying latent structure or the inducing paths that give rise to their adjacencies. We therefore use edge visibility to identify directed edges that cannot be confounded in any represented causal diagram. To generalize the UC-territory, we introduce a possible c-component (Jaber et al., 2018), which provides a necessary condition for nodes to belong to the same c-component in an underlying causal diagram.

Definition 0 (pc-component (Jaber et al., 2018)).

Two nodes are in the same possible c-component (pc-component) if there is a path between them such that:

  • 1.

    all non-endpoint nodes along the path are colliders; and

  • 2.

    none of the edges are visible.

The pc-component relation need not be transitive. We use 𝗉𝖼​(X)𝒬\mathsf{pc}(X)_{\mathcal{Q}} for the set of vertices related to XX by the path condition in the definition, including XX itself, and define 𝗉𝖼​(𝐗)𝒬≜⋃X∈𝐗𝗉𝖼​(X)𝒬\mathsf{pc}(\mathbf{X})_{\mathcal{Q}}\triangleq\bigcup_{X\in\mathbf{X}}\mathsf{pc}(X)_{\mathcal{Q}}. Thus, these sets need not form a partition.

For example, AA and BB are in the same pc-component in the PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P} in Fig. 4(e) because they are connected by the collider path A∘⁣→C←⁣∘BA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C\mathrel{\leftarrow\!\!\circ\!}B, whose edges are all invisible, and indeed 𝗉𝖼​(A)𝒫={A,B,C}\mathsf{pc}(A)_{\mathcal{P}}=\{A,B,C\}. Furthermore, because A∉𝗉𝖼​(Y)𝒫={B,Y}A\notin\mathsf{pc}(Y)_{\mathcal{P}}=\{B,Y\}, AA and YY cannot belong to the same c-component in any causal diagram conforming to 𝒫\mathcal{P}. We now generalize MUCT and IB for PMGs.

Definition 0 (Unobserved confounders’ territory for PMGs).

Given information ⟨𝒬,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{Q},Y\rangle and intervention set 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\}, let ℋ=𝒬⁡[𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒬∖𝐗]\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{Q}[\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{Q}\setminus\mathbf{X}}]. A set of variables 𝐓⊆𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒬∖𝐗\mathbf{T}\subseteq\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{Q}\setminus\mathbf{X}} containing YY is called a UC-territory with respect to ⟨𝒬,Y,𝐗⟩\langle\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X}\rangle if 𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙳𝚎​(𝐓)ℋ=𝐓\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{De}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathbf{T} and 𝗉𝖼​(𝐓)ℋ=𝐓\mathsf{pc}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathbf{T}. A UC-territory 𝐓\mathbf{T} is called a minimal UC-territory (MUCT) if no 𝐓′⊊𝐓\mathbf{T}^{\prime}\subsetneq\mathbf{T} is a UC-territory.

Definition 0 (Interventional border for PMGs).

Let 𝐓\mathbf{T} be a minimal UC-territory with respect to ⟨𝒬,Y,𝐗⟩\langle\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X}\rangle. Then 𝙿𝚊​(𝐓)𝒬∖𝐓\mathtt{Pa}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{Q}}\setminus\mathbf{T} is called an interventional border (IB) with respect to ⟨𝒬,Y,𝐗⟩\langle\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X}\rangle.

We denote MUCT and IB with respect to ⟨𝒬,Y,𝐗⟩\langle\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X}\rangle as 𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(𝒬,Y,𝐗)\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X}) and 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒬,Y,𝐗)\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X}), respectively. Note that the MUCT is unique. Starting from {Y}\{Y\} and repeatedly adding possible descendants and pc-related vertices in ℋ\mathcal{H} yields a closed set contained in every UC-territory. Since the graph is finite, this process terminates at the unique minimal UC-territory.

For concreteness, consider ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐗={A,B}\mathbf{X}=\{A,B\} in Fig. 15(b). Here, we omit 𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜\mathtt{Poss} because we are working with a MAG. Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be the induced graph ℳ⁡[𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℳ∖𝐗]\mathcal{M}[\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{M}\setminus\mathbf{X}}] (shown in Fig. 15(c)). In ℋ\mathcal{H}, the nodes CC and YY are in the same pc-component, and DD is a descendant of CC. This implies that 𝐓={C,D,Y}\mathbf{T}=\{C,D,Y\} is the minimal closed set for 𝙳𝚎ℋ\mathtt{De}_{\mathcal{H}} and 𝗉𝖼ℋ\mathsf{pc}_{\mathcal{H}}. Therefore, we have:

𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\displaystyle\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}) =𝐓={C,D,Y}\displaystyle=\mathbf{T}=\{C,D,Y\} (89)
𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\displaystyle\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}) =𝙿𝚊​(𝐓)ℳ∖𝐓\displaystyle=\mathtt{Pa}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{M}}\setminus\mathbf{T} (90)
={A,B}.\displaystyle=\{A,B\}. (91)
4.2.1 Characterization of POMIS for MAGs

The MUCT and IB construction gives a necessary and sufficient condition for POMIS membership in a MAG.

Theorem 46 (Graphical characterization of POMIS for MAGs).

𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} is a POMIS relative to ⟨ℳ,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{M},Y\rangle if and only if 𝐗=𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\mathbf{X}=\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}).

The proof is given in Sec. C.0.3. For the empty intervention in each MAG in Figs. 12(b) and 12(c), the MUCT consists of YY and its parent, and the IB is empty. Thus, Thm. 46 confirms the POMIS membership stated above.

For any intervention set, we seek a causal diagram whose corresponding MAG is ℳ\mathcal{M} and whose MUCT and IB after intervention agree with those computed from ℳ\mathcal{M}. Lemma 117 establishes that such a diagram always exists. We also retain exactly the directed edges of ℳ\mathcal{M}, so that the two graphs have the same proper directed paths and hence the same MISs.

Start by copying all directed and bidirected edges of ℳ\mathcal{M} into a causal diagram, and compute its MUCT after intervention. If this set is smaller than the MUCT computed from the MAG, choose a variable inside the current set that has invisible parents outside it but within 𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℳ∖𝐗\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{M}\setminus\mathbf{X}}. For every such parent, add a bidirected edge to the chosen variable, while keeping the original directed edge. All these edges to the chosen variable are added together. Recompute the MUCT and repeat until it agrees with the MAG’s MUCT. The proof explains both why a variable can always be chosen when the sets differ and why these additions preserve the corresponding MAG.

Fig. 16 applies the construction to the running example in Fig. 15(b). With 𝐗={A,B}\mathbf{X}=\{A,B\}, the relevant non-intervened ancestors are 𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℳ∖𝐗={C,D,Y}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{M}\setminus\mathbf{X}}=\{C,D,Y\}. The copied causal diagram has no bidirected edges, so its MUCT after intervention is initially just {Y}\{Y\}. In the original MAG, however, both C→YC\to Y and D→YD\to Y are invisible: every other vertex is adjacent to YY, so neither edge can have a visibility witness. The construction therefore adds C↔YC\leftrightarrow Y and D↔YD\leftrightarrow Y together. The three vertices are now connected by bidirected edges, giving IB {A,B}=𝐗\{A,B\}=\mathbf{X}, as required. Therefore, we conclude that 𝐗={A,B}\mathbf{X}=\{A,B\} is a POMIS with respect to ⟨ℳ,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{M},Y\rangle.

The constructed diagram retains exactly the directed edges of the MAG and need not coincide with 𝒢\mathcal{G} in Fig. 15(a). That original diagram is also represented by ℳ\mathcal{M} and has {A,B}\{A,B\} as a POMIS: after intervention, C↔YC\leftrightarrow Y places CC in the territory, descendant closure includes DD, and the border is again {A,B}\{A,B\}.

4.2.2 Searching for POMISs in Represented MAGs

The remainder of this section targets ℙ^𝒫,Y≜⋃ℳ∈[𝒫]ℙℳ,Y\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathcal{P},Y}\triangleq\bigcup_{\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}]}\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{M},Y}, where ℙℳ,Y\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{M},Y} is the collection of POMISs of a represented MAG. By Prop. 42, the PAG-wide collection of POMISs in Def. 41 satisfies ℙ𝒫,Y⊆ℙ^𝒫,Y\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{P},Y}\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathcal{P},Y}, and this inclusion can be strict. The search below is sound and complete for the union.

This union retains an optimal action for every compatible SCM. Fix such an SCM and its corresponding MAG ℳ\mathcal{M}. For any intervention set 𝐗\mathbf{X}, let 𝐓=𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\mathbf{T}=\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}) and 𝐖=𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\mathbf{W}=\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}). The necessity proof of Thm. 46 gives μ𝐱∗≤μ𝐰∗\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}}\leq\mu_{\mathbf{w}^{\ast}} in this SCM. Moreover, 𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℳ∖𝐖=𝐓\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{M}\setminus\mathbf{W}}=\mathbf{T}: descendant closure keeps a directed path from every member of 𝐓\mathbf{T} to YY inside 𝐓\mathbf{T}, while any directed path from outside 𝐓\mathbf{T} to YY enters 𝐓\mathbf{T} through a parent in 𝐖\mathbf{W}. Every path used to generate 𝐓\mathbf{T} by descendant and pc closure also stays inside 𝐓\mathbf{T}. With visibility inherited from the same full MAG, restricting the closure construction to ℳ⁡[𝐓]\mathcal{M}[\mathbf{T}] therefore leaves its result unchanged. Thus 𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐖)=𝐓\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{W})=\mathbf{T} and 𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐖)=𝐖\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{W})=\mathbf{W}. By Thm. 46, 𝐖\mathbf{W} is a POMIS of ℳ\mathcal{M}. Applying this argument to an optimal intervention set proves that the union retains an optimal action.

To search for ℙ^𝒫,Y\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathcal{P},Y}, we partition [𝒫][\mathcal{P}] according to the possible orientations of circle marks at vertices in 𝐗∪{Y}\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\}. Each part of this partition is represented by a locally oriented PMG, whose graphical structure is used in the terminal IB test. To this end, we first review local transformations of Wang et al. (2023), which orient the circle marks incident to a given variable.

Local transformation.

We define a local transformation (Wang et al., 2023) at A∈𝐕A\in\mathbf{V} as a set:

𝐂A𝒬⊆{V∈𝙰𝚍𝚓​(A)𝒬∣A∘−∗V}.\displaystyle\mathbf{C}^{\mathcal{Q}}_{A}\subseteq\{V\in\mathtt{Adj}(A)_{\mathcal{Q}}\mid A\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}V\}. (92)

The vertices in 𝐂A𝒬\mathbf{C}^{\mathcal{Q}}_{A} are those whose edges with a circle mark at AA will be oriented with arrowheads at AA. That is, for V∈𝐂A𝒬V\in\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}} and V′∈{U∈𝙰𝚍𝚓​(A)𝒬:A∘−∗U}∖𝐂A𝒬V^{\prime}\in\{U\in\mathtt{Adj}(A)_{\mathcal{Q}}:A\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}U\}\setminus\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}, the local transformation places an arrowhead at AA on the first edge and a tail at AA on the second edge, with ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} completing the latter as a directed edge.

  • ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}}

    If X−⁣∘YX\mathrel{-\!\circ\!}Y, then orient X−⁣∘YX\mathrel{-\!\circ\!}Y as X→YX\to Y.

The rule ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} naturally follows from the absence of selection bias1616 16 Additional rules for more general local transformations are studied by Venkateswaran and Perković (2024); Wang et al. (2024b) and Wang et al. (2025).. The resulting local orientation is:

V∗−∘A∘−∗V′⟹V∗⁣→A→V′.\displaystyle V\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}A\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}V^{\prime}\implies V\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}A\to V^{\prime}. (93)

We say that a local transformation is valid if at least one MAG in [𝒬][\mathcal{Q}] is consistent with all of its chosen orientations. A local transformation can be viewed as a candidate statement: it resolves the circle marks at one vertex. In the search below, we consider alternative statements of this kind and retain those compatible with at least one represented MAG. Notably, Wang et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2023) and Wang et al. (2024a) demonstrated that the rules ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}–ℛ3\mathcal{R}_{3}, ℛ4′\mathcal{R}_{4}^{\prime}, ℛ8\mathcal{R}_{8}–ℛ10\mathcal{R}_{10}, and ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} are complete for incorporating local transformations.

  • ℛ4′\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{4}

    If ⟨X,⋯,W,Z,Y⟩\langle X,\cdots,W,Z,Y\rangle is a discriminating path between XX and YY for ZZ, and Z∘−∗YZ\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}Y, then orient Z∘−∗YZ\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}Y as Z→YZ\to Y.

In other words, after applying a valid local transformation and then applying the rules until no further orientation is possible, the orientations in the resulting PMG are complete. The following theorem shows that the validity of a given local transformation can be verified in 𝒪⁡(|𝐕|3)\mathcal{O}(\lvert\mathbf{V}\rvert^{3}) time.

Theorem 47 (Theorem 3 and Remark 3 in Wang et al. (2023)).

Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be a PMG obtained from a PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P} by applying valid local transformations and the orientation rules ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}–ℛ3\mathcal{R}_{3}, ℛ4′\mathcal{R}_{4}^{\prime}, ℛ8\mathcal{R}_{8}–ℛ10\mathcal{R}_{10}, and ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} to closure after each transformation.     where 𝐅Vl={V∈𝐂A𝒬∪{A}∣V∗−∘Vl∈𝒬}\mathbf{F}_{V_{l}}=\{V\in\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}\cup\{A\}\mid V\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}V_{l}\in\mathcal{Q}\} is computed before these orientations. For concreteness, consider the PMG 𝒬\mathcal{Q} shown in Fig. 17(a), in which ZZ is a parent of every other vertex. The choice 𝐂A𝒬={B,C}\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}=\{B,C\} supplies the local transformation shown in Fig. 17(b):
