For ​𝐂A𝒬\displaystyle\text{For~}\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}} ={B,C},𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙳𝚎​(A)𝒬∖𝐂A𝒬∩𝙿𝚊​(𝐂A𝒬)𝒬\displaystyle=\{B,C\},~\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{De}(A)_{\mathcal{Q}\setminus\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}}\cap\mathtt{Pa}(\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}})_{\mathcal{Q}} (95)
={A,V1,V2,V3}∩{Z}\displaystyle=\{A,V_{1},V_{2},V_{3}\}\cap\{Z\} (96)
=∅.\displaystyle=\emptyset. (97)

All arrows incident to ZZ point away from ZZ, preventing a possibly directed path from AA back to this parent of BB and CC. Thus, the local choice cannot close a directed or almost directed cycle through ZZ.

Next, the second condition checks whether the local transformation introduces a new v-structure at AA. Since BB and CC are adjacent, 𝒬⁡[{B,C}]\mathcal{Q}[\{B,C\}] is complete. Their adjacency shields the triple B∘⁣→A←⁣∘CB\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}A\mathrel{\leftarrow\!\!\circ\!}C, so the two new arrowheads do not create a v-structure at AA.

Finally, the third condition checks whether orientations propagated to possible descendants of AA create new v-structures or require conflicting directions. The induced subgraph in Fig. 17(c) is V1∘−∘V2∘−∘V3V_{1}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}V_{2}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}V_{3}, with:

𝐅V1={A,C},𝐅V2=𝐅V3={A}.\displaystyle\mathbf{F}_{V_{1}}=\{A,C\},\qquad\mathbf{F}_{V_{2}}=\mathbf{F}_{V_{3}}=\{A\}. (98)

Here AA is excluded from the induced subgraph but retained in the 𝐅\mathbf{F} sets. The first subcondition requires V1→V2V_{1}\to V_{2} because 𝐅V1∖𝐅V2={C}≠∅\mathbf{F}_{V_{1}}\setminus\mathbf{F}_{V_{2}}=\{C\}\neq\emptyset. Since 𝐅V2=𝐅V3\mathbf{F}_{V_{2}}=\mathbf{F}_{V_{3}} and V1→V2∘−∘V3V_{1}\to V_{2}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}V_{3} is unshielded, the second subcondition then requires V2→V3V_{2}\to V_{3}. Both orientations avoid new v-structures and conflicting directions.

All three conditions hold, so the local transformation is valid. Orientation closure yields the PMG shown in Fig. 17(d), with C→V1→V2→V3C\to V_{1}\to V_{2}\to V_{3} fixed. The edges B∘−∘CB\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}C, B∘⁣→AB\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}A, and C∘⁣→AC\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}A retain four circle marks. Therefore, the resulting PMG represents multiple MAGs consistent with the local transformation.

The PMG incorporating local transformations satisfies the properties below.

Theorem 48 (Theorem 1 in Wang et al. (2023)).

Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be a PMG obtained from a PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P} by applying valid local transformations and applying the orientation rules ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}–ℛ3\mathcal{R}_{3}, ℛ4′\mathcal{R}_{4}^{\prime}, ℛ8\mathcal{R}_{8}–ℛ10\mathcal{R}_{10}, and ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} to closure after each transformation. Then 𝒬\mathcal{Q} satisfies the following properties:

  • •

    Closed.  𝒬\mathcal{Q} is closed under the orientation rules.

  • •

    Invariant.  The arrowheads (>\mathord{>}) and tails (−-) in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} are invariant in all the MAGs consistent with 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

  • •

    Chordal. 1717 17 A graph is chordal if any cycle of length four or more has a chord, which refers to an edge joining two vertices that are not adjacent in the cycle. Circle components in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} are chordal.

  • •

    Balanced.  For any three nodes A,B,CA,B,C in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, if A∗⁣→B∘−∗CA\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}B\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}C, then there is an edge between AA and CC with an arrowhead at CC, namely, A∗⁣→CA\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}C. Furthermore, if the edge between AA and BB is A→BA\to B, then the edge between AA and CC is either A→CA\to C or A∘⁣→CA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C (i.e., it is not A↔CA\leftrightarrow C).

  • •

    Complete.  For each circle at AA on any edge A∘−∗BA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}B in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, there exist MAGs ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2} consistent with 𝒬\mathcal{Q} such that A←⁣∗BA\mathrel{\leftarrow\!\!\ast\!}B in ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and A→BA\to B in ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}.

Thus, PMGs obtained by valid local transformations retain the listed graphical properties of PAGs, while representing a class of MAGs restricted by the incorporated local transformations.

Properties: inherited from PAGs.

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be a PAG, and let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be obtained from 𝒫\mathcal{P} through a sequence of valid local transformations, applying the orientation rules ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}–ℛ3\mathcal{R}_{3}, ℛ4′\mathcal{R}_{4}^{\prime}, ℛ8\mathcal{R}_{8}–ℛ10\mathcal{R}_{10}, and ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} to closure after each transformation. For any 𝐀⊆𝐕\mathbf{A}\subseteq\mathbf{V}, let 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}] be the induced graph on 𝐀\mathbf{A}.

Lemma 0.

For any distinct vertices A,B,C∈𝐀A,B,C\in\mathbf{A}, if A∗⁣→B∘−∗CA\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}B\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}C in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}], then A∗⁣→CA\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}C is also present. Furthermore, if A→BA\to B, then the edge between AA and CC is either A→CA\to C or A∘⁣→CA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C.

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 49] By Thm. 48, 𝒬\mathcal{Q} satisfies the balanced property. Since A,B,C∈𝐀A,B,C\in\mathbf{A}, every edge among these vertices, together with its endpoint marks, is preserved in the induced graph 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]. Both conclusions therefore hold in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}].

Lemma 0.

Suppose that distinct vertices A,B∈𝐀A,B\in\mathbf{A} are connected by a circle path in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]. Then the following properties hold:

  • 1.

    If AA and BB are adjacent, their edge is A∘−∘BA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}B.

  • 2.

    For every C∈𝐀∖{A,B}C\in\mathbf{A}\setminus\{A,B\}, C∗⁣→AC\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}A if and only if C∗⁣→BC\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}B. Furthermore, C↔AC\leftrightarrow A if and only if C↔BC\leftrightarrow B.

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 50] Let p:V0(=A)∘−∘V1∘−∘⋯∘−∘Vk(=B)p:V_{0}(=A)\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}V_{1}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}\cdots\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}V_{k}(=B) be a circle path in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}].

For the first property, the case k=1k=1 is immediate. Suppose that k≥2k\geq 2 and the edge between AA and BB has an arrowhead at BB. Applying Lemma 49 to A∗⁣→Vk∘−∘Vk−1A\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}V_{k}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}V_{k-1} gives A∗⁣→Vk−1A\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}V_{k-1}. Repeating this argument along pp yields A∗⁣→V1A\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}V_{1}, contradicting A∘−∘V1A\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}V_{1}. Reversing the roles of AA and BB also excludes an arrowhead at AA. Since selection bias is absent and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is closed under ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}}, the edge must therefore be A∘−∘BA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}B.

For the second property, if CC belongs to the same circle component as AA and BB, the first property excludes all four relations under consideration. Otherwise, repeated application of Lemma 49 along pp shows that C∗⁣→AC\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}A implies C∗⁣→BC\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}B. Traversing pp in reverse gives the converse.

It remains to establish the equivalence for bidirected edges. Consider consecutive vertices U,VU,V on pp and suppose that C↔UC\leftrightarrow U. The balanced property gives C∗⁣→VC\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}V. If this edge were C→VC\to V, applying the stronger part of Lemma 49 to C→V∘−∘UC\to V\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}U would exclude C↔UC\leftrightarrow U. If it were C∘⁣→VC\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}V, applying the balanced property to U↔C∘⁣→VU\leftrightarrow C\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}V would give U∗⁣→VU\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}V, contradicting U∘−∘VU\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}V. Thus, C↔VC\leftrightarrow V. Iterating along pp, and then applying the same argument in reverse, proves the desired equivalence.

Lemma 0.

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be any causal diagram consistent with 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and let X,Y∈𝐀X,Y\in\mathbf{A}. If X∈𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢⁡[𝐀]X\in\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]}, then X∈𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒬⁡[𝐀]X\in\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]}.

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 51] The case X=YX=Y is immediate. Otherwise, let pp be a directed path from XX to YY in 𝒢⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}], and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be the MAG corresponding to 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Each directed edge on pp is also present with the same orientation in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Since ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}], no endpoint mark in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} can contradict these orientations. Hence, the same vertex sequence forms a possibly directed path from XX to YY in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. All its vertices belong to 𝐀\mathbf{A}, so this path is also present in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]. Therefore, X∈𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒬⁡[𝐀]X\in\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]}.

Lemma 0.

For every directed edge X→YX\to Y in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}], if X→YX\to Y is visible in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, then it remains visible in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}].

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 52] Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be any DAG with explicit latent vertices, whose corresponding MAG belongs to [𝒬][\mathcal{Q}], and let 𝐔\mathbf{U} be its latent vertex set. Since X→YX\to Y is visible in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, 𝒢\mathcal{G} contains no inducing path between XX and YY, relative to 𝐔\mathbf{U}, that is into XX.

Suppose that such a path existed in 𝒢⁡[𝐀∪𝐔]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}\cup\mathbf{U}]. Its edges would also be present in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, as would the directed paths from each collider to at least one endpoint. It would therefore be an inducing path in 𝒢\mathcal{G} relative to the same latent set 𝐔\mathbf{U}, contradicting visibility in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. As 𝒢\mathcal{G} was arbitrary, X→YX\to Y is visible in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}].

Lemma 0.

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be any causal diagram consistent with 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and let X,Y∈𝐀X,Y\in\mathbf{A}. If X∈𝖼𝖼​(Y)𝒢⁡[𝐀]X\in\mathsf{cc}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]}, then X∈𝗉𝖼​(Y)𝒬⁡[𝐀]X\in\mathsf{pc}(Y)_{\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]}.

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 53] The case X=YX=Y is immediate. Otherwise, let pp be a bidirected path between XX and YY in 𝒢⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}], and let ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}] be the MAG corresponding to 𝒢\mathcal{G}. By Lemma 109, some subsequence of the vertices of pp forms a collider path p′p^{\prime} in ℳ\mathcal{M} whose directed edges, if any, are invisible in ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Among the paths between XX and YY in ℳ\mathcal{M} whose vertex sequences are subsequences of p′p^{\prime}, choose a shortest path qq subject to the requirements that every internal vertex is a collider and every directed edge is invisible in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Such a path exists because p′p^{\prime} satisfies these requirements. The proof of Lemma 110 in Jaber et al. (2018) shows that the internal vertices of this chosen path are definite colliders in the corresponding PAG 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Their arrowheads are preserved when 𝒫\mathcal{P} is refined to 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Moreover, every vertex of qq belongs to 𝐀\mathbf{A}. Thus, the corresponding path in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}] has only definite colliders as internal vertices.

We next show that no edge on this path is visible in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]. Consider any directed edge V→WV\to W on the path in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]. Because ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}], the corresponding edge in ℳ\mathcal{M} is also V→WV\to W, and it is invisible by the choice of qq. By Lemma 101, a DAG represented by ℳ\mathcal{M} can be chosen to contain V←U→WV\leftarrow U\to W for a latent vertex UU. Since V,W∈𝐀V,W\in\mathbf{A}, this common-parent path survives restriction to 𝐀\mathbf{A} and the latent vertices. As ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}], this DAG belongs to the class used to interpret visibility in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]. Hence, V→WV\to W is invisible in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]. The witnessing DAG may be chosen separately for each directed edge, since visibility is defined edge by edge.

Every remaining edge on the path is non-directed and is therefore invisible by definition. Consequently, qq is a path in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}] whose internal vertices are colliders and whose edges are all invisible. By Def. 43, this proves X∈𝗉𝖼​(Y)𝒬⁡[𝐀]X\in\mathsf{pc}(Y)_{\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]}.

Lemma 0.

pto (Alg. 12) is sound over 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}].

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 54] Construct an auxiliary directed graph 𝒯\mathcal{T} whose vertices are the circle components of 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]. For distinct components 𝐁\mathbf{B} and 𝐂\mathbf{C}, include the directed edge 𝐁→𝐂\mathbf{B}\to\mathbf{C} if 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}] contains U→VU\to V or U∘⁣→VU\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}V for some U∈𝐁U\in\mathbf{B} and V∈𝐂V\in\mathbf{C}.

We first show that 𝒯\mathcal{T} is acyclic. Suppose instead that it contains a directed cycle 𝐁1→⋯→𝐁k→𝐁1\mathbf{B}_{1}\to\cdots\to\mathbf{B}_{k}\to\mathbf{B}_{1}. For each directed edge on this cycle, choose an edge Ui?→ViU_{i}\mathrel{\!~{{}^{{}_{\bm{?}}}}\!\!\to}V_{i} in 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}] with Ui∈𝐁iU_{i}\in\mathbf{B}_{i} and Vi∈𝐁i+1V_{i}\in\mathbf{B}_{i+1}, where indices are interpreted cyclically. Since ViV_{i} and Ui+1U_{i+1} lie in the same circle component, the arrowhead and bidirected-edge equivalences in Lemma 50 imply Ui?→Ui+1U_{i}\mathrel{\!~{{}^{{}_{\bm{?}}}}\!\!\to}U_{i+1}. Indeed, the arrowhead at ViV_{i} propagates to Ui+1U_{i+1}, while a bidirected edge to Ui+1U_{i+1} would imply a bidirected edge to ViV_{i}, contrary to the choice of Ui?→ViU_{i}\mathrel{\!~{{}^{{}_{\bm{?}}}}\!\!\to}V_{i}.

By the chordal property in Thm. 48 and Lemma 115, there exists a MAG ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}] obtained by replacing every ∘⁣→\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to} edge with a directed edge and orienting the circle components into DAGs without v-structures. The edges identified above would then form U1→U2→⋯→Uk→U1U_{1}\to U_{2}\to\cdots\to U_{k}\to U_{1} in ℳ\mathcal{M}, contradicting its ancestral property. Therefore, 𝒯\mathcal{T} is acyclic.

Every nonempty induced subgraph of 𝒯\mathcal{T} consequently has a vertex with no outgoing directed edge. Such a vertex corresponds to a remaining circle component 𝐁\mathbf{B} for which every edge to another remaining component has an arrowhead at its endpoint in 𝐁\mathbf{B}. Thus, 𝐁\mathbf{B} satisfies the condition for removal in pto. Removing a whole circle component leaves the other circle components unchanged. Repeatedly choosing and removing a component with this property therefore removes every component and terminates.

Finally, let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be any causal diagram consistent with 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Every directed edge U→VU\to V in 𝒢⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}] is also directed from UU to VV in its corresponding MAG. If UU and VV belong to different circle components of 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}], their edge in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} must be U→VU\to V or U∘⁣→VU\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}V. There is therefore a directed edge in 𝒯\mathcal{T} from the component of UU to the component of VV. The component of VV must be removed before that of UU, because the latter still has an outgoing directed edge while both remain. Reversing the removal order thus places the component of UU before that of VV, as required by every directed edge between components in 𝒢⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]. The resulting partial topological order is therefore valid for 𝒢⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{A}]. Building on these properties, we can treat PMGs obtained through local transformations in much the same way as PAGs.

Orienting according to local transformations.

Fix an ordering of the vertices in 𝐗∪{Y}\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\}. Starting from 𝒫\mathcal{P}, process these vertices in this order, considering every valid local transformation at each step. After each transformation, apply the orientation rules ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}–ℛ3\mathcal{R}_{3}, ℛ4′\mathcal{R}_{4}^{\prime}, ℛ8\mathcal{R}_{8}–ℛ10\mathcal{R}_{10}, and ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} until no further orientation is possible. Let 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i} denote the resulting PMGs, where ii indexes the sequences of local transformation choices. The constructed PMGs 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i} inherit these graphical properties.

Corollary 0 (Inherited properties).

Lemmas 49, 50, 51, 52, 53 and 54 apply with 𝒬=𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i}.

{proof}

[Proof of Cor. 55] By Thm. 48, the resulting PMG is orientation-complete. It also satisfies the common hypotheses of the lemmas. Their conclusions therefore hold for 𝒬𝐗i​[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i}[\mathbf{A}].

Proposition 0.

Let ℳ∈[𝒫]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}], and suppose that 𝐗\mathbf{X} is an MIS relative to ⟨ℳ,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{M},Y\rangle. Then there exists a PMG 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i} representing ℳ\mathcal{M} such that:

  • 1.

    Every circle mark at a vertex in 𝐗∪{Y}\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\} in 𝒫\mathcal{P} is replaced by a tail or an arrowhead in 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i}.

  • 2.

    𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i} is closed under ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}–ℛ3\mathcal{R}_{3}, ℛ4′\mathcal{R}_{4}^{\prime}, ℛ8\mathcal{R}_{8}–ℛ10\mathcal{R}_{10}, and ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}}.

  • 3.

    For every X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X}, 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i} contains a proper directed path from XX to YY with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X}.

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 56] We first construct a sequence of local transformations that preserves ℳ\mathcal{M}. Initially, ℳ∈[𝒫]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}]. At each step, let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be the current PMG and let A∈𝐗∪{Y}A\in\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\} be the vertex being processed. Choose the local transformation at AA so that every circle mark at AA is oriented as in ℳ\mathcal{M}. This choice is valid because ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}] provides a compatible MAG realizing all the selected marks simultaneously. The subsequent orientation rules are sound and therefore preserve compatibility with ℳ\mathcal{M}. Inductively, the resulting PMG 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i} satisfies ℳ∈[𝒬𝐗i]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i}]. Every vertex in 𝐗∪{Y}\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\} is processed, and orientation closure is applied after each step. Hence, the first two conditions hold.

To prove the third condition, fix X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X}. By Thm. 31, choose a shortest proper directed path p:V0(=X)→V1→⋯→Vk(=Y)p:V_{0}(=X)\to V_{1}\to\cdots\to V_{k}(=Y) with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X} in ℳ\mathcal{M}. This path is uncovered; otherwise, a chord between nonconsecutive vertices must point forward, since the earlier vertex is an ancestor of the later one and ℳ\mathcal{M} is ancestral. Such a chord would give a shorter proper directed path, a contradiction.

Since ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i} have the same adjacencies, the corresponding path is also uncovered in 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i}. The mark at XX on the edge between XX and V1V_{1} is fixed in 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i} and agrees with ℳ\mathcal{M}. It is therefore a tail. Thus, closure under ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} gives X→V1X\to V_{1} in 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i}.

Now suppose that Vj−1→VjV_{j-1}\to V_{j} has been established for some 1≤j<k1\leq j<k. Because ℳ∈[𝒬𝐗i]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i}] and Vj→Vj+1V_{j}\to V_{j+1} in ℳ\mathcal{M}, the mark at VjV_{j} on the edge between VjV_{j} and Vj+1V_{j+1} cannot be an arrowhead. If it is a circle, the uncovered configuration Vj−1→Vj∘−∗Vj+1V_{j-1}\to V_{j}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}V_{j+1} is oriented as Vj→Vj+1V_{j}\to V_{j+1} by ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}, since Vj−1V_{j-1} and Vj+1V_{j+1} are not adjacent. If the mark is already a tail, the edge is Vj→Vj+1V_{j}\to V_{j+1}, using ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} if necessary. Thus, closure implies Vj→Vj+1V_{j}\to V_{j+1} in either case.

Thus, the path is a proper directed path from XX to YY with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X} in 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i}. The same PMG 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i} was constructed by preserving ℳ\mathcal{M} throughout all local transformations. Hence, this conclusion holds simultaneously for every X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X}, establishing the third condition.

Algorithmic characterization.

Building on the theoretical results above, we present IsPOMIS (Alg. 3), which searches locally oriented PMGs and applies a terminal IB test. The following theorem establishes that the algorithm decides whether 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a POMIS in at least one MAG represented by 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

Theorem 57.

IsPOMIS (Alg. 3) returns True if and only if 𝐗∈ℙ^𝒫,Y\mathbf{X}\in\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathcal{P},Y}.

The proof in Sec. C.0.5 combines Thm. 46 with the terminal PMG–MAG correspondence in Lemma 122. The latter constructs one compatible MAG with the required IB. The algorithm can therefore stop while circle marks remain at vertices outside 𝐗∪{Y}\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\}.

The algorithm first checks whether 𝐗\mathbf{X} is an MIS using Prop. 34. If this necessary condition fails, it returns False. Otherwise, it calls subIsPOMIS directly on 𝒫\mathcal{P}, with 𝐀=𝐗∪{Y}\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\}. When enumerating the full union, the candidates for these individual calls are the sets returned by MISs in Alg. 2.

At each recursive call, the algorithm selects the first vertex A∈𝐀A\in\mathbf{A} in a fixed order and considers local transformations 𝐂A𝒬\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}} satisfying Thm. 47.

For each valid transformation, it additionally checks:

A∈𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒬∖(𝐂A𝒬∪(𝐗∖{A})).\displaystyle A\in\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{Q}\setminus\left(\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}\cup(\mathbf{X}\setminus\{A\})\right)}. (99)

Here, we set 𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℋ=∅\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{H}}=\emptyset whenever YY is not a vertex of ℋ\mathcal{H}. When A=YA=Y, the condition holds automatically because possible ancestors include the vertex itself and Y∉𝐂Y𝒬∪𝐗Y\notin\mathbf{C}_{Y}^{\mathcal{Q}}\cup\mathbf{X}. When A∈𝐗A\in\mathbf{X}, the condition checks for a possibly directed path to YY that avoids both 𝐂A𝒬\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}} and the other intervention variables.

If the condition holds, the algorithm applies the selected local transformation and then the orientation rules ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}–ℛ3\mathcal{R}_{3}, ℛ4′\mathcal{R}_{4}^{\prime}, ℛ8\mathcal{R}_{8}–ℛ10\mathcal{R}_{10}, and ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} until none applies, obtaining 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}. The following proposition shows that, for A∈𝐗A\in\mathbf{X}, this update establishes a proper directed path from AA to YY.

Proposition 0.

Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be obtained from a PAG by valid local transformations and orientation closure, let 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} and let A∈𝐗∪{Y}A\in\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\}. Consider a MAG ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}] consistent with the valid local transformation 𝐂A𝒬\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}. Then the following equivalence holds:

A∈𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒬∖(𝐂A𝒬∪(𝐗∖{A}))⇔A∈𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℳ∖(𝐗∖{A}).\displaystyle A\in\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{Q}\setminus\left(\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}\cup(\mathbf{X}\setminus\{A\})\right)}\iff A\in\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{M}\setminus(\mathbf{X}\setminus\{A\})}. (100)

If either graph does not contain YY, the corresponding ancestor set of YY is interpreted as empty.

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 58] The case A=YA=Y is immediate because ancestors include the vertex itself. Hence assume A∈𝐗A\in\mathbf{X}.

(Only if) Suppose that the left-hand condition holds. There is a possibly directed path from AA to YY in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} avoiding 𝐂A𝒬∪(𝐗∖{A})\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}\cup(\mathbf{X}\setminus\{A\}). By Lemma 114, the path has an uncovered possibly directed subsequence with the same endpoints. Since taking a subsequence introduces no vertices, the resulting path still avoids the deleted vertices.

Its first neighbor of AA lies outside 𝐂A𝒬\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}. If the first edge already has a tail at AA, it points out of AA by closure under ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}}. Otherwise, its mark at AA is a circle, which the selected local transformation replaces by a tail; ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} then completes the directed edge. The rules ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} and ℛSB\mathcal{R}_{\texttt{SB}} then propagate this orientation along the uncovered path. Consequently, the resulting PMG 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} contains a proper directed path from AA to YY with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X}. The fixed MAG ℳ\mathcal{M} agrees with the selected local transformations, so sound orientation closure preserves ℳ∈[𝒬′]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}]. The directed path in 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} is therefore also present in this ℳ\mathcal{M}, establishing the right-hand condition.

(If) Conversely, suppose that the right-hand condition holds. Then ℳ\mathcal{M} contains a directed path from AA to YY avoiding 𝐗∖{A}\mathbf{X}\setminus\{A\}. Since ℳ\mathcal{M} is consistent with the selected local transformation, the edge between AA and every C∈𝐂A𝒬C\in\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}} has an arrowhead at AA. By ancestrality, no such CC can be a descendant of AA. Hence, the directed path also avoids 𝐂A𝒬\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}. Its corresponding path in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is possibly directed, establishing the left-hand condition.

The recursion continues with 𝐀∖{A}\mathbf{A}\setminus\{A\}. Once established, the proper directed paths are preserved by all subsequent valid transformations and orientation updates. Thus, when 𝐀=∅\mathbf{A}=\emptyset, every intervention variable has a proper directed path to YY in the resulting orientation-complete PMG 𝒬𝐗i\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i}. The algorithm then checks 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒬𝐗i,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{X}}^{i},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}. It returns True if any recursive branch satisfies this condition and False otherwise.

Corollary 0.

Define IsDMIS by running Alg. 3 with the terminal return value 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒬,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X} replaced by True, while retaining all other tests and recursive steps. For any 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\}, this procedure terminates and returns True if and only if 𝐗∈𝔻𝒫,Y\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{D}_{\mathcal{P},Y}.

{proof}

[Proof of Cor. 59] The search has finite branching, and each recursive descent removes one vertex from 𝐀\mathbf{A}, so it terminates.

If it accepts, the valid transformations and sound orientation closure yield a terminal PMG 𝒬\mathcal{Q} with ∅≠[𝒬]⊆[𝒫]\emptyset\neq[\mathcal{Q}]\subseteq[\mathcal{P}]. By Prop. 58, every X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X} has a proper directed path to YY with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X} in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, preserved by subsequent orientations. Any ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}] therefore makes 𝐗\mathbf{X} an MIS by Thm. 31, and Prop. 39 gives DMIS membership.

Conversely, a DMIS has a witnessing MAG ℳ∈[𝒫]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}] in which it is an MIS, and it passes the initial MIS screen. Follow the local choices agreeing with this same ℳ\mathcal{M}, as in Prop. 56. These choices are valid and preserve ℳ\mathcal{M}; Prop. 58 ensures that every proper path test passes. The test at YY holds by reflexivity. Thus an accepting terminal branch is reached. The argument includes 𝐗=∅\mathbf{X}=\emptyset, for which the proper path requirements are vacuous.

To illustrate the POMIS search, we return to the MAG in Fig. 16(a) and consider its PAG in Fig. 18(a). The candidate is 𝐗={A,B}\mathbf{X}=\{A,B\}, and the processing order is ⟨A,B,Y⟩\langle A,B,Y\rangle. Both A∘⁣→YA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y and B∘⁣→YB\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y are proper possibly directed paths, so this candidate belongs to the collection returned by MISs and passes the initial MIS check. The subsequent search determines whether this candidate is a POMIS in at least one represented MAG.

At AA, choose 𝐂A𝒫=∅\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{P}}=\emptyset. This is valid, and the additional path test deletes only BB, leaving the path A∘⁣→YA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y. The transformation orients A→BA\to B, A→CA\to C, and A→YA\to Y. Orientation closure gives the PMG 𝒬A\mathcal{Q}_{A} in Fig. 18(b). To see the role of the additional test, compare the valid choice 𝐂A𝒫={Y}\mathbf{C}_{A}^{\mathcal{P}}=\{Y\}. This choice instead places an arrowhead at AA on its edge to YY, but the path test deletes YY and therefore rejects the branch. Validity alone does not ensure a proper path to YY.

At BB, the only remaining circle mark is on B∘⁣→YB\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y. Choose 𝐂B𝒬A=∅\mathbf{C}_{B}^{\mathcal{Q}_{A}}=\emptyset. The path test deletes AA and retains B∘⁣→YB\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y, so the branch continues and fixes B→YB\to Y.

At YY, all incident marks are already arrowheads. Its only local choice is empty, and the reflexive possible ancestor condition holds after deleting {A,B}\{A,B\}. No further orientations are needed. The resulting PMG 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is shown in Fig. 18(c). After deleting 𝐗\mathbf{X}, the possible ancestors of YY are {C,D,Y}\{C,D,Y\}. The invisible edges C∘⁣→YC\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y and D∘⁣→YD\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y place both CC and DD in the territory reached from YY. Hence:

For 𝐗={A,B}\mathbf{X}=\{A,B\}, 𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(𝒬,Y,𝐗)={C,D,Y}\displaystyle\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X})=\{C,D,Y\} (101)
⇒𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒬,Y,𝐗)={A,B}=𝐗.\displaystyle\Rightarrow\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X})=\{A,B\}=\mathbf{X}. (102)

The algorithm therefore returns True. Two circle marks remain, one at CC and one at DD. Thus, the terminal graph is still a PMG. Replacing these two circles by tails gives the MAG in Fig. 16(a). Its construction example in Fig. 16(c) realizes the same territory and border in a compatible causal diagram. Thus, the local search and the earlier MAG construction establish the same candidate’s POMIS membership from their respective graph representations.

Runtime analysis.

Let n=|𝐕|n=\lvert\mathbf{V}\rvert, let mm be the number of edges in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and let k=|𝐗|+1k=\lvert\mathbf{X}\rvert+1. The initial MIS check can be implemented in 𝒪⁡(n+m)\mathcal{O}(n+m) time using a reverse reachability search from YY along possibly directed adjacencies. Vertices in 𝐗\mathbf{X} are marked when reached but are not expanded, ensuring that the corresponding paths avoid other intervention variables.

Let p≤n−1p\leq n-1 bound the number of circle marks at any vertex being processed. Each recursive call considers at most 2p2^{p} local transformations. Checking the validity of one transformation takes 𝒪⁡(n3)\mathcal{O}(n^{3}) time (Wang et al., 2023), while the condition in Prop. 58 can be evaluated by a reachability search in 𝒪⁡(n+m)\mathcal{O}(n+m) time.

The recursion has depth kk and examines at most k⋅2k​pk\cdot 2^{kp} candidate transformations and 2k​p2^{kp} terminal states. Let 𝒯𝚌𝚕𝚘𝚜𝚞𝚛𝚎\mathcal{T}_{\mathtt{closure}} denote the worst-case cost of one orientation closure and 𝒯𝙸𝙱\mathcal{T}_{\mathtt{IB}} the worst-case cost of evaluating the terminal IB condition. A conservative upper bound for one call to IsPOMIS is therefore:

𝒪⁡(n+m+2k​p​[k⁡(n3+𝒯𝚌𝚕𝚘𝚜𝚞𝚛𝚎)+𝒯𝙸𝙱]).\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\left(n+m+2^{kp}\left[k\bigl(n^{3}+\mathcal{T}_{\mathtt{closure}}\bigr)+\mathcal{T}_{\mathtt{IB}}\right]\right). (103)

To enumerate all members of ℙ^𝒫,Y\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathcal{P},Y}, first obtain 𝕄𝒫,Y\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{P},Y} using MISs, and then retain the sets accepted by IsPOMIS. Every POMIS in a represented MAG is an MIS for the PAG, so this restriction preserves every member of the union. There are κ\kappa candidates. The total cost is the MIS enumeration cost in Eq. 83, plus the sum of the individual IsPOMIS costs in Eq. 103 over these κ\kappa sets.

An alternative is to enumerate the MAGs represented by 𝒫\mathcal{P} and evaluate their IB conditions. For example, MagList (Wang et al., 2024a) enumerates these MAGs without duplication by recursively determining local structures throughout 𝐕\mathbf{V}. For a given candidate 𝐗\mathbf{X}, IsPOMIS branches only on local transformations at 𝐗∪{Y}\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\}, while applying orientation closure to the entire graph. A terminal PMG may therefore represent multiple MAGs. Its IB test is justified by Thm. 57.

For the PMGs visited by the algorithm, Cor. 120 shows that visibility is exactly characterized by the graphical criterion in Lemma 17, evaluated in the full PMG. For each directed edge R→BR\to B, this criterion can be checked by finding the bidirected connections among parents of BB and inspecting the edges entering those vertices. Starting from RR, retain only parents of BB along these bidirected connections, and check whether an edge entering a reached vertex starts at a vertex nonadjacent to BB. Each search takes 𝒪⁡(n+m)\mathcal{O}(n+m) time, so all directed edges can be checked in 𝒪⁡(m⁡(n+m))\mathcal{O}(m(n+m)) time. With their visibility fixed, the territory is reached from YY by traversing invisible edges in either direction and visible edges only from tail to arrowhead, within the possible-ancestor graph. Ancestor restriction, this traversal, and the border calculation each take 𝒪⁡(n+m)\mathcal{O}(n+m) time. Thus 𝒯𝙸𝙱=𝒪⁡((m+1)​(n+m))\mathcal{T}_{\mathtt{IB}}=\mathcal{O}((m+1)(n+m)) is a valid bound.

4.3 Experiments

We evaluate six settings, each with a fixed binary SCM whose structural functions combine AND (∧\land), OR (∨\lor), exclusive OR (⊕\oplus), and negation (¬\neg), with independent Bernoulli exogenous variables. The complete structural functions and exogenous distributions are specified in Appendix D. The agent receives the oracle PAG of the model’s causal diagram, and observes the reward of its selected intervention at each round. This PAG is obtained from graphical separation relations in the causal diagram, rather than from conditional independence tests on samples of the fixed SCM. Task 1 uses the PAG already shown in Fig. 13(a). Fig. 19 places the causal diagrams of the SCMs for Tasks 2–6 beside their oracle PAGs.

We compare three candidate action spaces. Brute force (BF) includes every assignment to every subset of 𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\}, including the empty intervention. With binary variables, its size is |𝒜BF|=∑k=0|𝐕|−1(|𝐕|−1k)2k=3|𝐕|−1\lvert\mathcal{A}_{\texttt{BF}}\rvert=\sum_{k=0}^{\lvert\mathbf{V}\rvert-1}\binom{\lvert\mathbf{V}\rvert-1}{k}2^{k}=3^{|\mathbf{V}\rvert-1}. The DMIS strategy retains all assignments to DMISs. We obtain these sets by applying IsDMIS in Cor. 59 to the MIS candidates. The POMIS union strategy retains all assignments to the intervention sets in the union ℙ^𝒫,Y\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathcal{P},Y} over represented MAGs, as returned by the POMIS membership procedure. Thus, the label POMIS union in the figures and tables denotes this union, rather than ℙ𝒫,Y\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{P},Y}. Table 2 reports the number of intervention sets and arms in each action space.

Each action space is paired with Thompson sampling (TS) (Thompson, 1933) and Bernoulli KL-UCB (Garivier and Cappé, 2011; Cappé et al., 2013). TS uses a 𝙱𝚎𝚝𝚊⁡(1,1)\mathtt{Beta}(1,1) prior for each arm. KL-UCB initially samples arms once in a random order and then uses Bernoulli KL upper confidence indices with exploration function f⁡(s)=log⁡s+3​log⁡log⁡sf(s)=\log s+3\log\log s for s≥3s\geq 3 and f⁡(s)=1f(s)=1 otherwise, where ss is the number of completed rounds. Thus, after initialization, the decision at round tt uses f⁡(t−1)f(t-1). All tasks use T=50,000T=50{,}000 rounds, so each candidate action space completes this initial exploration. The reward mean of each intervention is computed from the fixed SCM to simulate Bernoulli rewards and evaluate regret. Arm selection uses only the selected arms and observed rewards from previous rounds.

The performance measure is the cumulative (pseudo-)regret defined in Sec. 3:

RT=∑t=1T(μ⋆−μAt),μ⋆=maxa∈𝒜BF⁡μa,\displaystyle R_{T}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}(\mu^{\star}-\mu_{A_{t}}),\qquad\mu^{\star}=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{\texttt{BF}}}\mu_{a}, (104)

using the same full action space benchmark for all strategies. For each of the six fixed SCMs, we verify that all three candidate action spaces retain an arm attaining this optimal mean. Each of the 36 configurations—six tasks, three strategies, and two solvers—is run 100100 times. In Fig. 20, curves show the mean cumulative pseudo-regret and shaded regions show one standard deviation across these runs.

At T=50,000T=50{,}000, POMIS union has the lowest mean cumulative regret in all twelve task–solver comparisons in Table 3. Task 3 illustrates the benefit of substantial action reduction. POMIS union retains 5454 arms, compared with 19,68319{,}683 for BF, and both solvers incur much less regret. However, fewer arms do not guarantee lower finite-horizon regret. In Task 6, KL-UCB incurs mean regret 4,374.84{,}374.8 with DMIS, compared with 4,194.84{,}194.8 with BF. These results illustrate the benefit of the POMIS union action space on the six fixed SCMs with oracle PAGs.

5 On Transportability for Structural Causal Bandits

Secs. 3 and 4 used causal structure to reduce the action space while preserving an optimal action. Substantial exploration may nevertheless remain, and each intervention can be costly. A complementary strategy is to use data already collected from related source environments. Such data can narrow the possible rewards before interaction begins and reduce the cold-start problem.

However, an intervention that performs well in one environment may perform poorly in another. Transferring its reward distribution therefore requires accounting for the mechanisms that may change.

This section considers a known causal diagram and addresses these environmental discrepancies through transportability (Pearl and Bareinboim, 2011; Bareinboim and Pearl, 2012; Bareinboim and Pearl, 2016). Zhang and Bareinboim (2017) studied the transfer of prior observations for particular structures, including bow and instrumental-variable graphs. Bellot et al. (2023) and Deng et al. (2025) considered more general causal diagrams with single-variable interventions. Here, the available source experiments may involve several variables, and some variables may be non-manipulable in the target environment.

We first explain how non-manipulable variables change the POMIS action space. Then, we introduce the following contributions of this section.

  • •

    We derive causal bounds on individual action rewards by combining source distributions.

  • •

    We next provide dominance bounds, which compare the best rewards under different intervention constraints.

  • •

    Finally, we use these bounds to guide exploration in the target environment.

Relation to the published version.

This section revises Park and Lee (2026b). The assumptions of Proposition 1 of Park and Lee (2026b) are corrected to allow 𝐂⊆𝐂′⊆𝐃\mathbf{C}\subseteq\mathbf{C}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathbf{D} with 𝐂\mathbf{C} ancestral in 𝒢⁡[𝐂′]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{C}^{\prime}] (Prop. 63). For the online policy, the variance interval uses the action-specific lower bound ℓ𝐱\ell_{\mathbf{x}}, and a Bernstein index and its corresponding regret guarantee replace the published index and bound (Eqs. 166, 169 and 70). The experiments in Sec. 5.7 use this revised policy. Task 2 also uses a revised reward mechanism and controlled comparisons to isolate the effect of the upper dominance bound: the improvement reported for the original Task 2 did not establish that effect. The resulting regret measurements replace the published numerical results.

5.1 Structural Causal Bandits with Non-manipulable Variables

Sec. 3 allowed interventions on every observed variable except the reward. In many applications, an observed variable can be measured but cannot be set directly. For example, a treatment can be assigned while a patient’s physiological response must follow its natural mechanism. Let 𝐍⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{N}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\} denote these non-manipulable variables. The agent may now intervene only on sets 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}∖𝐍\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\}\setminus\mathbf{N} (Lee and Bareinboim, 2019). The variables in 𝐍\mathbf{N} continue to respond to their causes, including interventions on other variables. Thus, this restriction changes which actions are available while preserving the SCM and reward notation introduced earlier. As before, the agent chooses an intervention based on the past history, before observing the variables generated in the current round.

MISs and POMISs under constraint.

The definitions of MIS and POMIS in Sec. 3 extend by restricting their candidate intervention sets to the manipulable variables. We denote the resulting collections by 𝕄𝒢,Y𝐍\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}} and ℙ𝒢,Y𝐍\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}, respectively. Minimality is unchanged because every subset of a feasible intervention set is also feasible. Consequently:

𝕄𝒢,Y𝐍={𝐗∈𝕄𝒢,Y:𝐗∩𝐍=∅}.\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}=\{\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y}:\mathbf{X}\cap\mathbf{N}=\emptyset\}. (105)

In particular, the ancestral criterion in Sec. 3 applies directly after checking that 𝐗\mathbf{X} is feasible.

Possible optimality also depends on which competing intervention sets remain available. A feasible MIS 𝐗\mathbf{X} belongs to ℙ𝒢,Y𝐍\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}} if some SCM conforming to 𝒢\mathcal{G} satisfies:

μ𝐱∗>μ𝐰∗for every ​𝐖∈𝕄𝒢,Y𝐍∖{𝐗}.\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}}>\mu_{\mathbf{w}^{\ast}}\quad\text{for~every~}\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}\setminus\{\mathbf{X}\}. (106)

An unconstrained POMIS that remains feasible still satisfies this requirement, because its witnessing SCM has fewer competitors to beat. Therefore:

{𝐗∈ℙ𝒢,Y:𝐗∩𝐍=∅}⊆ℙ𝒢,Y𝐍⊆𝕄𝒢,Y𝐍.\displaystyle\{\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G},Y}:\mathbf{X}\cap\mathbf{N}=\emptyset\}\subseteq\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}\subseteq\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}. (107)

The first inclusion can be strict. An MIS previously dominated by an intervention on a non-manipulable variable may become a necessary candidate once that intervention is unavailable. Hence, simply removing infeasible sets from ℙ𝒢,Y\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G},Y} can discard an optimal feasible action.

Graphical characterization for POMISs under constraint.

To account for this change, we use the latent projection from Def. 10 of 𝒢\mathcal{G} onto 𝐕∖𝐍\mathbf{V}\setminus\mathbf{N}, denoted by ℋ=𝒢​⟨𝐕∖𝐍⟩\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{G}\langle\mathbf{V}\setminus\mathbf{N}\rangle.

The reason for projection is that an unavailable intervention cannot interrupt a causal pathway through 𝐍\mathbf{N}. Algebraically, each non-manipulable variable’s structural function can be substituted into the functions of its children. Repeating this substitution gives a model on ℋ\mathcal{H} with the same reward distribution for every feasible intervention.

The graphical characterization ranges over SCMs compatible with the diagram, allowing the domains of non-manipulable variables to vary so their mechanisms can encode the inputs needed by their children.

Theorem 60 (Constrained POMISs (Lee and Bareinboim, 2019)).

With ℋ=𝒢​⟨𝐕∖𝐍⟩\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{G}\langle\mathbf{V}\setminus\mathbf{N}\rangle, ℙ𝒢,Y𝐍=ℙℋ,Y\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}=\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{H},Y}, and a feasible set 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a constrained POMIS if and only if 𝖨𝖡⁡(ℋ𝐗¯,Y)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{H}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}},Y)=\mathbf{X}.

{proof}

[Proof of Thm. 60] Latent projection preserves directed paths between retained vertices that avoid an intervention set. The ancestral MIS criterion therefore gives 𝕄𝒢,Y𝐍=𝕄ℋ,Y\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}=\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{H},Y}. Substituting the mechanisms in 𝐍\mathbf{N} preserves every feasible reward distribution, so each constrained POMIS witness on 𝒢\mathcal{G} is also a witness on ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Conversely, the constructive proof of Thm. 28 provides a POMIS witness on ℋ\mathcal{H} whose independent exogenous variables each affect at most two observed variables (Lee and Bareinboim, 2018). The reverse construction of Proposition 3 in Lee and Bareinboim (2019) expands this witness to 𝒢\mathcal{G} by letting restored variables encode the inputs needed by their children. The allowed choice of their domains permits this construction. It preserves the feasible reward distributions and hence the strict comparisons against the common MIS collection. This proves equality; the IB criterion follows from Thm. 28. For instance, consider the causal diagram in Fig. 21(a). Its MISs are:

𝕄𝒢,Y={∅,{X1},{X2}}.\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y}=\{\emptyset,\{X_{1}\},\{X_{2}\}\}. (108)

The joint set {X1,X2}\{X_{1},X_{2}\} is redundant because fixing X2X_{2} removes the effect of X1X_{1} on YY.

When both X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} are manipulable, the minimal UC-territory of 𝒢\mathcal{G} contains all three variables, and thus its border is empty. Hence ∅\emptyset is a POMIS. After intervening on X2X_{2}, the border is {X2}\{X_{2}\}. By contrast, intervening on X1X_{1} removes its bidirected edge and leaves the border {X2}\{X_{2}\}. Hence:

ℙ𝒢,Y={∅,{X2}}.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G},Y}=\{\emptyset,\{X_{2}\}\}. (109)

Now suppose that X2X_{2} is non-manipulable, so 𝐍={X2}\mathbf{N}=\{X_{2}\}. Projecting out X2X_{2} gives X1→YX_{1}\to Y together with X1↔YX_{1}\leftrightarrow Y, as shown in Fig. 21(b). In this projected graph, the border is empty before intervention and becomes {X1}\{X_{1}\} after intervening on X1X_{1}. Therefore:

For 𝐍={X2},ℙ𝒢,Y𝐍={∅,{X1}}.\displaystyle\text{For $\mathbf{N}=\{X_{2}\}$,}\quad\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}=\{\emptyset,\{X_{1}\}\}. (110)

Filtering the unconstrained POMISs would retain only ∅\emptyset and miss {X1}\{X_{1}\}.

To see this, consider the following binary SCM conforming to the causal diagram in Fig. 21(a):

ℳ={𝐔={U,U1,U2,UY}𝐕={X1,X2,Y}ℱ={fX1​(u,u1)=u⊕u1fX2​(x1,u2)=x1⊕u2fY​(x2,u,uY)=x2⊕u⊕uYP⁡(𝐔)={U∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(25),U1,U2,UY∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(14)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{U}=\{U,U_{1},U_{2},U_{Y}\}\\ \mathbf{V}=\{X_{1},X_{2},Y\}\\ \mathcal{F}=\begin{cases}f_{X_{1}}(u,u_{1})=u\oplus u_{1}\\ f_{X_{2}}(x_{1},u_{2})=x_{1}\oplus u_{2}\\ f_{Y}(x_{2},u,u_{Y})=x_{2}\oplus u\oplus u_{Y}\\ \end{cases}\\ P(\mathbf{U})=\{U\thicksim\mathtt{Bern}(\frac{2}{5}),U_{1},U_{2},U_{Y}\sim\mathtt{Bern}(\frac{1}{4})\}.\end{cases} (111)

The exogenous variables are mutually independent. The shared variable UU induces X1↔YX_{1}\leftrightarrow Y, while U1U_{1}, U2U_{2}, and UYU_{Y} supply separate random variation in the three mechanisms. In particular, P⁡(X2=1∣X1=0)=14P(X_{2}=1\mid X_{1}=0)=\frac{1}{4} and P⁡(X2=1∣X1=1)=34P(X_{2}=1\mid X_{1}=1)=\frac{3}{4}. Every assignment to (X1,X2,Y)(X_{1},X_{2},Y) has positive observational probability. The observational and interventional means are:

μ∅\displaystyle\mu_{\emptyset} =716,\displaystyle=\frac{7}{16}, μX1=0\displaystyle\mu_{X_{1}=0} =1940,\displaystyle=\frac{19}{40}, μX1=1\displaystyle\mu_{X_{1}=1} =2140,\displaystyle=\frac{21}{40}, (112)
μX2=0\displaystyle\mu_{X_{2}=0} =920,\displaystyle=\frac{9}{20}, μX2=1\displaystyle\mu_{X_{2}=1} =1120.\displaystyle=\frac{11}{20}. (113)

Thus, when both variables can be manipulated, d​o​(X2=1)do(X_{2}=1) attains the optimal mean 1120\frac{11}{20}. When 𝐍={X2}\mathbf{N}=\{X_{2}\}, the optimal feasible action is d​o​(X1=1)do(X_{1}=1), with mean 2140\frac{21}{40}.

For the remainder of this section, we write the actions induced by constrained POMISs as:

𝒜𝒢,Y𝐍={𝐱:𝐗∈ℙ𝒢,Y𝐍,𝐱∈Ω𝐗}.\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}=\{\mathbf{x}:\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}},\mathbf{x}\in\Omega_{\mathbf{X}}\}. (114)

This reduction preserves the best achievable expected reward under the constraint. It does not determine which feasible actions are most informative during learning: observations from an excluded action may still help estimate rewards of retained actions. In the transportability setting considered next, the same distinction applies to prior experiments, including experiments on variables that cannot be manipulated in the target environment.

5.2 Structural Causal Bandits under Transportability

Let π∗\pi^{\ast} denote the target environment and ℳ∗\mathcal{M}^{\ast} its SCM, with reward Y∈[0,1]Y\in[0,1] and non-manipulable variables 𝐍∗\mathbf{N}^{\ast}. The agent also has information from source environments Π={π1,⋯,πn}\Pi=\{\pi^{1},\cdots,\pi^{n}\}, associated with SCMs ℳ1,⋯,ℳn\mathcal{M}^{1},\cdots,\mathcal{M}^{n} over the same observed variables and domains, all conforming to the known causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G}. We use P𝐱∗P^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}} and P𝐱iP^{i}_{\mathbf{x}} for the distributions under d​o​(𝐱)do(\mathbf{x}) in the target and source πi\pi^{i}, respectively. Thus, μ𝐱∗=𝔼P𝐱∗​Y\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbb{E}_{P^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}}Y is the target mean reward. A superscript ∗\ast on a distribution or mean specifies the target environment; the superscripts on assignments 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{\ast} and 𝐱⋆\mathbf{x}^{\star} retain their meanings from Sec. 3.

The target action space is 𝒜𝒢,Y𝐍∗\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}^{\ast}}. At round tt, the agent selects AtA_{t} from this space and observes the outcome of its intervention. The cumulative pseudo-regret from Sec. 3, evaluated in the target, is:

RT=T​μ𝐱⋆∗−∑t=1TμAt∗=∑𝐱∈𝒜𝒢,Y𝐍∗Δ𝐱​NT​(𝐱),\displaystyle R_{T}=T\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu^{\ast}_{A_{t}}=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}^{\ast}}}\Delta_{\mathbf{x}}N_{T}(\mathbf{x}), (115)

where Δ𝐱=μ𝐱⋆∗−μ𝐱∗\Delta_{\mathbf{x}}=\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}-\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}} and 𝐱⋆\mathbf{x}^{\star} is optimal under the target constraint. The objective is to minimize 𝔼​RT\mathbb{E}R_{T}. Source data do not contribute rewards to this objective; they provide information for choosing target interventions.

Environmental discrepancies.

For source πi\pi^{i}, let ℤi\mathbb{Z}^{i} contain the intervention sets for which experimental distributions are available. The empty set denotes observational data. We write:

ℤ={ℤi}i=1n,𝒫ℤΠ={P𝐳i:πi∈Π,𝐙∈ℤi,𝐳∈Ω𝐙}.\displaystyle\mathbb{Z}=\{\mathbb{Z}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},\qquad\mathcal{P}^{\Pi}_{\mathbb{Z}}=\{P^{i}_{\mathbf{z}}:\pi^{i}\in\Pi,\ \mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{Z}^{i},\ \mathbf{z}\in\Omega_{\mathbf{Z}}\}. (116)

A source may permit interventions that are unavailable in the target. For example, a laboratory experiment may directly control a biological mediator that cannot be assigned in a deployment population. Such experiments may still inform the rewards of feasible target actions.

For the probability bound algorithms below, observed variables have finite domains, with ΩY⊆[0,1]\Omega_{Y}\subseteq[0,1]. Source probabilities are treated as exact population quantities.

Definition 0 (Environment discrepancy and selection diagram).

Let Δi=Δ∗,i\Delta^{i}=\Delta^{\ast,i}1818 18 The superscript in Δi\Delta^{i} denotes an environmental discrepancy; the subscript in Δ𝐱\Delta_{\mathbf{x}} denotes a reward gap. contain the variables whose mechanisms may differ between π∗\pi^{\ast} and πi\pi^{i}. For each V∈ΔiV\in\Delta^{i}, add a root node SVS_{V} and an edge SV→VS_{V}\to V to 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The resulting graph is the selection diagram 𝒢Δi\mathcal{G}^{\Delta^{i}}.

A selection node marks a possible discrepancy between environments. Its absence asserts invariance of the corresponding mechanism, including the relevant exogenous variation. When a shared unobserved cause changes, its effects on all affected mechanisms must be represented. Equality of observed marginal distributions alone does not establish this invariance.

Let 𝚫={Δi}i=1n\bm{\Delta}=\{\Delta^{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}, 𝐒i={SV:V∈Δi}\mathbf{S}^{i}=\{S_{V}:V\in\Delta^{i}\}, and 𝐒=⋃i𝐒i\mathbf{S}=\bigcup_{i}\mathbf{S}^{i}. Adding all these selection edges gives the collective selection diagram 𝒢𝚫\mathcal{G}^{\bm{\Delta}}. We assume that the environments admit a unified SCM with this diagram, in which selection nodes are independent roots controlling the environment-specific mechanisms. With 𝐒−i=𝐒∖𝐒i\mathbf{S}^{-i}=\mathbf{S}\setminus\mathbf{S}^{i}, its distributions satisfy:

P𝐱𝚫​(𝐲∣𝐒=𝟎)\displaystyle P^{\bm{\Delta}}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{S}=\bm{0}) =P𝐱∗​(𝐲),\displaystyle=P^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}), (117)
P𝐱𝚫​(𝐲∣𝐒i=𝐢,𝐒−i=𝟎)\displaystyle P^{\bm{\Delta}}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{S}^{i}=\mathbf{i},\mathbf{S}^{-i}=\bm{0}) =P𝐱i​(𝐲).\displaystyle=P^{i}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}). (118)

The assignment 𝐒i=𝐢\mathbf{S}^{i}=\mathbf{i} sets every selection node in 𝐒i\mathbf{S}^{i} to ii. In this representation, do-calculus can compare distributions across environments by determining whether the relevant selection nodes affect the queried outcome.

Example 0 (Treatment selection).

Consider the schematic treatment system in Fig. 22(a). Let X1X_{1} indicate an antihypertensive treatment, X2X_{2} an anti-diabetic treatment, WW blood pressure, and YY a favorable health outcome. The unobserved variable UU influences both WW and X2X_{2}.

Suppose that the agent can assign the two treatments but cannot directly set blood pressure, so 𝐍∗={W}\mathbf{N}^{\ast}=\{W\}. Prior data from another population can help evaluate treatment choices. However, if the distribution of UU differs across populations, both mechanisms involving WW and X2X_{2} may change. The collective selection diagram in Fig. 22(b) represents this possibility by Δ1={W,X2}\Delta^{1}=\{W,X_{2}\}. The mechanism for YY, conditional on its causes and exogenous inputs, remains shared. We will return to this distinction when comparing feasible treatments with hypothetical interventions on WW.

5.3 Partial Transportability and Causal Bounds

A target mean μ𝐱∗\mu_{\mathbf{x}}^{\ast} is transportable from 𝒫ℤΠ\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\Pi} if it has the same value in every collection of SCMs compatible with both these source distributions and the collective selection diagram (Lee et al., 2020). Equivalently, the available information uniquely determines the target mean. Different factors in a formula may come from different environments.

For the collective selection diagram shown in Fig. 22(c), suppose that source π1\pi^{1} supplies observational data and source π2\pi^{2} supplies experiments on {A,C}\{A,C\}, i.e., ℤ1={∅}\mathbb{Z}^{1}=\{\emptyset\} and ℤ2={{A,C}}\mathbb{Z}^{2}=\{\{A,C\}\}. Let 𝐍∗={C}\mathbf{N}^{\ast}=\{C\}. Although CC cannot be manipulated in the target, experiments on CC in π2\pi^{2} can still identify the target reward of d​o​(a)do(a). Specifically:

Pa∗​(y)\displaystyle P^{\ast}_{a}(y) =∑b,cPa∗​(b)​Pa∗​(c∣b)​Pa∗​(y∣b,c)\displaystyle=\sum_{b,c}P^{\ast}_{a}(b)P^{\ast}_{a}(c\mid b)P^{\ast}_{a}(y\mid b,c) (119)
=(a)​∑b,cPa,c∗​(b)​P∅∗​(c∣a,b)​Pa,c∗​(y∣b)\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{=}\sum_{b,c}P^{\ast}_{a,c}(b)P^{\ast}_{\emptyset}(c\mid a,b)P^{\ast}_{a,c}(y\mid b) Rules 2 and 3 (120)
=∑b,cP∅∗​(c∣a,b)​Pa,c∗​(b,y)\displaystyle=\sum_{b,c}P^{\ast}_{\emptyset}(c\mid a,b)P^{\ast}_{a,c}(b,y) (121)
=(b)​∑b,cP∅1​(c∣a,b)​Pa,c2​(b,y).\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(b)}}{=}\sum_{b,c}P^{1}_{\emptyset}(c\mid a,b)P^{2}_{a,c}(b,y). (122)

Intermediate conditional probabilities are evaluated on conditioning events with positive probability; the final expression requires only the displayed source conditionals. Step (a) uses Rules 2 and 3 of do-calculus: the intervention on CC does not affect BB, conditioning on CC can be exchanged with intervention in the reward factor, and the conditional mechanism for CC is recovered observationally given A,BA,B. In step (b), source π1\pi^{1} supplies this conditional mechanism because its discrepancy is confined to AA. Source π2\pi^{2} supplies the joint distribution of B,YB,Y under d​o​(a,c)do(a,c) because intervening on CC removes its changed mechanism. Neither source needs to reproduce the entire target system. Multiplying these two contributions and summing over B,CB,C gives the target reward distribution. The example illustrates why heterogeneous experiments can be useful even when they cannot be repeated in the target.

5.3.1 Partial Transportability

Exact transportability need not hold for every action. We call a mean partially transportable when the source information restricts it to an informative interval [ℓ𝐱,u𝐱]⊊[0,1][\ell_{\mathbf{x}},u_{\mathbf{x}}]\subsetneq[0,1] that is valid for every compatible target SCM. To construct such intervals, we decompose the query into causal factors and bound the factors that cannot be determined exactly.

Q-decomposition.

Recall the c-components from Sec. 3, and write 𝖼𝖼𝒢\mathsf{cc}_{\mathcal{G}} for their collection. For 𝐂⊆𝐕\mathbf{C}\subseteq\mathbf{V}, define the causal factor:

Q⁡[𝐂]​(𝐯)=P𝐯∖𝐂​(𝐜).\displaystyle Q[\mathbf{C}](\mathbf{v})=P_{\mathbf{v}\setminus\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{c}). (123)

It is the distribution of 𝐂\mathbf{C} when every observed variable outside 𝐂\mathbf{C} is fixed by intervention. Thus, Q⁡[𝐂]Q[\mathbf{C}] is shorthand for an interventional distribution; its displayed arguments also record those fixed values. We usually suppress its assignment argument 𝐯\mathbf{v}. Superscripts distinguish target and source factors, as in Q∗​[𝐂]Q^{\ast}[\mathbf{C}] and Qi​[𝐂]Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}].

Let 𝐘+=𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢∖𝐗\mathbf{Y}^{+}=\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}\setminus\mathbf{X}}. Only these remaining ancestors can affect YY after d​o​(𝐱)do(\mathbf{x}). The Q-decomposition (Tian and Pearl, 2003) gives:

P𝐱∗​(y)\displaystyle P^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}(y) =∑𝐲+∖{Y}∏𝐂∈𝖼𝖼𝒢⁡[𝐘+]Q∗​[𝐂],\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{y}^{+}\setminus\{Y\}}\prod_{\mathbf{C}\in\mathsf{cc}_{\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{Y}^{+}]}}Q^{\ast}[\mathbf{C}], (124)
μ𝐱∗\displaystyle\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}} =∑𝐲+y​∏𝐂∈𝖼𝖼𝒢⁡[𝐘+]Q∗​[𝐂].\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{y}^{+}}y\prod_{\mathbf{C}\in\mathsf{cc}_{\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{Y}^{+}]}}Q^{\ast}[\mathbf{C}]. (125)

The fixed intervention arguments in each factor agree with 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Other fixed variables outside 𝐘+∪𝐗\mathbf{Y}^{+}\cup\mathbf{X} do not affect these remaining mechanisms.

If 𝐂∩Δi=∅\mathbf{C}\cap\Delta^{i}=\emptyset, then all mechanisms retained in Q⁡[𝐂]Q[\mathbf{C}] are shared, and Q∗​[𝐂]=Qi​[𝐂]Q^{\ast}[\mathbf{C}]=Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}]. When the latter factor is identifiable from an available source distribution and its graph, this equality transports the factor. Transporting every factor in Eq. 125 is sufficient to determine the reward distribution and hence its mean.

Fig. 23 depicts the decomposition as a jigsaw puzzle. The query determines the pieces needed, and different source experiments may provide different pieces. A missing exact piece does not require discarding the entire query: a lower or upper bound for that piece may still constrain the final reward.

Bounds for unavailable factors.

Return to the collective selection diagram in Fig. 22(c), but now suppose that ℤ1={∅,{C}}\mathbb{Z}^{1}=\{\emptyset,\{C\}\} and ℤ2={{B}}\mathbb{Z}^{2}=\{\{B\}\}. The target mean decomposes into:

μa∗=∑b,c,yy​Q∗​[C]​Q∗​[B,Y].\displaystyle\mu^{\ast}_{a}=\sum_{b,c,y}yQ^{\ast}[C]Q^{\ast}[B,Y]. (126)

Source π1\pi^{1} still identifies Q∗​[C]=P∅1​(c∣a,b)Q^{\ast}[C]=P^{1}_{\emptyset}(c\mid a,b). It does not identify Q1​[B,Y]Q^{1}[B,Y]: within the available factor on {A,B,Y}\{A,B,Y\}, latent confounding prevents removal of the mechanism for AA. Source π2\pi^{2} intervenes on BB and therefore does not provide the required joint factor on B,YB,Y. Nevertheless, Q∗​[B,Y]=Q1​[B,Y]Q^{\ast}[B,Y]=Q^{1}[B,Y], since neither BB nor YY is in Δ1\Delta^{1}.

The natural bounds (Manski, 1990; Robins, 1989),

P⁡(𝐱,𝐲)≤P𝐱​(𝐲)≤P⁡(𝐱,𝐲)+1−P⁡(𝐱),\displaystyle P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\leq P_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})\leq P(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})+1-P(\mathbf{x}), (127)

give the starting point. For units whose natural value is 𝐱\mathbf{x}, replacing the corresponding mechanisms by 𝐱\mathbf{x} leaves the values received by all other mechanisms unchanged. Their outcome is therefore unchanged, so their observed joint probability supplies the lower bound. The remaining units can contribute at most their total probability, 1−P⁡(𝐱)1-P(\mathbf{x}), to the upper bound. The same argument applies within an available causal factor.

For the next proposition, take 𝐂⊆𝐂′⊆𝐃\mathbf{C}\subseteq\mathbf{C}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathbf{D}, where 𝐂\mathbf{C} is ancestral in 𝒢⁡[𝐂′]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{C}^{\prime}], 𝐂∩Δi=∅\mathbf{C}\cap\Delta^{i}=\emptyset, and Qi​[𝐃]Q^{i}[\mathbf{D}] is available or identifiable from source information. Ancestral marginalization gives Qi​[𝐂]=∑𝐜′∖𝐂Qi​[𝐂′]Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}]=\sum_{\mathbf{c}^{\prime}\setminus\mathbf{C}}Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}^{\prime}].

Proposition 0 (Bounds for a shared causal factor).

The target factor satisfies:

∑𝐜′∖𝐂Qi​[𝐃]≤Q∗​[𝐂]≤∑𝐜′∖𝐂{Qi​[𝐃]+1−∑𝐜′Qi​[𝐃]}.\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{c}^{\prime}\setminus\mathbf{C}}Q^{i}[\mathbf{D}]\leq Q^{\ast}[\mathbf{C}]\leq\sum_{\mathbf{c}^{\prime}\setminus\mathbf{C}}\left\{Q^{i}[\mathbf{D}]+1-\sum_{\mathbf{c}^{\prime}}Q^{i}[\mathbf{D}]\right\}. (128)

If Qi​[𝐂′]Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}^{\prime}] is identifiable, then Q∗​[𝐂]=∑𝐜′∖𝐂Qi​[𝐂′]Q^{\ast}[\mathbf{C}]=\sum_{\mathbf{c}^{\prime}\setminus\mathbf{C}}Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}^{\prime}].

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 63] Fix the arguments outside 𝐃\mathbf{D} and apply Eq. 127 within the resulting SCM, with the intervention variables 𝐃∖𝐂′\mathbf{D}\setminus\mathbf{C}^{\prime}. This gives, at every assignment:

Qi​[𝐃]≤Qi​[𝐂′]≤Qi​[𝐃]+1−∑𝐜′Qi​[𝐃].\displaystyle Q^{i}[\mathbf{D}]\leq Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}^{\prime}]\leq Q^{i}[\mathbf{D}]+1-\sum_{\mathbf{c}^{\prime}}Q^{i}[\mathbf{D}]. (129)

The inner sum varies only 𝐂′\mathbf{C}^{\prime}, holding all other arguments fixed. Because 𝐂\mathbf{C} is ancestral in 𝒢⁡[𝐂′]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{C}^{\prime}], ancestral marginalization gives Qi​[𝐂]=∑𝐜′∖𝐂Qi​[𝐂′]Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}]=\sum_{\mathbf{c}^{\prime}\setminus\mathbf{C}}Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}^{\prime}] by Lemma 3 in Tian and Pearl (2003). Also Q∗​[𝐂]=Qi​[𝐂]Q^{\ast}[\mathbf{C}]=Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}] by the shared mechanisms. Summing the pointwise bounds proves the claim; the same marginalization of an identified Qi​[𝐂′]Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}^{\prime}] gives the exact case.

In the example, use 𝐂=𝐂′={B,Y}\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}^{\prime}=\{B,Y\} and 𝐃={A,B,Y}\mathbf{D}=\{A,B,Y\}. The enclosing factor is observed under the source experiment on CC:

Q1​[A,B,Y]=Pc1​(a,b,y).\displaystyle Q^{1}[A,B,Y]=P^{1}_{c}(a,b,y). (130)

Combining its bounds with the exact factor for CC yields:

μa∗\displaystyle\mu^{\ast}_{a} ≥∑b,c,yy​P∅1​(c∣a,b)​Pc1​(a,b,y)\displaystyle\geq\sum_{b,c,y}yP^{1}_{\emptyset}(c\mid a,b)P^{1}_{c}(a,b,y) (131)
μa∗\displaystyle\mu^{\ast}_{a} ≤∑b,c,yy​P∅1​(c∣a,b)​{Pc1​(a,b,y)+1−Pc1​(a)}.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{b,c,y}yP^{1}_{\emptyset}(c\mid a,b)\left\{P^{1}_{c}(a,b,y)+1-P^{1}_{c}(a)\right\}. (132)

Thus, the experiment on CC contributes information about a target intervention on AA, even though it does not identify its reward exactly.

Algorithmic partial transportability.

paTR in Alg. 4 constructs lower or upper expressions for a target query, following the recursive structure of general transportability (Lee et al., 2020).

Its arguments are the outcome assignment 𝐲\mathbf{y}, intervention assignment 𝐱\mathbf{x}, current graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}, current discrepancy sets 𝚫\bm{\Delta}, and bound direction 𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾∈{ℓ,u}\mathsf{type}\in\{\ell,u\}. In every call, 𝐕=𝐕⁡(𝒢)\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{G}) denotes the current vertex set, and 𝐗,𝐘⊆𝐕\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}\subseteq\mathbf{V} are the disjoint variable sets of 𝐱,𝐲\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}. The sources Π\Pi, experimental sets ℤ\mathbb{Z}, and available distributions 𝒫ℤΠ\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\Pi} are fixed global information. Each yielded expression is a candidate lower bound when 𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾=ℓ\mathsf{type}=\ell or upper bound when 𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾=u\mathsf{type}=u for the current target probability; an exact expression serves both directions.

A yield emits an expression, and a recursive yield forwards every expression obtained by that call. A following return ends the current call. If no source supplies a required expression, that call yields nothing. Whenever a source experiment is used, all available assignments 𝐳\mathbf{z} agreeing with the current query on 𝐙∩𝐕\mathbf{Z}\cap\mathbf{V} are considered. Values 𝐳∖𝐕\mathbf{z}\setminus\mathbf{V} remain fixed external arguments. A source distribution supplied to a recursive call is first marginalized to the vertices of that call’s graph, with its intervention arguments held fixed.

The lines of Alg. 4 have the following roles:

  • •

    Use a direct source expression (lines 2–3). The experiment must set exactly 𝐗\mathbf{X} among the current vertices. The separation condition checks that its source discrepancy does not affect 𝐘\mathbf{Y} after those vertices are removed. Every qualifying source expression is then exact for the current target query, and the call ends.

  • •

    Remove non-ancestors (lines 4–5). Variables outside 𝙰𝚗​(𝐘)𝒢\mathtt{An}(\mathbf{Y})_{\mathcal{G}} cannot affect the query. The recursive call removes them from the graph, intervention assignment, and discrepancy sets, then forwards its expressions.

  • •

    Add irrelevant interventions (lines 6–9). Among the variables remaining after 𝐗\mathbf{X} is removed, those outside the ancestors of 𝐘\mathbf{Y} may be fixed to any assignment 𝐯′\mathbf{v}^{\prime} by Rule 3. For every assignment 𝐯′∈Ω𝐕′\mathbf{v}^{\prime}\in\Omega_{\mathbf{V}^{\prime}}, the target query satisfies P𝐱∗​(𝐲)=P𝐱𝐯′∗​(𝐲)P^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})=P^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{v}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{y}). The algorithm forwards the candidate expressions from all these assignments before ending the call. Although the target probability is invariant to this choice, the available source factors used to bound it may differ. CausalBound intersects the resulting bounds, which can tighten the interval without claiming sharpness.

  • •

    Decompose the query (lines 10–11). If several c-components remain, the algorithm queries the causal factor of each component 𝐂\mathbf{C} by fixing the other current variables. It forms every combination of one yielded expression per component, multiplies them, and sums over variables outside 𝐗∪𝐘\mathbf{X}\cup\mathbf{Y}. Components may use different sources; a combination contributes no expression if any required component yields none.

  • •

    Choose a source for the remaining component (lines 12–13). A source is eligible when its discrepancies avoid all remaining mechanisms, 𝐕∖𝐗\mathbf{V}\setminus\mathbf{X}, and its experiment intervenes only within 𝐗\mathbf{X} among the current vertices. The variables already fixed by that experiment are removed from the graph and from the intervention still to be performed. The resulting source distribution and query are passed to paID, which supplies exact expressions or natural bounds.

The subroutine paID in Alg. 5 works within the selected source. Its arguments are 𝐲,𝐱,P,𝒢,𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x},P,\mathcal{G},\mathsf{type}, with the same local graph, assignment, and bound-direction conventions. Here PP is the source distribution or a causal factor over the current vertices, with outside assignments held fixed. The reductions in paTR ensure that each call satisfies:

𝐂=𝐕∖𝐗=𝙰𝚗​(𝐘)𝒢∖𝐗,𝖼𝖼𝒢∖𝐗={𝐂}.\displaystyle\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{V}\setminus\mathbf{X}=\mathtt{An}(\mathbf{Y})_{\mathcal{G}\setminus\mathbf{X}},\qquad\mathsf{cc}_{\mathcal{G}\setminus\mathbf{X}}=\{\mathbf{C}\}. (133)

The recursive calls of paID preserve this condition. The subroutine yields lower or upper expressions for the intervention query within PP; the source-invariance check in paTR makes these expressions valid for the corresponding target query. In the factor products in Alg. 5, 𝐯≺j\mathbf{v}_{\prec j} denotes values preceding VjV_{j} in a topological ordering of the current graph, and the conditionals are formed from the current PP while holding its outside assignments fixed.

  • •

    Finish an observational query (lines 2–3). If no intervention remains, marginalizing PP to 𝐘\mathbf{Y} gives an exact expression.

  • •

    Restrict to ancestors (lines 4–6). Set 𝐃=𝙰𝚗​(𝐘)𝒢\mathbf{D}=\mathtt{An}(\mathbf{Y})_{\mathcal{G}}, sum out variables outside 𝐃\mathbf{D} from PP, and retain only the graph and intervention on 𝐃\mathbf{D}.

  • •

    Bound an unavailable factor (lines 7–13). Line 7 names the unique remaining c-component 𝐂\mathbf{C}. If the whole current graph is one c-component, exact extraction stops. Lines 9–12 apply the lower or upper natural bound from Prop. 63 and marginalize to 𝐘\mathbf{Y}, after which the call ends. In the preceding example, this is the step that bounds Q1​[B,Y]Q^{1}[B,Y] using Q1​[A,B,Y]Q^{1}[A,B,Y].

  • •

    Extract an exact factor (lines 14–15). If 𝐂\mathbf{C} is already a c-component of the current graph, its Q-factor is the product of the displayed conditionals for Vj∈𝐂V_{j}\in\mathbf{C}. Summing over 𝐂∖𝐘\mathbf{C}\setminus\mathbf{Y} gives the exact query.
