    Reduce to an enclosing component (lines 16–18). Otherwise, locate the c-component 𝐂′\mathbf{C}^{\prime} containing 𝐂\mathbf{C} and extract its identifiable factor Q⁡[𝐂′]Q[\mathbf{C}^{\prime}] from PP. Recurse using this factor, the induced graph on 𝐂′\mathbf{C}^{\prime}, and the interventions still inside 𝐂′\mathbf{C}^{\prime}. Assignments outside 𝐂′\mathbf{C}^{\prime} remain fixed arguments of the extracted factor.

Theorem 64.

Every expression yielded by paTR is a valid lower or upper bound, according to 𝗍𝗒𝗉𝖾\mathsf{type}, for the queried target probability.

The proof is given in Sec. F.0.1. Several expressions can bound the same probability. The theorem guarantees that these bounds are valid, although the source information may permit tighter bounds.

5.3.2 Causal Bounds

CausalBound in Alg. 6 takes the reward Y∈[0,1]Y\in[0,1], an intervention assignment 𝐱\mathbf{x}, the diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and discrepancies 𝚫\bm{\Delta}, together with the fixed source experiments ℤ\mathbb{Z} and distributions 𝒫ℤΠ\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\Pi}. It returns an interval [ℓ𝐱,u𝐱][\ell_{\mathbf{x}},u_{\mathbf{x}}] containing the target mean μ𝐱∗\mu_{\mathbf{x}}^{\ast}. Its calls to paTR use the fixed source information specified above.

Before checking support, we combine products of source probabilities by the chain rule, preserving their source and fixed experimental arguments. For example, for disjoint assignments a,b,c,da,b,c,d, the product P(a,b∣c,d)P(c∣d)P(a,b\mid c,d)P(c\mid d) is evaluated through the merged expression P⁡(a,b,c∣d)P(a,b,c\mid d). The merged conditional requires P⁡(d)>0P(d)>0 and is defined even when P⁡(c,d)=0P(c,d)=0. This rule uses the joint-probability expression supplied by the chain rule; it does not permit arbitrary cancellation of zero-denominator ratios or numerical evaluation of undefined conditionals.

After these simplifications, we evaluate a formula only when every remaining source conditional it uses has a conditioning event with positive probability. Otherwise, that formula is omitted; another formula may still provide a bound. If none is usable, we retain 0≤μ𝐱∗≤10\leq\mu_{\mathbf{x}}^{\ast}\leq 1. Thus, the graph determines which source mechanisms can be transferred, while the source probabilities determine whether a particular formula can be evaluated.

Line 1 starts from the valid interval [0,1][0,1]. Lines 2–4 evaluate each available lower expression, sum it against the nonnegative reward values, and retain the largest resulting lower bound. Lines 5–7 apply the same operation to upper expressions, truncating each probability bound at one before taking the smallest reward upper bound. Lines 3 and 6 apply the support test after the stated chain-rule simplifications and discard a formula if any remaining source conditional required for its evaluation is undefined. Thus a missing formula does not invalidate the other bounds, and a direction with no usable formula retains its trivial endpoint. Line 8 returns the intersection of the usable bounds. These operations are sound because multiplying pointwise probability bounds by y≥0y\geq 0 and summing preserves their direction.

Corollary 0.

CausalBound returns ℓ𝐱≤μ𝐱∗≤u𝐱\ell_{\mathbf{x}}\leq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}\leq u_{\mathbf{x}}. If this interval is a proper subinterval of [0,1][0,1], the target mean is partially transportable.

{proof}

By Thm. 64, every usable lower and upper expression satisfies 0≤P𝐱ℓ​(y)≤P𝐱∗​(y)≤min⁡{1,P𝐱u​(y)}0\leq P^{\ell}_{\mathbf{x}}(y)\leq P^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}(y)\leq\min\{1,P^{u}_{\mathbf{x}}(y)\}. Multiplying by y≥0y\geq 0 and summing over yy gives valid bounds on μ𝐱∗\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}. Taking the maximum of these lower bounds and the minimum of these upper bounds, starting from [0,1][0,1], preserves validity. A proper resulting subinterval is informative by the definition of partial transportability.

Computational cost.

The cost includes graph operations, expression generation, and evaluation of source probabilities. Enumeration can be large: if each of dd components has zz candidate expressions, their product can yield zdz^{d} combinations. Each Rule 3 branch also visits |Ω𝐕′|\lvert\Omega_{\mathbf{V}^{\prime}}\rvert assignments; these finite-domain branching factors compound across recursive calls. The total cost must therefore account for the number and size of returned expressions, as well as the assignments summed over in their evaluation. Source quantities and repeated subqueries can be reused. These computations occur before target interaction; once the bounds are available, the online policy uses their numerical endpoints.

5.4 Dominance Bounds

Causal bounds constrain individual rewards. The graph also relates the best rewards attainable from different action spaces. We say that one action space dominates another when its maximum expected reward is at least as large. This comparison concerns the maxima over the two spaces, rather than every pair of their actions.

5.4.1 Lower Dominance Bound

Under the target constraint 𝐍∗\mathbf{N}^{\ast}, the POMIS action space attains at least the reward of every feasible MIS action. Therefore, any lower bound for a feasible MIS action also lower-bounds the target optimum. Define:

ℓ⋆=max𝐖∈𝕄𝒢,Y𝐍∗𝐰∈Ω𝐖⁡ℓ𝐰.\displaystyle\ell^{\star}=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}^{\ast}}\\ \mathbf{w}\in\Omega_{\mathbf{W}}\end{subarray}}\ell_{\mathbf{w}}. (134)

If 𝐰†\mathbf{w}^{\dagger} attains this maximum, then:

ℓ⋆=ℓ𝐰†≤μ𝐰†∗≤μ𝐱⋆∗.\displaystyle\ell^{\star}=\ell_{\mathbf{w}^{\dagger}}\leq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{w}^{\dagger}}\leq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}. (135)

The maximizing lower bound may come from an MIS that is not a POMIS. Its reward is still achievable, so it can certify that another action is suboptimal. In particular, u𝐱<ℓ⋆u_{\mathbf{x}}<\ell^{\star} implies μ𝐱∗<μ𝐱⋆∗\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}<\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}} and permits safe removal of 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

5.4.2 Upper Dominance Bound

A non-manipulable variable restricts the interventions available to the agent. Allowing an additional intervention cannot reduce the best attainable reward. The constrained POMIS construction makes this comparison explicit.

Proposition 0.

A POMIS under ⟨𝒢,Y,𝐍⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y,\mathbf{N}\rangle is an MIS under ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle.

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 66] A constrained POMIS 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a minimal feasible intervention set. If it were not an unconstrained MIS, a proper subset of 𝐗\mathbf{X} would be interventionally equivalent for YY in every compatible SCM. That subset is also feasible because 𝐗∩𝐍=∅\mathbf{X}\cap\mathbf{N}=\emptyset, contradicting constrained minimality. A constrained POMIS can nevertheless fail to be an unconstrained POMIS: an intervention that dominates it may become available when the constraint is removed.

Example 0 (Continued).

Return to Example 62, with 𝐍∗={W}\mathbf{N}^{\ast}=\{W\}. Its constrained POMISs are:

ℙ𝒢,Y{W}={{X1},{X1,X2}}.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\{W\}}=\{\{X_{1}\},\{X_{1},X_{2}\}\}. (136)

Thus, an optimal feasible treatment can be selected among interventions on X1X_{1} alone or on both treatments. Now consider the unconstrained intervention set 𝐑={W,X2}\mathbf{R}=\{W,X_{2}\}. Fixing both direct causes of YY can match or improve the mean attained by any distribution over their natural values. For the best intervention on X1X_{1}:

μx1∗∗\displaystyle\mu^{\ast}_{x_{1}^{\ast}} =∑𝐫𝔼Px1∗∗​[Y∣𝐫]​Px1∗∗​(𝐫)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{r}}\mathbb{E}_{P^{\ast}_{x_{1}^{\ast}}}[Y\mid\mathbf{r}]P^{\ast}_{x_{1}^{\ast}}(\mathbf{r}) (137)
=(a)​∑𝐫𝔼Px1∗,𝐫∗​[Y]​Px1∗∗​(𝐫)\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{=}\sum_{\mathbf{r}}\mathbb{E}_{P^{\ast}_{x_{1}^{\ast},\mathbf{r}}}[Y]P^{\ast}_{x_{1}^{\ast}}(\mathbf{r}) Rule 2 (138)
=(b)​∑𝐫μ𝐫∗​Px1∗∗​(𝐫)\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(b)}}{=}\sum_{\mathbf{r}}\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{r}}P^{\ast}_{x_{1}^{\ast}}(\mathbf{r}) Rule 3 (139)
≤μ𝐫∗∗.\displaystyle\leq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{r}^{\ast}}. (140)

Step (a) uses Rule 2, since the relevant paths from W,X2W,X_{2} to YY are unconfounded after fixing X1X_{1}. Step (b) uses Rule 3: once WW is fixed, X1X_{1} no longer affects YY. The last inequality bounds an average by its largest term.

The same argument applies to an intervention on {X1,X2}\{X_{1},X_{2}\}, averaging only over WW. Consequently, the best reward under the target constraint is no greater than the best reward under d​o​(w,x2)do(w,x_{2}). The latter interventions remain unavailable to the target agent, but an upper bound on their rewards can still constrain every feasible treatment.

Theorem 68.

Let 𝐍⊊𝐍∗\mathbf{N}\subsetneq\mathbf{N}^{\ast}, and let 𝐫⋆\mathbf{r}^{\star} be optimal in 𝒜𝒢,Y𝐍\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}. Then μ𝐱⋆∗≤μ𝐫⋆∗\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}\leq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{r}^{\star}}.

{proof}

[Proof of Thm. 68] Every intervention feasible under 𝐍∗\mathbf{N}^{\ast} is feasible under 𝐍⊊𝐍∗\mathbf{N}\subsetneq\mathbf{N}^{\ast}. The maximum target mean over all feasible interventions therefore cannot decrease when the constraint is relaxed. POMIS reduction preserves each maximum, giving μ𝐱⋆∗≤μ𝐫⋆∗\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}\leq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{r}^{\star}}.

The optimal action 𝐫⋆\mathbf{r}^{\star} under the weaker constraint is unknown. To obtain a computable upper bound, maximize the available upper bounds over all POMIS actions under the weaker constraint:

μ𝐱⋆∗≤max𝐫∈𝒜𝒢,Y𝐍⁡μ𝐫∗≤max𝐫∈𝒜𝒢,Y𝐍⁡u𝐫.\displaystyle\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}\leq\max_{\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}}\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{r}}\leq\max_{\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}}u_{\mathbf{r}}. (141)

Combining these bounds, including the original constraint, gives:

u⋆=min𝐍⊆𝐍∗⁡max𝐫∈𝒜𝒢,Y𝐍​u𝐫.\displaystyle u^{\star}=\min_{\mathbf{N}\subseteq\mathbf{N}^{\ast}}\max_{\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}}u_{\mathbf{r}}. (142)

Every reward in this calculation is a target reward. Source experiments are used to bound those rewards; the optimum of a source environment is not itself a bound on the target optimum.

5.4.3 Traversing the Constraint Hierarchy

Removing one variable from 𝐍\mathbf{N} gives an immediately weaker constraint. Repeating this step reaches every subset of 𝐍\mathbf{N}. Exact optimal rewards increase weakly along these paths, but their computed upper bounds need not: source experiments can constrain a hypothetical intervention more tightly than the original feasible actions.

udb in Alg. 7 takes 𝒢\mathcal{G}, YY, the current non-manipulable set 𝐍\mathbf{N}, and valid target mean bounds 𝕃={ℓ𝐫}\mathbb{L}=\{\ell_{\mathbf{r}}\} and 𝕌={u𝐫}\mathbb{U}=\{u_{\mathbf{r}}\} for the actions queried during recursion. It returns an upper bound on the best target reward under 𝐍\mathbf{N}. The diagram, reward, and causal bounds remain fixed, and an initially empty collection of stored results is shared across the recursive calls.

The lines of Alg. 7 have the following roles:

  • •

    Construct the current candidates (lines 2–6). Reuse a stored result if this constraint was visited before. Otherwise, project out 𝐍\mathbf{N}, enumerate its POMIS actions, and select an action 𝐫†\mathbf{r}^{\dagger} with the largest upper bound. Ties are resolved by preferring the larger lower bound, with a fixed rule for any remaining tie. Its upper endpoint supplies the local candidate.

  • •

    Stop when no improvement is possible (lines 7–8). If the maximizing action has ℓ𝐫†=u𝐫†\ell_{\mathbf{r}^{\dagger}}=u_{\mathbf{r}^{\dagger}}, the exact constrained optimum is known. An exact interval for another action does not suffice. At 𝐍=∅\mathbf{N}=\emptyset, no constraint remains to relax.

  • •

    Visit weaker constraints (lines 9–11). Remove one non-manipulable variable at a time and take the minimum of the resulting bounds and the local candidate. Store the returned value for later visits.

Corollary 0.

udb returns the bound in Eq. 142; in particular, μ𝐱⋆∗≤u⋆\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}\leq u^{\star}.

{proof}

[Proof of Cor. 69] At a constraint 𝐍\mathbf{N}, the local value max𝐫∈𝒜𝒢,Y𝐍⁡u𝐫\max_{\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G},Y}^{\mathbf{N}}}u_{\mathbf{r}} bounds its constrained optimum. Every recursive value bounds an optimum under a weaker constraint, which is at least the current optimum by Thm. 68. Taking their minimum is therefore valid. Removing one variable recursively visits every proper subset, so induction on |𝐍|\lvert\mathbf{N}\rvert gives the subset-minimum in Eq. 142. For an early return, the maximizing action 𝐫†\mathbf{r}^{\dagger} satisfies ℓ𝐫†=u𝐫†\ell_{\mathbf{r}^{\dagger}}=u_{\mathbf{r}^{\dagger}}, so its known mean equals the local maximum upper bound and hence the exact constrained optimum. Every bound at a weaker constraint is at least this value; omitting those calls therefore leaves the subset-minimum unchanged.

The same constraint can be reached by removing variables in different orders. Reusing its result limits the traversal to at most 2|𝐍∗|2^{\lvert\mathbf{N}^{\ast}\rvert} distinct constraints and |𝐍∗|​2|𝐍∗|−1\lvert\mathbf{N}^{\ast}\rvert 2^{\lvert\mathbf{N}^{\ast}\rvert-1} one-variable relaxations when 𝐍∗≠∅\mathbf{N}^{\ast}\neq\emptyset. The cost at each constraint additionally includes latent projection, POMIS enumeration, and any causal bounds not already computed. Early termination can reduce this cost.

Combining the bounds.

The lower dominance bound certifies an achievable target reward; the upper dominance bound certifies a ceiling on the target optimum. Together with an action’s causal bounds, they provide two ways to reduce exploration. If u𝐱<ℓ⋆u_{\mathbf{x}}<\ell^{\star}, the action can be removed. Otherwise, its reward still satisfies:

ℓ𝐱≤μ𝐱∗≤min⁡{u𝐱,u⋆}.\displaystyle\ell_{\mathbf{x}}\leq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}\leq\min\{u_{\mathbf{x}},u^{\star}\}. (143)

The upper dominance bound can therefore improve the interval even when no additional action can be pruned.

5.5 Worked Examples of Bound Construction

Every endogenous and exogenous variable is binary, and the exogenous variables within each SCM are mutually independent. For these worked examples, the source environments use the displayed structural functions and exogenous distributions, and their distributions are known at the population level. The discrepancy sets specify mechanisms that are allowed to differ, without requiring an actual change. The agent uses the collective selection diagram and available source distributions, while the displayed target means serve only to check the bounds. Numerical results are rounded to four decimal places; all comparisons use unrounded values.
