5.6 Online Learning with Transferred Bounds

We now use the bounds in a UCB policy. The clipping principle (Zhang and Bareinboim, 2017; Gong et al., 2023) limits an optimistic empirical estimate by a valid prior upper bound. trUCB in Alg. 8 first computes the causal and dominance bounds, removes actions with u𝐱<ℓ⋆u_{\mathbf{x}}<\ell^{\star}, and then interacts only through the retained action space 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{\ast}.

Its inputs are 𝒢\mathcal{G}, YY, 𝐍∗\mathbf{N}^{\ast}, the source information (𝚫,ℤ,𝒫ℤΠ)(\bm{\Delta},\mathbb{Z},\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\Pi}), and an integer horizon T≥1T\geq 1. It produces the target actions A1,⋯,ATA_{1},\cdots,A_{T} and records their rewards. The causal queries include feasible MIS actions used for ℓ⋆\ell^{\star} and POMIS actions under the weaker constraints visited by udb; their bounds can be computed when first needed and reused.

Clipped exploration.

Let κ=|𝒜∗|\kappa=\lvert\mathcal{A}^{\ast}\rvert and suppose that the horizon TT is known. The analysis uses the stationary, independent reward draws from Sec. 3. For each retained action, set:

b𝐱\displaystyle b_{\mathbf{x}} =min⁡{u𝐱,u⋆},\displaystyle=\min\{u_{\mathbf{x}},u^{\star}\}, σ𝐱2\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathbf{x}}^{2} =maxμ∈[ℓ𝐱,b𝐱]⁡μ⁡(1−μ).\displaystyle=\max_{\mu\in[\ell_{\mathbf{x}},b_{\mathbf{x}}]}\mu(1-\mu). (166)

Because Y∈[0,1]Y\in[0,1], its variance is no greater than μ𝐱∗​(1−μ𝐱∗)\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}(1-\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}), and hence no greater than σ𝐱2\sigma_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}. For example, an interval lying near zero or one gives a smaller variance bound than an interval containing 12\frac{1}{2}.

Using the counts Nt​(𝐱)N_{t}(\mathbf{x}) from Sec. 3, the empirical target mean after at least one pull is:

μ^𝐱,t∗=1Nt​(𝐱)∑s=1tYs 1{As=𝐱}.\displaystyle\widehat{\mu}^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x},t}=\frac{1}{N_{t}(\mathbf{x})}\sum_{s=1}^{t}Y_{s}\,\mathds{1}\{A_{s}=\mathbf{x}\}. (167)

Each retained action is initially played once. With ζT=log⁡(2​κ​T2)\zeta_{T}=\log(2\kappa T^{2}), a Bernstein confidence radius gives the index:

U𝐱​(t)\displaystyle U_{\mathbf{x}}(t) =μ^𝐱,t−1∗+2​σ𝐱2​ζTNt−1​(𝐱)+2​ζT3​Nt−1​(𝐱),\displaystyle=\widehat{\mu}^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x},t-1}+\sqrt{\frac{2\sigma_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}\zeta_{T}}{N_{t-1}(\mathbf{x})}}+\frac{2\zeta_{T}}{3N_{t-1}(\mathbf{x})}, (168)
U¯𝐱​(t)\displaystyle\bar{U}_{\mathbf{x}}(t) =min⁡{U𝐱​(t),b𝐱}.\displaystyle=\min\{U_{\mathbf{x}}(t),b_{\mathbf{x}}\}. (169)

The square-root term uses the variance information supplied by the bounds. The linear term ensures the confidence guarantee for general bounded rewards. Both the count and the empirical mean use observations through round t−1t-1, as required when selecting AtA_{t}.

Lines 1–5 perform the action reduction and bound construction before interaction. Lines 6–8 set the confidence parameter and variance bounds, then obtain one reward per retained action. At each subsequent round, lines 10–14 form the indices, clip them, select an action maximizing U¯𝐱​(t)\bar{U}_{\mathbf{x}}(t), observe its target reward, and update only that action’s empirical mean and count. Directly evaluating the κ\kappa indices costs 𝒪⁡(κ)\mathcal{O}(\kappa) per round; updating the selected mean and count costs 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1). Since b𝐱≥μ𝐱∗b_{\mathbf{x}}\geq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}}, clipping preserves optimism whenever the empirical confidence bounds are valid. On the event that all confidence bounds hold, an action whose prior upper bound lies below the optimal mean need not be explored after initialization.

Regret guarantee.

Assume valid population bounds and T≥κT\geq\kappa. If the horizon is shorter, initialization stops after TT pulls.

Theorem 70.

The expected regret satisfies:

𝔼RT≤∑𝐱∈𝒜∗Δ𝐱+ζT∑𝐱∈𝒜∗:b𝐱≥μ𝐱⋆∗,Δ𝐱>0(32​σ𝐱2Δ𝐱+83)+1.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}R_{T}\leq\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{A}^{\ast}}\Delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\zeta_{T}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{A}^{\ast}:\\ b_{\mathbf{x}}\geq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}},\ \Delta_{\mathbf{x}}>0\end{subarray}}\left(\frac{32\sigma_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}}{\Delta_{\mathbf{x}}}+\frac{8}{3}\right)+1. (170)

The proof is given in Sec. F.0.2. The three terms have direct interpretations. The first accounts for playing each retained action once. The logarithmic term accounts for suboptimal actions whose upper bounds still permit optimality. The last term accounts for failure of the simultaneous confidence event, whose probability is at most 1T\frac{1}{T}. In particular, initialization can incur regret even when no suboptimal action remains in the logarithmic sum.

More explicitly, actions removed before interaction are never selected. For a retained action with b𝐱<μ𝐱⋆∗b_{\mathbf{x}}<\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}, the expected number of pulls is at most two. For the other retained suboptimal actions, it is at most 2+32​σ𝐱2​ζTΔ𝐱2+8​ζT3​Δ𝐱2+\frac{32\sigma_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}\zeta_{T}}{\Delta_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}}+\frac{8\zeta_{T}}{3\Delta_{\mathbf{x}}}. Thus, transferred bounds can remove actions entirely, prevent repeated exploration, or reduce the variance term for actions that remain competitive. Since u⋆≥μ𝐱⋆∗u^{\star}\geq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}, the condition b𝐱≥μ𝐱⋆∗b_{\mathbf{x}}\geq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}} is equivalent to u𝐱≥μ𝐱⋆∗u_{\mathbf{x}}\geq\mu^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}. The dominance bound nevertheless affects the indices and σ𝐱2\sigma_{\mathbf{x}}^{2}.

5.7 Experiments

We evaluate the bounds and online policy on three binary SCMs. Tasks 1 and 3 use the models in the previous examples with Figs. 24(a) and 24(c), respectively. Task 2 uses the diagram, source experiments, discrepancy sets, and target constraint of Fig. 24(b), with the reward mechanism and exogenous probabilities specified below.

Task 2: upper dominance and interval variance.

The agent cannot manipulate AA or CC in the target environment. Source 1 supplies observational data with Δ1={A}\Delta^{1}=\{A\}, and source 2 supplies experiments on CC with Δ2={B}\Delta^{2}=\{B\}. All exogenous variables are mutually independent. The SCM is specified as follows: Let 𝐕={A,B,C,Y}\mathbf{V}=\{A,B,C,Y\}. The exogenous variables are:

𝐔={UA,UB,UC,UY,UB​C,UB​Y,UG}.\displaystyle\mathbf{U}=\{U_{A},U_{B},U_{C},U_{Y},U_{BC},U_{BY},U_{G}\}. (171)

The structural functions are:

fA=uAfB=(uB​Y∧uB​C)⊕uBfC=b⊕(uB​C∧((1−uC)⊕a))fY=uG∧[(c∧(1−uY))⊕(a∧uB​Y)].\displaystyle\begin{aligned} f_{A}&=u_{A}\\ f_{B}&=(u_{BY}\land u_{BC})\oplus u_{B}\\ f_{C}&=b\oplus\bigl(u_{BC}\land((1-u_{C})\oplus a)\bigr)\\ f_{Y}&=u_{G}\land\bigl[(c\land(1-u_{Y}))\oplus(a\land u_{BY})\bigr].\end{aligned} (172)

The exogenous distributions are:

UA∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.8)UB∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.9)UC∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.6)UY∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.6)UB​C∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.1)UB​Y∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.4)UG∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.2).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} U_{A}&\sim\mathtt{Bern}(0.8)&U_{B}&\sim\mathtt{Bern}(0.9)&U_{C}&\sim\mathtt{Bern}(0.6)\\ U_{Y}&\sim\mathtt{Bern}(0.6)&U_{BC}&\sim\mathtt{Bern}(0.1)&U_{BY}&\sim\mathtt{Bern}(0.4)\\ U_{G}&\sim\mathtt{Bern}(0.2).\end{aligned} (173)

The additional private noise UGU_{G} enters only fYf_{Y}, so the causal diagram is unchanged. The three feasible actions are observation, d​o​(B=0)do(B=0), and d​o​(B=1)do(B=1), with d​o​(B=1)do(B=1) attaining the largest mean. Their source-derived intervals appear in Table 8.

For the hypothetical intervention d​o​(A=a,C=c)do(A=a,C=c), source 2 identifies:

μA=a,C=c∗=PC=c2​(Y=1∣A=a)=0.2​(0.4​c+0.4​a−0.32​a​c).\displaystyle\mu^{\ast}_{A=a,C=c}=P^{2}_{C=c}(Y=1\mid A=a)=0.2\bigl(0.4c+0.4a-0.32ac\bigr). (174)

These means are 00, 0.080.08, 0.080.08, and 0.0960.096 for (a,c)=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)(a,c)=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1), respectively. The other unconstrained POMIS, {A}\{A\}, gives means approximately 0.06890.0689 and 0.09310.0931. The largest local upper bounds under the other constraints all exceed 0.0960.096. Thus udb returns u⋆=0.096u^{\star}=0.096, reducing the upper limits of both interventions on BB to this value. All three actions remain after pruning. Since their intervals lie below 12\frac{1}{2}, the reduced upper limits also tighten the Bernoulli variance bounds in Eq. 166: from approximately 0.12410.1241 to 0.08680.0868 for d​o​(B=0)do(B=0) and from 0.09030.0903 to 0.08680.0868 for d​o​(B=1)do(B=1). The larger reduction applies to the suboptimal action.

Source information and target interaction.

The agent receives the causal diagram, the target constraint, and the permitted population source distributions. The source and target SCMs share the displayed numerical parameters in these tasks; the discrepancy sets specify which mechanisms may differ without requiring an actual change. Thus, these experiments study the use of source information under the asserted invariances. They do not assess uncertainty from finite source datasets. Table 9 reports the numbers of intervention sets and arms considered by the three main strategies in each task.

At every target round, the agent observes a fresh reward from its chosen intervention. We compute each target mean by summing over the SCM’s exogenous assignments and generate an independent Bernoulli reward with that mean. This gives the same reward distribution as simulating the full binary SCM. Exact target means are used only for reward generation and evaluation; the policy uses its permitted prior bounds and previously observed rewards. All methods are evaluated against the same optimum over target-feasible interventions: 11, approximately 0.09140.0914, and 11 in Tasks 1–3. In particular, hypothetical interventions used by udb do not enlarge the agent’s feasible actions or change its regret benchmark.

Compared policies.

We first compare UCB, poUCB, and trUCB. The first uses all assignments to all manipulable subsets, including the empty intervention. The second restricts these assignments to constrained POMISs. After playing each candidate action once, both use the standard UCB1 index (Auer et al., 2002), μ^𝐱,t−1∗+2​log⁡tNt−1​(𝐱)\widehat{\mu}^{\ast}_{\mathbf{x},t-1}+\sqrt{\frac{2\log t}{N_{t-1}(\mathbf{x})}}. The third uses Alg. 8, including the Bernstein index in Eq. 169. These main comparisons therefore combine differences in action selection and confidence rules.

To distinguish the effects of the transferred bounds, we also compare four policies using the same Bernstein rule as trUCB. Bernstein-POMIS uses all POMIS actions with upper limit one and variance bound 14\frac{1}{4}. Pruning only removes actions with u𝐱<ℓ⋆u_{\mathbf{x}}<\ell^{\star} but otherwise keeps these trivial bounds. Pruning + clipping additionally uses b𝐱=min⁡{u𝐱,u⋆}b_{\mathbf{x}}=\min\{u_{\mathbf{x}},u^{\star}\}, while retaining variance bound 14\frac{1}{4}. Finally, trUCB without UDB uses the causal upper bound u𝐱u_{\mathbf{x}} in both clipping and the variance interval, omitting only the upper dominance bound. Each policy sets κ\kappa to its number of retained actions when computing ζT\zeta_{T}.

Evaluation.

Every task–policy configuration is run for T=10,000T=10{,}000 rounds and repeated 1,0001{,}000 times. Before interaction, each repetition draws an action order independently of the reward draws and keeps it fixed for initialization and index ties. All policies in that repetition use the same order restricted to their candidate actions and share the same sequence of independent uniform draws for generating rewards. The random sequences used for this evaluation were not used to choose the parameters of Task 2. We record cumulative pseudo-regret. Curves in Fig. 26 show its mean, and shaded regions show one population standard deviation across repetitions, matching the presentation in Sec. 4.3. Table 10 reports the final mean and standard deviation.

Performance.

In Task 1, POMIS reduction decreases the number of actions from nine to six, and the source bounds remove two more. At T=10,000T=10{,}000, the mean regret decreases from 247.1247.1 for UCB to 94.894.8 for poUCB and 13.013.0 for trUCB. The controlled comparison isolates the additional effect of pruning: Bernstein-POMIS incurs mean regret 38.138.1, whereas Pruning only incurs 13.013.0. Since every retained upper limit is one, clipping does not further tighten these limits.

In Task 2, all methods retain the same three actions. Thus UCB and poUCB coincide, with mean regret 67.167.1, and pruning alone does not change the Bernstein policy, whose mean regret is 63.863.8. Full trUCB gives 55.455.4, compared with 123.9123.9 without upper dominance. However, Pruning + clipping, which fixes the variance bound at 14\frac{1}{4}, gives 121.7121.7. A common clipping level can produce index ties, so tightening a cap alone need not improve finite-horizon regret. The full policy also uses the smaller variance bounds supplied by the intervals. The additional comparison below isolates how upper dominance contributes through these two uses.

In Task 3, the action counts decrease from 2727 to 77 after POMIS reduction and to 44 after pruning. The corresponding main-policy regrets are 248.6248.6, 132.7132.7, and 32.232.2. With the Bernstein rule held fixed, pruning reduces mean regret from 74.174.1 to 32.232.2. The source experiment identifies an optimal mean of one, but several retained actions still have uncertain means. Consequently, initialization and subsequent exploration can incur regret even though the optimal value is known.

In Tasks 1 and 3, trUCB without UDB and Pruning + clipping select exactly the same actions as full trUCB under the shared random draws. Task 2 instead exhibits an additional gain from upper dominance and interval variance information. Together, the tasks distinguish action reduction from changes to the exploration of retained actions.

Separating the two uses of upper dominance.

For Task 2, Fig. 27 further separates the effect of u⋆u^{\star} on clipping from its effect on the variance interval. All four policies retain the same three actions and use the same Bernstein rule, initialization, reward draws, and action order. Starting from trUCB without UDB, UDB cap only replaces u𝐱u_{\mathbf{x}} by b𝐱b_{\mathbf{x}} only in the clipping step, while retaining the variance bound computed from [ℓ𝐱,u𝐱][\ell_{\mathbf{x}},u_{\mathbf{x}}]. Conversely, UDB variance only uses the variance bound computed from [ℓ𝐱,b𝐱][\ell_{\mathbf{x}},b_{\mathbf{x}}] but clips at u𝐱u_{\mathbf{x}}. Full trUCB applies both changes. The cap-only comparison therefore differs from Pruning + clipping, which fixes the variance bound at 14\frac{1}{4}.

The mean regrets are 123.9123.9 without upper dominance, 75.275.2 with the cap adjustment alone, 91.291.2 with the variance adjustment alone, and 55.455.4 with both. Full trUCB reduces mean regret by 55.3%55.3\% relative to trUCB without UDB. The mean paired reduction is 68.568.5, with a 95%95\% confidence interval of [64.8,72.3][64.8,72.3] across repetitions. Both uses of upper dominance therefore contribute to the improvement. The common cap removes the larger upper limit initially assigned to the suboptimal action, and the tighter variance bound further reduces its exploration. These effects do not require removing an action.

The improvement also persists when the horizon is changed: the mean regrets without and with upper dominance are 51.951.9 and 24.724.7 at T=2,000T=2{,}000, and 145.4145.4 and 64.664.6 at T=50,000T=50{,}000. Each horizon uses its own ζT\zeta_{T} and 1,0001{,}000 repetitions. In a further sensitivity check, changing each of the seven exogenous success probabilities by ±0.05\pm 0.05, one at a time, gives 1414 settings. Using 256256 new repetitions per setting at T=10,000T=10{,}000, the mean reductions range from 40.0%40.0\% to 58.2%58.2\%. These results illustrate a setting in which upper dominance improves learning; they do not imply an improvement for every SCM or every reward sequence.

6 Counterfactual Structural Causal Bandits

The preceding sections use causal structure to reduce the search space of a decision-making agent. This section extends the available interventions themselves.

Example 0 (AI-assisted clinical decision support system).

Consider a hospital aiming to improve the quality of patient care. Let YY denote the treatment outcome, XX a patient’s report of their health status, WW an expert physician’s assessment, and ZZ the score from an AI-assisted clinical tool. Fig. 28(a) illustrates the setting, where bidirected edges represent unobserved confounders such as historical bias (Peiffer-Smadja et al., 2020).

For fixed report values xx and x′x^{\prime}, a standardized symptom-reporting interface can supply xx to the expert assessment and x′x^{\prime} to the AI tool. Supplying xx to both assessments gives the same expected outcome as d​o​(X=x)do(X=x), namely 𝔼​Yx\mathbb{E}Y_{x} (Fig. 28(b)). Alternatively, xx can describe a current health condition, while x′x^{\prime} describes a prospective condition, such as the anticipated health benefits of beginning regular exercise (Fig. 28(c)). These report values are selected for the experiment before the patient’s natural report is observed. Supplying the two values separately gives 𝔼​YWx,Zx′\mathbb{E}Y_{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}}, allowing one to ask counterfactual-level questions:

“What if the AI assistant had perceived the patient’s prospective health status x′x^{\prime} rather than the current one xx?”

and to design decision strategies that improve patient outcomes. Here WxW_{x} is the physician’s assessment under report xx, and Zx′Z_{x^{\prime}} is the AI score under report x′x^{\prime}. Both concern the same patient, so their evaluation retains the same unobserved characteristics. The reporting interface changes the information received by each assessment; it does not itself change the patient’s physical health.

The example raises two questions.

  • •

    First, which counterfactuals can actually be produced through interaction with the system?

  • •

    Second, among the available actions, which can be removed without losing an optimal decision?

The first question requires a notion of realizability. The second extends the equivalence and partial-order arguments developed for ordinary interventions in Sec. 3.

We extend the SCB framework to accommodate a broader class of decision-making scenarios. Our key contributions in this section are as follows:

  • •

    We first formulate the counterfactual structural causal bandit problem, enabling an agent to consider actions beyond ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2}-level interventions.

  • •

    We investigate equivalence and partial-order relations among these actions and develop graphical characterizations for reducing the action space.

  • •

    Building on these results, we present an algorithm that removes redundant or weakly dominated choices while retaining an optimal action.

Relation to the published version.

This section revises Park and Lee (2026a). The counterfactual regime graph in Section 3.2 of Park and Lee (2026a) is corrected by deleting directed edges whose inputs are fixed to constants, retaining bidirected edges, and then restricting to reward ancestors (Thm. 87). The sufficiency proof of Theorem 2 of Park and Lee (2026a) is replaced by a construction using reserved values and propagation of invalid inputs (Sec. H.0.3). The illustrative SCM in Section 3.2 of Park and Lee (2026a) is also corrected: fXf_{X} is set to uX∨zu_{X}\lor z, and fZf_{Z} is specified as uZ∨(w⊕uZ​Y)u_{Z}\lor(w\oplus u_{ZY}). Finally, Sec. 6.6 uses distinct realizable parent-input assignments, corrected ctf-POMIS arm counts, and a ctf-MIS baseline that includes nested actions. Its action counts and regret results replace those in Tables 1 and 2 of Park and Lee (2026a).

6.1 Background: Counterfactuals and Realizability

6.1.1 Counterfactual Distributions

We use the SCM, submodel, and PCH notation of Sec. 2. The counterfactual X𝐰​(𝐮)X_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{u}) evaluates XX in the submodel ℳ𝐰\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{w}}. Its random counterpart is X𝐰=X𝐰​(𝐔)X_{\mathbf{w}}=X_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{U}). Layer 3 of the PCH permits joint events involving counterfactuals from several such submodels. All counterfactuals are evaluated at the same exogenous realization (Bareinboim et al., 2022).

Definition 0 (Counterfactual distribution (Bareinboim et al., 2022)).

An SCM ℳ\mathcal{M} induces joint distributions over counterfactual events by:

P⁡(𝐲𝐱,⋯,𝐳𝐰)=∑𝐮𝟙​{𝐘𝐱​(𝐮)=𝐲,⋯,𝐙𝐰​(𝐮)=𝐳}​P​(𝐮).\displaystyle P(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{x}},\cdots,\mathbf{z}_{\mathbf{w}})=\sum_{\mathbf{u}}\mathds{1}\{\mathbf{Y}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{y},\cdots,\mathbf{Z}_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{z}\}P(\mathbf{u}). (175)

Shared exogenous inputs preserve the dependence between counterfactuals, including dependence induced by unobserved confounders. In the clinical example, WxW_{x} and Zx′Z_{x^{\prime}} describe two assessments of one patient under different reports. Separately sampling patients for the two assessments generally produces a different joint distribution. A fully specified SCM determines the joint counterfactual distribution, but its semantic definition alone supplies neither an identification formula from available data nor an experiment that measures the counterfactuals.

We write a collection of counterfactuals as 𝐗∗={Xi⁡[𝐰i]}i=1k\mathbf{X}_{\ast}=\{X_{i[\mathbf{w}_{i}]}\}_{i=1}^{k} and its targets as 𝐗=𝐕⁡(𝐗∗)={Xi}i=1k\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{X}_{\ast})=\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}. The brackets separate the variable index ii from its subscript assignment, and the symbol ∗\ast indexes the collection of counterfactual subscripts. Targets are distinct and exclude YY; every specified counterfactual has a nonempty subscript set. For example, 𝐗∗={Wx,Zx′}\mathbf{X}_{\ast}=\{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}\} has target set 𝐗={W,Z}\mathbf{X}=\{W,Z\}. Different terms may use different values, including x≠x′x\neq x^{\prime}. Within a single counterfactual ZwZ_{w}, however, the same assignment ww is used throughout its defining submodel.

Nested counterfactuals.

Counterfactuals can themselves supply the values of an intervention. For instance, Y𝐙𝐱​(𝐮)Y_{\mathbf{Z}_{\mathbf{x}}}(\mathbf{u}), equivalently Y𝐙=𝐙𝐱​(𝐮)​(𝐮)Y_{\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{Z}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{u})}(\mathbf{u}), first computes 𝐙𝐱​(𝐮)\mathbf{Z}_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{u}) and then substitutes those values for 𝐙\mathbf{Z} in the mechanism for the outer counterfactual (Correa et al., 2021). The inner and outer counterfactuals use the same 𝐮\mathbf{u} even though they may be evaluated under different interventions. More generally, Y𝐗∗​(𝐮)Y_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast}}(\mathbf{u}) evaluates the specified counterfactuals and substitutes their values for the corresponding targets.

We write 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} when the assigned counterfactuals may themselves have counterfactuals in their subscripts. The double asterisk allows arbitrary nesting and includes 𝐗∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast} as a special case. This distinction concerns the assigned counterfactuals; the reward Y𝐗∗Y_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast}} already involves a counterfactual substitution.

Counterfactual calculus.

The ctf-calculus provides rules for manipulating counterfactual probability quantities (Correa and Bareinboim, 2025). We recall the consistency and exclusion rules used below.

CTF-Rule 1 (Consistency).  Once a counterfactual already takes the value 𝐱\mathbf{x}, explicitly setting it to that same value does not change the remaining counterfactuals:

P⁡(𝐲𝐓∗⁣∗,𝐱,𝐱𝐓∗⁣∗,𝐰∗)=P⁡(𝐲𝐓∗⁣∗,𝐱𝐓∗⁣∗,𝐰∗)\displaystyle P(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{T}_{\ast\ast},\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{T}_{\ast\ast}},\mathbf{w}_{\ast})=P(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{T}_{\ast\ast}},\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{T}_{\ast\ast}},\mathbf{w}_{\ast}) (176)

This rule allows a computed counterfactual to replace an explicit assignment when their values agree.

The extension from 𝐓∗\mathbf{T}_{\ast} in the original rule to 𝐓∗⁣∗\mathbf{T}_{\ast\ast} follows from unit-level composition: at a fixed exogenous realization 𝐮\mathbf{u}, evaluate the nested assignments recursively, apply consistency to the resulting values, and then average over 𝐮\mathbf{u}. All nested counterfactuals use that same exogenous realization.

CTF-Rule 3 (Exclusion).  An assignment can be removed when its variables cannot affect the counterfactual after the other interventions:

P⁡(𝐲𝐱𝐳,𝐰∗)=P⁡(𝐲𝐳,𝐰∗), if ​𝐗∩𝙰𝚗​(𝐘)𝒢𝐙¯=∅.\displaystyle P(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{w}_{\ast})=P(\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{w}_{\ast}),\qquad\text{~if~}\mathbf{X}\cap\mathtt{An}(\mathbf{Y})_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{Z}}}}=\emptyset. (177)

The ancestor condition is checked after cutting the incoming edges of 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. In the clinical example, fixing both WW and ZZ blocks every directed path from XX to YY, so an additional assignment to XX cannot change Yw​zY_{wz}. Consistency and exclusion will be used to identify counterfactual assignments that do not change the reward.

Counterfactual unnesting theorem.

Nested distributions can also be expanded into joint events involving counterfactuals with less nesting. This is useful because each term then states explicitly which values must occur together on the same unit.

Lemma 0 (Counterfactual Unnesting Theorem (CUT); Theorem 4 in Correa et al. (2021)).

For a collection of counterfactuals 𝐓∗⁣∗\mathbf{T}_{\ast\ast}:

P⁡(Y𝐓∗⁣∗,X𝐳=y)=∑xP⁡(Y𝐓∗⁣∗,x=y,X𝐳=x).\displaystyle P(Y_{\mathbf{T}_{\ast\ast},X_{\mathbf{z}}}=y)=\sum_{x}P(Y_{\mathbf{T}_{\ast\ast},{x}}=y,X_{\mathbf{z}}={x}). (178)

For example, applying CUT to the two assessments gives:

P⁡(YWx,Zx′=y)=∑w​zP⁡(Yw​z=y,Wx=w,Zx′=z).\displaystyle P(Y_{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}}=y)=\sum_{wz}P(Y_{wz}=y,W_{x}=w,Z_{x^{\prime}}=z). (179)

For each possible pair w,zw,z, the event requires both assessments to produce that pair and the outcome under those values to equal yy. Summing over the pairs recovers the nested distribution. These counterfactuals cannot generally be sampled independently because they retain the same exogenous realization. CUT is an identity between distributions; the expansion alone does not supply an experiment for the joint events or a single unnested action equivalent to the nested regime.

6.1.2 Realizability

Throughout this section, endogenous variables have finite discrete domains, as in Raghavan and Bareinboim (2025). These domains are fixed within each bandit instance but may vary across the compatible SCMs used in a graphical characterization, as specified in Sec. 3. The exogenous variables may have general distributions.

Experimental capabilities.

Layer 1 distributions can be sampled through passive observation of the system’s natural behavior. Layer 2 distributions require interventions, such as Fisherian randomization (Fisher, 1935). Counterfactual randomization further permits changing the value transmitted to selected child mechanisms while allowing other children to receive the original value (Raghavan and Bareinboim, 2025).

Definition 0 (Feasible operations).

An operation collection 𝔸\mathbb{A} specifies which of the following physical operations are available:

  • 1.

    Select: select a unit from the target population.

  • 2.

    Read(V)(V): observe the output of the mechanism generating VV on that unit.

  • 3.

    Rand(X)(X): replace the natural mechanism of XX by an externally randomized value whose support is ΩX\Omega_{X}.

  • 4.

    ctf-Rand(X→𝐙)(X\to\mathbf{Z}): randomize the value of XX received by selected directed children 𝐙⊆𝙲𝚑​(X)𝒢\mathbf{Z}\subseteq\mathtt{Ch}(X)_{\mathcal{G}}, using suitable counterfactual mediators.

A counterfactual mediator for X→ZX\to Z is a manipulable interface through which fZf_{Z} receives the information about XX. Its ordinary states must encode XX so that the input received by fZf_{Z} agrees with the original mechanism; changing the interface reproduces the intended alternative input. The reporting interface plays this role in the introductory example. Availability of such an interface is an experimental capability assumption: observing the edge X→ZX\to Z alone does not establish it. The formal mediator conditions are given by Raghavan and Bareinboim (2025).

Realizability.

Counterfactual semantics specify a counterfactual even when no available experiment can measure it. Realizability asks whether physical operations can produce samples from the required distribution, including the dependence among counterfactuals on the same unit.

Definition 0 (Realizability).

A counterfactual distribution is realizable from 𝔸\mathbb{A} if operations in 𝔸\mathbb{A} produce samples from it for every SCM conforming to 𝒢\mathcal{G} and the specified experimental capabilities.

Throughout this section, we use the maximal collection 𝔸†\mathbb{A}^{\dagger}, which permits the operations above at every relevant variable and parent-child interface. Each external randomizer assigns positive probability to every value in the corresponding finite domain. The randomizers for separately selected inputs are independent of one another and of the unit’s exogenous variables. Assigned inputs can therefore be obtained by retaining units whose randomized inputs match the selected assignment. Retention depends only on these randomized inputs. As in Sec. 3, each bandit round uses a fresh independent retained unit. Discarded randomization attempts are outside the round count. Even with these capabilities, a mechanism cannot be evaluated twice under conflicting inputs on the same unit. Different reports sent to different mechanisms, as in WxW_{x} and Zx′Z_{x^{\prime}} in the clinical example, are allowed. The difficulty arises when the requested counterfactuals require two different versions of the same mechanism. Counterfactual ancestors make these requirements explicit.

Counterfactual ancestors.

Before listing required mechanisms, we simplify the counterfactuals. Effectiveness gives Xx​𝐰=xX_{x\mathbf{w}}=x, so a directly assigned constant requires no evaluation of fXf_{X}. For other counterfactuals, interventional minimization removes assignments that cannot affect the counterfactual (Correa et al., 2021):

∥X𝐰∥=X𝐰∩𝙰𝚗​(X)𝒢𝐖¯.\displaystyle\lVert X_{\mathbf{w}}\rVert=X_{\mathbf{w}\cap\mathtt{An}(X)_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{W}}}}}. (180)

For a collection, ∥𝐗∗∥\lVert\mathbf{X}_{\ast}\rVert applies this operation to each term. We apply this simplification before checking realizability.

The counterfactual ancestors of X𝐰X_{\mathbf{w}}, denoted 𝙰𝚗​(X𝐰)𝒢\mathtt{An}(X_{\mathbf{w}})_{\mathcal{G}}, record the counterfactuals needed to compute it. A counterfactual T𝐳T_{\mathbf{z}} belongs to this set when:

  • 1.

    T∈𝙰𝚗​(X)𝒢𝐖¯∖𝐖T\in\mathtt{An}(X)_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{W}}}}\setminus\mathbf{W}, and

  • 2.

    𝐳=𝐰∩𝙰𝚗​(T)𝒢𝐖¯\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{w}\cap\mathtt{An}(T)_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{W}}}}.

The first condition traces the mechanisms that remain upstream of XX after fixing 𝐖\mathbf{W}. The second retains only the assignments that can affect each such mechanism. For a collection, 𝙰𝚗​(𝐗∗)𝒢\mathtt{An}(\mathbf{X}_{\ast})_{\mathcal{G}} is the union of the counterfactual ancestor sets of its terms. Natural variables may occur as intermediate ancestors; they need not be among the assigned counterfactuals. Two required versions conflict when their subscript assignments differ after interventional minimization, including the variables to which those assignments apply.

For instance, the causal diagram in Fig. 29(a) with 𝐗∗={Wx,Zx′}\mathbf{X}_{\ast}=\{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}\} gives:

𝙰𝚗​(𝐗∗)𝒢\displaystyle\mathtt{An}(\mathbf{X}_{\ast})_{\mathcal{G}} =𝙰𝚗​(Wx)𝒢∪𝙰𝚗​(Zx′)𝒢\displaystyle=\mathtt{An}(W_{x})_{\mathcal{G}}\cup\mathtt{An}(Z_{x^{\prime}})_{\mathcal{G}} (181)
={Wx,Zx}∪{Zx′}={Wx,Zx,Zx′}.\displaystyle=\{W_{x},Z_{x}\}\cup\{Z_{x^{\prime}}\}=\{W_{x},Z_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}\}. (182)

Computing WxW_{x} first requires ZxZ_{x}, because ZZ lies between XX and WW. The separate counterfactual Zx′Z_{x^{\prime}} then asks for a second version of ZZ. If x′=xx^{\prime}=x, these requirements coincide and one evaluation of fZf_{Z} supplies both. If x′≠xx^{\prime}\neq x, however, they require conflicting inputs to that mechanism. This leads to the graphical criterion below.

Lemma 0 (Realizability; Corollary 3.7 of Raghavan and Bareinboim (2025)).

Under 𝔸†\mathbb{A}^{\dagger}, a counterfactual distribution is realizable if and only if its ancestor set contains no conflicting required versions of the same mechanism.

Thus P⁡(Wx,Zx′)P(W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}) in Fig. 29(a) is not realizable when x≠x′x\neq x^{\prime}. The obstacle concerns producing both counterfactuals on one unit, even though either counterfactual can be measured separately.

For an action, realizability concerns the mechanisms actually required to evaluate its reward on the same unit, including the inner counterfactuals that the reward uses. In Fig. 29(b), ZwZ_{w} requires XwX_{w} as an input. However, the outer counterfactual YZwY_{Z_{w}} also receives the natural XX through the direct edge X→YX\to Y. Producing the required counterfactuals would therefore require both versions of XX. If the action instead supplies XwX_{w} to the outer reward as well, giving YXw,ZwY_{X_{w},Z_{w}}, the conflicting requirement disappears. This example explains why checking the assigned counterfactuals alone is insufficient: the complete nested evaluation determines which mechanisms are needed.

6.2 Counterfactual Structural Causal Bandits

We now formalize the counterfactual structural causal bandit (ctf-SCB) problem. As in Sec. 3, an agent interacts with a target system modeled by an SCM with a reward variable YY. The agent knows 𝒢\mathcal{G} and YY, while the structural functions and the exogenous distribution remain unknown. Traditional SCB (Lee and Bareinboim, 2018) optimizes the mean reward of an ordinary intervention:

μ𝐱=𝔼​Y𝐱=𝔼⁡[Y∣d​o​(𝐗=𝐱)].\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbb{E}Y_{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid do(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})]. (183)

A counterfactual action 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} can instead supply computed counterfactuals to the system. We write its mean reward as:

μ𝐗∗⁣∗=𝔼​Y𝐗∗⁣∗.\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}=\mathbb{E}Y_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}. (184)

When the action is given by counterfactual assignments, each Xi⁡[𝐰i]X_{i[\mathbf{w}_{i}]} is computed under the indicated submodel and substituted for its target XiX_{i}. The required mechanisms and the reward are evaluated on the same unit.

For concreteness, return to Fig. 28. The mean reward μx\mu_{x} is obtained by setting X=xX=x, whereas μWx,Zx′\mu_{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}} uses the physician’s counterfactual under xx and the AI counterfactual under x′x^{\prime}. Since WW and ZZ are the only children of XX in this graph, μx=μWx,Zx\mu_{x}=\mu_{W_{x},Z_{x}}. Indeed, setting X=xX=x sends xx to both assessments, and assigning xx separately to the two inputs produces the same reward. Allowing x′x^{\prime} to differ from xx makes additional decisions available. The ordinary intervention is recovered when both input values agree.

Parent inputs of counterfactual actions.

In the preceding example, counterfactuals describe the action. For computation, we describe the same experiment through the inputs received by each mechanism. At fXf_{X}, the map 𝚙𝚊⁡[X]\mathtt{pa}[X] records the parents whose inputs are assigned constants. Each selected input has a separately selectable value, and every other input receives the output of its parent’s mechanism on the same unit. Inputs to fYf_{Y} may also be fixed, while the reward mechanism itself is retained. Each required mechanism is evaluated once, in a topological order of 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

We use 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} for this counterfactual action specified by these inputs and Y𝐗∗⁣∗Y_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} for its reward. The parent-input specification preserves the constant inputs and counterfactual substitutions of the original action. Values within each counterfactual subscript remain unchanged. Inputs that cannot affect YY may be discarded.

Let ℳ𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} be the SCM obtained by fixing these selected parent arguments, retaining every other argument and the original exogenous inputs. Furthermore, let 𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} be a graph obtained from 𝒢\mathcal{G} by deleting W→VW\to V whenever a required evaluation of fVf_{V} receives a constant in place of its WW argument. All vertices, other directed edges, and bidirected edges are retained.

A directed path in 𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} therefore follows inputs that still receive their parent’s computed counterfactual. In particular, a vertex loses a parent precisely when that incoming edge is replaced by a constant input.

Definition 0 (Action space).

The action space 𝒜ctf\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}} consists of all counterfactual actions realizable under 𝔸†\mathbb{A}^{\dagger}, with their selected input values specified.

This space includes realizable nested counterfactual actions. Their constant inputs can be recorded at the receiving mechanisms, as established below.

Proposition 0.

Every realizable nested counterfactual action can be implemented by the parent-input choices described above.

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 78] Expand Y𝐗∗⁣∗Y_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} into its required structural equations, applying effectiveness and identifying equal counterfactuals. Realizability gives one evaluation of each required mechanism. Record in 𝚙𝚊⁡[X]\mathtt{pa}[X] every parent input fixed to a constant at fXf_{X}, retaining its value. All other arguments are outputs of parent mechanisms on the same unit. These choices define an action in 𝒜ctf\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}.

To compare the two evaluations, proceed in topological order. Each first required mechanism receives the same fixed inputs and exogenous realization in both evaluations, and hence produces the same output. At a subsequent mechanism, the parent outputs already agree, and the fixed inputs and exogenous realization also agree. Its output is therefore unchanged. Continuing to YY proves equality of the reward on every unit.

Constructing the SCM for a counterfactual action.

Alg. 9 starts from the original mechanisms and replaces only the selected parent arguments. Each remaining argument receives its parent’s output on the same unit, and every exogenous input is retained. Evaluating these mechanisms in topological order gives the intended reward Y𝐗∗⁣∗Y_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}. Selecting an input of fYf_{Y} changes that argument while leaving its other inputs available; the reward mechanism itself is retained.

The construction specifies how an action is evaluated in an SCM. As in the previous sections, the bandit agent need not know these mechanisms. Instead, it performs the corresponding experiment and observes the reward.

Counterfactual structural causal bandits objective.

As in Sec. 3, at round tt the agent chooses At∈𝒜ctfA_{t}\in\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}, performs the corresponding experiment on a fresh unit, and observes its reward YtY_{t}. Repeated selections provide samples for estimating the mean of that action, just as ordinary interventions do in SCB.

We use the best-action convention of Sec. 3: a superscript ∗\ast optimizes the subscript values of a fixed set of counterfactuals, and ⋆\star selects an optimal action over the entire space. The cumulative pseudo-regret is:

RT𝒜ctf=T​μ𝐗∗⁣∗⋆−∑t=1TμAt=∑𝐗∗⁣∗∈𝒜ctfΔ𝐗∗⁣∗​NT​(𝐗∗⁣∗),\displaystyle R_{T}^{\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}}=T\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\star}}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mu_{A_{t}}=\sum_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}\in\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}}\Delta_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}N_{T}(\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}), (185)

where Δ𝐗∗⁣∗=μ𝐗∗⁣∗⋆−μ𝐗∗⁣∗\Delta_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}=\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\star}}-\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} and NT​(𝐗∗⁣∗)N_{T}(\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}) counts the rounds t≤Tt\leq T with At=𝐗∗⁣∗A_{t}=\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}. The learning objective has the same form as before; the available experiments and the benchmark reward have been extended.

Corollary 0.

The optimal ordinary intervention cannot outperform the optimal counterfactual action, i.e., μ𝐱⋆≤μ𝐗∗⁣∗⋆\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}\leq\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\star}}.

{proof}

[Proof of Cor. 79] An ordinary intervention is obtained by assigning the same value to every outgoing input of each intervened variable. Hence its reward is represented in 𝒜ctf\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}.

A larger space can offer a higher reward, but it also gives the agent more actions to explore. The following sections use causal structure to reduce this exploration burden. We first ask when removing a counterfactual assignment leaves the reward unchanged, and then compare the best rewards attainable by non-equivalent counterfactual actions.

6.3 Equivalence among Actions

In Sec. 3, an ordinary intervention set is reduced by removing variables whose assigned values cannot affect the reward once the other interventions are in place. For example, if every directed path from ZZ to YY passes through an intervened variable WW, the additional assignment to ZZ does not change YY. An MIS retains the intervention variables needed to distinguish that intervention set from its proper subsets.

Counterfactual minimal intervention sets.

The same question arises for a set of counterfactuals 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} with outer targets 𝐗=𝐕⁡(𝐗∗⁣∗)\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}). Each target now receives a counterfactual, which may itself contain nested counterfactuals. Such an assignment can be redundant for two reasons:

  • 1.

    The target may have no remaining directed path to the reward.

  • 2.

    The counterfactuals assigned to the other targets may already induce the same counterfactual at that target.

We examine both possibilities using the consistency and exclusion rules of ctf-calculus.

We first apply effectiveness and interventional minimization within the nested counterfactuals. For the special case 𝐗∗={Xi⁡[𝐰i]}i\mathbf{X}_{\ast}=\{X_{i[\mathbf{w}_{i}]}\}_{i}, this gives 𝐗∗=∥𝐗∗∥\mathbf{X}_{\ast}=\lVert\mathbf{X}_{\ast}\rVert. We then ask whether the assignment to a target variable can be removed altogether. Retained counterfactuals keep all their inner substitutions and constant assignments. As in the MIS definition of Sec. 3, this comparison concerns an expression with variable assignments: retained terms keep their assignments, and equivalence must hold for all admissible values and all compatible SCMs.

Definition 0 (Counterfactual minimal intervention set).

A set of counterfactuals 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} is a counterfactual minimal intervention set (ctf-MIS) if no proper subset 𝐙∗⁣∗⊊𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{Z}_{\ast\ast}\subsetneq\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} satisfies μ𝐗∗⁣∗=μ𝐙∗⁣∗\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}=\mu_{\mathbf{Z}_{\ast\ast}} for every compatible SCM and every admissible subscript assignment.

Thus, deleting a term requires equality for every admissible assignment and every compatible SCM. The following examples show how the causal diagram can justify removing an assignment for all such values and SCMs.

For example, consider the causal diagram shown in Fig. 29(a), and take the realizable counterfactual 𝐗∗={Wx,Zx}\mathbf{X}_{\ast}=\{W_{x},Z_{x}\}. The two assigned counterfactuals use the same assignment xx. To generate the reward, the outer system receives WxW_{x} at WW and ZxZ_{x} at ZZ. However, once WW receives its assigned counterfactual, the value supplied separately at ZZ has no directed path to YY. CUT makes this explicit:

μWx,Zx\displaystyle\mu_{W_{x},Z_{x}} =∑y​w​zy​P​(yw​z,wx,zx)\displaystyle=\sum_{ywz}yP(y_{wz},w_{x},z_{x}) (186)
=∑y​w​zy​P​(yw,wx,zx)=∑y​wy​P​(yw,wx)=μWx.\displaystyle=\sum_{ywz}yP(y_{w},w_{x},z_{x})=\sum_{yw}yP(y_{w},w_{x})=\mu_{W_{x}}. (187)

The second line uses ctf-Rule 3 and then sums over zz. Removing the outer assignment ZxZ_{x} still leaves the evaluation of ZxZ_{x} needed inside the submodel that computes WxW_{x}. It is the separate assignment at the outer target ZZ that is redundant. Therefore {Wx,Zx}\{W_{x},Z_{x}\} is not a ctf-MIS.

In Fig. 29(b), consider 𝐗∗={Xw,Zw′}\mathbf{X}_{\ast}=\{X_{w},Z_{w^{\prime}}\}. Both targets have directed edges to YY, so neither is excluded by the ordinary MIS condition. Nevertheless, computing Zw′Z_{w^{\prime}} requires Xw′X_{w^{\prime}}, while the first assignment requires XwX_{w}. Realizability therefore requires w′=ww^{\prime}=w.

With this shared value, assigning XwX_{w} already makes ZZ behave as ZwZ_{w} since the only directed path from WW to ZZ passes through XX. ctf-Rule 1 permits substituting XwX_{w} into the submodel for ZwZ_{w}, and ctf-Rule 3 then removes the assignment to WW: Zw=Zw,Xw=ZXwZ_{w}=Z_{w,X_{w}}=Z_{X_{w}} and thus YXw,Zw=YXwY_{X_{w},Z_{w}}=Y_{X_{w}}.

The other parent TT of ZZ retains its natural value on the same unit in both evaluations. Thus every admissible assignment satisfies μXw,Zw=μXw\mu_{X_{w},Z_{w}}=\mu_{X_{w}}, and the assignment ZwZ_{w} can be removed even though ZZ has a directed edge to YY.

Graphical characterization for CTF-MISs.

Throughout the remainder of this section, we assume that 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} is realizable and every assigned counterfactual is nonconstant, i.e., after effectiveness, it still requires its target mechanism. Constant values are free apart from equalities required by realizability.

The graph 𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} deletes the directed edges replaced by constant inputs. Thus a vertex VV receives a fixed input exactly when its parent set in this graph is strictly smaller than in 𝒢\mathcal{G}. In the second condition below, deleting the other outer targets from this graph ensures that the entire path, including its starting vertex, avoids those targets.

Theorem 81 (Graphical characterization of ctf-MIS).

A counterfactual action 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} is a ctf-MIS if and only if the following two conditions hold:

  • 1.

    𝐗⊆𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢𝐗¯\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}}.

  • 2.

    For every Xi∈𝐗X_{i}\in\mathbf{X}, there exists V∈𝙰𝚗​(Xi)𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗∖(𝐗∖{Xi})V\in\mathtt{An}(X_{i})_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}\setminus(\mathbf{X}\setminus\{X_{i}\})} such that
    𝙿𝚊​(V)𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗⊊𝙿𝚊​(V)𝒢\mathtt{Pa}(V)_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}}\subsetneq\mathtt{Pa}(V)_{\mathcal{G}}.

The proof is given in Sec. H.0.1. The first condition is the ordinary MIS condition applied to the outer target set 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Each target must have a directed path to YY that avoids the other targets. In the first example, ZZ fails this test because its only path to YY passes through WW. In contrast, {Wx,Zx′}\{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}\} in Fig. 30(a) has the two paths W→T→YW\to T\to Y and Z→R→YZ\to R\to Y. Therefore, both targets satisfy the first condition.

The second condition traces the counterfactual’s computation in the other direction. A directed edge deleted from 𝒢\mathcal{G} must enter a vertex with a retained directed path to XiX_{i} avoiding every other outer target. The path may have length zero: a fixed input received by XiX_{i} itself suffices. A fixed input received only at another outer target does not suffice, because that target’s counterfactual is still supplied when the assignment to XiX_{i} is removed.

In the second example, the fixed input W→XW\to X enters XX. The counterfactual XwX_{w} therefore satisfies the second condition. For ZwZ_{w}, however, this input reaches ZZ only through the other target XX. Deleting XX from the graph removes that path, and ZwZ_{w} fails the condition. In contrast, for {Wx,Zx′}\{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}\} in Fig. 30(a), both WW and ZZ receive a fixed input directly, so both conditions hold.

Corollary 0.

For 𝐗∗={Xi⁡[𝐰i]}i\mathbf{X}_{\ast}=\{X_{i[\mathbf{w}_{i}]}\}_{i} satisfying the first condition, the second condition is equivalent to 𝐖i∩𝙰𝚗​(Xi)𝒢𝐗∖{Xi}¯≠∅\mathbf{W}_{i}\cap\mathtt{An}(X_{i})_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}\setminus\{X_{i}\}}}}\neq\emptyset for every XiX_{i}.

{proof}

[Proof of Cor. 82] The first condition in Thm. 81 ensures that every assigned target computation is required by the reward. For the second condition, suppose a vertex of 𝐖i\mathbf{W}_{i} has a directed path to XiX_{i} in 𝒢𝐗∖{Xi}¯\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}\setminus\{X_{i}\}}}. Take the last vertex of 𝐖i\mathbf{W}_{i} on this path. Its input to the next mechanism is fixed, whereas the remaining path to XiX_{i} contains no further subscript intervention or other outer target. Realizability preserves these inputs in 𝒢𝐗∗\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast}}, giving the mechanism and path required by the general condition.

Conversely, a fixed input received by a mechanism on such a path to XiX_{i} must be an assignment from 𝐖i\mathbf{W}_{i}: these are exactly the constants used in the submodel computing Xi⁡[𝐰i]X_{i[\mathbf{w}_{i}]}. Prepending that input edge to the path gives a directed path from 𝐖i\mathbf{W}_{i} to XiX_{i} whose internal vertices avoid the other outer targets. Consequently, the general condition is equivalent to 𝐖i∩𝙰𝚗​(Xi)𝒢𝐗∖{Xi}¯≠∅\mathbf{W}_{i}\cap\mathtt{An}(X_{i})_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}\setminus\{X_{i}\}}}}\neq\emptyset, proving the specialization.

Consider the causal diagram in Fig. 31(a) with 𝐗∗⁣∗={Xw,Zw′,Xw}\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}=\{X_{w},Z_{w^{\prime},X_{w}}\}. The first counterfactual gives fXf_{X} the input W=wW=w. The second gives fZf_{Z} the input W=w′W=w^{\prime} together with the previously computed XwX_{w}. Consequently, W→XW\to X and W→ZW\to Z are deleted, while X→ZX\to Z remains in 𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} (Fig. 31(b)). Both targets have a directed edge to YY and receive a fixed input themselves. Thus, 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} is a ctf-MIS.

Reducing an action to a CTF-MIS.

ctf-MISify (Alg. 10) applies these conditions to a supplied counterfactual set. It first removes all targets blocked from YY by other outer targets. A reverse search from YY, stopping at each outer target, identifies exactly the assignments to retain. It then examines each remaining target once, deleting its assignment if the second condition fails. The nested counterfactuals and constant values inside every retained term are unchanged.

Each deletion preserves the reward on every unit. The initial deletions are valid together: every path from an omitted target to YY meets a retained target. Moreover, these deletions preserve the required mechanism evaluations and their fixed inputs, so 𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} is unchanged. A target that passes either condition continues to pass after other targets are deleted, because its witnessing path remains available. Thus a single pass suffices, and the returned set satisfies both conditions.

Corollary 0.

ctf-MISify returns an equivalent and realizable ctf-MIS subset of its input.

{proof}

[Proof of Cor. 83] In the first step, every directed path from a discarded target to YY meets a retained target: the last outer target on that path satisfies the first condition. Thus these assignments can be removed together, while keeping every retained nested counterfactual unchanged.

By the necessity proof of Thm. 81, both deletion steps preserve the reward on every unit, for every compatible SCM and every admissible assignment. They also preserve the required mechanism evaluations and their fixed inputs. Hence realizability and the initially computed graph 𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} are preserved.

Deleting other outer targets cannot destroy a path witnessing either condition for a retained target. Therefore, a target that passes a condition continues to pass it throughout the algorithm. After the single pass, every remaining target satisfies both conditions. Therefore, Thm. 81 gives the conclusion.

Computational cost.

Let n=|𝐕|n=\lvert\mathbf{V}\rvert and mm be the number of edges in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and let k=|𝐗|+1k=\lvert\mathbf{X}\rvert+1 for the initial outer target set. Comparing the two graphs’ parent sets and performing the initial reverse search take 𝒪⁡(n+m)\mathcal{O}(n+m) time. Each remaining target requires at most one further reverse search, also taking 𝒪⁡(n+m)\mathcal{O}(n+m) time. Therefore ctf-MISify uses 𝒪⁡(k⁡(n+m))\mathcal{O}(k(n+m)) time and 𝒪⁡(n+m)\mathcal{O}(n+m) auxiliary space. These bounds concern the graphical reduction after the action graph has been formed; retained nested terms are reused without expanding them.

Equivalent CTF-MISs.

Different ctf-MISs can still describe the same input action even when neither target set contains the other. Two counterfactual sets are equivalent if every admissible subscript assignment to either set has a corresponding assignment to the other, independent of the SCM, that gives the same reward on every unit. To see this, consider the causal diagram shown in Fig. 30(a). The counterfactual sets {Tx,Zx′}\{T_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}\} and {Wx,Zx′}\{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}\} satisfy both ctf-MIS conditions. The first assigns TxT_{x} directly to TT; the second assigns WxW_{x} to WW, which induces the same counterfactual TxT_{x} through the mechanism for TT. In particular, WW receives the fixed input xx, and the retained path W→TW\to T avoids the other target ZZ. This verifies the second condition for TxT_{x}, and its edge T→YT\to Y verifies the first condition.

To compare the two actions, first compute WxW_{x} on a unit. Feeding this value into the unchanged mechanism for TT produces TxT_{x}. The counterfactual Zx′Z_{x^{\prime}} on the other branch is identical under both actions, as is the natural value of XX received directly by YY. Thus the reward mechanism receives the same inputs on the same unit. These substitutions give:

μTx,Zx′\displaystyle\mu_{T_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}} =∑y,t,zy​P​(yt​z,tx,zx′)\displaystyle=\sum_{y,t,z}yP(y_{tz},t_{x},z_{x^{\prime}}) CUT (188)
=∑y,t,z,wy​P​(yt​z,tx,zx′,wx)\displaystyle=\sum_{y,t,z,w}yP(y_{tz},t_{x},z_{x^{\prime}},w_{x}) marg. over WxW_{x} (189)
=∑y,t,z,wy​P​(yt​w​z,tw​x,zx′,wx)\displaystyle=\sum_{y,t,z,w}yP(y_{twz},t_{wx},z_{x^{\prime}},w_{x}) ctf-Rules 1 and 3 (190)
=∑y,t,z,wy​P​(yt​w​z,tw,zx′,wx)\displaystyle=\sum_{y,t,z,w}yP(y_{twz},t_{w},z_{x^{\prime}},w_{x}) ctf-Rule 3 (191)
=∑y,t,z,wy​P​(yt​w​z,tw​z,zx′,wx)\displaystyle=\sum_{y,t,z,w}yP(y_{twz},t_{wz},z_{x^{\prime}},w_{x}) ctf-Rule 3 (192)
=∑y,t,z,wy​P​(yw​z,tw​z,zx′,wx)\displaystyle=\sum_{y,t,z,w}yP(y_{wz},t_{wz},z_{x^{\prime}},w_{x}) ctf-Rule 1 (193)
=∑y,z,wy​P​(yw​z,zx′,wx)\displaystyle=\sum_{y,z,w}yP(y_{wz},z_{x^{\prime}},w_{x}) sum. over Tw​zT_{wz} (194)
=μWx,Zx′.\displaystyle=\mu_{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}}. CUT (195)

Similarly, {Tx,Rx′}\{T_{x},R_{x^{\prime}}\} has the same reward. These ctf-MISs assign the same inputs xx on X→WX\to W and x′x^{\prime} on X→ZX\to Z, as shown in Fig. 30(b). The action space 𝒜ctf\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}} identifies these sets through their common input choices.

6.4 Counterfactual Possibly-Optimal Minimal Intervention Sets

The preceding section identifies redundant outer assignments in a realizable set 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}. Removing these assignments preserves the reward for every admissible choice of values. We now compare non-equivalent counterfactual actions after optimizing their subscript values. As in Sec. 3, the causal diagram can imply that one optimized counterfactual always performs at least as well as another, regardless of the parameterization of the underlying SCM. These partial-order relations allow the agent to exclude further actions before estimating their rewards.

From ordinary interventions to counterfactual interventions.

First consider ordinary interventions in the causal diagram of Fig. 32(a). Let w∗w^{\ast} maximize the reward under d​o​(W=w)do(W=w), and choose w†w^{\dagger} to maximize μWw∗,Zw\mu_{W_{w^{\ast}},Z_{w}}. Choosing w=w∗w=w^{\ast} in {Ww∗,Zw}\{W_{w^{\ast}},Z_{w}\} reproduces the ordinary intervention by effectiveness and ctf-Rule 1. Hence:

μw∗=μWw∗,Zw∗≤μWw∗,Zw†.\displaystyle\mu_{w^{\ast}}=\mu_{W_{w^{\ast}},Z_{w^{\ast}}}\leq\mu_{W_{w^{\ast}},Z_{w^{\dagger}}}. (196)

The action {Ww∗,Zw∗}\{W_{w^{\ast}},Z_{w^{\ast}}\} sends the same value to both children of WW. In contrast, for {Ww∗,Zw†}\{W_{w^{\ast}},Z_{w^{\dagger}}\}, the input received directly by YY remains w∗w^{\ast}, while ZZ may listen to w†w^{\dagger}. The best reward cannot decrease, since the choice w†=w∗w^{\dagger}=w^{\ast} is still available. A different value may improve the reward, depending on the underlying mechanisms.

For a concrete example, consider the following binary SCM with independent exogenous variables:

ℳ={𝐔={UW,UZ,UX,UY,UZ​Y}𝐕={W,Z,X,Y}ℱ={fW​(uW)=uWfZ​(w,uZ,uZ​Y)=uZ∨(w⊕uZ​Y)fX​(z,uX)=uX∨zfY​(w,x,uY,uZ​Y)=1−(uY⊕uZ​Y⊕x⊕(1−w))P⁡(𝐔)={U∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.1):∀U∈𝐔}.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{U}=\{U_{W},U_{Z},U_{X},U_{Y},U_{ZY}\}\\ \mathbf{V}=\{W,Z,X,Y\}\\ \mathcal{F}=\begin{cases}f_{W}(u_{W})=u_{W}\\ f_{Z}(w,u_{Z},u_{ZY})=u_{Z}\lor(w\oplus u_{ZY})\\ f_{X}(z,u_{X})=u_{X}\lor z\\ f_{Y}(w,x,u_{Y},u_{ZY})=1-(u_{Y}\oplus u_{ZY}\oplus x\oplus(1-w))\\ \end{cases}\\ P(\mathbf{U})=\{U\thicksim\mathtt{Bern}(0.1):\forall U\in\mathbf{U}\}.\end{cases} (197)

Then w∗=0w^{\ast}=0 and w†=1w^{\dagger}=1 give:

μ∅=0.22464<μw∗=0.2368<μWw∗,Zw†=0.8848.\displaystyle\mu_{\emptyset}=0.22464<\mu_{w^{\ast}}=0.2368<\mu_{W_{w^{\ast}},Z_{w^{\dagger}}}=0.8848. (198)

The first increase is obtained by replacing the natural value of WW with its best constant. The much larger second increase is obtained by keeping this zero at the input of YY and sending one to the input of ZZ, as in Fig. 32(b).

Counterfactual possibly-optimal minimal intervention sets.

We now extend possible optimality from Sec. 3 to counterfactuals. The comparisons below concern counterfactual sets with each retained parent input independently selectable; equivalent sets are treated as the same action.

Definition 0 (Counterfactual possibly-optimal minimal intervention set).

A counterfactual action 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} is a ctf-POMIS if there exists an SCM conforming to 𝒢\mathcal{G} such that μ𝐗∗⁣∗∗>μ𝐙∗⁣∗∗\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\ast}}>\mu_{\mathbf{Z}_{\ast\ast}^{\ast}} for every non-equivalent counterfactual action 𝐙∗⁣∗\mathbf{Z}_{\ast\ast}.

For a retained counterfactual set, one compatible SCM makes its best subscript assignment outperform every assignment to any set that is not equivalent to it. Several counterfactual sets may satisfy this condition, with different SCMs establishing their possible optimality. The agent must still learn their rewards to determine which action is best in the actual environment.

6.4.1 CTF-POMIS under Unconfounded Rewards

We first consider the case in which the exogenous inputs of YY are independent of those generating its other ancestors. For any upstream intervention, the reward mechanism receives values from its parents. These values may be random. The agent can instead supply a fixed assignment directly to the same parent inputs. If conditioning on the received values does not change the distribution of the reward’s exogenous inputs, the resulting mean is a weighted average of the means under these direct assignments. Choosing the best parent assignment is therefore at least as good as that average.

Fig. 33 illustrates this comparison. An upstream intervention changes the distribution of the inputs reaching YY. An intervention on 𝙿𝚊​(Y)𝒢\mathtt{Pa}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}} can instead fix those inputs to the values most favorable to the reward.

Proposition 0.

If YY is not confounded with 𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢∖{Y}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}}\setminus\{Y\}, the ordinary intervention set 𝙿𝚊​(Y)𝒢\mathtt{Pa}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}} is the only ctf-POMIS up to equivalence.

The proof is given in Sec. H.0.2.

Corollary 0.

If 𝒢\mathcal{G} is Markovian, meaning that it has no bidirected edges, the ordinary intervention set 𝙿𝚊​(Y)𝒢\mathtt{Pa}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}} is the only ctf-POMIS up to equivalence.

{proof}

[Proof of Cor. 86] Prop. 85 applies because a Markovian diagram has no unobserved confounding.

Thus, in the Markovian case it suffices to intervene on the parents of YY. With unobserved confounding, a parent counterfactual may carry information about the exogenous inputs of the reward. Fixing that parent to a constant removes this dependence, so the preceding averaging argument need not apply. For example, in Fig. 32, the best ordinary intervention on the parents 𝙿𝚊​(Y)𝒢={W,X}\mathtt{Pa}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}}=\{W,X\} has mean 0.820.82, below the mean 0.88480.8848 of {Ww∗,Zw†}\{W_{w^{\ast}},Z_{w^{\dagger}}\}.

6.4.2 Graphical Characterization of CTF-POMISs
Counterfactual regime graph.

Recall that ℳ𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} fixes the selected parent inputs, and its graph 𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} deletes the corresponding directed edges while retaining the bidirected edges. We now define ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗≜𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗​[𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗]\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}\triangleq\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}[\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}}].

For concreteness, consider the causal diagram in Fig. 34(a) and the action 𝐗∗⁣∗={Wx,Zx′}\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}=\{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}\}. The two counterfactuals assign separate inputs from XX, giving the substitutions fW​(X,𝐔W)⇒fW​(x,𝐔W)f_{W}(X,\mathbf{U}_{W})\Rightarrow f_{W}(x,\mathbf{U}_{W}) and fZ​(X,𝐔Z)⇒fZ​(x′,𝐔Z)f_{Z}(X,\mathbf{U}_{Z})\Rightarrow f_{Z}(x^{\prime},\mathbf{U}_{Z}), respectively. Consequently, X→WX\to W and X→ZX\to Z are deleted. The natural output of XX no longer reaches YY. Hence, the ancestral restriction removes XX, as illustrated in Fig. 34(b).

Figs. 34(b), 34(c), 34(d) and 34(e) show how the same construction changes with the action. Under 𝐗∗⁣∗={Tx}\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}=\{T_{x}\} in Fig. 34(c), only the input X→WX\to W is fixed to produce TxT_{x}, while the natural value of XX still reaches YY through ZZ and RR. Under 𝐗∗⁣∗={Rx}\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}=\{R_{x}\} in Fig. 34(d), only X→ZX\to Z is fixed, while X→W→T→YX\to W\to T\to Y remains. Thus XX is retained in both graphs. Under 𝐗∗⁣∗={Rz}\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}=\{R_{z}\} in Fig. 34(e), the substitution is instead fR​(Z,𝐔R)⇒fR​(z,𝐔R)f_{R}(Z,\mathbf{U}_{R})\Rightarrow f_{R}(z,\mathbf{U}_{R}). This removes Z→RZ\to R and makes the natural output of ZZ irrelevant to YY. Its vertex is omitted, while the exogenous inputs of RR remain unchanged.

MUCT and IB for counterfactual actions.

We reuse the c-components, minimal unobserved confounders’ territory 𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳\mathsf{MUCT}, and interventional border 𝖨𝖡\mathsf{IB} from Definitions 26 and 27. For 𝐗∗⁣∗={Wx,Zx′}\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}=\{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}\} in Fig. 34(b), the c-component containing YY is 𝖼𝖼​(Y)ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗={Y,R,Z,W}\mathsf{cc}(Y)_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}}=\{Y,R,Z,W\}. Including descendants adds TT, thus:

For 𝐗∗⁣∗={Wx,Zx′}\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}=\{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}\}, 𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗,Y)={W,Z,T,R,Y}\displaystyle\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}},Y)=\{W,Z,T,R,Y\} (199)
⇒𝖨𝖡⁡(ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗,Y)=∅.\displaystyle\Rightarrow\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}},Y)=\emptyset. (200)

In Figs. 34(c) and 34(d), the retained bidirected connection X↔ZX\leftrightarrow Z also includes XX in the c-component of YY. Adding TT by descendant closure therefore gives all six vertices, again leaving an empty border.

In contrast, consider 𝐗∗⁣∗={Rz}\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}=\{R_{z}\} in Fig. 34(e). After removing ZZ, we obtain 𝖼𝖼​(Y)ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗={Y,R,W}\mathsf{cc}(Y)_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}}=\{Y,R,W\}. Including descendants adds TT, and neither closure operation adds XX. Thus:

For 𝐗∗⁣∗={Rz}\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}=\{R_{z}\}, 𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗,Y)={W,T,R,Y}\displaystyle\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}},Y)=\{W,T,R,Y\} (201)
⇒𝖨𝖡⁡(ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗,Y)={X}.\displaystyle\Rightarrow\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}},Y)=\{X\}. (202)

The remaining input from XX enters the territory through WW. Fixing it to xx adds the counterfactual WxW_{x} to the action. Since the territory’s exogenous inputs are independent of those generating XX, conditioning on X=xX=x gives the same reward mean as supplying this value directly. Hence:

μRz\displaystyle\mu_{R_{z}} =∑x𝔼⁡[YRz∣X=x]​P​(x)\displaystyle=\sum_{x}\mathbb{E}[Y_{R_{z}}\mid X=x]P(x) (203)
=∑xμRz,Wx​P​(x)≤μ{Rz,Wx}∗.\displaystyle=\sum_{x}\mu_{R_{z},W_{x}}P(x)\leq\mu_{\{R_{z},W_{x}\}^{\ast}}. (204)

This shows why a nonempty border provides an additional input choice that weakly improves the best reward. An empty border leaves no such external input to fix. These examples suggest that possible optimality can be characterized by the absence of an interventional border.

Theorem 87 (Graphical characterization of ctf-POMIS).

A counterfactual action 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} is a ctf-POMIS with respect to ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle if and only if 𝖨𝖡⁡(ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗,Y)=∅\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}},Y)=\emptyset.

The proof is given in Sec. H.0.3. When the border is nonempty, fixing its inputs gives a counterfactual action whose optimized mean is at least as large. When the border is empty, the retained mechanisms and shared exogenous inputs can make this counterfactual uniquely optimal up to equivalence.

When YY is unconfounded with its ancestors, its minimal UC-territory is {Y}\{Y\}. Its border is empty precisely when every incoming reward argument has been fixed. These counterfactuals are equivalent to intervening on 𝙿𝚊​(Y)𝒢\mathtt{Pa}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}}.

6.5 Enumerating the CTF-POMIS Action Space

The graphical characterization in Thm. 87 identifies counterfactual sets that can be optimal. As in the preceding sections, their subscript assignments are then treated as actions.

Enumerating counterfactual sets.

Alg. 11 enumerates each choice of children in ℋ=𝒢⁡[𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢]\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{G}[\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}}]. For a parent WW, the choice 𝐗W⊆𝙲𝚑​(W)ℋ\mathbf{X}_{W}\subseteq\mathtt{Ch}(W)_{\mathcal{H}} lists the mechanisms that will receive a fixed value in place of their input from WW. The map 𝚙𝚊⁡[X]\mathtt{pa}[X] collects these choices at the receiving mechanism fXf_{X}. Thus the children choices enumerate the selected edges, and 𝚙𝚊⁡[X]\mathtt{pa}[X] records how to execute the resulting action. Deleting those edges gives the graph of the remaining causal dependence. Restricting this graph to the ancestors of YY then removes mechanisms that cannot affect the reward.

An accepted choice.

Consider the causal diagram in Fig. 34(a). Choose 𝐗X={W,Z}\mathbf{X}_{X}=\{W,Z\} and choose no children for the other parents. The resulting map has 𝚙𝚊⁡[W]=𝚙𝚊⁡[Z]={X}\mathtt{pa}[W]=\mathtt{pa}[Z]=\{X\}, with every other entry empty. The algorithm deletes X→WX\to W and X→ZX\to Z. Since XX then has no directed path to YY, the ancestral restriction removes XX, giving Fig. 34(b). Both selected inputs remain in the specification: their receiving mechanisms, fWf_{W} and fZf_{Z}, still affect YY. The rule for pruning a selected input therefore concerns its receiving mechanism, even when its source vertex has disappeared from the graph.

The retained graph has an empty interventional border, so this choice is returned. Assigning xx to the input of fWf_{W} and x′x^{\prime} to the input of fZf_{Z} gives the counterfactuals {Wx,Zx′}\{W_{x},Z_{x^{\prime}}\}. These two values are independently selectable.

A rejected choice and a redundant specification.

Now choose only 𝐗Z={R}\mathbf{X}_{Z}=\{R\}. This gives 𝚙𝚊⁡[R]={Z}\mathtt{pa}[R]=\{Z\} and, after assigning its value, the action {Rz}\{R_{z}\}. Cutting Z→RZ\to R removes ZZ from the reward ancestry but retains its fixed input at fRf_{R}. The resulting graph is Fig. 34(e). Since its border is not empty, the algorithm rejects this counterfactual. Adding the choice 𝐗X={W}\mathbf{X}_{X}=\{W\} fixes the remaining input from this border into the territory. The resulting counterfactual set {Wx,Rz}\{W_{x},R_{z}\} has empty border and is returned.

If a retained specification passes the condition of Thm. 87, the algorithm returns it only once, regardless of how many original choices produce it. The returned action 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} retains its selected-input specification and may contain nested counterfactuals. All subscript assignments of these returned counterfactuals form 𝒜ctf⋆\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}^{\star}.

Theorem 88.

Alg. 11 returns exactly the ctf-POMISs with respect to ⟨𝒢,Y⟩\langle\mathcal{G},Y\rangle.

{proof}

[Proof of Thm. 88] Every selection of parent inputs occurs in the children-choice loop. Deleting its selected edges and restricting to the ancestors of YY gives exactly ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}. Removing fixed inputs at mechanisms outside this ancestral graph preserves the reward counterfactual on every unit, and each remaining selected input can affect YY along an uncut path. The characterization in Thm. 87 therefore accepts exactly the ctf-POMISs. Identifying repeated specifications changes no available action.

Corollary 0.

No two counterfactual sets returned by Alg. 11 are equivalent.

{proof}

[Proof of Cor. 89] The final check compares all retained entries 𝚙𝚊⁡[X]\mathtt{pa}[X] and returns each map once. It remains to show that distinct retained maps are not equivalent.

Choose an edge selected in one map but not the other. Its receiving child has a retained directed path to YY in the first map. If the other map retains this entire path, the chosen edge is followed by a path retained in both maps. Otherwise, take the last edge of that path selected by the other map. Again, the edge is fixed in one map and retained in the other, and its remaining path to YY is retained in both.

Choose a binary SCM in which the source of this edge outputs a private 𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(12)\mathtt{Bern}(\frac{1}{2}) variable, and each mechanism along the edge and remaining path copies the preceding variable. Other inputs do not affect these mechanisms. Fixing the edge then gives a constant reward, whereas retaining it gives a non-constant reward on the same units, regardless of the other selected values. Thus the two maps cannot be equivalent.

Corollary 0.

For every SCM compatible with 𝒢\mathcal{G}:

max𝐗∗⁣∗∈𝒜ctf⋆⁡μ𝐗∗⁣∗=max𝐗∗⁣∗∈𝒜ctf⁡μ𝐗∗⁣∗.\displaystyle\max_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}\in\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}^{\star}}\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}=\max_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}\in\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}}\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}. (205)

The proof is given in Sec. H.0.4.

Computational cost.

The initial ancestral restriction takes time linear in the size of 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Let nn and mm be the numbers of vertices and edges in ℋ\mathcal{H}, and let m^\hat{m} count its directed edges. The children-choice loop examines 2m^2^{\hat{m}} choices. For each choice, deleting edges, finding reward ancestors, and computing the territory and border take 𝒪⁡(n+m)\mathcal{O}(n+m) time.

If κ\kappa distinct counterfactual sets are returned, comparing a retained specification against all previously returned specifications takes at most 𝒪⁡(κ⁡(n+m))\mathcal{O}(\kappa(n+m)) time per choice. Thus a direct implementation takes 𝒪⁡(2m^​(κ+1)​(n+m))\mathcal{O}(2^{\hat{m}}(\kappa+1)(n+m)) time and 𝒪​((κ+1)​(n+m))\mathcal{O}((\kappa+1)(n+m)) space, including the returned specifications. These bounds enumerate counterfactual sets; assigning their constant values to form bandit arms is a subsequent step.

6.6 Experiments

We evaluate how the counterfactual action space and its graphical reduction affect bandit learning. Each task uses a fixed binary SCM with independent Bernoulli exogenous variables, and the agent observes the reward of its selected action on a fresh unit at each round. Here the agent is given the causal diagram and may perform the counterfactual experiments admitted by 𝒜ctf\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}. Task 1 uses the causal diagram in Fig. 32(a), and Task 2 uses the diagram in Fig. 29(b). Tasks 3(a) and 3(b) share the diagram in Fig. 35. We use one SCM for each of the first two tasks and two SCMs for Task 3, giving four experimental cases. Their complete specifications appear in Appendix I.

Candidate action spaces.

We compare three strategies. The CTF-POMIS strategy uses the actions returned by Alg. 11; each selected parent argument has its own binary value. Identical choices of fixed parent inputs and their assigned values are counted once.

The CTF-MIS baseline covers all realizable ctf-MIS actions, including nested counterfactuals. It enumerates the selected parent inputs as in Alg. 11, but omits the interventional border test. Every selection entering a mechanism required to evaluate YY is retained, together with all binary assignments. This includes ordinary interventions and the empty action. By Prop. 78, every realizable nested action can be evaluated through these parent-input choices; removing redundant outer assignments preserves its reward. Different expressions giving the same fixed inputs and values are counted once. Both counterfactual strategies count the same choice of fixed inputs and values only once. Their comparison measures the exploration savings from the graphical ctf-POMIS condition over the complete nested ctf-MIS baseline.

Finally, POMIS retains all assignments to ordinary POMISs, as in Sec. 3. Table 11 reports the numbers of sets and arms.

Solvers and evaluation.

Each action space is paired with Thompson sampling (TS) (Thompson, 1933) and Bernoulli KL-UCB (Garivier and Cappé, 2011; Cappé et al., 2013), using the same settings as Sec. 4.3. TS uses a 𝙱𝚎𝚝𝚊⁡(1,1)\mathtt{Beta}(1,1) prior for each arm. KL-UCB initially selects each arm once and subsequently uses f⁡(s)=log⁡s+3​log⁡log⁡sf(s)=\log s+3\log\log s for s≥3s\geq 3, with f⁡(s)=1f(s)=1 otherwise, where ss is the number of completed rounds. Thus, after initialization, the decision at round tt uses f⁡(t−1)f(t-1). Tasks 1 and 2 use T=10,000T=10{,}000 rounds, and Tasks 3(a) and 3(b) use T=100,000T=100{,}000. Each of the 24 task–strategy–solver configurations is repeated 1,0001{,}000 times.

The reward means are computed exactly from the fixed SCMs by summing over their exogenous assignments. These means generate Bernoulli rewards and evaluate cumulative regret; the solvers use only the selected arms and observed rewards. All strategies are evaluated against the same optimal counterfactual mean μ𝐗∗⁣∗⋆\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\star}}, using the cumulative regret defined earlier in this section. In particular, the ordinary POMIS baseline is compared with the counterfactual optimum even when its own best arm has a smaller mean. Curves in Fig. 36 show mean cumulative regret, and shaded regions show one population standard deviation across repeated runs. Displayed reward means in Appendix I are rounded to at most three decimal places.

Tasks 1 and 2: enlarging and reducing the action space.

Task 1 corresponds to the causal diagram in Fig. 32. Its best ordinary intervention has mean 0.820.82, while separately choosing the two values supplied by WW raises the optimal mean to 0.88480.8848. The CTF-POMIS strategy retains this optimum with 88 arms, compared with 2121 for the CTF-MIS baseline. Task 2 uses the causal diagram in Fig. 29(b), where realizability constrains the simultaneous use of counterfactuals. For its fixed SCM, the optimal counterfactual and ordinary means are approximately 0.67590.6759 and 0.57970.5797, respectively. Both counterfactual strategies retain the former mean, while CTF-POMIS reduces the number of arms from 6767 to 3636.

Task 3: whether ordinary interventions attain the optimum.

The two seven-variable SCMs share a causal diagram and therefore the same candidate action spaces: 5252 arms for CTF-POMIS, 187187 for the CTF-MIS baseline, and 3636 for POMIS. Their structural functions determine whether ordinary interventions can attain the counterfactual optimum. In Task 3(a), the optimal counterfactual and ordinary means are approximately 0.61800.6180 and 0.59320.5932, respectively, leaving a positive gap of about 0.02480.0248 per round. In Task 3(b), all three spaces attain the same optimal mean, approximately 0.43650.4365. The latter case isolates the exploration cost of the larger counterfactual spaces when ordinary interventions already suffice.

For a strategy restricted to ordinary interventions, every selected arm has mean at most μ𝐱⋆\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}. Consequently, RT𝒜ctf≥T⁡(μ𝐗∗⁣∗⋆−μ𝐱⋆)R_{T}^{\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}}\geq T(\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\star}}-\mu_{\mathbf{x}^{\star}}). The positive gaps in Tasks 1, 2, and 3(a) therefore impose a linear contribution to the ordinary strategy’s regret, regardless of how quickly it learns its own best arm. This contribution vanishes in Task 3(b).

Observed learning performance.

Table 12 reports the simulation results. The CTF-POMIS strategy has lower mean cumulative regret than the CTF-MIS baseline in all eight task–solver comparisons. In Task 1, its regret is 37.7%37.7\% and 37.5%37.5\% of the baseline under TS and KL-UCB, respectively. In Task 3(a), these ratios are 29.9%29.9\% and 36.7%36.7\%. The CTF-POMIS strategy also has lower mean regret than ordinary POMIS under both solvers in Tasks 1, 2, and 3(a). Ordinary POMIS has the lowest mean regret under both solvers in Task 3(b), where it retains an optimal arm with fewer candidates. These results illustrate both the gain from additional counterfactual actions and the exploration savings from graphical reduction on the fixed SCMs considered here.

7 Conclusion

Across the three settings studied in this paper, causal structure clarifies which decisions merit exploration even when their rewards remain unknown. Under structural uncertainty, graphical criteria support action reduction over compatible models. Information from source environments constrains target rewards through transferable mechanisms and dominance relations. Counterfactual actions expand the available decisions when the required experiments are realizable. These results separate the construction of an action space from learning the rewards of its members, while preserving an optimal action under the stated assumptions.

The scope of these guarantees is determined by their inputs and assumptions. The Markov equivalence experiments use oracle PAGs, and the transportability analysis assumes correct structural information and valid population reward bounds. The counterfactual formulation uses finite endogenous domains and specified experimental capabilities. The numerical studies use fixed finite SCMs and do not establish performance across arbitrary environments. Moreover, graphical action reduction does not eliminate the cost of constructing the reduced space: candidate enumeration and searches over compatible structures can still grow exponentially.

Several questions remain open. A direct graphical criterion for DMIS membership in PAGs and the complexity of deciding that membership deserve further study, as discussed in Sec. 4.1.2. Another direction is to propagate uncertainty from learned causal structures and estimated source distributions into action pruning and online confidence bounds. Extending the analysis to richer domains and to settings in which counterfactual experiments have unequal costs would help connect these guarantees to a wider range of decision problems.
