The argument set in the first line specifies the variables whose values are supplied to fVf_{V}. Every parent value and every LeL_{e} is either zero or one. Consequently, the threshold on the right-hand side is at least αV>0\alpha_{V}>0 and at most the sum of the coefficients, which is strictly less than one. Acyclicity lets us evaluate these equations in a topological order, with each parent evaluated before its child, and every resulting observed variable is binary.

The equation for VV contains exactly its directed parents in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, each with a positive coefficient. The only exogenous variables shared by different equations are the LeL_{e} variables, one for each specified bidirected edge. Equivalently, each bidirected edge can be represented by an unobserved common parent of its two endpoints. Adding the directed edges UV→VU_{V}\to V for the separate exogenous variables gives the DAG underlying this causal diagram. The SCM therefore conforms to 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Fix this SCM as 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} for all comparisons below.

Expected values under an intervention. For any intervention set 𝐒\mathbf{S}, write ηV𝐒=𝔼⁡[V∣d​o​(𝐒=𝟏)]\eta_{V}^{\mathbf{S}}=\mathbb{E}[V\mid do(\mathbf{S}=\bm{1})] in the fixed SCM. If V∈𝐒V\in\mathbf{S}, its equation is replaced by the constant one, so ηV𝐒=1\eta_{V}^{\mathbf{S}}=1. If V∉𝐒V\notin\mathbf{S}, its original mechanism remains. The private variable UVU_{V} is independent of both the parent values and the shared variables appearing in that equation: it is independent of all other exogenous variables, and acyclicity prevents any parent of VV from depending on UVU_{V}. Conditional on those parent values and shared variables, the probability that V=1V=1 thus equals its threshold.

An intervention changes structural equations but leaves the exogenous distributions unchanged. Hence each LeL_{e} still has mean 12\frac{1}{2}. For V∉𝐒V\notin\mathbf{S}, taking the expectation of the threshold gives:

ηV𝐒=αV+∑P∈𝙿𝚊​(V)𝒢βP​VηP𝐒+12∑e:V∈eγe​V,0<ηV𝐒<1.\displaystyle\eta_{V}^{\mathbf{S}}=\alpha_{V}+\sum_{P\in\mathtt{Pa}(V)_{\mathcal{G}}}\beta_{PV}\eta_{P}^{\mathbf{S}}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{e:V\in e}\gamma_{eV},\qquad 0<\eta_{V}^{\mathbf{S}}<1. (208)

Only the independence of the private variable UVU_{V} was needed for the conditional probability calculation. In particular, a parent of VV may depend on a shared LeL_{e} and therefore be correlated with it. Linearity of expectation still gives the displayed formula; it does not require independence between the terms in the threshold. The two strict inequalities hold because the threshold stays strictly between zero and one for every assignment of the parents and shared variables.

Comparing two intervention sets. Now choose any 𝐙⊊𝐗\mathbf{Z}\subsetneq\mathbf{X} satisfying the condition in the lemma, and let δV=ηV𝐗−ηV𝐙\delta_{V}=\eta_{V}^{\mathbf{X}}-\eta_{V}^{\mathbf{Z}}. There are three cases. If V∈𝐙V\in\mathbf{Z}, both interventions set VV to one, thus δV=0\delta_{V}=0. If V∈𝐗∖𝐙V\in\mathbf{X}\setminus\mathbf{Z}, only the first intervention sets VV to one, whereas its mean under the second is strictly below one; thus δV=1−ηV𝐙>0\delta_{V}=1-\eta_{V}^{\mathbf{Z}}>0. Finally, if V∉𝐗V\notin\mathbf{X}, its structural equation is unchanged under both interventions. Subtracting the two expectation formulas cancels the constant and the terms involving the shared exogenous variables, leaving:

δV=∑P∈𝙿𝚊​(V)𝒢βP​V​δP.\displaystyle\delta_{V}=\sum_{P\in\mathtt{Pa}(V)_{\mathcal{G}}}\beta_{PV}\delta_{P}. (209)

In a topological order, the differences for the parents have already been evaluated when this last formula is used. The first two cases give nonnegative differences directly, and the last case is a sum of nonnegative differences for the parents with positive coefficients. Induction therefore gives δV≥0\delta_{V}\geq 0 at every vertex.

By the condition in the lemma, some W∈𝐗∖𝐙W\in\mathbf{X}\setminus\mathbf{Z} has a proper directed path W(=V0)→V1→⋯→Vk(=Y)W(=V_{0})\to V_{1}\to\cdots\to V_{k}(=Y) with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Every vertex after WW on this path lies outside 𝐗\mathbf{X} and hence also outside 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. The displayed equation for the difference in expected values therefore applies at each such vertex. The terms for its other parents are nonnegative, thus δVi≥βVi−1​Vi​δVi−1\delta_{V_{i}}\geq\beta_{V_{i-1}V_{i}}\delta_{V_{i-1}} for i=1,⋯,ki=1,\cdots,k. Applying these inequalities successively yields the explicit bound:

δY≥δW​∏i=1kβVi−1​Vi=(1−ηW𝐙)​∏i=1kβVi−1​Vi>0.\displaystyle\delta_{Y}\geq\delta_{W}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\beta_{V_{i-1}V_{i}}=(1-\eta_{W}^{\mathbf{Z}})\prod_{i=1}^{k}\beta_{V_{i-1}V_{i}}>0. (210)

The final inequality is strict because ηW𝐙<1\eta_{W}^{\mathbf{Z}}<1 and every coefficient on the path is positive. Since δY=μ𝐗=𝟏𝒮∗−μ𝐙=𝟏𝒮∗\delta_{Y}=\mu_{\mathbf{X}=\bm{1}}^{\mathcal{S}^{\ast}}-\mu_{\mathbf{Z}=\bm{1}}^{\mathcal{S}^{\ast}}, this is the required reward comparison. The argument applies to every pair 𝐗,𝐙\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Z} satisfying the condition in the lemma within the same fixed SCM, and all reward means are bounded because YY is binary.

C.0.2 Constructing a Causal Diagram from a MAG
Lemma 0 (Causal diagram with the same MUCT and IB).

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a MAG and let 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\}. There exists a causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G} whose corresponding MAG is ℳ\mathcal{M} and whose directed edges are exactly those of ℳ\mathcal{M} such that 𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(𝒢𝐗¯,Y)=𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}},Y)=\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}) and 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒢𝐗¯,Y)=𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}},Y)=\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}).

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 117] Let 𝐇=𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℳ∖𝐗\mathbf{H}=\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{M}\setminus\mathbf{X}} and 𝐑=𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\mathbf{R}=\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}). The set 𝐇\mathbf{H} contains exactly the vertices that can reach YY by a directed path avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}. The set 𝐑\mathbf{R} is the MUCT of the MAG that we want to obtain as the MUCT of a causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G}. We will retain every edge of ℳ\mathcal{M} and add selected bidirected edges. The proof has two tasks:

  • •

    showing that these additions give the desired territory; and

  • •

    showing that they preserve the corresponding MAG.

The second task requires considering all the added edges together.

All decisions about visibility refer to the original MAG. For a directed edge retained in ℳ⁡[𝐇]\mathcal{M}[\mathbf{H}], we use the causal model class represented by the full ℳ\mathcal{M} and retain its latent variables, as in the definition of visibility for induced subgraphs. A visible edge in ℳ\mathcal{M} remains visible when the observed vertices are restricted to 𝐇\mathbf{H}. An invisible directed edge remains invisible because Lemma 101 provides a corresponding DAG in which its endpoints share a latent parent. This parent and its two edges remain when observed vertices outside 𝐇\mathbf{H} are removed.

An observation about invisible directed edges. We first establish a fact that will be used when checking preservation of the MAG. Suppose that A→BA\to B is invisible and that there is a bidirected path from CC to AA in ℳ\mathcal{M} whose vertices are all parents of BB. Then C→BC\to B is also invisible.

To see this, suppose instead that C→BC\to B were visible. By the graphical visibility criterion in Lemma 17, there would be a vertex VV nonadjacent to BB and a collider path from VV into CC whose non-endpoint vertices are parents of BB. This includes the possibility of a single edge from VV into CC. Starting from VV, follow this path up to its first intersection with the bidirected path, and then follow the latter path to AA. The resulting path has no repeated vertices: the part before the first intersection is disjoint from the bidirected path.

If the intersection is not AA, both incident edges have arrowheads there; if it is AA, the resulting path ends with an arrowhead at AA. Every non-endpoint vertex of the resulting path is a parent of BB. Thus it is a collider path from VV into AA satisfying the visibility criterion for A→BA\to B. This contradicts the invisibility of A→BA\to B and proves the observation.

Constructing the causal diagram. Begin with 𝒢=ℳ\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{M}, viewed as a causal diagram. For the current 𝒢\mathcal{G}, start with YY and repeatedly include directed descendants and vertices connected by bidirected paths in 𝒢⁡[𝐇]\mathcal{G}[\mathbf{H}], until no more vertices can be included. Call the resulting set 𝐓\mathbf{T}. Equivalently, 𝐓\mathbf{T} is the least subset of 𝐇\mathbf{H} containing YY that is closed under these two operations. As shown below, after intervention on 𝐗\mathbf{X} this is precisely the MUCT of the current causal diagram.

If 𝐓≠𝐑\mathbf{T}\neq\mathbf{R}, choose a vertex B∈𝐓B\in\mathbf{T} for which there is an invisible directed edge C→BC\to B with C∈𝐇∖𝐓C\in\mathbf{H}\setminus\mathbf{T}. For this one chosen BB, add the bidirected edge C↔BC\leftrightarrow B for every such CC at the same time, retaining the original directed edges C→BC\to B and all other edges. Recompute 𝐓\mathbf{T} and repeat this step until 𝐓=𝐑\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{R}.

The requirement to include every eligible parent of the chosen BB is part of the construction. Each such parent becomes connected to a vertex already in 𝐓\mathbf{T} and therefore enters 𝐓\mathbf{T} in this step. Once a vertex has entered 𝐓\mathbf{T}, it remains there, because edges are only added. Consequently, a vertex CC can occur as the parent in an addition of C↔BC\leftrightarrow B only once. In a later step, it cannot qualify as a parent outside the current territory.

For example, Fig. 16 illustrates this step with 𝐗={A,B}\mathbf{X}=\{A,B\} and 𝐇={C,D,Y}\mathbf{H}=\{C,D,Y\}. Initially the current territory is 𝐓={Y}\mathbf{T}=\{Y\}. The directed edges C→YC\to Y and D→YD\to Y are invisible, thus choosing YY requires adding both C↔YC\leftrightarrow Y and D↔YD\leftrightarrow Y before recomputing the territory. It then becomes 𝐓={C,D,Y}\mathbf{T}=\{C,D,Y\}, whose parents outside the set are {A,B}\{A,B\}. All original directed edges are retained in the constructed causal diagram; only the intervention removes edges into {A,B}\{A,B\} in the manipulated panels.

The construction reaches the required territory. We verify both that 𝐓\mathbf{T} never exceeds 𝐑\mathbf{R} and that another addition is possible whenever 𝐓\mathbf{T} is smaller than 𝐑\mathbf{R}. Initially 𝐓⊆𝐑\mathbf{T}\subseteq\mathbf{R}, because 𝐑\mathbf{R} contains YY and is closed under directed descendants and original bidirected connections in ℳ⁡[𝐇]\mathcal{M}[\mathbf{H}]. Suppose this inclusion holds before a step choosing B∈𝐓B\in\mathbf{T}. For every added C↔BC\leftrightarrow B, the original directed edge C→BC\to B is invisible, which gives:

C∈𝗉𝖼​(B)ℳ⁡[𝐇]⊆𝐑.\displaystyle C\in\mathsf{pc}(B)_{\mathcal{M}[\mathbf{H}]}\subseteq\mathbf{R}. (211)

Thus both endpoints of every added edge belong to 𝐑\mathbf{R}. The directed descendant relation is unchanged, and the original bidirected connections also remain within 𝐑\mathbf{R} whenever they start there. Recomputing 𝐓\mathbf{T} therefore preserves 𝐓⊆𝐑\mathbf{T}\subseteq\mathbf{R}.

Now suppose that 𝐓≠𝐑\mathbf{T}\neq\mathbf{R}. By construction, 𝐓\mathbf{T} is already closed under directed descendants and original bidirected connections in ℳ⁡[𝐇]\mathcal{M}[\mathbf{H}]. It cannot also satisfy 𝗉𝖼​(𝐓)ℳ⁡[𝐇]=𝐓\mathsf{pc}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{M}[\mathbf{H}]}=\mathbf{T}. Otherwise it would be a UC-territory in ℳ⁡[𝐇]\mathcal{M}[\mathbf{H}] containing YY and properly contained in 𝐑\mathbf{R}, contrary to the minimality of 𝐑\mathbf{R}. Hence, by Def. 43, there is a collider path in ℳ⁡[𝐇]\mathcal{M}[\mathbf{H}] from a vertex of 𝐓\mathbf{T} to a vertex outside 𝐓\mathbf{T}, and none of its edges are visible. Traverse it from the vertex in 𝐓\mathbf{T} and consider the first edge crossing to the complement of 𝐓\mathbf{T}. This edge cannot be bidirected, because 𝐓\mathbf{T} is closed under original bidirected connections. It cannot be directed from 𝐓\mathbf{T} to its complement, because 𝐓\mathbf{T} is closed under directed descendants. It must therefore be an invisible directed edge from a vertex outside 𝐓\mathbf{T} into a vertex B∈𝐓B\in\mathbf{T}. This supplies the next choice required by the construction.

Every step adds at least one vertex to 𝐓\mathbf{T}, and Y∈𝐓⊆𝐑⊆𝐇Y\in\mathbf{T}\subseteq\mathbf{R}\subseteq\mathbf{H} throughout. The procedure therefore terminates with 𝐓=𝐑\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{R} after at most |𝐇|−1\lvert\mathbf{H}\rvert-1 steps. Since each vertex outside the initial territory can occur as CC in an added edge C↔BC\leftrightarrow B with original directed edge C→BC\to B at most once, at most |𝐇|−1\lvert\mathbf{H}\rvert-1 bidirected edges are added.

The corresponding MAG is preserved. We next check that the final 𝒢\mathcal{G} still has corresponding MAG ℳ\mathcal{M}. The following argument extends the single-edge argument in the proof of Lemma 101 to all edges added by the construction. All original adjacencies and ancestral relations among observed vertices are retained because no original edge is removed and no directed edge is added. It remains to show that the added bidirected edges do not create an adjacency between vertices that were nonadjacent in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Such a new adjacency would require an inducing path between those vertices in 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

For the sake of contradiction, suppose that pp is an inducing path between vertices S,TS,T nonadjacent in ℳ\mathcal{M}. For a causal diagram, such a path has only colliders as non-endpoint vertices, each of which is an ancestor of SS or TT. Among all these inducing paths, choose one with the fewest vertices; among paths with that number of vertices, choose one using the fewest added bidirected edges. Both parts of this choice will be used: a path with fewer vertices contradicts the first part, and a path with the same vertices but fewer added edges contradicts the second. The chosen path uses an added edge. Otherwise the same path, with every non-endpoint collider still an ancestor of SS or TT, would already be an inducing path in ℳ\mathcal{M}, contradicting maximality.

We first rule out a particular arrangement of two consecutive added edges on pp. Here consecutive means that no other added edge occurs between them; original edges may occur between them. Since all vertices between these two edges are non-endpoint colliders, the intervening original edges must be bidirected. The arrangement we rule out is:

B↔A(=U0)↔U1↔⋯↔C(=Uk)↔D,A→B​ and ​C→D​ in ​ℳ,\displaystyle B\leftrightarrow A(=U_{0})\leftrightarrow U_{1}\leftrightarrow\cdots\leftrightarrow C(=U_{k})\leftrightarrow D,\qquad A\to B\text{~and~}C\to D\text{~in~}\mathcal{M}, (212)

where the first and last bidirected edges were added and the middle ones were already in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Thus the two original directed edges point toward BB and DD, away from the intervening bidirected segment. The case k=0k=0, with A=CA=C, is included. The vertices BB and DD may be endpoints of pp, but they are distinct because pp has no repeated vertices.

If k=0k=0, the two added edges have the same original parent A=CA=C. They cannot occur because each parent participates in at most one addition, as shown above. Hence assume k≥1k\geq 1. Suppose first that A↔BA\leftrightarrow B was added before C↔DC\leftrightarrow D. We show that every UiU_{i} is a parent of BB in ℳ\mathcal{M}. The first vertex U0(=A)U_{0}(=A) is a parent by assumption. For the induction step, suppose U0,⋯,Ui−1U_{0},\cdots,U_{i-1} are parents of BB. If UiU_{i} were nonadjacent to BB, the original collider path Ui↔⋯↔AU_{i}\leftrightarrow\cdots\leftrightarrow A, whose non-endpoint vertices are parents of BB, would make A→BA\to B visible. Therefore, UiU_{i} is adjacent to BB.

The edge cannot be B→UiB\to U_{i}: together with Ui−1→BU_{i-1}\to B, it would make Ui−1U_{i-1} an ancestor of UiU_{i} despite the original edge Ui−1↔UiU_{i-1}\leftrightarrow U_{i}. The edge cannot be Ui↔BU_{i}\leftrightarrow B either: replacing the segment from BB through AA to UiU_{i} by this original bidirected edge would shorten pp. All retained non-endpoint vertices would still be colliders and ancestors of SS or TT, thus the shortened path would still be inducing. The only remaining possibility is Ui→BU_{i}\to B, completing the induction.

In particular, CC and AA are joined by an original bidirected path whose vertices are all parents of BB. The observation at the beginning of the proof therefore implies that C→BC\to B is invisible. Consider the step in which A↔BA\leftrightarrow B was added. If CC was already in the territory at that time, it could not be eligible for a later addition of C↔DC\leftrightarrow D. If CC was outside the territory, then C∈𝐇∖𝐓C\in\mathbf{H}\setminus\mathbf{T} and its invisible directed edge into the chosen BB required C↔BC\leftrightarrow B to be added in that same step. This would place CC in the territory, again preventing the later addition C↔DC\leftrightarrow D. Both possibilities contradict the construction. If C↔DC\leftrightarrow D was added first, the same argument read from DD towards BB gives the symmetric contradiction. Finally, the two edges cannot have been added in the same step, because that step chooses a single vertex, whereas B≠DB\neq D. Thus the displayed arrangement cannot occur on pp.

Now list the added edges in their order from SS to TT, and consider the direction of each one’s original directed edge in ℳ\mathcal{M}. The arrangement just excluded is exactly a left-pointing original directed edge followed by a right-pointing original directed edge at consecutive positions in this list. Consequently, if the first directed edge points to the left, the last directed edge must also point to the left; otherwise such a change would occur somewhere in the list. We can therefore read pp from one of its endpoints so that the first added edge is traversed from AA to BB with A→BA\to B in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Indeed, use the endpoint SS if its first directed edge points to the right, and otherwise read the path from TT. Rename the chosen starting endpoint SS and the other endpoint TT. All edges preceding this first added A↔BA\leftrightarrow B are original edges.

If A=SA=S, replace A↔BA\leftrightarrow B on the path by the original directed edge A→BA\to B. The mark at AA is irrelevant because AA is an endpoint, and the arrowhead at BB is unchanged. Hence every non-endpoint vertex remains a collider and an ancestor of SS or TT. The result is an inducing path with the same number of vertices but one fewer added edge, contradicting the second part of our choice of pp. This replacement is used only when the original parent AA is the path endpoint; it does not assume that every added edge touching an endpoint can be replaced in this way.

It remains to consider A≠SA\neq S. Write the original path segment from SS to AA as ⟨S,O1,⋯,Ok(=A)⟩\langle S,O_{1},\cdots,O_{k}(=A)\rangle. It is a collider path into AA, and all edges between the OiO_{i} are original bidirected edges. We show backwards that every OiO_{i} is a parent of BB. Starting with Ok=AO_{k}=A, suppose that Oi+1,⋯,OkO_{i+1},\cdots,O_{k} are parents of BB. The invisibility of A→BA\to B makes OiO_{i} adjacent to BB, since otherwise Oi↔⋯↔AO_{i}\leftrightarrow\cdots\leftrightarrow A would satisfy the visibility criterion for A→BA\to B. The edge B→OiB\to O_{i} would create an almost directed cycle consisting of Oi+1→B→OiO_{i+1}\to B\to O_{i} and Oi↔Oi+1O_{i}\leftrightarrow O_{i+1}. The edge Oi↔BO_{i}\leftrightarrow B would shorten pp, and all remaining non-endpoint vertices would still be colliders and ancestors of SS or TT. Therefore Oi→BO_{i}\to B. This proves the claim for all vertices O1,⋯,OkO_{1},\cdots,O_{k}.

The same visibility criterion implies that SS is adjacent to BB. Otherwise, the path ⟨S,O1,⋯,Ok⟩\langle S,O_{1},\cdots,O_{k}\rangle would establish visibility of A→BA\to B. This adjacency cannot be B→SB\to S. If the first original edge is S→O1S\to O_{1}, then S→O1→B→SS\to O_{1}\to B\to S would be a directed cycle. If it is S↔O1S\leftrightarrow O_{1}, then O1→B→SO_{1}\to B\to S together with that bidirected edge would form an almost directed cycle. Thus the edge between SS and BB has an arrowhead at BB. If B=TB=T, this is already a contradiction, since SS and TT were assumed nonadjacent in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Otherwise replace the path segment ⟨S,O1,⋯,Ok(=A),B⟩\langle S,O_{1},\cdots,O_{k}(=A),B\rangle by this original edge from SS into BB. The arrowhead at BB is preserved, and all other retained non-endpoint vertices remain colliders and ancestors of SS or TT. We have obtained a shorter inducing path, again a contradiction.

We conclude that no inducing path in 𝒢\mathcal{G} creates a new adjacency. Its corresponding MAG therefore has exactly the adjacencies of ℳ\mathcal{M}. It also has exactly the same endpoint marks, because the ancestral relations used to determine those marks have not changed. Hence its corresponding MAG is ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Identifying the resulting territory and border. Finally, we connect the set 𝐓\mathbf{T} used in the construction with the ordinary MUCT after intervention on 𝐗\mathbf{X}. The directed edges of 𝒢\mathcal{G} and ℳ\mathcal{M} coincide, and a directed path from a vertex outside 𝐗\mathbf{X} to YY survives this intervention exactly when it avoids 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Thus:

𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢𝐗¯∖𝐗=𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℳ∖𝐗=𝐇.\displaystyle\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}}}\setminus\mathbf{X}=\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{M}\setminus\mathbf{X}}=\mathbf{H}. (213)

Some intervened vertices may themselves remain ancestors of YY. However, they cannot enter the territory grown from YY since the intervention removes every edge into them, so neither a bidirected connection nor a directed path from the current territory can reach a vertex in 𝐗\mathbf{X}. The ordinary MUCT computation in the ancestral subgraph of 𝒢𝐗¯\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}} therefore takes place entirely within 𝐇\mathbf{H} and uses exactly the two closure operations defining 𝐓\mathbf{T}. Since the construction ended with 𝐓=𝐑\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{R}, this proves 𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(𝒢𝐗¯,Y)=𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}},Y)=\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}).

Every vertex of 𝐑\mathbf{R} is outside 𝐗\mathbf{X}, so intervention on 𝐗\mathbf{X} removes none of the directed edges entering 𝐑\mathbf{R}. Together with the fact that no directed edge was changed during the construction, this shows that the parents of 𝐑\mathbf{R} outside 𝐑\mathbf{R} are the same in 𝒢𝐗¯\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}} and ℳ\mathcal{M}. Consequently, 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒢𝐗¯,Y)=𝙿𝚊​(𝐑)ℳ∖𝐑=𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}},Y)=\mathtt{Pa}(\mathbf{R})_{\mathcal{M}}\setminus\mathbf{R}=\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}).

C.0.3 Proof of Theorem 46
{proof}

[Proof of Thm. 46] Necessity. Fix 𝐗\mathbf{X} and write:

ℋ\displaystyle\mathcal{H} =ℳ⁡[𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℳ∖𝐗],\displaystyle=\mathcal{M}[\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{M}\setminus\mathbf{X}}], 𝐓\displaystyle\mathbf{T} =𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗),\displaystyle=\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}),
𝐖\displaystyle\mathbf{W} =𝙿𝚊​(𝐓)ℳ∖𝐓,\displaystyle=\mathtt{Pa}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{M}}\setminus\mathbf{T}, 𝐖′\displaystyle\mathbf{W}^{\prime} =𝐖∖𝐗,𝐗′=𝐗∖𝐖.\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}\setminus\mathbf{X},\qquad\mathbf{X}^{\prime}=\mathbf{X}\setminus\mathbf{W}.

Thus 𝐖=𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\mathbf{W}=\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}). The defining closures are 𝙳𝚎​(𝐓)ℋ=𝐓\mathtt{De}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathbf{T} and 𝗉𝖼​(𝐓)ℋ=𝐓\mathsf{pc}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathbf{T}; these are closures in ℋ\mathcal{H}, not in the full MAG. Also, 𝐓∩𝐗=∅\mathbf{T}\cap\mathbf{X}=\emptyset.

Our aim is to show that intervening on 𝐖\mathbf{W} can achieve at least the optimal reward attainable by intervening on 𝐗\mathbf{X}, in every conforming SCM. If 𝐖≠𝐗\mathbf{W}\neq\mathbf{X}, this will provide a competing DMIS that prevents 𝐗\mathbf{X} from being strictly optimal. The set 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} consists of the border variables that are missing from the current intervention, whereas 𝐗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime} consists of intervention variables that are not on the border. The two separation claims below will allow us first to intervene on 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} and then to remove 𝐗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime} from the intervention.

First, 𝐖\mathbf{W} is an MIS for ℳ\mathcal{M}. For each W∈𝐖W\in\mathbf{W}, choose W→TW\to T with T∈𝐓T\in\mathbf{T}. Since TT is a vertex of ℋ\mathcal{H}, it has a directed path to YY within ℋ\mathcal{H}. Descendant closure keeps that path entirely in 𝐓\mathbf{T}, so the path from WW to YY avoids every other member of 𝐖\mathbf{W}. Now apply Thm. 31. Thus, 𝐖\mathbf{W} is also a DMIS by Prop. 38. This includes 𝐖=∅\mathbf{W}=\emptyset.

For MAGs, lower manipulation at 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} deletes visible directed edges out of 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} and replaces invisible directed edges out of 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} by bidirected edges. Apply this operation before upper manipulation at 𝐗\mathbf{X}, as required by the MAG manipulation convention (Zhang, 2008a).

Claim 1.

(Y⟂⁣⟂𝐖′∣𝐗)ℳ𝐗¯​𝐖′¯(Y\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}\mathbf{W}^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{X})_{\mathcal{M}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}\underline{\mathbf{W}^{\prime}}}}.

{proof}

[Proof of Claim 1] Suppose that an m-connecting path pp in ℳ𝐗¯​𝐖′¯\mathcal{M}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}\underline{\mathbf{W}^{\prime}}} joins W∈𝐖′W\in\mathbf{W}^{\prime} to YY given 𝐗\mathbf{X}. All incoming edges to 𝐗\mathbf{X} have been removed, so a collider on pp could neither belong to 𝐗\mathbf{X} nor be an ancestor of a vertex in 𝐗\mathbf{X}. It would therefore violate the condition for m-connection. Thus, pp has no colliders, and every non-endpoint vertex lies outside 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Lower manipulation leaves only arrowheads at vertices in 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime}. A non-endpoint vertex in 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} would therefore be a collider. Consequently, pp has no non-endpoint vertex in 𝐖\mathbf{W} and its first edge has an arrowhead at WW.

Every member of 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} is a vertex of ℋ\mathcal{H}: it is outside 𝐗\mathbf{X} and has a child in 𝐓\mathbf{T} followed by a directed path to YY in ℋ\mathcal{H}. Consider first a path whose first edge W↔VW\leftrightarrow V was created from an invisible W→VW\to V. If V≠YV\neq Y, the next edge must point away from VV; otherwise, VV would be a collider. Applying the same argument at each subsequent vertex shows that the remaining path is directed from VV to YY. The case V=YV=Y is included. Starting at Y∈𝐓Y\in\mathbf{T} and considering each preceding vertex on this directed path, any parent outside 𝐓\mathbf{T} would lie in 𝐖\mathbf{W}. Since there is no non-endpoint vertex of pp in 𝐖\mathbf{W}, VV must belong to 𝐓\mathbf{T}.

The edge W→VW\to V is invisible in ℋ\mathcal{H} under the inherited interpretation of visibility. Indeed, Lemma 101 gives a DAG whose corresponding MAG is ℳ\mathcal{M} and which contains W←U→VW\leftarrow U\to V for a latent vertex UU. This path remains when only observed vertices outside ℋ\mathcal{H} are removed. Hence W∈𝗉𝖼​(V)ℋ⊆𝐓W\in\mathsf{pc}(V)_{\mathcal{H}}\subseteq\mathbf{T}, contradicting W∈𝐖W\in\mathbf{W}.

Otherwise, all edges of pp are original MAG edges. Any added bidirected edge would have to meet a member of 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime}, but no non-endpoint vertex of pp belongs to that set. Since pp has no colliders and its first edge has an arrowhead at WW, it has one of the following forms:

W←⋯←L→⋯→Y,\displaystyle W\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow L\to\cdots\to Y, (214)
W←⋯←L↔R→⋯→Y.\displaystyle W\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow L\leftrightarrow R\to\cdots\to Y. (215)

To see this, start at WW and follow the path. The edges may initially point towards WW. Once an edge points towards the next vertex, or a bidirected edge is encountered, every subsequent edge must point towards YY to avoid a collider. In either form, the directed path ending at YY may have length zero and consist only of YY. In the second form, the directed path from LL to WW may also have length zero, with L=WL=W. In the first form, however, L≠WL\neq W, because the first edge has an arrowhead at WW.

All vertices of pp are in the vertex set of ℋ\mathcal{H}. The directed path ending at YY consists of ancestors of YY and avoids 𝐗\mathbf{X}. The directed path from LL to WW also avoids 𝐗\mathbf{X}, and W∈𝐕⁡(ℋ)W\in\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{H}) has a directed path to YY avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Its vertices are therefore also ancestors of YY in ℳ∖𝐗\mathcal{M}\setminus\mathbf{X}.

We now show that both forms imply W∈𝐓W\in\mathbf{T}. In the first form, start at Y∈𝐓Y\in\mathbf{T} and consider each preceding vertex on the directed path from LL to YY. As above, a parent outside 𝐓\mathbf{T} would belong to 𝐖\mathbf{W}, which is impossible for a non-endpoint vertex of pp. Thus, L∈𝐓L\in\mathbf{T}. In the second form, the same argument along the directed path from RR to YY gives R∈𝐓R\in\mathbf{T}. The bidirected edge L↔RL\leftrightarrow R is invisible, so L∈𝗉𝖼​(R)ℋ⊆𝐓L\in\mathsf{pc}(R)_{\mathcal{H}}\subseteq\mathbf{T}. In both forms, WW is a descendant of LL along a directed path in ℋ\mathcal{H}. Since 𝙳𝚎​(𝐓)ℋ=𝐓\mathtt{De}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathbf{T}, we obtain W∈𝐓W\in\mathbf{T}, contradicting W∈𝐖W\in\mathbf{W}.

Claim 2.

(Y⟂⁣⟂𝐗′∣𝐖)ℳ𝐖∪𝐗′¯(Y\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}\mathbf{X}^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{W})_{\mathcal{M}_{\overline{\mathbf{W}\cup\mathbf{X}^{\prime}}}}.

{proof}

[Proof of Claim 2] An m-connecting path from X∈𝐗′X\in\mathbf{X}^{\prime} would start with an outgoing edge. No collider can be activated by conditioning on 𝐖\mathbf{W}, whose vertices have no incoming edges after manipulation. The path must therefore be directed towards YY and avoid 𝐖\mathbf{W}. Since Y∈𝐓Y\in\mathbf{T} and X∉𝐓X\notin\mathbf{T}, this directed path has a first edge entering 𝐓\mathbf{T} from outside. The vertex just before that first member of 𝐓\mathbf{T} lies in 𝙿𝚊​(𝐓)ℳ∖𝐓=𝐖\mathtt{Pa}(\mathbf{T})_{\mathcal{M}}\setminus\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{W}, a contradiction. For any assignment 𝐱\mathbf{x} in any conforming SCM, marginalization and Rules 2 and 3 for MAGs yield:

μ𝐱\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{x}} =∑𝐰′𝔼[Y∣do(𝐱),𝐰′]P(𝐰′∣do(𝐱))\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{w}^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}[Y\mid do(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{w}^{\prime}]P(\mathbf{w}^{\prime}\mid do(\mathbf{x}))
=∑𝐰′𝔼⁡[Y∣d​o​(𝐱,𝐰′)]​P​(𝐰′∣d​o​(𝐱))\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{w}^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}[Y\mid do(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}^{\prime})]P(\mathbf{w}^{\prime}\mid do(\mathbf{x})) (216)
=∑𝐰′𝔼⁡[Y∣d​o​(𝐱∩𝐖,𝐰′)]​P​(𝐰′∣d​o​(𝐱))\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{w}^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}[Y\mid do(\mathbf{x}\cap\mathbf{W},\mathbf{w}^{\prime})]P(\mathbf{w}^{\prime}\mid do(\mathbf{x})) (217)
≤μ𝐰∗.\displaystyle\leq\mu_{\mathbf{w}^{\ast}}.

The first rule application exchanges observation of 𝐖′\mathbf{W}^{\prime} for intervention, using Claim 1. The second removes the interventions on 𝐗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime}, using Claim 2. Both rule applications are within the same fixed SCM. What remains is an average of rewards under assignments to 𝐖=(𝐗∩𝐖)∪𝐖′\mathbf{W}=(\mathbf{X}\cap\mathbf{W})\cup\mathbf{W}^{\prime}. Each term is at most the best reward attainable on 𝐖\mathbf{W}, and the nonnegative averaging weights sum to one. This gives the last inequality. For general domains, replace the sum by the corresponding integral. The bound holds for every 𝐱\mathbf{x}, so it also holds after maximizing over assignments to 𝐗\mathbf{X}. If 𝐖≠𝐗\mathbf{W}\neq\mathbf{X}, the DMIS 𝐖\mathbf{W} is therefore a distinct competitor whose optimal reward is never smaller. Thus 𝐗\mathbf{X} cannot be a POMIS, proving necessity.

Sufficiency. Suppose 𝐗=𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\mathbf{X}=\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}). By Lemma 117, there is a causal diagram 𝒢\mathcal{G} with corresponding MAG ℳ\mathcal{M}, exactly the same directed edges, and 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒢𝐗¯,Y)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}}},Y)=\mathbf{X}. By Thm. 28, 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a POMIS, and hence an MIS, for 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Thus there is one SCM 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} conforming to 𝒢\mathcal{G} in which the optimal reward attainable on 𝐗\mathbf{X} is strictly greater than that attainable on every other MIS of 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Because 𝒢\mathcal{G} and ℳ\mathcal{M} have exactly the same directed edges, their proper directed paths agree for every intervention set. Hence Prop. 23 and Thm. 31 imply:

𝕄𝒢,Y=𝕄ℳ,Y=𝔻ℳ,Y.\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{G},Y}=\mathbb{M}_{\mathcal{M},Y}=\mathbb{D}_{\mathcal{M},Y}. (218)

The final equality follows from Props. 37 and 38. The same 𝒮∗\mathcal{S}^{\ast} conforms to ℳ\mathcal{M} and supplies all strict inequalities required by Def. 41. Therefore, 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a POMIS for ℳ\mathcal{M}.

C.0.4 Terminal PMG–MAG Correspondence

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be a PAG on 𝐕\mathbf{V}, and let 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\}. The PMG 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is obtained from 𝒫\mathcal{P} by valid local transformations and the orientation rules in Thm. 48 applied to closure after each transformation. We first explain how to compare the territories of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and its represented MAGs. We then show how to choose the remaining orientations so that one represented MAG has the required interventional border. Visibility in every induced graph retains the model class of its full PMG.

Visibility in induced graphs.

Consider a directed edge A→BA\to B in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and an observed vertex set 𝐀\mathbf{A} containing both endpoints. Visibility relative to the inherited model class is the same in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and 𝒬⁡[𝐀]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}]. We verify both directions because the ancestor sets used later depend on the graph.

First suppose that A→BA\to B is visible in the full PMG. If a represented DAG restricted to 𝐀\mathbf{A} and its latent vertices had an inducing path into AA between AA and BB, the same path would be present in the full DAG. The directed paths that establish the ancestry of any colliders would also remain present in the full DAG. This contradicts visibility in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, so the edge is visible after restriction.

Conversely, suppose that A→BA\to B is invisible in the full PMG. There is then a represented DAG with an inducing path between AA and BB that is into AA. Its corresponding MAG has an invisible A→BA\to B by Lemma 100. By Lemma 101, a DAG represented by this same MAG can be chosen to contain a latent common parent A←U→BA\leftarrow U\to B. The vertices A,B,UA,B,U and these two edges survive restriction to 𝐀\mathbf{A} and the latent vertices. They therefore establish invisibility after restriction as well. Non-directed edges are invisible by definition. For each fixed full graph and its represented model class, these observations allow us to use the same visibility status when an edge appears in different induced ancestor graphs.

Expressing the territory using individual edges.

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be 𝒬\mathcal{Q} or a MAG in [𝒬][\mathcal{Q}], let 𝐀𝒟=𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒟∖𝐗\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}=\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{D}\setminus\mathbf{X}} and let 𝐓𝒟=𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(𝒟,Y,𝐗)\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}}=\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{D},Y,\mathbf{X}). Then 𝐓𝒟\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}} is the set reachable from YY in 𝒟⁡[𝐀𝒟]\mathcal{D}[\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}] when invisible edges can be traversed in both directions and visible edges can be traversed from tail to arrowhead.

An invisible edge is itself a path satisfying the possible c-component (pc) condition: it has no internal vertices, so its internal-collider condition is vacuous. Consequently, if a set is closed under 𝗉𝖼\mathsf{pc} and contains one endpoint of an invisible edge, it must also contain the other endpoint.

Conversely, suppose that a set is closed under this operation on individual invisible edges. A pc path consists entirely of invisible edges. Starting from an endpoint in the set, we can follow its edges one at a time and conclude that every vertex of the path, including the other endpoint, is in the set. Thus closure under 𝗉𝖼\mathsf{pc} is equivalent to closure under traversing individual invisible edges in either direction. This argument does not require the pc relation itself to be transitive.

Possible descendant closure additionally permits movement along a possibly directed path. Each invisible edge on such a path is already covered by the preceding operation, 𝗉𝖼\mathsf{pc}. Any visible edge is directed, and a possibly directed path can use it only from tail to arrowhead. It follows that the set reached from YY by the movements in the statement is closed under both operations. Every set containing YY and closed under both operations must contain all vertices reached in this way. Hence the reached set is precisely the minimal such set, 𝐓𝒟\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}}.

Lemma 0.

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be 𝒬\mathcal{Q} or a MAG in [𝒬][\mathcal{Q}], let 𝐀𝒟=𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒟∖𝐗\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}=\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{D}\setminus\mathbf{X}} and let 𝐓𝒟=𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(𝒟,Y,𝐗)\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}}=\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{D},Y,\mathbf{X}). If every X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X} has a proper directed path to YY in 𝒟\mathcal{D}, then 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒟,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{D},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X} if and only if 𝐓𝒟=𝐀𝒟\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}}=\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}.

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 118] An unchanged border requires the entire ancestor set. Suppose that 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒟,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{D},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}, and assume for a contradiction that some WW belongs to 𝐀𝒟∖𝐓𝒟\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}\setminus\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}}. By the definition of 𝐀𝒟\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}, there is a possibly directed path from WW to YY avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Every vertex on this path belongs to 𝐀𝒟\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}, since the remaining part of the path is also a possibly directed path to YY avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}.

The path starts outside 𝐓𝒟\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}} and ends at Y∈𝐓𝒟Y\in\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}}. Let U∗−∗VU\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}V be the first edge with U∉𝐓𝒟U\notin\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}} and V∈𝐓𝒟V\in\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}}. This edge cannot be invisible. Otherwise, UU belongs to 𝐓𝒟\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}}. It must therefore be visible. Because the path is possibly directed from UU toward VV, its orientation is U→VU\to V. Thus UU is a parent outside the territory and belongs to 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒟,Y,𝐗)\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{D},Y,\mathbf{X}). But UU lies on a path avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}, so U∉𝐗U\notin\mathbf{X}. This contradicts the assumed border equality 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒟,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{D},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}. Therefore, 𝐓𝒟=𝐀𝒟\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}}=\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}.

Recover the border from the entire ancestor set. Now suppose that 𝐓𝒟=𝐀𝒟\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}}=\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}. Let W→VW\to V be any edge with V∈𝐀𝒟V\in\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}} and W∉𝐀𝒟W\notin\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}. If W∉𝐗W\notin\mathbf{X}, this edge can be followed by a possibly directed path from VV to YY avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Such a path cannot already contain WW, since its remaining part from WW would make WW a member of 𝐀𝒟\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}. The concatenation is therefore a possibly directed path from WW to YY avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}, again a contradiction. Hence every parent outside the territory belongs to 𝐗\mathbf{X}, giving 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒟,Y,𝐗)⊆𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{D},Y,\mathbf{X})\subseteq\mathbf{X}.

For the reverse inclusion, fix X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X} and take its proper directed path to YY with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X}. The first child on this path is an ancestor of YY along a path avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}, and thus belongs to 𝐀𝒟=𝐓𝒟\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}=\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{D}}. Since XX itself is excluded from 𝐀𝒟\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{D}}, it is a parent outside the territory. This proves 𝐗⊆𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒟,Y,𝐗)\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{D},Y,\mathbf{X}) and completes the equivalence.

Choosing the remaining orientations.

We will obtain a MAG from 𝒬\mathcal{Q} by replacing every ∘⁣→\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to} edge with a directed edge and orienting each circle component as a DAG without unshielded colliders. Lemma 115 applies to the simultaneous orientation of all these components and ensures that the resulting graph belongs to [𝒬][\mathcal{Q}].

Within a circle component, we can require any specified vertex RR to have no incoming edges from that component. To see this, choose RR first, then repeatedly choose a remaining vertex with the largest number of already chosen neighbors, breaking ties arbitrarily. Direct every edge from the earlier vertex to the later vertex in this order. For a chordal graph, each vertex’s earlier neighbors form a clique (Tarjan and Yannakakis, 1984). They therefore cannot form an unshielded collider at that vertex. The ordering also excludes a directed cycle.

Moreover, every vertex of the component is a descendant of RR in this orientation. Indeed, while a connected component is only partly visited, some unvisited vertex has a visited neighbor. The stated choice rule therefore selects a vertex with at least one earlier neighbor. Its edge from that neighbor is directed into the newly visited vertex. Starting with RR and repeating this argument gives a directed path from RR to every vertex of the component. The choices of RR made below can differ between components; the same cited lemma (Lemma 115) ensures that the resulting orientations together give one compatible MAG.

For example, consider the circle component in Fig. 37(a), formed by the two triangles on {R,A,B}\{R,A,B\} and {B,C,D}\{B,C,D\}. Choose RR first. Both AA and BB then have one already chosen neighbor, so we may choose AA. Now BB has two already chosen neighbors, RR and AA, whereas CC and DD have none; hence BB is chosen next. Both CC and DD now have BB as an already chosen neighbor. We may choose CC and then DD, giving the order R≺A≺B≺C≺DR\prec A\prec B\prec C\prec D. Directing each edge from the earlier vertex to the later vertex gives Fig. 37(b). The blue edges provide the paths: R→AR\to A, R→BR\to B, R→B→CR\to B\to C, and R→B→DR\to B\to D. Thus even CC and DD, which are not adjacent to RR, are descendants of RR. Each newly chosen vertex receives an edge from an earlier vertex that is already reachable from RR. This is the step repeated in the general argument above. The two incoming edges at BB have adjacent parents R,AR,A, and those at DD have adjacent parents B,CB,C; the resulting orientation therefore has no unshielded colliders.

For an edge R→BR\to B, a visibility witness is a path into RR whose first vertex is not adjacent to BB and whose internal vertices are colliders and parents of BB. A path consisting of one edge is allowed. These are the conditions in Lemma 17, which we use below to establish visibility.

Lemma 0.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be obtained from 𝒬\mathcal{Q} by replacing every ∘⁣→\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to} edge with a directed edge and orienting each circle component as a DAG without unshielded colliders. Suppose that RR has no incoming edges within its circle component in this orientation. If R→BR\to B is visible in ℳ\mathcal{M}, then the edge between RR and BB is already oriented as R→BR\to B in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and has a graphical visibility witness there. In particular, an invisible edge of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} that becomes R→BR\to B remains invisible in ℳ\mathcal{M}.

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 119] Step 1: Find a path that establishes visibility in the MAG. By Lemma 17, visibility of R→BR\to B supplies a path p=⟨C0,C1,⋯,Ck(=R)⟩p=\langle C_{0},C_{1},\cdots,C_{k}(=R)\rangle such that C0C_{0} is not adjacent to BB, the path has an arrowhead at RR, and all internal vertices are colliders on the path and parents of BB. The endpoint RR is also a parent of BB by the edge under consideration. Thus Ci→BC_{i}\to B in ℳ\mathcal{M} for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k. All these vertices are distinct from BB. When k≥2k\geq 2, every edge from C1C_{1} through RR has arrowheads at both endpoints, so this part of the path is bidirected.

Step 2: The path’s arrowheads were already in the PMG. The procedure used to obtain ℳ\mathcal{M} creates no bidirected edges. Consequently, the bidirected part from C1C_{1} through RR was already present in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. If the first edge is bidirected, it too was already present. If the first edge is directed into C1C_{1}, its arrowhead at C1C_{1} could be new only when C0∘−∘C1C_{0}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}C_{1} was oriented as C0→C1C_{0}\to C_{1}. For k=1k=1, such a new arrowhead would give RR an incoming edge from another vertex in its circle component, contrary to the assumption on RR. For k≥2k\geq 2, suppose that this possibility does occur. We then have C0∘−∘C1↔C2C_{0}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}C_{1}\leftrightarrow C_{2} in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. The bidirected edge equivalence in Lemma 50 gives C0↔C2C_{0}\leftrightarrow C_{2}. We may therefore replace the beginning ⟨C0,C1,C2⟩\langle C_{0},C_{1},C_{2}\rangle by ⟨C0,C2⟩\langle C_{0},C_{2}\rangle. This deletes one vertex and preserves the collider condition, the arrowhead at RR, and all the remaining parent conditions. It also leaves the same endpoint C0C_{0}, which is still not adjacent to BB. After this possible deletion, every arrowhead required by the resulting path is already present in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

Step 3: Every required parent mark was already fixed. Relabel the resulting path as ⟨C0,C1,⋯,Ck(=R)⟩\langle C_{0},C_{1},\cdots,C_{k}(=R)\rangle. We prove in order, for i=1,⋯,ki=1,\cdots,k, that the edge is already oriented as Ci→BC_{i}\to B in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Because the corresponding edge is directed from CiC_{i} to BB in ℳ\mathcal{M}, the possibilities in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} are Ci→BC_{i}\to B, Ci∘⁣→BC_{i}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}B, or Ci∘−∘BC_{i}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}B.

For i=1i=1, the circle edge possibility C1∘−∘BC_{1}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}B is excluded by balance: together with the already present C0∗⁣→C1C_{0}\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}C_{1}, it would make C0C_{0} adjacent to BB. If the remaining possibility is C1∘⁣→BC_{1}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}B, the triple C0∗⁣→C1∘⁣→BC_{0}\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}C_{1}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}B is unshielded, and ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} orients C1→BC_{1}\to B. Since 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is closed under this rule, the tail at C1C_{1} must already be displayed in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

Now take i>1i>1 and assume that C1,⋯,Ci−1C_{1},\cdots,C_{i-1} have already been shown to be parents of BB in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. If Ci∘−∘BC_{i}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}B, the edge Ci−1↔CiC_{i-1}\leftrightarrow C_{i} and circle balance would imply Ci−1↔BC_{i-1}\leftrightarrow B. This contradicts the orientation Ci−1→BC_{i-1}\to B in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} just established. Hence only Ci→BC_{i}\to B or Ci∘⁣→BC_{i}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}B remains.

To exclude the latter possibility, consider ⟨C0,C1,⋯,Ci,B⟩\langle C_{0},C_{1},\cdots,C_{i},B\rangle. Its first endpoint C0C_{0} is not adjacent to BB, while CiC_{i} is adjacent to BB. Every intermediate vertex C1,⋯,Ci−1C_{1},\cdots,C_{i-1} is a collider on this path, by Step 2, and a parent of BB in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, by the induction hypothesis. The vertices are distinct. Thus this is a discriminating path for CiC_{i}, and ℛ4′\mathcal{R}_{4}^{\prime} would orient Ci∘⁣→BC_{i}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}B as Ci→BC_{i}\to B. Closure again implies that this tail is already fixed in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. This completes the induction.

Step 4: Apply the visibility criterion in the PMG. The path now has all its required arrowheads in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and all its internal vertices are parents of BB in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Its endpoint C0C_{0} remains nonadjacent to BB. It therefore establishes visibility of the edge R→BR\to B, already oriented in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, in every represented MAG and in the inherited causal model class of 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. The last assertion of the lemma is the contrapositive of this conclusion.

Corollary 0.

A directed edge R→BR\to B is visible in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} if and only if it has a graphical visibility witness in the full graph 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

{proof}

[Proof of Cor. 120] Suppose first that R→BR\to B is visible in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Choose RR first when orienting its circle component as described above, and orient all other circle components as DAGs without unshielded colliders. Replace every ∘⁣→\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to} edge by a directed edge. By Lemma 115, these simultaneous choices give a MAG ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}] in which RR has no incoming edges from its circle component. Every DAG represented by ℳ\mathcal{M} belongs to the model class specified by 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, so R→BR\to B is visible in ℳ\mathcal{M}. By Lemma 119, it has a graphical visibility witness in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

Conversely, suppose that such a witness is present in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Its nonadjacency, required arrowheads, and directed parent edges are preserved in every MAG in [𝒬][\mathcal{Q}]. The criterion in Lemma 17 therefore makes R→BR\to B visible in every such MAG, and hence in the full causal model class specified by 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

Lemma 0.

Let B,CB,C lie in the same circle component of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and let RR lie outside that component. If R→BR\to B has a graphical visibility witness in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, then the edge between RR and CC is already oriented as R→CR\to C in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and has a graphical visibility witness there.

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 121] If B=CB=C, the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise, it suffices to prove the result for adjacent vertices B∘−∘CB\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}C and repeat it along a circle path from BB to CC.

Step 1: Obtain the possible parent edges into CC. Choose a visibility witness ⟨C0,C1,⋯,Ck(=R)⟩\langle C_{0},C_{1},\cdots,C_{k}(=R)\rangle for R→BR\to B. For every 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, 𝒬\mathcal{Q} already contains the directed edge Ci→BC_{i}\to B. The stronger balanced property applied to Ci→B∘−∘CC_{i}\to B\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}C therefore gives Ci→CC_{i}\to C or Ci∘⁣→CC_{i}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C. In particular, each CiC_{i} is adjacent to CC, with an arrowhead at CC. Each CiC_{i} lies outside the circle component of BB: if it lay in that component, its adjacency to BB would have to be a circle edge by Lemma 50(1), contradicting Ci→BC_{i}\to B. Thus none of these vertices equals CC.

Step 2: The first endpoint stays nonadjacent to CC. For the sake of contradiction, suppose that C0C_{0} is adjacent to CC. We consider all possible forms of this edge.

If C0∘−∘CC_{0}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}C, then C0C_{0} lies in the same circle component as BB. Since C1C_{1} is outside that component, the arrowhead equivalence in Lemma 50(2), applied to C1→BC_{1}\to B, gives an arrowhead at C0C_{0} on the C1∗−∗C0C_{1}\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}C_{0} edge. Its bidirected edge equivalence also excludes C1↔C0C_{1}\leftrightarrow C_{0}, because C1→BC_{1}\to B is not bidirected. The edge must therefore be C1→C0C_{1}\to C_{0} or C1∘⁣→C0C_{1}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C_{0}. Both possibilities contradict the witness arrowhead at C1C_{1}.

Next suppose that the edge has no arrowhead at CC and is not a circle edge. In any MAG obtained by replacing all ∘⁣→\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to} edges with directed edges and orienting the circle components as DAGs without unshielded colliders, this edge is C→C0C\to C_{0}. Step 1 also gives C1→CC_{1}\to C in that MAG. The first edge of the witness still points into C1C_{1}. If it is C0→C1C_{0}\to C_{1}, these three edges form C→C0→C1→CC\to C_{0}\to C_{1}\to C. If it is C0↔C1C_{0}\leftrightarrow C_{1}, then C1→C→C0C_{1}\to C\to C_{0} together with C0↔C1C_{0}\leftrightarrow C_{1} is an almost directed cycle. Both conclusions contradict the ancestral property of the MAG, whose existence follows from Lemma 115.

The remaining possibility is an arrowhead at CC on the C0∗−∗CC_{0}\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}C edge. The balanced property applied to C0∗⁣→C∘−∘BC_{0}\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}C\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}B then gives an adjacency between C0C_{0} and BB. This contradicts the defining nonadjacency of the visibility witness. All possibilities lead to contradictions; therefore, C0C_{0} is not adjacent to CC.

Step 3: Fix the parent marks into CC in order. For C1C_{1}, Step 1 leaves C1→CC_{1}\to C or C1∘⁣→CC_{1}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C. Since C0C_{0} is not adjacent to CC, the triple C0∗⁣→C1∘⁣→CC_{0}\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!\to}C_{1}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C would trigger ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1}. Since 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is closed under the rule, C1→CC_{1}\to C is already oriented in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

For i>1i>1, assume that the vertices C1,⋯,Ci−1C_{1},\cdots,C_{i-1} have already been shown to be parents of CC in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. The path ⟨C0,⋯,Ci,C⟩\langle C_{0},\cdots,C_{i},C\rangle has distinct vertices, its first endpoint is nonadjacent to CC, and its intermediate vertices are colliders and parents of CC in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Thus it is a discriminating path for CiC_{i}. If Ci∘⁣→CC_{i}\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}C remained, ℛ4′\mathcal{R}_{4}^{\prime} would orient Ci→CC_{i}\to C. Closure shows that this tail is already fixed. The induction reaches Ck=RC_{k}=R.

The edge R→CR\to C is therefore already oriented in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. The same collider path into RR now has all its internal vertices as parents of CC in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Step 2 supplies the required nonadjacency of its first endpoint. This is the desired visibility witness for R→CR\to C.

Lemma 0.

Suppose that every circle mark at a vertex in 𝐗∪{Y}\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\} has been resolved in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and that every X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X} has a proper directed path to YY with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X} in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Then 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒬,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X} if and only if there exists a MAG ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}] satisfying 𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}.

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 122] Let 𝐀ℳ=𝙰𝚗​(Y)ℳ∖𝐗\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}=\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{M}\setminus\mathbf{X}} and let 𝐓ℳ=𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}=\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X}). Similarly, let 𝐀𝒬=𝙿𝚘𝚜𝚜𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒬∖𝐗\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}=\mathtt{Poss}\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{Q}\setminus\mathbf{X}} and let 𝐓𝒬=𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(𝒬,Y,𝐗)\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{Q}}=\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X}). For a represented MAG, 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}} consists of the actual ancestors of YY after 𝐗\mathbf{X} is deleted. For the PMG, 𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}} consists of possible ancestors under the same deletion. We always have 𝐀ℳ⊆𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}, since a directed path in ℳ\mathcal{M} is possibly directed in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. This inclusion can be strict. The argument below keeps the two sets separate.

From a Represented MAG to the PMG

Step 1: Transfer membership in the MAG territory to the PMG. Suppose that ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}] satisfies 𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}. The proper directed paths from 𝐗\mathbf{X} in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} remain directed in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Thus Lemma 118 gives 𝐓ℳ=𝐀ℳ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}=\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}. We next show that 𝐓ℳ⊆𝐓𝒬\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{Q}}.

Every vertex used to reach 𝐓ℳ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}} lies in 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}} and hence in 𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}. If an edge traversed in ℳ\mathcal{M} is invisible, its counterpart in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is invisible as well. If its counterpart is not directed, it is invisible by definition. If its counterpart is directed, the same edge is directed in ℳ\mathcal{M}, and a DAG represented by ℳ\mathcal{M} that establishes its invisibility also belongs to the causal model class specified by 𝒬\mathcal{Q}; the visibility-under-restriction observation at the beginning of this subsection applies to both induced graphs. Such an edge can therefore also be traversed in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. If a traversed edge in ℳ\mathcal{M} is visible, it is traversed in its directed direction. Its counterpart in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is either invisible, allowing either direction, or is a visible directed edge with the same orientation, allowing that forward direction. Thus every step used to reach a vertex of 𝐓ℳ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}} can also be made in 𝒬⁡[𝐀𝒬]\mathcal{Q}[\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}]. This proves the claimed inclusion 𝐓ℳ⊆𝐓𝒬\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{Q}}.

Step 2: Include the remaining possible ancestors in the PMG territory. Fix W∈𝐀𝒬W\in\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}. The case W=YW=Y is immediate. Otherwise, Lemma 114 supplies an uncovered possibly directed path from WW to YY avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Before its first arrowhead, all edges are circle edges. Once an arrowhead appears, each following uncovered triple triggers ℛ1\mathcal{R}_{1} if the next edge still has a circle at its starting vertex. Closure therefore makes the rest of the path directed. The path has the form W∘−∘⋯∘−∘V?→U→⋯→YW\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}\cdots\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!-\!\!\circ\!}V\mathrel{\!~{{}^{{}_{\bm{?}}}}\!\!\to}U\to\cdots\to Y, where V?→UV\mathrel{\!~{{}^{{}_{\bm{?}}}}\!\!\to}U denotes either V→UV\to U or V∘⁣→UV\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}U, and the initial circle segment or the final directed segment may have length zero. A nontrivial path consisting entirely of circle edges is excluded because the marks at YY are resolved.

The vertex UU has a directed path to YY avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X} in every represented MAG. In particular:

U∈𝐀ℳ=𝐓ℳ⊆𝐓𝒬.\displaystyle U\in\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}=\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{Q}}. (219)

If V→UV\to U, then VV also has a directed path to YY avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}, so the same reasoning puts VV in 𝐓𝒬\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{Q}}. If V∘⁣→UV\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}U, this edge is invisible in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Since U∈𝐓𝒬U\in\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{Q}} and both endpoints lie in 𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}, closure along invisible edges also puts VV in 𝐓𝒬\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{Q}}. Each preceding circle edge is also invisible. Following them back toward WW gives W∈𝐓𝒬W\in\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{Q}}.

Since WW was arbitrary, 𝐀𝒬⊆𝐓𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}\subseteq\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{Q}}. The reverse inclusion is part of the definition of the territory, so these sets are equal. Lemma 118 gives 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒬,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}.

From the PMG to One Represented MAG

Step 1: Choose one vertex in each relevant circle component. Suppose that 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒬,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}. By Lemma 118, 𝐓𝒬=𝐀𝒬\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{Q}}=\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}.

The set 𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}} is a union of entire circle components. To see this, suppose a component contains a possible ancestor of YY in 𝒬∖𝐗\mathcal{Q}\setminus\mathbf{X}. Any other vertex in the component can follow a circle path to that vertex and then its possibly directed path to YY. Removing repeated vertices, if necessary, leaves a possibly directed path. This path avoids 𝐗\mathbf{X}: every vertex in 𝐗\mathbf{X} has all its marks resolved and therefore lies in a singleton circle component.

Consider the components contained in 𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}. By the closure characterization, every vertex in them can be reached from YY using invisible edges in either direction and visible edges in their directed direction. Start with the singleton component {Y}\{Y\}. If some components remain unvisited, choose an allowed path from YY to one of them and take its first edge leaving the already visited components. Let TT be its endpoint in a visited component and RR its endpoint in the new component. Record this edge and choose RR as the vertex from which to orient the new component. Mark the new component as visited and repeat. Every repetition adds one component, so eventually every component contained in 𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}} has been visited. Each receives exactly one such choice.

Step 2: Make all the choices into one MAG. Within each component, orient its circle edges as a DAG without unshielded colliders, with no incoming component edges at its chosen vertex RR. The preceding discussion of chordal components shows that this can be done and that RR then has a directed path to every vertex of its component. The component of YY is a singleton, so there is no internal choice there. Orient any components outside 𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}} as DAGs without unshielded colliders as well, and replace every ∘⁣→\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to} edge by a directed edge.

These choices specify the orientation of every remaining circle mark. Lemma 115 applies to the simultaneous choices and gives a single MAG ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}]. We use this same MAG throughout the rest of the proof.

For concreteness, consider the PMG in Fig. 38(a), with 𝐗={X}\mathbf{X}=\{X\}. Its relevant ancestor set and territory are both 𝐀𝒬=𝐓𝒬={A,B,C,D,Y}\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}=\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{Q}}=\{A,B,C,D,Y\}, and its relevant circle components are {Y}\{Y\}, {A,B}\{A,B\}, and {C,D}\{C,D\}. The singleton {X}\{X\} is outside this set because XX has been deleted when computing ancestors.

Start with {Y}\{Y\} visited. To visit {A,B}\{A,B\}, use the invisible edge A∘⁣→YA\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y in the direction from YY to AA. Record this edge with T=YT=Y and R=AR=A, and choose AA as the vertex from which to orient the new component (Fig. 38(b)). The visited vertices are now {Y,A,B}\{Y,A,B\}. Next use C∘⁣→YC\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y in the direction from YY to CC, record it with T=YT=Y and R=CR=C, and choose CC for the component {C,D}\{C,D\} (Fig. 38(c)). All relevant components have now been visited. Recording these two edges does not change their endpoint marks; it specifies the connection and the chosen vertex for each new component.

Make both choices in the same graph: orient A→BA\to B and C→DC\to D, and replace V∘⁣→YV\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}Y by V→YV\to Y for every V∈{A,B,C,D}V\in\{A,B,C,D\}, while keeping X→YX\to Y. These choices give the single MAG ℳ\mathcal{M} in Fig. 38(d). The selected vertex AA reaches both vertices of its component, and CC does the same for its component. Every vertex other than XX has a directed path to YY avoiding XX, so in this example 𝐀ℳ=𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}=\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}.

The recorded edges become A→YA\to Y and C→YC\to Y and remain invisible in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Indeed, YY is adjacent to every other vertex, so no visibility witness can have the required first vertex nonadjacent to YY. Starting from YY, invisible edge closure therefore includes AA and CC; descendant closure along A→BA\to B and C→DC\to D then includes BB and DD. Thus 𝐓ℳ={A,B,C,D,Y}\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}=\{A,B,C,D,Y\} and its only outside parent is XX, giving 𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,{X})={X}\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\{X\})=\{X\}. This illustrates the reverse traversal of invisible edges in Step 4 below. The remaining argument also covers completions in which 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}} is strictly smaller than 𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}.

Step 3: Verify ancestry for the chosen vertices. For every component contained in 𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}, its chosen vertex RR belongs to 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}. This is immediate for R=YR=Y. For any other RR, take an uncovered possibly directed path from RR to YY avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}. As in the first direction of this proof, it consists of circle edges, then one directed or partially directed edge, followed by directed edges to YY. The initial circle segment stays in the component of RR. In ℳ\mathcal{M}, there is a directed path from RR to its last vertex because of the orientation chosen in Step 2. The next edge is directed in ℳ\mathcal{M}, and the remaining part of the path is already directed in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Since ℳ\mathcal{M} has no directed cycle, concatenating these edges gives a directed path from RR to YY.

It avoids 𝐗\mathbf{X} because the circle component is disjoint from 𝐗\mathbf{X} and the remaining path was chosen to avoid 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Hence R∈𝐀ℳR\in\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}.

A component may also contain vertices that are in 𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}} but not in 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}. The following induction will require territory membership only for its vertices in 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}.

Step 4: Include the actual ancestors component by component. Consider the components in the order recorded in Step 1. We prove that every vertex in an already considered component that belongs to 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}} also belongs to 𝐓ℳ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}. The first component is {Y}\{Y\}, and Y∈𝐓ℳY\in\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}} by definition.

For the next component, use its recorded edge T∗−∗RT\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}R, where TT is in an earlier component and RR is the chosen vertex of the new component. Let SS be the chosen vertex of the component containing TT. Step 3 gives R,S∈𝐀ℳR,S\in\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}. The induction hypothesis in particular gives S∈𝐓ℳS\in\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}. We show that RR also belongs to 𝐓ℳ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}} by considering the recorded edge.

  • •

    The edge points from the earlier component to the new one. Suppose that the edge in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is T→RT\to R or T∘⁣→RT\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}R. It is T→RT\to R in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Because RR has a directed path to YY avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}, so does TT. Thus T∈𝐀ℳT\in\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}, and the induction hypothesis puts TT in 𝐓ℳ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}. The edge T→RT\to R lies in the induced graph on 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}, so descendant closure puts RR in 𝐓ℳ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}.

  • •

    The edge is bidirected. Suppose that the recorded edge is R↔TR\leftrightarrow T. If T=ST=S, it directly connects RR to the known territory vertex SS. Otherwise, TT and SS are in the same circle component, and Lemma 50 gives R↔SR\leftrightarrow S. This edge is unchanged in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Both endpoints belong to 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}, and SS already belongs to 𝐓ℳ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}. Closure along this invisible edge therefore includes RR.

  • •

    The edge points toward the earlier component and is invisible. The remaining possibility is an invisible R→TR\to T or R∘⁣→TR\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}T, used in the reverse direction when visiting the new component. If T=ST=S, retain this edge. Otherwise, the arrowhead equivalence in Lemma 50(2) gives an arrowhead at SS on the R∗−∗SR\mathrel{\!\ast\!\!-\!\!\ast\!}S edge. The bidirected edge equivalence excludes R↔SR\leftrightarrow S, since it would imply R↔TR\leftrightarrow T. Thus the edge to SS is R→SR\to S or R∘⁣→SR\mathrel{\!\circ\!\!\to}S, and in either case it becomes R→SR\to S in ℳ\mathcal{M}.

    We must also show that R→SR\to S is invisible in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Suppose instead that it is visible. The choice of RR in Step 2 satisfies Lemma 119, which then shows that R→SR\to S is already oriented in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and has a graphical visibility witness there. If T≠ST\neq S, Lemma 121 shows that R→TR\to T is also already oriented in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and has such a witness. If T=ST=S, the same conclusion already holds.

    In both cases the edge originally used to visit the component would be visible in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, contradicting its selection as an invisible edge. Therefore R→SR\to S is invisible in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Since both endpoints are in 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}} and S∈𝐓ℳS\in\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}, invisible edge closure includes RR.

These cases exhaust the possibilities. Circle edges cannot join different circle components, and a visible edge was allowed only in its directed direction. We have shown that the chosen vertex RR of the new component belongs to 𝐓ℳ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}.

Now let VV be any other vertex of this component with V∈𝐀ℳV\in\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}. Step 2 supplies a directed path from RR to VV inside the component. Every vertex on that path is also in 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}: it reaches VV, and VV reaches YY along a directed path avoiding 𝐗\mathbf{X}. The component itself contains no vertex of 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Thus the path from RR to VV lies entirely in the induced ancestor graph. Descendant closure puts VV in 𝐓ℳ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}, completing the induction step.

All vertices of 𝐀ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}} lie in 𝐀𝒬\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}, whose components have all been considered. The induction therefore proves 𝐀ℳ⊆𝐓ℳ\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}. The reverse inclusion is definitional, giving 𝐓ℳ=𝐀ℳ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{M}}=\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{M}}. Finally, the proper directed paths from 𝐗\mathbf{X} present in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} are preserved in this same ℳ\mathcal{M}. Lemma 118 now gives 𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}, which proves the required existence statement.

C.0.5 Proof of Theorem 57
{proof}

[Proof of Thm. 57] Termination. A recursive call considers finitely many local transformations at its chosen vertex. Each recursive descent removes that vertex from the set still to be processed, so the depth is at most |𝐗∪{Y}|\lvert\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\}\rvert. The orientation closure within each call also terminates: each effective rule application resolves at least one circle mark, and there are only finitely many marks. Thus every branch and the entire search terminate.

The terminal correspondence applies. By the time a branch reaches its terminal PMG, it has processed every vertex in 𝐗∪{Y}\mathbf{X}\cup\{Y\}. The local transformations have therefore resolved all circle marks at these vertices.

Furthermore, at each processed X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X} the branch passed the proper path check. By Prop. 58, the resulting PMG contains a proper directed path from XX to YY with respect to 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Later valid transformations preserve the tails and arrowheads already displayed along this path, so it remains directed and proper in the terminal PMG. Consequently, each terminal PMG satisfies both conditions of Lemma 122.

Soundness. Suppose that IsPOMIS returns True. Then there is an accepting terminal PMG 𝒬\mathcal{Q} for which the tested equality is 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒬,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}. Every local transformation on this branch was valid. It therefore retains at least one compatible MAG, and sound orientation closure preserves the MAGs consistent with the chosen transformations. Since the branch started from 𝒫\mathcal{P}, we have ∅≠[𝒬]⊆[𝒫]\emptyset\neq[\mathcal{Q}]\subseteq[\mathcal{P}]. The terminal correspondence supplies a single ℳ∈[𝒬]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{Q}] with 𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}. By Thm. 46, 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a POMIS for this MAG. Because ℳ∈[𝒫]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}], the set 𝐗\mathbf{X} belongs to ℙ^𝒫,Y\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathcal{P},Y}. Thus every True output has the claimed meaning.

Completeness. Suppose that 𝐗∈ℙ^𝒫,Y\mathbf{X}\in\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathcal{P},Y}. Fix one MAG ℳ∈[𝒫]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}] for which 𝐗\mathbf{X} is a POMIS. In particular, 𝐗\mathbf{X} is an MIS for ℳ\mathcal{M}, so each of its vertices has a proper directed path to YY in ℳ\mathcal{M}. The corresponding paths in 𝒫\mathcal{P} are possibly directed and remain proper. Hence 𝐗\mathbf{X} passes the algorithm’s initial MIS screen.

Now follow choices that agree with this fixed ℳ\mathcal{M} at every processed vertex. We verify that these choices define an admissible branch. Initially ℳ∈[𝒫]\mathcal{M}\in[\mathcal{P}]. Whenever the current PMG represents ℳ\mathcal{M}, the local choice agreeing with ℳ\mathcal{M} is valid, since this same MAG realizes all the chosen marks. Sound orientation closure preserves it; thus, the resulting PMG again represents ℳ\mathcal{M}. This argument applies successively throughout the branch, as in Prop. 56.

It remains to check that the possible ancestor test never rejects this branch. At a processed X∈𝐗X\in\mathbf{X}, the proper directed path already present in ℳ\mathcal{M} avoids 𝐗∖{X}\mathbf{X}\setminus\{X\}. Since ℳ\mathcal{M} also agrees with the local choice, the reverse implication in Prop. 58 shows that the required possible ancestor test holds in the current PMG. At the processed vertex YY, the test holds by reflexivity: neither 𝐗\mathbf{X} nor the local transformation set contains YY.

Thus the search either returns True on an earlier branch or reaches a terminal PMG 𝒬\mathcal{Q} representing this same ℳ\mathcal{M}. The necessary direction of Thm. 46 gives 𝖨𝖡⁡(ℳ,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{M},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}. Applying Lemma 122 to the terminal PMG then gives 𝖨𝖡⁡(𝒬,Y,𝐗)=𝐗\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{Q},Y,\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}.

This branch therefore returns True. Every member of ℙ^𝒫,Y\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\mathcal{P},Y} is accepted, which completes the proof.

This section specifies the six fixed SCMs used in Sec. 4.3. All observed and exogenous variables are binary, and the reward is YY. Within each task, all distinct exogenous variables are mutually independent, with the Bernoulli distributions specified in each model. A variable UVU_{V} appears only in the equation for VV. Each variable UV​WU_{VW} appears in two structural functions. Sharing an exogenous variable in this way allows dependence between observed variables, even though distinct exogenous variables are independent.

E Supporting Results for Transportability

Appendix F Omitted Proofs

This section proves the soundness and regret guarantees from Sec. 5. Source distributions and the resulting causal bounds are population quantities. All fixed arguments of a causal factor remain fixed during its marginalization or extraction.

F.0.1 Proof of Theorem 64

The source-selection test has a useful equivalent form once the graphical reductions in paTR have been applied.

Lemma 0 (Proposition 1 in Lee et al. (2020)).

Suppose that 𝐕∖𝐗=𝙰𝚗​(𝐘)𝒢∖𝐗\mathbf{V}\setminus\mathbf{X}=\mathtt{An}(\mathbf{Y})_{\mathcal{G}\setminus\mathbf{X}}. Then (𝐒i⟂⁣⟂𝐘)𝒢𝚫∖𝐗(\mathbf{S}^{i}\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\displaystyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\displaystyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\textstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\textstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptstyle\perp}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{$\scriptscriptstyle\perp$\hss}\mkern 3.0mu{\scriptscriptstyle\perp}}}\mathbf{Y})_{\mathcal{G}^{\bm{\Delta}}\setminus\mathbf{X}} if and only if Δi∩(𝐕∖𝐗)=∅\Delta^{i}\cap(\mathbf{V}\setminus\mathbf{X})=\emptyset.

{proof}

[Proof of Lemma 123] If Δi∩(𝐕∖𝐗)=∅\Delta^{i}\cap(\mathbf{V}\setminus\mathbf{X})=\emptyset, removing 𝐗\mathbf{X} removes every child of 𝐒i\mathbf{S}^{i}, giving the separation. Otherwise, a remaining child V∈Δi∖𝐗V\in\Delta^{i}\setminus\mathbf{X} has a directed path to 𝐘\mathbf{Y} by the assumed ancestry condition. Its selection edge followed by that path is unblocked, so separation fails.

{proof}

[Proof of Thm. 64] We first check the transformations in paTR, then the expressions supplied by paID. The direct-source branch, ancestral restriction, addition of irrelevant interventions, and c-component decomposition follow the sound transformations of general transportability (Lee et al., 2020).

The first branch uses the source experiment only when its selection nodes are separated from the query. Removing non-ancestors leaves its distribution unchanged, as does fixing the remaining non-ancestors by Rule 3 of do-calculus. Decomposition expresses the query as a sum of products of causal factors. Source experiments may differ between factors because each expression bounds the corresponding target factor.

Each graphical reduction forwards its recursive expressions and ends the current call. Consequently, when the source loop is reached:

𝐂=𝐕∖𝐗=𝙰𝚗​(𝐘)𝒢∖𝐗,𝖼𝖼𝒢∖𝐗={𝐂}.\displaystyle\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{V}\setminus\mathbf{X}=\mathtt{An}(\mathbf{Y})_{\mathcal{G}\setminus\mathbf{X}},\qquad\mathsf{cc}_{\mathcal{G}\setminus\mathbf{X}}=\{\mathbf{C}\}. (235)

The source test ensures Δi∩𝐂=∅\Delta^{i}\cap\mathbf{C}=\emptyset and hence Q∗​[𝐂]=Qi​[𝐂]Q^{\ast}[\mathbf{C}]=Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}]. Lemma 123 also shows why this test agrees with the separation test at this stage. The selected experiment fixes only variables in 𝐗\mathbf{X} among the current vertices. Removing those variables therefore leaves 𝐂\mathbf{C}, its induced graph, and Eq. 235 unchanged.

Consider the resulting call to paID. Its input PP is an available source distribution marginalized to its current vertices, with the experimental arguments fixed. Subsequent ancestral marginalization and c-component extraction make each input distribution or causal factor an identifiable source factor Qi​[𝐕l]Q^{i}[\mathbf{V}_{l}], where the subscript ll denotes the variables and graph local to that call. Ancestral marginalization and the products of topologically ordered conditionals are the causal factor identities of Tian and Pearl (2003).

The set of non-intervened vertices remains 𝐂\mathbf{C} throughout these calls. Indeed, each vertex in 𝐂\mathbf{C} has a directed path to 𝐘\mathbf{Y} entirely inside 𝐂\mathbf{C}, so an ancestral restriction keeps all of 𝐂\mathbf{C}. An enclosing c-component 𝐂′\mathbf{C}^{\prime} contains 𝐂\mathbf{C}, so restriction to 𝐂′\mathbf{C}^{\prime} also keeps these paths and the same induced graph on 𝐂\mathbf{C}. Thus the singleton component specified by paID is always well defined. The source invariance of Q⁡[𝐂]Q[\mathbf{C}] is preserved as well. In particular, the query at every such call is the marginal ∑𝐜∖𝐘Qi​[𝐂]=∑𝐜∖𝐘Q∗​[𝐂]\sum_{\mathbf{c}\setminus\mathbf{Y}}Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}]=\sum_{\mathbf{c}\setminus\mathbf{Y}}Q^{\ast}[\mathbf{C}] with its inherited arguments fixed.

With no remaining intervention, the marginal of PP is exact. Extraction and marginalization are also exact when 𝐂\mathbf{C} is a c-component of the current graph. It remains to check the branch where the whole current graph is one c-component. Write Pl=Qi​[𝐕l]P_{l}=Q^{i}[\mathbf{V}_{l}] and 𝐂=𝐕l∖𝐗l\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{V}_{l}\setminus\mathbf{X}_{l}. Apply Prop. 63 with both smaller sets equal to 𝐂\mathbf{C} and the enclosing set equal to 𝐕l\mathbf{V}_{l}. Therefore, the following pointwise inequality holds:

Pl​(𝐯l)≤Q∗​[𝐂]=Qi​[𝐂]≤Pl​(𝐯l)+1−∑𝐜Pl​(𝐯l).\displaystyle P_{l}(\mathbf{v}_{l})\leq Q^{\ast}[\mathbf{C}]=Q^{i}[\mathbf{C}]\leq P_{l}(\mathbf{v}_{l})+1-\sum_{\mathbf{c}}P_{l}(\mathbf{v}_{l}). (236)

The inner sum varies only 𝐂\mathbf{C}, holding the local intervention and all external arguments fixed. Summing over 𝐂∖𝐘\mathbf{C}\setminus\mathbf{Y} gives exactly the lower or upper expression yielded by the fallback branch.

Every yielded bound is nonnegative: the consistency upper expression adds to PlP_{l} the complement of a marginal probability. Products of nonnegative lower bounds, or of nonnegative upper bounds, therefore preserve their inequality, as does summation. Induction through the c-component products and the preceding exact transformations proves soundness for every expression yielded by the original call. If a recursive call returns no expression, it contributes no candidate bound. Only expressions whose required source conditionals are defined are evaluated. These conventions can remove a candidate formula without invalidating any retained bound.
