H.0.1 Proof of Theorem 81

We assume that 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} is realizable and every assigned counterfactual is nonconstant, i.e., after effectiveness, it still requires its target mechanism.

The proof follows the two parts of the graphical condition. If either part fails, we identify an assignment that can be removed without changing the reward. If both hold, we use the binary SCM of Lemma 116 to make every proper subset give a strictly smaller mean reward. One such SCM is enough to rule out equality in every compatible SCM.

{proof}

[Proof of Thm. 81] (Only if) We show that failure of either condition permits deleting one counterfactual from 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}.

Failure of the first condition. Suppose the first condition fails for XiX_{i}. Let 𝐗∗⁣∗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast} omit the counterfactual assigned to XiX_{i}, keeping all other terms. Every directed path from XiX_{i} to YY then meets a target whose counterfactual is still assigned. Consequently, changing the value assigned to XiX_{i} cannot affect the reward once the values at those other targets have been supplied.

To apply ctf-Rule 3 explicitly, a path starting at XiX_{i} cannot use an edge entering XiX_{i}. The failed ancestor condition therefore gives Xi∉𝙰𝚗​(Y)𝒢𝐗∖{Xi}¯X_{i}\notin\mathtt{An}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}_{\overline{\mathbf{X}\setminus\{X_{i}\}}}}. Therefore, we have:

P⁡(Y𝐗∗⁣∗=y)\displaystyle P(Y_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}=y) =∑𝐱P⁡(y𝐱,𝐗∗⁣∗=𝐱)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}P(y_{\mathbf{x}},\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}=\mathbf{x}) CUT (248)
=∑𝐱P⁡(y𝐱∖{Xi},𝐗∗⁣∗=𝐱)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}P(y_{\mathbf{x}\setminus\{X_{i}\}},\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}=\mathbf{x}) ctf-Rule 3 (249)
=∑𝐱∖{Xi}P⁡(y𝐱∖{Xi},𝐗∗⁣∗′=𝐱∖{Xi})\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\setminus\{X_{i}\}}P(y_{\mathbf{x}\setminus\{X_{i}\}},\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}=\mathbf{x}\setminus\{X_{i}\}) marg. over XiX_{i} (250)
=P⁡(Y𝐗∗⁣∗′=y).\displaystyle=P(Y_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}}=y). CUT (251)

Counterfactuals inside the remaining terms are unchanged. Only the separate assignment to XiX_{i} has disappeared. Thus the deletion preserves the reward on every unit and introduces no new required evaluation. The resulting action is realizable and has the same mean reward. If no assignment remains, its reward is simply YY.

Failure of the second condition. Suppose the first condition holds but the second fails for XiX_{i}. Again, let 𝐗∗⁣∗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast} remove only the counterfactual assigned to XiX_{i}. The question is now whether computing XiX_{i} through its mechanism, with the remaining assignments in place, reproduces that counterfactual.

For example, consider {Xw,Zw}\{X_{w},Z_{w}\} in Fig. 29(b). The mechanism of ZZ still receives XwX_{w}, together with the same natural value of TT and the same exogenous realization. It therefore produces ZwZ_{w} without a separate assignment to ZZ. As explained in the main text, Zw=ZXwZ_{w}=Z_{X_{w}} and thus YXw,Zw=YXwY_{X_{w},Z_{w}}=Y_{X_{w}}. In this example, the second condition fails for ZZ because the fixed value ww reaches its computation only through the other target XX.

For the general case, compare the computations in three steps:

  • 1.

    Starting at XiX_{i}, follow parent edges backwards in 𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}. Stop a branch when another target in 𝐗∖{Xi}\mathbf{X}\setminus\{X_{i}\} is reached. Its assigned counterfactual is still supplied under 𝐗∗⁣∗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}.

  • 2.

    At each vertex VV visited before these stopping points, failure of the second condition gives 𝙿𝚊​(V)𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗=𝙿𝚊​(V)𝒢\mathtt{Pa}(V)_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}}=\mathtt{Pa}(V)_{\mathcal{G}}. Thus no parent value received by fVf_{V} was replaced by a constant. Each such value is calculated by its parent mechanism or supplied by the counterfactual at a stopping point. At a stopping point, realizability ensures that the counterfactual needed by this calculation is the one assigned to that remaining target.

  • 3.

    Evaluate the visited mechanisms in topological order. The values supplied at the stopping points are unchanged. Every other parent value is obtained from an earlier mechanism whose value already agrees, and the exogenous realization is the same. Hence each mechanism returns the same value, including fXif_{X_{i}}.

Consequently, removing the assignment to XiX_{i} reproduces its assigned counterfactual through the same mechanisms. ctf-Rule 1 gives Y𝐗∗⁣∗=Y𝐗∗⁣∗′Y_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}=Y_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}}. The deletion preserves realizability because it reuses evaluations already needed by the original action. Both cases establish equality for every compatible SCM and every admissible subscript assignment, proving necessity.

(If) Suppose both conditions hold. We will use the second condition to obtain a strict difference at a removed target, and the first condition to carry that difference to YY.

Step 1: Choose the binary SCM and set the subscript values. We first take ℳ\mathcal{M} from Lemma 116 and set every constant subscript value to one. This choice respects the equalities required by realizability. Recall three properties of the construction:

  • •

    Every observed variable is binary. Increasing a parent value while keeping the exogenous realization fixed cannot decrease the child’s value.

  • •

    Every parent has a strictly positive coefficient βP​V\beta_{PV} in the expectation formula. A positive difference in a parent’s mean therefore increases the child’s mean when the other differences are nonnegative.

  • •

    Every value computed by a mechanism has mean strictly between zero and one. In particular, it does not equal one with probability one, even when all its parent values are one.

Fix any proper subset 𝐗∗⁣∗′⊊𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}\subsetneq\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}. We compare it with the original set in this same SCM, using the same exogenous realization and leaving every remaining counterfactual unchanged.

Step 2: Compare the values used in the two calculations. First consider a target whose counterfactual remains in 𝐗∗⁣∗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}. Its assigned value is identical in the two rewards. For every other mechanism fVf_{V} required by the original action, VV is evaluated under the subset through its structural mechanism. Compare the values received from each parent as follows:

  • •

    If 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} fixes the value received from PP, that value is one. The corresponding value under the subset is P𝐗∗⁣∗′P_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}}, which is either zero or one.

  • •

    If the value received from PP is calculated by its mechanism, compare that calculation with P𝐗∗⁣∗′P_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}} first. In topological order, this parent comparison has already been made before evaluating its child.

Starting with the earliest mechanisms, monotonicity therefore makes every value required by the original action at least as large as its counterpart in the subset’s reward calculation. In particular, for each target:

Xi⁡[𝐗∗⁣∗]​(𝐮)≥Xi⁡[𝐗∗⁣∗′]​(𝐮).\displaystyle X_{i[\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}]}(\mathbf{u})\geq X_{i[\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}]}(\mathbf{u}). (252)

For the next step, the notation 𝔼ℳ𝐗∗⁣∗​V\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}}V denotes the mean of the value returned by the mechanism for VV when computing the original action. The notation 𝔼ℳ​V𝐗∗⁣∗′\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}}V_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}} denotes the mean of VV in the subset’s reward calculation. These may refer to different counterfactuals. For instance, computing ZwZ_{w} may require XwX_{w} even when the reward after a deletion also receives the natural XX. The comparison above keeps these calculations distinct. It remains valid when the subset is not realizable, because both counterfactuals are defined in the same SCM.

Step 3: Find a strict difference where a parent value was fixed. Consider a required mechanism fVf_{V} for which the subset supplies no assigned counterfactual at VV. There are two contributions to the difference of its means. A parent edge deleted from 𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}} contributes the difference between the fixed value one and the calculated value P𝐗∗⁣∗′P_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}}. A parent edge retained in that graph contributes the difference between the two calculated values of PP. The expectation formula from Lemma 116 gives:

𝔼ℳ𝐗∗⁣∗​V\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}}V −𝔼ℳ​V𝐗∗⁣∗′\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}}V_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}} (253)
=∑P∈𝙿𝚊​(V)𝒢∖𝙿𝚊​(V)𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗βP​V​(1−𝔼ℳ​P𝐗∗⁣∗′)\displaystyle=\sum_{P\in\mathtt{Pa}(V)_{\mathcal{G}}\setminus\mathtt{Pa}(V)_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}}}\beta_{PV}(1-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}}P_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}}) (254)
+∑P∈𝙿𝚊​(V)𝒢𝐗∗⁣∗βP​V(𝔼ℳ𝐗∗⁣∗P−𝔼ℳP𝐗∗⁣∗′).\displaystyle+\sum_{P\in\mathtt{Pa}(V)_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}}}\beta_{PV}(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}}P-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}}P_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}}). (255)

The first sum is over the parent values replaced by one; the second is over the parent values still computed by their mechanisms. The constant and shared latent terms cancel because the structural function and exogenous distribution are unchanged. Every summand is nonnegative by Step 2.

Moreover, every P𝐗∗⁣∗′P_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}} has mean strictly below one. If PP is a remaining target, its counterfactual still requires its mechanism by assumption. Otherwise, its mechanism is evaluated with the values produced under the subset. In both cases, the threshold of the binary construction stays strictly between zero and one. Therefore, whenever fVf_{V} receives a fixed parent value in the original action, the corresponding summand in the first sum is strictly positive.

The expectation calculation remains valid for nested counterfactuals. The private noise UVU_{V} is independent of all values supplied by parent mechanisms, since these use only ancestral mechanisms and their exogenous variables. Parents may be correlated with shared latent variables; the calculation uses independence only of UVU_{V}.

Step 4: Use the second condition to reach a removed target. Choose any target XiX_{i} whose counterfactual was removed. The second condition provides a vertex VV that receives a fixed parent value and a retained directed path from VV to XiX_{i}. This path, including VV, avoids every other target in 𝐗\mathbf{X}, so none of its mechanisms is replaced by a remaining assignment.

Step 3 gives a strictly positive difference at VV. At each next vertex on the path, the contribution of the preceding parent appears in Eq. 255, multiplied by a strictly positive coefficient. All other contributions are nonnegative. The difference therefore stays strictly positive until it reaches XiX_{i}. If V=XiV=X_{i}, no propagation is needed.

Step 5: Use the first condition to reach the reward. The first condition provides a directed path from XiX_{i} to YY that avoids every other target in 𝐗\mathbf{X}. After XiX_{i}, these mechanisms are evaluated in both rewards with their original structural mechanisms. The strict difference at XiX_{i} therefore propagates along this path to YY by the same positive coefficient calculation. The other parent differences are nonnegative by Eq. 252 and monotonicity. Hence μ𝐗∗⁣∗>μ𝐗∗⁣∗′\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}>\mu_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}}.

The proper subset was arbitrary: it may remove several assignments, and the resulting counterfactual need not be realizable. The same SCM and the same subscript values, all equal to one, distinguish the original set from every such subset. Thus no proper subset preserves its mean reward for every compatible SCM and every admissible assignment. This proves that 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} is a ctf-MIS.

{proof}

[Proof of Prop. 85] Fix an assigned counterfactual 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} and condition on the values received by the parent inputs of fYf_{Y}. These values are determined by upstream exogenous variables and fixed constants, independently of the exogenous inputs of YY. The conditional reward mean is therefore 𝔼​Y𝐩𝐚Y\mathbb{E}Y_{\mathbf{pa}_{Y}}. Averaging over the received values gives:

μ𝐗∗⁣∗≤max𝐩𝐚Y⁡𝔼​Y𝐩𝐚Y=μ𝐩𝐚Y∗.\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}\leq\max_{\mathbf{pa}_{Y}}\mathbb{E}Y_{\mathbf{pa}_{Y}}=\mu_{\mathbf{pa}_{Y}^{\ast}}. (256)

Consequently, no non-equivalent counterfactual can be strictly better than the best parent intervention. To establish that the parent intervention set itself is a ctf-POMIS, we also need one SCM in which the comparison is strict against every non-equivalent counterfactual.

Choose binary domains and independent private noises UV∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(ϵ)U_{V}\sim\mathtt{Bern}(\epsilon) for V≠YV\neq Y and UY∼𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(1−ϵ)U_{Y}\sim\mathtt{Bern}(1-\epsilon), where 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1. Set fV=UV​∏P∈𝙿𝚊​(V)𝒢Pf_{V}=U_{V}\prod_{P\in\mathtt{Pa}(V)_{\mathcal{G}}}P for V∈𝐕V\in\mathbf{V}, where an empty product equals one. Fixing every parent input of YY to one gives mean 1−ϵ1-\epsilon. Any non-equivalent counterfactual leaves some input P→YP\to Y natural: if all these inputs are fixed, every upstream assignment is irrelevant to the reward. The natural output supplied by PP is at most UPU_{P}, whatever its other inputs. Hence every choice of subscript values has mean at most ϵ⁡(1−ϵ)<1−ϵ\epsilon(1-\epsilon)<1-\epsilon. This single SCM establishes strictness against all non-equivalent counterfactuals. When 𝙿𝚊​(Y)𝒢=∅\mathtt{Pa}(Y)_{\mathcal{G}}=\emptyset, every input assignment is irrelevant and every counterfactual is equivalent to the empty action.

H.0.3 Proof of Theorem 87

The two proof directions of Thm. 87 use different properties of the minimal UC-territory. When its border is empty, we construct an SCM in which the given counterfactual preserves useful dependence between the reward and its ancestors. Replacing a retained input by a constant breaks this dependence. When the border is nonempty, the inputs entering the territory are independent of its exogenous variables. Their random values can then be replaced by the best fixed values.

An SCM construction.

For each shared binary exogenous variable, blue and red vertices carry its value along the two sides of the corresponding bidirected edge. Purple vertices compare these values after the directed paths meet. The mechanisms retain a separate coordinate for each confounder, so all these comparisons take place in one SCM. Thus the colors specify the structural functions used in the proof.

Consider Fig. 39(a). Fix the inputs A→BA\to B, A→CA\to C, and E→DE\to D to aa, a′a^{\prime}, and ee, respectively. Choose a≠a′a\neq a^{\prime} and reserve these assigned values separately from the values naturally output by the mechanisms. Deleting the three selected edges and restricting to the ancestors of YY leaves {B,C,D,Y}\{B,C,D,Y\}. Starting from YY, the bidirected edge Y↔DY\leftrightarrow D includes DD, descendant closure includes CC, and C↔BC\leftrightarrow B includes BB. The retained graph is therefore its own minimal UC-territory, with empty border.

Let U1U_{1} be the fair bit shared by BB and CC, and let U2U_{2} be the independent fair bit shared by DD and YY. In Fig. 39(b), the blue vertex BB carries U1U_{1} and the red vertex CC carries 1−U11-U_{1}. The purple vertex YY checks that these two values are complementary, recording 22 for (0,1)(0,1) and 11 for (1,0)(1,0). In Fig. 39(c), the red vertices DD and CC carry 1−U21-U_{2}. At YY, this value is checked against the genuine U2U_{2} available to its own mechanism. The same purple encoding records 2−U22-U_{2}. Table 13 shows the calculations for U1U_{1} and U2U_{2} separately as ℳ1\mathcal{M}_{1} and ℳ2\mathcal{M}_{2}, then combines them into ℳ\mathcal{M}. The two coordinates of BB, DD, and CC are (U1,0)(U_{1},0), (0,1−U2)(0,1-U_{2}), and (1−U1,1−U2)(1-U_{1},1-U_{2}), respectively; zero fills a coordinate unused at that vertex. The intermediate value Y′Y^{\prime} contains the two comparison results, and Y=1Y=1 exactly when both are valid. Before making these calculations, the mechanisms of BB, CC, and DD check their selected inputs against aa, a′a^{\prime}, and ee. Under the specified counterfactual, all checks succeed for every (u1,u2)(u_{1},u_{2}), giving reward one.

This example also explains why fixing a retained input can be harmful. If B→YB\to Y is fixed while C→YC\to Y remains natural, its first coordinate must agree with a fair bit carried through CC. If D→CD\to C is fixed while C→YC\to Y remains natural, its second coordinate must agree with the genuine U2U_{2} at YY. If C→YC\to Y is fixed, its second coordinate must again agree with that U2U_{2}, even when the other inputs are fixed as well. Each comparison succeeds with probability at most 12\frac{1}{2}. If all retained inputs remain natural, omitting a selected input fails its assigned value check. The following construction applies these comparisons to arbitrary retained paths, including paths that merge.

{proof}

[Proof of Thm. 87] (If) Suppose 𝖨𝖡⁡(ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗,Y)=∅\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}},Y)=\emptyset. Every vertex of the graph is ancestral to YY. If a vertex lay outside the minimal UC-territory, a directed path from it to YY would have a first edge entering the territory. The parent of this edge would belong to the border, a contradiction. Therefore:

𝐕†=𝐕⁡(ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗)=𝖬𝖴𝖢𝖳⁡(ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗,Y).\displaystyle\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}=\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}})=\mathsf{MUCT}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}},Y). (257)

Selected inputs whose children lie outside 𝐕†\mathbf{V}^{\dagger} cannot affect YY and may be discarded. We compare the remaining selections of fixed inputs, allowing each selected value to vary freely and identifying equivalent counterfactual sets.

Choosing the assigned values. Choose the subscript values of 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} so that distinct selected occurrences of the same parent variable receive distinct values. Reserve separate values for the coordinate tuples used below and for an invalid output.

Each mechanism checks every input selected by 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} against its chosen value. No natural output will take one of these reserved assigned values. Consequently, a competing counterfactual cannot pass a selected-input check merely by leaving that input natural.

Constructing the mechanisms for one confounder.

Let U1,⋯,UkU_{1},\cdots,U_{k} be independent fair binary confounders, one for each bidirected edge of ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}. Denote the endpoints of UjU_{j} by B(j)B^{(j)} and R(j)R^{(j)}. Descendants in the following coloring are computed in the retained graph:

blue:\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.4922,0.7227}\texttt{blue}}:\quad 𝙳𝚎⁡(B(j))∖𝙳𝚎⁡(R(j)),\displaystyle\mathtt{De}(B^{(j)})\setminus\mathtt{De}(R^{(j)}), (258)
red:\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.8945,0.1016,0.1094}\texttt{red}}:\quad 𝙳𝚎⁡(R(j))∖𝙳𝚎⁡(B(j)),\displaystyle\mathtt{De}(R^{(j)})\setminus\mathtt{De}(B^{(j)}), (259)
purple:\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.5977,0.3047,0.6406}\texttt{purple}}:\quad 𝙳𝚎⁡(B(j))∩𝙳𝚎⁡(R(j)).\displaystyle\mathtt{De}(B^{(j)})\cap\mathtt{De}(R^{(j)}). (260)

The blue endpoint supplies uju_{j} as an additional blue input to its mechanism, and the red endpoint supplies 1−uj1-u_{j} as an additional red input. This convention also applies when an endpoint is itself purple because it is a descendant of the other endpoint.

At a blue or red vertex, the mechanism returns the common value of its inputs of that color, provided they agree and belong to {0,1}\{0,1\}. At a purple vertex, the valid input combinations and outputs are:

blueredpurpleoutput01221011\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{ccc|c}{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.4922,0.7227}\texttt{blue}}&{\color[rgb]{0.8945,0.1016,0.1094}\texttt{red}}&{\color[rgb]{0.5977,0.3047,0.6406}\texttt{purple}}&\textbf{output}\\ 0&1&2&2\\ 1&0&1&1\end{array}

Each entry specifies the common value required of all inputs of that color; a color with no input imposes no condition. An unequal or malformed input, a failed selected-input check, or an invalid parent output gives the invalid value 33. Invalid outputs propagate along every retained directed edge. A vertex outside the two descendant sets has an unused zero coordinate.

These rules have a simple interpretation. Blue values encode uju_{j}, red values encode 1−uj1-u_{j}, and purple values encode 2−uj2-u_{j}. Thus every mechanism compares copies of the same bit, with the encoding determined by the sender’s color. For example, a purple input equal to 22 is consistent with a blue input equal to 00 and a red input equal to 11. Keeping the purple value allows subsequent mechanisms to make the same comparison after paths have already merged.

Combining the mechanisms into one SCM.

Represent each variable in 𝐕†∖{Y}\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}\setminus\{Y\} by the kk coordinates just constructed, using two bits per coordinate as in Table 13. Its mechanism applies all selected-input checks and all coordinate comparisons. A coordinate tuple with an incorrect number of coordinates or a nonzero unused coordinate is invalid. Any failure makes the whole output invalid. The mechanism of YY makes the corresponding comparisons, including any exogenous bits it receives directly, and returns one exactly when every check succeeds. Natural mechanisms outside 𝐕†\mathbf{V}^{\dagger} also avoid the reserved assigned values. Other allowed exogenous inputs may be ignored.

Under the chosen subscript values, every coordinate carries the genuine shared bit in its designated encoding, and every selected-input check succeeds. Hence:

μ𝐗∗⁣∗=μ𝐗∗⁣∗∗=1.\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}=\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\ast}}=1. (264)

If 𝐕†={Y}\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}=\{Y\}, there are no colored coordinates: checking the selected parent inputs of YY is sufficient. In either case, this fixes one SCM before any competing counterfactual is considered.

Comparing every competing counterfactual.

Consider an assigned counterfactual 𝐙∗⁣∗\mathbf{Z}_{\ast\ast} with mean greater than 12\frac{1}{2}. We first show that it fixes no input retained in ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}}.

Start at YY, whose length-zero path to itself is unchanged. Suppose every directed path from a vertex to YY is unchanged, and that vertex shares UjU_{j} with another endpoint. On every accepted outcome, its genuine copy of UjU_{j} reaches YY. If a path from the other endpoint to YY contains an input fixed by 𝐙∗⁣∗\mathbf{Z}_{\ast\ast}, take the last such input on that path. This input supplies a constant coordinate tuple. Its jjth coordinate must propagate along the unchanged remainder of the path and agree with the genuine copy, either at an earlier merge or at YY. A malformed coordinate is rejected. Otherwise, the constant can agree with the fair bit in only one of its two states, so the competing reward mean is at most 12\frac{1}{2}, a contradiction.

Every directed path from the other endpoint to YY must therefore be unchanged. The same conclusion holds for each of its descendants: any fixed input on a descendant’s path would also lie on a path from that endpoint. Repeatedly applying these bidirected and descendant steps reaches precisely the minimal UC-territory. Since that territory is 𝐕†\mathbf{V}^{\dagger}, all its retained inputs must remain natural under an assignment with mean greater than 12\frac{1}{2}.

Every input selected by 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} must also retain its designated value. Omitting its assignment supplies a natural output, which never takes that value and therefore fails its check. Since all retained paths are unchanged, the resulting invalid output reaches YY. If the competing counterfactual keeps every selected input, any further selections outside 𝐕†\mathbf{V}^{\dagger} are irrelevant: their paths to YY already pass through fixed inputs. Removing them leaves the same selected inputs with the same unrestricted choices of values. The two counterfactuals are then equivalent. We have proved, in one SCM, that:

μ𝐙∗⁣∗∗≤12<1=μ𝐗∗⁣∗∗\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{Z}_{\ast\ast}^{\ast}}\leq\tfrac{1}{2}<1=\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\ast}} (265)

for every non-equivalent counterfactual. This establishes possible optimality.

(Only if) Suppose 𝐓=𝖨𝖡⁡(ℋ𝐗∗⁣∗,Y)≠∅\mathbf{T}=\mathsf{IB}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}},Y)\neq\emptyset, and fix the best assignment 𝐗∗⁣∗∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\ast} in an arbitrary compatible SCM. The minimal UC-territory is closed under descendants and bidirected connections. Its exogenous inputs are therefore independent of those generating 𝐓\mathbf{T}. Indeed, if an ancestor of a border vertex shared an exogenous input with the territory, bidirected closure would include that ancestor, and descendant closure would then include the border vertex. This contradicts the definition of the border. All parents entering the territory from outside belong to 𝐓\mathbf{T}.

Construct 𝐗∗⁣∗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast} by retaining the original input assignments and fixing every remaining input from 𝐓\mathbf{T} into the territory. For any value 𝐭\mathbf{t}, supply its component for TT to all newly selected inputs from that border variable, while retaining the original optimizing values. The resulting reward has the same mean as the original reward conditional on 𝐓=𝐭\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{t}: the inputs received by the territory are the same, and conditioning does not change its exogenous distribution.

The border values here are evaluated in the modified SCM ℳ𝐗∗⁣∗∗\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\ast}}. In the summand below, 𝐗∗⁣∗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast} denotes the assignment corresponding to 𝐭\mathbf{t}. Conditioning gives:

μ𝐗∗⁣∗∗\displaystyle\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\ast}} =∑𝐭𝔼ℳ𝐗∗⁣∗∗​[Y∣𝐓=𝐭]​Pℳ𝐗∗⁣∗∗​(𝐓=𝐭)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{t}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\ast}}}[Y\mid\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{t}]P_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\ast}}}(\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{t}) (266)
=∑𝐭μ𝐗∗⁣∗′​Pℳ𝐗∗⁣∗∗​(𝐓=𝐭)≤μ𝐗∗⁣∗′∗.\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{t}}\mu_{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}}P_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast}^{\ast}}}(\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{t})\leq\mu_{{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast}}^{\ast}}. (267)

The last optimization allows independent values at the newly selected inputs, including the common-value assignments appearing in the sum. The best such assignment is at least as good as their average. Thus 𝐗∗⁣∗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast} dominates 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} in every compatible SCM.

The two counterfactuals are non-equivalent. Choose T∈𝐓T\in\mathbf{T} and a directed path from TT into the territory and onward to YY. Let TT be an independent fair bit and let the mechanisms along this path copy it, ignoring their other inputs. Every assignment of 𝐗∗⁣∗\mathbf{X}_{\ast\ast} then has mean 12\frac{1}{2}, whereas fixing the new input from TT to one gives mean one. Finally, discard selected inputs in 𝐗∗⁣∗′\mathbf{X}^{\prime}_{\ast\ast} whose children are no longer ancestral to YY. This preserves the reward and leaves the corresponding counterfactual action. The original counterfactual therefore cannot be strictly better than every non-equivalent counterfactual in any compatible SCM, so it is not a ctf-POMIS.

H.0.4 Proof of Corollary 90
{proof}

[Proof of Cor. 90] For a rejected counterfactual set, fix the remaining inputs from its interventional border into its minimal UC-territory, retaining the originally selected inputs and their values. The argument in Eq. 267 shows that optimizing the new inputs weakly improves the best mean. The remaining graph is the subgraph induced by that territory and has empty border, so the algorithm returns the resulting counterfactual set. Every omitted action is thus weakly dominated by an action in 𝒜ctf⋆\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}^{\star}; the reverse inequality follows from 𝒜ctf⋆⊆𝒜ctf\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}^{\star}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{\textsc{ctf}}.

Appendix I Experimental Structural Causal Models

This section specifies the fixed SCMs used in Sec. 6.6. All observed and exogenous variables are binary. Distinct exogenous variables are mutually independent. A variable UVU_{V} is specific to the mechanism of VV, while a shared variable UV​WU_{VW} appears in the two mechanisms connected by the corresponding bidirected edge. The symbols ∧\land, ∨\lor, ⊕\oplus, and ¬\neg denote AND, OR, exclusive OR, and negation. Parentheses specify the order of the logical operations.

Task 1.

The graph is shown in Fig. 32(a). The structural functions are:

fW=uWfX=z∨uXfZ=uZ∨(w⊕uZ​Y)fY=¬(uY⊕x⊕(¬w)⊕uZ​Y).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} f_{W}&=u_{W}&f_{X}&=z\lor u_{X}\\ f_{Z}&=u_{Z}\lor(w\oplus u_{ZY})&f_{Y}&=\neg\bigl(u_{Y}\oplus x\oplus(\neg w)\oplus u_{ZY}\bigr).\end{aligned} (268)

Each of UW,UX,UZ,UY,UZ​YU_{W},U_{X},U_{Z},U_{Y},U_{ZY} follows 𝙱𝚎𝚛𝚗⁡(0.1)\mathtt{Bern}(0.1). The action supplying w=0w=0 to fYf_{Y} and w=1w=1 to fZf_{Z} has mean approximately 0.8850.885, whereas the optimal ordinary intervention has mean 0.820.82.

fT=uTfW=uWfX=(¬uX​Y)⊕(uX∨w)fZ=(¬(t⊕(¬uZ))∨x)⊕uZ​YfY=¬(uZ​Y∨(¬uX​Y))⊕uY⊕(x∨z).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} f_{T}&=u_{T}\qquad f_{W}=u_{W}\\ f_{X}&=(\neg u_{XY})\oplus(u_{X}\lor w)\\ f_{Z}&=\bigl(\neg(t\oplus(\neg u_{Z}))\lor x\bigr)\oplus u_{ZY}\\ f_{Y}&=\neg\bigl(u_{ZY}\lor(\neg u_{XY})\bigr)\oplus u_{Y}\oplus(x\lor z).\end{aligned} (269)

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
